Principia Humanitatis · Experimental File

Heartburst

Love as a Wavefront — a treatment through gestalt, complexity and energy, as an organisational phenomenon

Mark Downham

In response to Donald Innes Davies, The Saturday Signatures 09, “The Humanities as a Living Field” — with Papworth on compassion, McQuade on ethical agency, and Nielsen, Bévort and Henriksen on paradox

Filed as
experimental and experiential
Extent
c. 101,000 words · seven movements · forty-three chapters · 366 reversible explainer cards · 50 reversible file notes
Registers
E experiential M measured A argued C conjecture

The Proposition, As Filed

Love is an affective-cognitive cardial-toroidal state where the noetic-communicative energetic field it creates and emanates extends beyond the human body in a super-luminous way, as a wavefront, to the point where light becomes a photonic language and has real substance and you can feel it crossing the room. You become light-emitting. Love literally is a 'heart-burst'. You can become Love and that is what Hans Urs von Balthasar saw and said "love alone is credible" and why he stopped negotiating to rejoin the Jesuits. I do not have a steady language for this so file it as experimental and experiential.

That paragraph is the whole of the evidence with which this work begins. It was not written as a thesis. It was written as a report — the report of someone who has stood in a room and felt something cross it, and who afterwards went looking for words and found that the words available were either too small or too borrowed. Everything that follows is an attempt to keep faith with the report while refusing to flatter it. The proposition is treated here as a filed statement: taken down exactly, examined clause by clause, tested against three bodies of thought that have each, in their own idiom, already tried to say what a whole is, how order arises without a designer, and what it means for something to be at work between people — gestalt thinking, complexity, and the long philosophy of energy. And it is tested in the place where it is least expected and most needed: the organisation.

The occasion is a short chapter by Donald Innes Davies — Signature 09 of his fifty-four Saturday Signatures, "The Humanities as a Living Field", from Principia Humanitatis: We Are Energy. Davies names a Circulatory Energy that renews meaning through exchange and resonance. He writes that human energy propagates beyond direct contact, the way electromagnetic waves do. He says ideas travel, gather, transform and return. He does not say what it is that circulates when circulation is most alive. This file proposes an answer to the question his chapter leaves standing at the door. WHAT CIRCULATES IS LOVE. The rest is commentary, and correction, and experiment.

How This File Is Kept

The author of the proposition asked for it to be filed as experimental and experiential. That instruction is taken literally and it governs the form of the whole work.

Experiential means that first-person report is admitted as evidence — as a particular kind of evidence, with its own strengths and its own failure modes. A person who says "I felt it cross the room" is reporting a fact about their experience that no instrument can overrule. An instrument can only ask what, in the world, the experience was an experience of. The history of this subject is full of people who made the same report in different centuries and different languages: a hermit in Yorkshire who put his hand to his chest to check whether he was actually on fire; a priest in Rome whose ribs were found, after his death, arched outward over his heart; a Russian landowner who could not look at an old monk's face because it was brighter than the sun on the snow. These reports will be laid side by side. Their agreement is data. It is not proof.

Experimental means two things. It means that the language is provisional — every term in the proposition is put on the bench, loaded until it creaks, and either kept, repaired, or replaced, with the repairs shown. And it means that the work issues in experiments: things that can be tried in a team, a boardroom, a ward, a workout meeting, with something that can be observed afterwards. A doctrine of love that cannot be tried on a Tuesday afternoon is a doctrine of something else.

To keep the two honest, each chapter closes with a short FILE NOTE that says in which register its main claims were made. There are four:

  • E Experiential. Reported from the first person, by the author of the proposition or by a witness in the tradition. True as experience; open as to cause.
  • M Measured. Something an instrument or a study has found, stated at the strength the finding can bear and no stronger.
  • A Argued. A claim that follows, if it follows, from reasons given on the page. Open to counter-argument.
  • C Conjecture. A reach. Offered because it is illuminating, flagged because it is unproven. The file's most interesting pages are of this kind, and the reader should know when they are standing on one.

One discipline above all. The proposition uses the word literally. This file will not use that word loosely. Where the physics supports a literal reading, it will say so, and the reader may be surprised at how much there is — the human body does emit light; the heart does generate a field that extends beyond the skin; a heart can change its shape under the pressure of an emotion. Where the physics does not support the claim at the magnitude the experience seems to require, the file will say that too, plainly, and will then ask the better question: if not by that channel, then by which? Because the crossing of the room is not in doubt. Rooms are crossed. The only question is by what.

A note on a second deposit. While this file was being drafted, three further books were laid on it with the instruction to analyse, synthesise, distil and apply: Kirstie Papworth on compassionate leadership, Aidan McQuade on ethical decision under pressure, and Rikke Kristine Nielsen and colleagues on navigating paradox. None is about love. Each turned out to supply something the proposition lacks — an account of what the state must learn in order to act well — and they are woven in from the third movement onward, treated together in chapter twenty-nine, and indexed in the Apparatus.

A last note on voice. This is written in the register the imprint has made its own — scholastic in its distinctions, vatic in its pressure, with the occasional sentence set in capitals where an argument has earned the right to be carried out of the room in the pocket. The capitals are not decoration. They are the places where the file thinks it has found something that will bear weight.

Overture: The Room, Before Anyone Speaks

Begin with the commonest version of the event, the one almost everybody has had and almost nobody has filed.

A meeting is going badly. It is the third hour. The numbers on the screen are worse than the numbers in the pack, and the person who must explain the difference is explaining it in the passive voice. Around the table the bodies have arranged themselves into the small architectures of self-protection: folded arms, the laptop lid raised an extra ten degrees, the gaze that goes to the window. Nobody is lying. Nobody is telling the truth either. The room has a temperature, and everyone in it could tell you what it is, and nobody could tell you where the thermometer is kept.

Then someone comes in late. She has not been briefed. She does not know the numbers. She sits down, and she looks — actually looks — at the man who has been talking, and something in her face says, without a word and without the least softness about the facts: I am for you. Go on. And he does. He stops in the middle of a sentence, and he says, "Let me say that again properly," and he says it properly, in the active voice, with himself as the subject of the verb. The arms unfold. The lids come down. Two people speak who had not spoken. The numbers have not changed by a single pound. The room has changed completely.

Ask the people who were there what happened and they will reach for one of two vocabularies. The first is managerial and it is too small: she has good interpersonal skills; she created psychological safety; she's an energiser. All true, all measured, all — as later chapters will show — backed by respectable literatures, and all of them sounding like a description of a sunrise given by someone reading the lux meter. The second vocabulary is the one people use afterwards in the corridor, lowered, half-embarrassed: I don't know what it is about her. She just — it's like the lights come on.

It is like the lights come on. This file takes that sentence seriously. It asks whether the corridor knows something the conference room has agreed not to know.

Three things the corridor is saying

It is saying, first, that what happened was a whole. Nobody in the corridor says, "her zygomatic muscle contracted, then her gaze held for 2.3 seconds, then her vocal pitch dropped a tone." They say she came in and it changed. The event had a form, and the form was grasped at once, before and beneath its parts — and it was the form, the way of her being for him, that did the work. This is the oldest claim of gestalt thinking: that wholes are perceived first, that they are other than the sum of their parts, and that their properties cannot be found by inspecting the parts one at a time. It will turn out that the founding experiment of Gestalt psychology was an experiment about light — two lamps, a dark gap, and a motion that crosses the gap although nothing travels. It will also turn out that the greatest Catholic theologian of the last century built his entire doctrine of love upon a single German word, and that the word was Gestalt.

It is saying, second, that what happened spread, and spread without being ordered to. Nobody instructed the arms to unfold. One relation changed — hers to him — and then his to himself, and then the room's to him, and within ninety seconds a pattern that had held eleven people in place for three hours had given way to a different pattern which no one of them had chosen and all of them were enacting. This is the signature of what the sciences of complexity study: order that arises from interaction, that has thresholds, that propagates, that can tip. It will turn out that the cleanest physical model of this — a crowd of independent emitters that suddenly, above a critical point, fall into step and begin to act as one — is the laser. Which is to say: the textbook example of self-organisation is a thing becoming light-emitting.

It is saying, third, that something was given off. The corridor's verbs are verbs of emission: she radiates, she lights up the room, she gives energy, he drains it. These are metaphors, and it would be easy to leave them as metaphors. But they are suspiciously stable metaphors. They recur across languages that have had no contact; they recur in the Greek of the Gospels and the Chinese of the Great Learning; they recur in the instruments of the organisational network analysts, who some years ago began asking people a simple question — when you interact with this person, how does it affect your energy? — and found that the answers mapped a structure more predictive of performance than the formal chart. When a metaphor is that stable, the working assumption should be that it is tracking something.

What the proposition adds

The proposition goes further than the corridor, and its further steps are precisely where the trouble and the interest lie. It makes seven claims. They are set out here so that the reader can watch each one being handled.

One: love is an affective-cognitive state. Not a feeling that then informs a thought, nor a judgement that then warms into feeling, but a single act in which knowing and being-moved are not yet two things. The proposition's own word for the knowing side is noetic. The tradition's phrase is older and harder: amor ipse notitia est — love is itself a kind of knowledge.

Two: it is cardial. It is of the heart — and the proposition means the organ, or at least refuses to not mean the organ. The heart of the Psalms and the heart in the chest are being held together on purpose.

Three: it is toroidal. It has the shape of a torus: a flow that goes out from a centre, curves round, and returns through the centre from which it left. This is a claim about form, and it will prove to be the most fertile word in the proposition, because it is the exact geometric figure of what Davies calls circulation.

Four: it creates and emanates a field that extends beyond the body — a field the proposition calls noetic-communicative and energetic. Something is there, between people, that carries meaning and does work.

Five: the field propagates as a wavefront, in a super-luminous way, such that light becomes a photonic language with real substance, felt crossing a room. This is the hardest sentence. It contains a word, super-luminous, that in a physics department means faster than light and in a sixth-century Greek treatise means something else entirely. Three chapters will be spent on it.

Six: the lover becomes light-emitting, and love is literally a heart-burst. A claim about transformation of the person, and a claim about the violence of the onset.

Seven: one can become Love — and this is what Balthasar saw. The proposition closes by leaving psychology altogether. It says that love is not finally a state one is in but something one can be; and it attaches that claim to a named man, a named book, and a decision he made about an institution.

Notice the shape of the list. It begins inside a person and ends inside an organisation — a religious order, a negotiation, a refusal. The proposition is already, in its own last clause, about organisational life. It says that a man who had seen what love was could no longer bargain over the terms of his belonging. That is not a pious detail. It is the thesis of this work in miniature: LOVE CHANGES WHAT CAN BE NEGOTIATED.

The road

The work moves in seven movements, and the names of the movements are the proposition's own vocabulary taken back to its roots.

GESTALT asks what kind of whole love is, and finds in Wertheimer's lamps, Köhler's physical fields, Lewin's rooms and Perls's contact boundary a grammar for it — before arriving at Balthasar, for whom Gestalt was the form through which glory shines. KARDIA takes the heart at its word: as organ, as symbol, as the place where knowing and feeling are one act; it gives the torus its geometry and the heart-burst its witnesses, and it submits the whole to the instruments. PHOS is about light: Grosseteste's, Tabor's, Huygens's, the laser's, and the light of a face. COMPLEXITY rebuilds the proposition in the language of thresholds, order parameters, synchrony and constraint, and lets Ralph Stacey object to the entire enterprise. THE ORGANISATION carries the result into the place it must finally be tried: the taboo on the word, the evidence that the thing is nevertheless there, the room, the leader, three disciplines for love under pressure, power, judgement, holding, and institutional memory. PHTHORA — corruption — is the dark mirror: counterfeit light, love extracted as labour, fusion, the wavefront of fear, and the burning-out of the luminous. BECOMING LOVE returns to the seventh claim, to Balthasar and his refusal, and ends in a room.

Then a CONTRA, where the strongest objections are stated at full strength and not all of them are answered; a CODA; and an APPARATUS — a lexicon for the unsteady language, a Chinese register, an evidence ledger, the experiments gathered for use, and the sources.

A word to two kinds of reader. The reader who comes from the sciences will find claims in the later movements that they cannot accept, and they should find them clearly labelled. The reader who comes from prayer will find the first half slow, full of lamps and apes and pendulum clocks, and may wonder when the subject will arrive. The subject has already arrived. It arrived in the third hour of a bad meeting, when a woman sat down and looked at a man, and the lights came on.

THE CORRIDOR KNOWS. THE CONFERENCE ROOM HAS AGREED NOT TO.

Movement I

GESTALT

The Form That Shines

What kind of whole is love? Two lamps and a dark gap; fields that are already wholes; a room whose geometry bends around what is loved; the boundary where contact happens; and a theologian who staked everything on the word form.

1The Signature and the Thing It Does Not Name

Davies's ninth Signature is nine pages long and it does a thing that most writing about the humanities fails to do: it declines to describe them as a possession. The humanities, he says, are usually called disciplines, collections, traditions — and that language "arrives too late." It names the artefacts and misses the movement that made them. What he wants in its place is a picture of a field: an energetic ecology in which meanings drift, gather force, meet resistance and come back changed. The humanities do not store human meaning. They circulate it.

Three features of his account matter for what follows, and the file wants them on the table before it adds anything of its own.

The first is propagation without contact. Davies writes that human energy, like electromagnetic waves, travels beyond direct touch — that a breakthrough or an ethical shift may show its significance only long after and far from its origin. He is careful to say, a page later, that he is not offering scientific analogy but "a way of perceiving." The analogy is a lens. It "does not explain society"; it sensitises attention. That is exactly the right caution and this file adopts it as its own rule — and will then press on it, because the proposition under examination does not want a lens. It wants the thing.

The second is latency. Ideas, he says, accumulate as stored potential within collective life — unspoken assumptions, unresolved questions, unrealised possibilities — and persist across generations awaiting activation. When conditions align the potential releases into movement. This is an account of charge and discharge, of capacitance: a culture as something that can hold what it cannot yet use. It will matter greatly when the file comes to institutions, because an institution is, among other things, a device for holding love across the intervals when no one in it is loving.

The third is return. The governing figure of We Are Energy is the Gyre — Yeats's widening spiral — used as a method: ideas revisited without repetition, transformation traced without assuming progress, contradiction held without collapse. "Meaning returns not to confirm itself, but to be reworked under changed conditions." Circulation, for Davies, is never a closed loop. What comes back is not what went out.

Now observe what the chapter does not say. It says that something circulates: energy, meaning, significance. It says the circulation is "not neutral" — that it carries emotional weight and ethical consequence, that what the field amplifies or marginalises decides what a society finds thinkable, sayable and — his word — feelable. It says the field is permeable, that it absorbs disruption and registers fracture. But on the question of what makes one circulation renewing and another merely busy — why one seminar leaves its members larger and another leaves them only better informed, why one retelling of an old story is an act of memory and another an act of taxidermy — the Signature is silent. Its three watchwords are Exchange, Resonance, Renewal. It does not say what must be exchanged for there to be resonance, or what resonance must carry for there to be renewal.

The silence is not a fault. A Signature is a vignette, and Davies's book has fifty-three others in which to say more. But it is an opening, and the proposition walks through it. The proposition says: there is a state in which a person becomes a source in this field — in which what goes out from them has the form of a wave, carries meaning as light carries signal, and returns to them through the centre from which it left. The proposition calls that state love. If it is right, then love is not one of the things the living field happens to contain, alongside justice and memory and obligation. Love is the name for the field when it is alive. Circulatory Energy at full strength, with a face.

What kind of claim is this?

It is, to begin with, a claim about a whole. This needs saying carefully, because everything in the next six chapters hangs on it.

There are two ways to go about studying love in organisations, and the literature has mostly taken the first. The first way is to decompose. Love — or its organisational proxies: care, compassion, trust, safety, belonging — is broken into behaviours that can be counted. Does your manager ask about your life outside work? Do colleagues express tenderness? Do people here console one another? These are good questions; a later chapter leans on a study built from exactly such items, and the study is one of the best things in the field. But the method carries an assumption which it never states: that the thing is the sum of the countable behaviours, so that an organisation can raise its score on love by raising the frequency of the items.

Everyone who has worked in an organisation that tried this knows what happens. The behaviours go up. The thing does not appear. Managers ask about your weekend in the tone in which they ask for the quarter's numbers. There is a wellbeing week. There is fruit. And the corridor, which is never fooled, begins to speak of the initiative in the particular flat voice it reserves for counterfeits.

The second way is to begin from the whole — to say that what the woman in the Overture did was not a sum of micro-behaviours but one act with one form, and that the form is what was received. On this view the behaviours are real, but they are expressions of the form, the way the notes are expressions of the melody; and just as you can play all the notes and miss the tune, you can perform all the behaviours and miss the love. Transposed into another key — a different person, a different culture, entirely different behaviours: a gruff silence, a hand on a shoulder, a hard truth told straight — the same form can be present and instantly recognised.

That second way has a name and a century of disciplined work behind it. It is the gestalt tradition, and it is the first of the three lenses the proposition asked to be looked through. It is commonly reduced to a slogan about wholes and sums and a few optical illusions in a first-year textbook. It was nothing of the kind. It was a revolt — begun in 1912, in the same year that Durkheim published his account of the collective effervescence in which a gathered people feels itself seized by a force greater than any of its members — against the idea that experience is built up out of atoms of sensation glued together by association. Its founders were physicists as much as psychologists. They believed that wholes are real, that they are found in the physical world and not merely in the eye, and that the nervous system is the kind of thing in which such wholes can form. Their first exhibit was a pair of lights.

DAVIES NAMES THE CIRCULATION. THE PROPOSITION NAMES WHAT CIRCULATES.

File note, in fullChapter 1

What this note commits the file to. The reading of Davies's Signature is an argument anyone can check against his nine pages: that he names propagation without contact, latency and return, and does not say what makes circulation renewing. The identification of love with the living field at full strength is the conjecture the whole work exists to test.

How to check it. Read Signature 09 and ask whether the silence is really there or has been read in. Then ask what would distinguish a field "at full strength" from one that is merely busy; if no observable difference can be named, the conjecture is empty.

What would count against it. A convincing account of renewing circulation in which love plays no part — for example, one driven wholly by rivalry or by curiosity.

Where the file returns to it. Apparatus VI, section by section; the Coda.

Registers used here
  • A Argued. A claim that follows, if it follows, from reasons given on the page. Open to counter-argument.
  • C Conjecture. A reach. Offered because it is illuminating, flagged because it is unproven. The file's most interesting pages are of this kind.

2Wertheimer's Light: What Crosses the Gap

The story is told that in the summer of 1910 Max Wertheimer, travelling by train toward the Rhineland, had an idea about the perception of movement, got off at Frankfurt, bought a toy stroboscope, and began experimenting in his hotel room. Whether or not every detail is true, what he did next is a matter of record. At the Frankfurt Psychological Institute, with two younger colleagues as his subjects — Wolfgang Köhler and Kurt Koffka, who with him would become the founding triumvirate — he ran the experiments published in 1912 as the "Experimental Studies on the Seeing of Motion."

The arrangement was as simple as an experiment can be. Two lights, a small distance apart. The first flashes and goes dark; after an interval, the second flashes. If the interval is long, the observer sees what is physically there: one light, then another. If the interval is very short, the observer sees two lights at once. But in between — at around a twentieth of a second — the observer sees something that is not physically there at all. They see movement. A single light travels across the gap.

And at a slightly different timing, something stranger still. The observer sees movement without anything that moves — not a light travelling from left to right, but pure passage, an objectless crossing. Wertheimer gave it a Greek letter so as not to prejudge what it was. He called it phi.

Why this mattered

The psychology Wertheimer had inherited held that perception is assembled from elements. First there are sensations — this patch of brightness here, that patch there — and then the mind, by association and inference, adds them up. On that view apparent movement had to be a kind of error: the mind receives sensation A, then sensation B, and wrongly infers that A has gone to B.

Wertheimer's observers did not infer anything. They saw the movement, immediately, as vividly as they saw the lights — in the case of pure phi, more vividly than they saw the lights. The movement was not a conclusion drawn from two sensations. It was a third thing, given directly, belonging to neither lamp, which existed only in the relation between them. And it could not be found in the parts. Examine lamp one as long as you like; examine lamp two; nothing in either contains the crossing.

This is the origin of the principle that Koffka later put in the form usually misquoted. He did not say the whole is greater than the sum of its parts — a merely arithmetical claim, as though the whole were the parts plus a bonus. He said the whole is other than the sum of its parts. The crossing is not more lamp. It is a different kind of thing from a lamp.

The first lesson for the proposition

Go back to the room in the Overture and look at it with Wertheimer's eyes.

There are two persons, a short distance apart. Something occurs at one — a look, a settling of the shoulders, a quality of attention. After an interval, something occurs at the other — a breath, a sentence begun again. A decomposing psychology will say: stimulus at A, response at B, and between them an inference; he read her expression, concluded that she was supportive, and decided to speak more candidly. And if you asked him, afterwards, he might even give you that account, because it is the account our culture supplies.

But it is not what he experienced. What he experienced was something crossing the room. He did not see a face and then infer goodwill; he was met. The meeting was given as immediately as the face — more immediately; he might be unable afterwards to tell you a single feature of her expression and yet be in no doubt about what came across. The crossing belongs to neither of them. You will not find it by examining her (she was only paying attention) or by examining him (he was only talking). It exists in the relation, as a whole, as a third thing.

The proposition says: you can feel it crossing the room. Wertheimer licenses the sentence — licenses it as a description of experience, with the full rigour of a founding experiment. That which crosses is real as a phenomenon; it is perceived directly and not inferred; it is a property of a relation and not of either pole. And — here is the point that will keep the whole inquiry honest — in Wertheimer's laboratory nothing physically travelled across the gap. No light went from the first lamp to the second. The crossing was real and it was not a transport of stuff.

This is a hinge, and the file wishes to oil it well. There are two wrong things to say about phi. The first: "It's only an illusion — nothing really moves." That treats the physical lamps as the only reality and the experienced crossing as a mistake. Wertheimer rejected this; the crossing is a genuine, lawful, reproducible fact about what happens when a perceiving organism meets that arrangement of the world. The second wrong thing: "Since I see something cross, some substance must be travelling through the gap." That insists the experience can only be real if it corresponds, point for point, to a movement of matter. Wertheimer rejected that too.

The proposition, as filed, leans toward the second. It says the light "has real substance." The file will not dismiss that — there are three chapters on light to come, and the tradition of the uncreated light makes a claim about substance that is not naive. But Wertheimer sets the terms on which the question must be asked. A crossing can be fully real without being a thing that travels. If love crosses a room, it may cross it the way phi crosses the gap: as the form of a relation between two sources, a form that appears only when the timing is right.

On timing

That last clause deserves more than a clause. Wertheimer's whole discovery was a discovery about intervals. Too slow, and there are two events in succession — no crossing. Too fast, and there is mere simultaneity — no crossing. The crossing lives in a window.

Every practitioner of anything relational knows this window without having a name for it. The comedian knows it. The analyst knows it, who has learned to let a silence run two seconds longer than is comfortable. The negotiator knows it. The woman in the Overture knew it: had she spoken at once — "I'm sure it's not as bad as it looks" — there would have been no crossing, only a remark, and the room would have filed her under reassurance and gone on as before. Had she waited until the agenda item was closed and caught him by the lifts, there would have been a kindness, in succession, after the fact. What she did happened in the window. He was mid-sentence; she looked; the two events fell within the interval in which they could be one event.

Responsiveness that arrives late is information. Responsiveness that arrives early is noise. Responsiveness that arrives in time is contact. Organisations are, among other things, vast machines for getting the interval wrong: the annual review that answers in December a question the heart asked in March; the engagement survey whose results are "cascaded" a quarter after the mood they measured has gone; the recognition scheme that thanks you by automated email. In each case both lamps flash. Stimulus is followed by response. And nothing crosses, because nothing can cross at that timing.

The second lesson: Prägnanz

Wertheimer and his colleagues went on to describe how the perceptual field organises itself — proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common fate — and they gathered these under a single tendency they called Prägnanz: the field settles into the best, simplest, most stable form that the prevailing conditions allow. Three dots are seen as a triangle. A circle with a gap is seen as a circle. A flock that wheels together is seen as one thing.

Two of these deserve to be carried forward.

Common fate. Elements that move together are seen as belonging together. The first thing that changed in the Overture's room, after the crossing, was that the bodies began to move together — the arms unfolding within seconds of one another, the lids coming down. An observer at the glass wall, hearing nothing, would have seen the room become one figure. The file will return to this under the heading of synchrony, with heart monitors. For now: one of the perceptible marks of the state the proposition describes is that a group which was an aggregate becomes, visibly, a gestalt.

Closure. The field completes what is incomplete. This is the gestalt law with the most to say about love and the least said about it. To be looked at by someone who loves you is to be seen as whole — to be perceived under the law of closure, with the gaps completed in the direction of your best form. He was, at that moment, a circle with a large gap: a competent man giving an incompetent account. The room's perception was organising him around the gap; the gap was becoming the figure. She perceived the circle. And — this is the mystery, and Gestalt psychology gives no more than its outline — he then became what she perceived. He closed.

There is nothing sentimental in this. To see someone under the law of closure is not to pretend the gap is not there. The circle with a gap is seen as a circle and as having a gap; the gap is perceived precisely as a gap in a circle, which is the only way a gap can be perceived as something to be closed and not as the end of the line. This is why love and honest judgement are not opposites, a point on which a whole later chapter will turn. The loveless eye sees fragments, and accurately. The loving eye sees the form the fragments belong to — also accurately, and more.

THE CROSSING IS REAL. NOTHING NEED TRAVEL FOR IT TO BE REAL.

What is measured. Wertheimer's 1912 result concerns the perception of motion between two lights flashed in succession, and nothing else. It has been replicated for a century.

What is argued. That meeting between two people has the same structure: a whole given directly, belonging to neither party, existing only within a window of timing. This is an analogy of form, and the note says so.

What is experiential. That goodwill is perceived and not inferred. Scheler and later phenomenologists defend direct perception of another's state; many cognitive scientists hold that it is rapid inference.

How to check it. Recall an occasion of being met and ask whether you could list the features of the other's face.

What would count against it. Evidence that such meetings are reliably reconstructed from separately noticed cues.

3Köhler's Physical Gestalten: The Field Is Already a Whole

Wertheimer showed that wholes are primary in perception. A sceptic may answer: very well, the mind organises; that tells us about minds. The world itself is still made of separate bits, and wholes are what we project.

Wolfgang Köhler set out to close that exit. He was a physicist by training — a student of Max Planck — and he spent the First World War marooned on Tenerife, where he had gone to direct a primate research station and from which, the war intervening, he could not easily leave. He used the years to watch chimpanzees solve problems by what he called insight, a sudden reorganisation of the whole situation. And he wrote a book almost no one now reads: Die physischen Gestalten in Ruhe und im stationären Zustand — "The Physical Gestalten at Rest and in the Stationary State", published in 1920. Its argument was that Gestalten are not confined to psychology. Physics is full of them.

What a physical gestalt is

Take a charged conductor of any shape. Put a quantity of electric charge on it. The charge distributes itself over the surface in a definite pattern, denser at the points, thinner on the flats. Now ask: what determines the density of charge at this point? The answer is: everything. The density here depends on the shape of the entire conductor and on the charge everywhere else on it. Change the shape at the far end and the density changes here. You cannot build up the distribution by deciding each local density separately and adding them; there are no separately decidable local densities. The pattern is settled all at once, as a whole, by the system relaxing into the configuration of least energy.

Or take a soap film on a wire frame. The film finds the surface of minimum area. No part of the film "knows" what that surface is. Every part pulls on its neighbours, and the global form is what the local pullings settle into; alter the frame at one corner and the whole surface re-forms.

These, said Köhler, are Gestalten in the strict sense. They have the two marks by which Christian von Ehrenfels had defined a gestalt-quality thirty years earlier: they are more than a sum (the pattern cannot be got by adding independently fixed parts), and they are transposable (the same form recurs on a larger conductor, a different frame, as the same melody recurs in another key). And they are not in anyone's mind. They are in the world.

The paradigm case, for Köhler, was the field. An electric or magnetic field is not an assembly of little independent forces at points. It is a single extended whole in which the state at each point is what it is because of the state at every other. Faraday had taught physics to think this way — to take the lines of force seriously as a real condition of space and not a bookkeeping device for forces between particles — and Maxwell had made it mathematics. Köhler made it a philosophy: THE FIELD IS THE FORM IN WHICH NATURE DOES WHOLES.

Isomorphism

From here Köhler made a bold step. If the perceived world is organised into wholes, and if the physical world also contains wholes of the field kind, then perhaps perception is organised because the brain processes underlying it are themselves physical Gestalten. He called this psychophysical isomorphism: the structure of experience and the structure of the underlying brain events are the same structure. In later decades he went looking for electrical field currents in the cortex, and the specific hypothesis did not survive experimental attack — Karl Lashley and Roger Sperry laid gold foil and mica plates through animals' visual cortex, which should have wrecked any such fields, and the animals went on seeing.

The specific hypothesis failed. The general idea did not die; it changed form. Contemporary neuroscience speaks freely of large-scale synchrony, of travelling waves across cortex, of global states that constrain local firing. No one now thinks perception is a direct-current field in the visual cortex. Almost everyone thinks that brain function involves coordinated wholes whose properties are not properties of single neurons. Köhler was wrong about the mechanism and right about the grammar.

The second lesson for the proposition

The proposition says love "creates and emanates" an "energetic field" that "extends beyond the human body." There are two ways to hear the word field there, and Köhler lets them be told apart.

The weak hearing: field is a figure of speech for "a sphere of influence" — as one speaks of a field of study. On this hearing the proposition says only that love affects people nearby. True, and thin.

The strong hearing, which is Köhler's: a field is a single extended whole in which the condition at each point depends on the condition at every other, and which settles as a whole into a form. To say that love creates a field in this sense is to say something exact and testable about a room. It is to say that when the state the proposition describes is present in one person, the condition of every other person in the room is altered — not one by one, by separate transactions, but as a pattern; that the alteration at each place depends on the whole configuration (who else is there, how they stand to one another, what the room is for); and that the pattern has a form to which it tends, a Prägnanz.

Is that true of rooms? Anyone who has chaired one knows that it is. A room is not eleven dyads. The effect of the newcomer's look upon the man was not a private wire between two terminals; it was received by him in front of nine others, and their reception of his reception was part of what he received. Had the finance director rolled her eyes, the same look would have distributed itself differently. The charge finds its distribution over the whole conductor.

But a Köhlerian field needs a medium and a quantity. Charge distributes over a conductor; tension over a film. If love is a field in the strong sense, across what does it extend, and what is the quantity that distributes?

The proposition's own answer is physical in the narrowest sense: the medium is space and the quantity is something electromagnetic — light, or the heart's field. That answer will be examined at the bench in the chapter called "What the Instruments Say," and the examination will be unsentimental. But Köhler's own practice suggests a less literal and more robust answer, and it should be stated now so the inquiry does not seem to stand or fall with the magnetometer.

The medium is the web of mutual perception — the fact that in a room each person is continuously perceiving each other person perceiving. This web is as physical as anything else in the room: it is made of photons reflected from faces, of pressure waves from larynxes, of volatile molecules, of the micro-timings of movement, all of them received by nervous systems exquisitely evolved to receive them. And the quantity that distributes over it is something like readiness — each person's moment-by-moment disposition to open or to guard, to approach or withdraw, to tell the truth or manage the impression. Readiness is not a private fact. It is expressed continuously in every channel the web has, it is read continuously by everyone, and each person's readiness is a function of everyone else's. That is a field in Köhler's exact sense. It relaxes toward a form. And one person in a particular state can change the boundary conditions and force the whole to re-form.

On this account the proposition's sentence — the field it creates and emanates extends beyond the human body — is strictly true, and the "beyond the body" is its most important part. Love is not located inside the lover, as a private feeling which is then, optionally, communicated. It exists as a condition of the space between. The lover is where the field is sourced. It is not where the field is.

A note on conductors

Köhler's charged conductor offers one more thing, almost as a gift. Charge concentrates at the points. On a smooth sphere it spreads evenly; on a body with a sharp projection it crowds to the tip, and if the crowding becomes great enough the field at the tip tears the air apart and there is a discharge — a visible glow, a corona, St Elmo's fire at the masthead.

A group's readiness distributes the same way. It does not spread evenly. It crowds at the points — at the person who is, at that moment, most exposed: the one giving the bad account, the newest, the most junior, the one who has just disagreed. That is where the field is most intense, and that is where a discharge will occur if one occurs: the outburst, the tears, the resignation, or — in the other direction — the truth told at last. The woman in the Overture did not address the room. She addressed the point. She put her attention exactly where the charge was densest, and the discharge, when it came, was not a breakdown but a glow: "Let me say that again properly."

Leaders who try to shift a room by addressing its smooth surfaces — the general exhortation, the all-hands slide on values — are working where the field is weakest. THE FIELD IS CHANGED AT ITS POINTS.

LOVE IS SOURCED IN A PERSON. IT IS NOT LOCATED IN ONE.

4Lewin's Room: Love Bends the Space

Kurt Lewin served in the German infantry in the First World War, was wounded, and during his convalescence wrote a short essay with an unpromising title: "War Landscape." It is one of the strangest and most consequential things in the literature of psychology, and it is about how a field looks to a man who might be killed in it.

In peacetime, Lewin observed, a landscape extends evenly in all directions. It is round; it has no front or back. As a soldier approaches the front the same countryside acquires a direction. It has a "this side" and a "that side." It ends — there is a boundary beyond which the land is theirs, and the boundary is felt as a property of the terrain as real as a river. A fold in the ground is no longer a fold in the ground; it is cover. A farmhouse is not a farmhouse; it is a position. And when the front moves on, the same field, which an hour ago was a combat thing, reverts with a kind of shock to being a peace thing — just a meadow, round again.

The physical geography had not changed. The psychological geography had changed completely, and it was the psychological geography in which the soldier actually lived and moved and made his decisions. Lewin spent the rest of his life — in Berlin, and after 1933 in Iowa and at MIT — building a science of that second geography. He called it the life space.

The life space

The life space is the totality of facts that determine a person's behaviour at a given moment — the person, and the environment as it exists for that person. Behaviour, in his famous compression, is a function of the person and the environment together, and the two are not independent variables but regions of one field.

The life space has structure. It is divided into regions — activities, states, memberships, possible futures — separated by boundaries that are more or less permeable. There are paths, and there are barriers. And — here is the concept that bears on love — the regions have valence. Lewin's German was Aufforderungscharakter: literally "invitation-character," the demand a thing makes. A postbox, to a man with a letter in his hand, asks to have the letter put in it. A cake, to a hungry child, pulls. A room containing someone who has humiliated you pushes. Valences are not opinions about things. They are forces in the field, and they have direction and strength. A person at a given moment is at a point in their life space, subject to a resultant of forces, and they move — locomote, he said — accordingly.

Three things about this account are radical and are routinely forgotten by the organisations that quote his name on change-management slides.

First, the field is contemporaneous. Only what is present in the field now can have effects now. The past matters only as it is present — as a current tension, a current expectation. This is not a denial of history. It is a demand that history be shown working.

Second, the field is the unit. Lewin thought it a pre-scientific habit — Aristotelian, he called it, as against Galilean — to explain behaviour by the properties of the object: he is hostile because he is a hostile person. Galileo stopped explaining the fall of a stone by the stone's nature and started explaining it by the stone's relation to a field. Lewin wanted psychology to make the same move. The hostility is a fact about the field in which that person stands.

Third, tension persists until discharged. His student Bluma Zeigarnik had noticed — the tale is that it began with a waiter in a Berlin café who could remember every unpaid order and nothing about the ones that had been settled — that interrupted tasks are recalled better than completed ones. An intention sets up a tension system; the system stays charged until the intention is carried out; the charge keeps the matter present. An unfinished thing is not simply absent. It is a force.

Love as a transformation of the life space

Now the proposition can be given its third piece of grammar. Wertheimer: love crosses as a whole, in the right interval. Köhler: what it crosses is a field in which each point depends on every other. Lewin: THE FIELD IS A SPACE, AND LOVE CHANGES ITS GEOMETRY.

Consider what the room in the Overture was, as a life space, for the man giving the account, in the minute before she came in. It had a front. It had sides. It ended: there was a boundary — somewhere about the edge of the table — beyond which the territory was theirs. The faces were positions. The questions were incoming. The region labelled "say plainly what went wrong" lay on the far side of a barrier with a strong negative valence, because in that geography it led directly to the region labelled "be the person who is blamed." The only paths with positive valence led sideways: qualify, contextualise, attribute to market conditions. He was not a coward. He was locomoting sensibly in a combat landscape.

What her look did was alter the geography. It did not give him courage — courage would have been a change in the person, an increase in his capacity to cross a barrier that remained in place. It removed the barrier. The region "say plainly what went wrong" was suddenly adjacent, and it led somewhere else: not to "be blamed" but to "be met." The room, for him, became round. And then he did the natural thing in a peace landscape, which was to walk in a straight line to where he needed to go.

This is a precise claim and it differs from the usual ones. The usual accounts of what love or support does are Aristotelian in Lewin's sense: they locate the effect in the object. Support "builds confidence"; care "increases resilience"; safety "enables voice." Something is added to the person. Lewin's account is Galilean: nothing is added to the person. The space is re-formed, and the person, unchanged, moves differently because the forces are different.

The practical difference is very large. If courage is a property of persons, then an organisation that wants more candour must hire braver people or train the ones it has — and its failure to hear the truth can be blamed on those who did not speak. If candour is a function of the geometry of the field, then the question is who is shaping the geometry, and the people with most power to shape it are precisely the ones who complain that nobody tells them anything.

Valence, and what love does to it

Lewin's valences give the proposition's word affective-cognitive a first clean meaning. A valence is not a feeling about a perceived object, added to a neutral perception. The cake is not first seen as a brown cylinder and then judged desirable. It is seen as inviting; the invitation is in the perception. Perceiving and being-moved are one act. The world comes already tilted.

Love is a wholesale re-tilting. The lover's life space is not the same space with one more attractive object in it. Everything is re-valenced by its relation to the beloved. The street they live on has a different gravity. A song is unbearable or indispensable. One's own time re-forms: hours with them and hours until. The beloved is not an object in the lover's field. The beloved is a new centre of it.

And here the proposition's noetic earns its keep. For the re-tilted world is not a distorted one — or need not be. The lover notices things about the beloved that the indifferent do not, and they are there: the particular way a sentence is abandoned, the exact shade of a courage. The tradition's maxim is ubi amor, ibi oculus — where there is love, there is an eye. Lewin lets it be said without mysticism: a positive valence draws locomotion toward a region; a region approached is a region differentiated; the lover's field is more finely articulated around the beloved because they have, in the plain sense, gone there more. Love is a way of knowing because it is a way of approaching, and only what is approached is known in detail.

Transpose to the organisation. A leader who loves the work — this particular work: this plant, this ward, this portfolio — has a life space densely differentiated around it. They see what a merely competent manager cannot, because for the latter the region is flat: a line in a report with a number on it. And a leader who loves the people sees them differentiated: sees that this one is quiet today in a way that is not his usual quiet; sees that the junior analyst's question was the best thing said in the meeting. None of this is soft. It is higher resolution. THE LOVING FIELD HAS MORE DETAIL IN IT. Which is one reason, among several the work will gather, why organisations in which love is present are frequently better at what they do — not because love is pleasant and pleasant people work harder, but because love is a cognitive instrument and they are, in a quite literal sense, seeing more.

The Zeigarnik charge of the unloved

One more thing from Lewin, and it is the darkest. Tension persists until discharged; the unfinished stays present as a force.

Every organisation carries a vast Zeigarnik load of interrupted relational acts. The apology not made after the restructuring. The founder who left and was never thanked. The colleague dismissed by email on a Friday, whose desk was cleared by Monday and whose name is not mentioned. The thing the chief executive said in the town hall that everyone knows was false and no one has said was false. None of these is over. Each is a tension system, still charged, still bending locomotion around itself. People route around the region. New joiners, who were not there, learn the detour without learning the reason — they simply find that certain subjects have a negative valence, as a walker in woodland finds the path curves for no visible cause, round the place where a tree once stood.

Davies's Signature speaks of stored energies that "persist across generations, awaiting activation." He means the hopeful kind. Lewin and Zeigarnik remind us that the same capacitance holds the other kind: unfinished grief, unacknowledged injury, unreturned loyalty. An organisational field is thick with them, and they are a large part of why a room has a front before anyone has spoken.

A great deal of what love does in an organisation is therefore not the generation of anything new. It is completion. Someone finally says the thing — "what was done to that team was wrong, and I was part of it" — and a tension that has bent the corridor for six years discharges in a minute, and the corridor is straight. No energy was added. A dam was let go. Much of the "energy" that people report flooding a room when love enters it is not her energy at all. It is the room's own, released.

COURAGE CROSSES THE BARRIER. LOVE REMOVES IT.

5The Contact Boundary: Where Love Actually Happens

Gestalt psychology, exiled from Germany, split in America into two streams that are now barely on speaking terms. One stayed in the laboratory and was absorbed into the psychology of perception. The other went into the consulting room, and from there into organisations, and it is this second stream — Gestalt therapy, and the organisational practice that grew from it — that has the most direct things to say about the proposition.

Its founding text is a strange, brilliant, uneven book of 1951, Gestalt Therapy: Excitement and Growth in the Human Personality, by Frederick Perls, Ralph Hefferline and Paul Goodman. Perls had trained as a psychoanalyst and had worked under Kurt Goldstein, the neurologist who insisted on the organism as a whole. His wife Laura had studied with Wertheimer and had been close to Martin Buber. Goodman was a poet and an anarchist. What they made together took the laboratory's concepts — figure and ground, the field, the tendency to completion — and turned them on the question of how a human being makes contact with what is not themselves.

The boundary is not a wall

Their central idea is the contact boundary, and it corrects an error that is nearly universal.

The common picture is that a person is a bounded thing, like a walled city, and that relationship is traffic across the wall: messages go out, messages come in. Experience happens inside. On this picture the boundary is where the self stops.

Perls, Hefferline and Goodman say the opposite. Experience occurs at the boundary between the organism and its environment. The boundary is not where the self stops; it is where the self happens. The skin does not merely separate the body from the air; it is the organ by which the body touches the air. Contact is the awareness of, and the movement toward, what is novel and assimilable in the environment — and the self is not a thing which then makes contact but is the system of contacts, the boundary at work. Where there is no contact — in habit, in routine, in sleep — there is, in their rather severe view, very little self.

The consequence for the proposition is direct. If the self is at the boundary, then a state of the self is a state of the boundary, and a state of the boundary is already between. The proposition says the field "extends beyond the human body." The contact-boundary theorists would say there never was a self that was merely within the body for the field to extend beyond. To be in the state the proposition calls love is not to have an interior condition that leaks. It is to be at one's boundary in a particular way: maximally present there, maximally permeable to the other as other.

Contact needs difference

As other. This is the second correction and it is the one that separates love from every one of its counterfeits.

Contact, in the Gestalt account, requires a boundary to make contact at. Two things that have merged are not in contact; they are simply one thing, and nothing is happening between them because there is no between. The Gestalt writers named the ways in which contact is interrupted, and the first on the list is confluence: the dissolving of the boundary, the pretence or the wish that there is no difference between me and you, us and them. Confluence feels like closeness. It is the absence of the conditions for closeness. The confluent couple "never argue." The confluent team "is totally aligned." What is missing in both is the friction of two real surfaces.

The others, briefly, since they will all come back in the movement on corruption. Introjection: swallowing whole what comes from outside, without chewing — the value statement accepted and never digested. Projection: placing outside what belongs inside — "they don't trust us" from a management that does not trust them. Retroflection: doing to oneself what one wants to do to another, or wants another to do — the anger at the director turned into a migraine; the care one longs to receive lavished on a pot plant. Deflection, added later by the Polsters: turning aside from the impact — the joke, the abstraction, the "let's take that offline."

Each of these is a way of being in a room without being at one's boundary in it. And each is so thoroughly normal in organisational life that their sum is what most people mean by "professional behaviour." An ordinary management meeting is a small masterpiece of deflection decorated with introjects, in which eleven people retroflect for two hours and then project in the car park.

Against that ground, the figure. The woman in the Overture was at her boundary. She did not merge with him — she did not take on his defensiveness, feel his shame for him, or signal "we're all in this together." Nor did she stay behind her wall. She was fully herself, there, and fully open to him, there. The Gestalt word for that quality is presence, and Edwin Nevis, who carried the Gestalt approach from the consulting room into organisational consulting at the Cleveland institute, made it the consultant's primary instrument: the use of oneself — one's whole, living, embodied response — as the means of evoking something in the client system which the system's own habits have suppressed.

LOVE IS CONTACT WITHOUT CONFLUENCE. It is the fullest possible meeting across a boundary that both parties keep. And this, the file wants to say as early and as loudly as it can, is why love in an organisation is compatible with — is in fact the condition of — disagreement, judgement, refusal, and the saying of hard things. A confluent "love" cannot tell you that your plan is wrong, because to do so would be to assert a difference and the whole point of confluence is that there are none. Only someone at a boundary can say no in a way that is still contact.

The cycle

The Cleveland school developed a map of how contact unfolds in time, usually called the Cycle of Experience. It runs: sensation (something stirs); awareness (it becomes figure — I know what it is); mobilisation of energy (the organism gathers itself); action (it moves toward the environment); contact (the meeting itself, the exchange); resolution or closure (the meeting is assimilated); withdrawal (the figure dissolves back into ground, and the organism rests, available for the next thing).

The map is crude and its users know that it is. Three features of it matter here.

First, energy sits in the middle of it. Between knowing what one wants and doing something about it there is a gathering — excitement, in the founders' term — and the gathering is felt in the body: the breath deepens, the chest opens, there is heat. The Gestalt tradition is one of the few in modern psychology to treat this bodily mobilisation not as a by-product of motivation but as its substance. This is a first, modest, entirely secular sighting of what the proposition calls energetic. And the founders made an observation about it that will be important later: excitement which is not supported — which is mobilised without enough breath, in a field that will not receive it — is experienced as anxiety. The same arousal. Anxiety, on this account, is excitement without oxygen.

Second, the cycle has a withdrawal phase, and it is as much a part of contact as the meeting. An organism that cannot withdraw cannot make the next contact; it is stuck to the last one. This will matter when the file comes to the torus — a form whose whole point is that what goes out comes back — and again when it comes to the burning-out of people who are asked to emit continuously.

Third, the cycle can be interrupted at every stage, and organisations have characteristic interruptions. Some never let sensation reach awareness — the data are all there, in every body in the building, and are never made figure. Some go from awareness directly to action with no gathering of energy — the initiative-a-quarter firm, where nothing has any charge. Some mobilise magnificently and never arrive at contact: the offsite is electric; nothing is said to anyone's face. Some cannot close: no project is ever declared over, no loss ever mourned, and the Zeigarnik load of the previous chapter accumulates.

Seen through the cycle, the event in the Overture was a contact completed in a system that had been interrupting contact for three hours. And it was her contact that made his possible; contact is contagious, and the reason is structural. A boundary can only be met by a boundary. When she arrived at hers, there was at last something there for him to arrive at.

The paradox of change

One more Gestalt idea, and it is the one with the sharpest implication for anyone who would take the proposition as a programme.

In 1970 the psychiatrist Arnold Beisser published a paper of four pages called "The Paradoxical Theory of Change." Its thesis: change occurs when one becomes what one is, not when one tries to become what one is not. The person who strains toward a different self divides into a reformer and a reformed, and the two fight to a standstill. The person who fully inhabits their present condition — owns it, feels it, stands in it — finds that it moves.

Apply this to love and to organisations and a warning sounds. An organisation that sets out to become loving — that makes love a target state, with a programme, metrics, a head of — has by that act divided itself into reformer and reformed, and it will get the standstill: the fruit, the wellbeing week, the flat voice in the corridor. Love cannot be the object of the will in that way. What Beisser's paradox suggests is that an organisation moves toward love by making contact with what it currently is — including its lovelessness: by someone standing up in the room and saying, in the active voice, "we are frightened of each other in here, and I am too." That sentence is not loving in its content. It is an act of contact. And contact, as the last pages have tried to show, is what love is made of.

So the proposition's seventh claim — you can become Love — arrives early at its first qualification. If Beisser is right, one does not become love by trying to be loving. One becomes love by ceasing to be anything other than what one is, at the boundary, in the presence of another. The saints, who are the tradition's experts on the seventh claim, say the same thing in their own way: it is not achieved. It is consented to.

A BOUNDARY CAN ONLY BE MET BY A BOUNDARY.

6Schau der Gestalt: The Form Through Which Glory Shines

The proposition names one thinker, and he is not a psychologist. Hans Urs von Balthasar was a Swiss priest, the most widely read man of his generation by the testimony of people who were themselves formidably read, and the author of a theological trilogy of fifteen volumes whose first part he called Herrlichkeit — The Glory of the Lord — and subtitled A Theological Aesthetics. The first volume, published in 1961, bears the title Schau der Gestalt. English translators render it "Seeing the Form."

It is not a coincidence of vocabulary. Balthasar took his doctorate in German literature; he was soaked in Goethe, for whom Gestalt was the living form which the morphologist's eye learns to behold whole in the plant — and it was from the same Goethean spring that von Ehrenfels and the Berlin psychologists had drawn. When Balthasar put Gestalt at the foundation of a theology he knew what freight the word carried. He was making, in his own field, the same revolt Wertheimer had made in his: against the dissolution of wholes into parts.

The revolt

The target was a way of doing theology — and, behind it, a way of doing thought generally — that Balthasar believed had lost the capacity to see. Modern rationality, as he read it, begins by taking a thing apart. The historical critic takes the Gospel apart into sources, strata, redactions. The apologist takes faith apart into a set of propositions and a set of evidences. The moralist takes the Christian life apart into rules. Each operation is legitimate; each yields real knowledge. But a figure that has been disassembled cannot be reassembled into the thing that was there before the knife. What was there was a form — one, whole, with its own inner necessity — and a form is perceived by beholding or not at all.

So Balthasar proposed to begin theology from the transcendental the tradition had most neglected. The scholastics taught that being has properties which belong to everything that is: unity, truth, goodness. A long tradition added a fourth: beauty. Modern theology had begun from truth (and become apologetics) or from goodness (and become ethics). Balthasar would begin from beauty — warning in a much-quoted passage that a world which loses the capacity to perceive beauty will find that the good loses its power to attract and the true its power to convince. Beauty is not ornament. It is how the real first shows itself as worth turning toward.

Form and splendour

What, then, is the beautiful? Here Balthasar gave the analysis that makes him the hinge of this work. Beauty, he said, has two moments which can be distinguished and never separated. The scholastics called them species and lumen, or forma and splendor. He called them Gestalt and Glanz: FORM AND RADIANCE.

The form is the thing's intelligible shape — its proportion, its wholeness, the way its parts cohere into this and no other. It is what can be studied and described.

The splendour is what shines through the form: the depth of being that the form makes present. It is not a second thing alongside the form, a glow added to the outline. It is the form's own interior coming to the surface. Aquinas had listed claritas — brightness, radiance — among the conditions of beauty, with wholeness and proportion; Balthasar reads it as the light of being itself breaking out through a finite shape.

And the two are perceived together, in a single act which has two sides. There is the beholding — the Schau — in which the form is taken in as a whole. And there is the being taken: the rapture, the transport, in which the beholder is seized by what shines through the form and carried out of themselves toward it. One does not first inspect the form and then decide to be moved. The seeing and the being-moved are one event. Balthasar's entire theological aesthetics is built on this double structure: a doctrine of perception and a doctrine of rapture, which are one doctrine.

Put that sentence beside the proposition. Love is an affective-cognitive state: a single act, cognitive (the form is seen) and affective (the beholder is moved), not yet two. Light becomes a photonic language and has real substance: a radiance that is not decoration but the showing-forth of what the thing is. You can feel it crossing the room: the splendour travels from the form to the beholder and takes hold. You become light-emitting: the form through which splendour shines is, for Balthasar, supremely a person — and those who behold it are, in the old Pauline phrase he loved, changed into the same image from glory to glory.

The proposition is not Balthasar's theology. It was written out of an experience, in an unsteady language of fields and photons, and he would have raised an eyebrow at some of the vocabulary. But it has exactly his structure. Whoever wrote it had seen what he saw: that there is a way of knowing which is also a being-seized; that it is occasioned by a form; that the form shines; and that the shining is not a property of the surface.

The third way

In 1963, two years after Schau der Gestalt, Balthasar published a short book intended as a kind of key to the whole trilogy. Its title was Glaubhaft ist nur Liebe. In English: Love Alone Is Credible.

Its argument can be put in a page. There have been, he says, two great ways of commending Christianity to the human mind. The first, the way of the ancients and the medievals, is cosmological: the faith is shown to be the fulfilment of the world's own order — it completes philosophy, it crowns the cosmos, it makes sense of everything else. The second, the way of the moderns, is anthropological: the faith is shown to be the fulfilment of the human being — it answers our deepest need, it corresponds to the structure of the heart.

Each, Balthasar says, is a reduction. In each, the thing to be believed is measured by a standard outside itself — the cosmos in one case, the human subject in the other — and is found credible in so far as it fits. But a love that is credible because it fits my need is not being received as love. It is being received as supply. Whatever can be deduced from the world or from the self is by that fact not gift.

There is, he says, a third way, and it is the only one adequate to the object. Love is credible as love: by its own evidence, its own form, its own radiance. It is not proved from something else. It shows itself, and the showing is its authority. When one is loved — really, gratuitously, beyond anything one could have required — one does not check the experience against a criterion. The experience is the criterion. It is self-attesting, as light is: one does not need a second light by which to see that the first is shining.

His central image for this is one of the most beautiful in modern theology, and it is not theological. It is a mother and a newborn. The infant, he says, is awakened to consciousness of itself by the smile of its mother. For days and weeks she smiles at the child; and one day the child smiles back. In that moment something has occurred that no theory of knowledge built on a solitary subject can explain. The child did not infer the mother's love from evidence. The love came across, as a form, in a face; and in receiving it the child received at once the mother, itself, the world, and the knowledge that being is good. The first act of the human mind is not I think. It is the reception of a smile.

What the organisation can take from a theologian

It may seem a long way from a theological aesthetics to a management meeting. It is one step.

Every organisation commends itself — to its staff, its customers, its lenders, its regulators — and it does so in one of Balthasar's two reductive ways. The cosmological commendation says: we fit the order of things. We are compliant, well-governed, sound; our ratios are within covenant; we are the sensible choice. The anthropological commendation says: we meet your need. We offer development, flexibility, purpose; work here and you will be fulfilled.

Both are legitimate and both are necessary. And everyone to whom they are addressed understands, with the infallibility of the corridor, that neither is a reason to trust. A firm that fits the order of things may be trusted to go on fitting it exactly as long as it pays. A firm that meets my needs will meet them as long as my needs coincide with its interests. These are grounds for a contract. They are not grounds for belief.

What makes an institution credible — believable in the way a person is believable — is the third thing, and it can only be shown, never claimed. It is the moment when the organisation, or someone acting as it, does something for a person that no contract required and no interest explains: stays with the supplier through the bad year; tells the borrower the truth early when silence would have been cheaper; keeps the promise after the person to whom it was made has lost the power to enforce it. Such acts have a form. The form is recognised instantly and at a distance — the story is told for twenty years. And they generate the one asset that cannot be manufactured from any quantity of the other two: the belief that this institution means it.

CREDIBILITY IS THE SPLENDOUR OF A FORM. It shines through acts; it cannot be applied to them. An organisation that sets out to appear credible has already begun to fail at being so, for the same reason that a person trying to seem sincere has stopped being it. Balthasar's title is thus not only a theological claim. It is the most compressed statement available of something every credit committee, every regulator, every patient and every employee already knows and has no official means to say: that in the end the only thing anyone believes is love — gratuitous, costly, formed, visible — and that everything else is terms.

The bridge to the heart

Gestalt thinking has now given the proposition its grammar. Love is a whole, perceived directly and not assembled (Wertheimer). It exists as a field in which each depends on all (Köhler). It re-forms the space in which people move (Lewin). It happens at a boundary which both parties keep (Perls and Goodman). And it is a form through which something shines, credible by its own light (Balthasar).

What the gestalt tradition has not given is any account of where in the body this occurs, or why the proposition should insist — as it does, twice — on the heart. The Berlin psychologists were interested in the visual cortex. Balthasar's organ was the eye. The proposition says: cardial. Heart-burst. It locates the source in the chest. The next movement goes there.

LOVE IS NOT PROVED. IT SHOWS ITSELF, AND THE SHOWING IS THE PROOF.
