Movement II

KARDIA

The Cardial

The proposition says the heart, and means it. The organ and the symbol; why love is a way of knowing; the torus as the shape of what goes out and returns; the witnesses of the heart-burst; hearts in step across a room; and what the instruments will and will not confirm.

7The Heart Is Not Only a Pump

In 1628 William Harvey published the demonstration that the heart is a muscle which drives the blood round the body in a circuit. It was one of the great acts of the scientific revolution, and its effect on the imagination was a demotion. Before Harvey the heart was the seat of life, heat, thought and feeling, the sun of the microcosm — Harvey himself, dedicating the book to his king, still called it that. After him it was, increasingly, a pump: a piece of plumbing, indispensable and dumb. The brain inherited everything else. By the twentieth century it was a mark of education to know that when one said "I know it in my heart" one was using a dead metaphor about an organ that knows nothing.

The proposition refuses the demotion. Its word is cardial, and the choice is exact: not "cordial," which has dwindled to a manner and a drink, but a coinage straight from the Greek kardia, with the anatomy still on it. The file must therefore ask what the heart is — in the languages that formed our idea of love, and in the physiology of the last forty years, which has turned out to be considerably less obedient to the pump theory than the educated assume.

The heart in the old languages

In the Hebrew Bible the word is lev or levav, and it occurs some eight hundred and fifty times. It almost never means the seat of emotion as opposed to thought. It is the centre of the whole person: where one thinks, plans, remembers, understands, decides, and also where one rejoices and grieves. Solomon asks for a hearing heart with which to judge the people — the organ of wisdom is a heart, and it works by listening. Pharaoh's heart is hardened: that is a failure of perception as much as of pity. The fool says in his heart that there is no God; the place where an atheist does his reasoning is cardiac. When the prophet promises that the heart of stone will be taken out and a heart of flesh put in, he is promising a new capacity to know.

The Greek of the New Testament keeps the usage. Kardia is where thoughts arise, where the word is sown, where one believes. On the road to Emmaus two disciples walk for hours beside a stranger without recognising him; afterwards they say to each other, Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way? The heart knew, and knew as heat, before the eyes were opened. And Paul, in a sentence that could stand as the epigraph to this whole work, writes that the God who commanded light to shine out of darkness hath shined in our hearts — the creation of light, relocated to the chest.

In classical Chinese the word is 心, xīn, and the difficulty of translating it is so notorious that sinologists have given up and write "heart-mind." The character is a drawing of the organ. It is the seat of thinking and feeling, and the tradition does not regard these as two functions which happen to share an address. Mencius, in the fourth century before Christ, says that the function of the xīn is to think — 思, sī — and in the same breath locates in it the four "sprouts" of virtue, the first of which is the feeling that seizes anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well: 惻隱之心, the heart of alarm and compassion. No one, he says, is without it. And it arrives before any calculation about the parents' gratitude or the neighbours' praise.

So the three literatures on which our vocabularies of love principally draw — Hebrew, Greek, Chinese — agree with one another against the modern West. The heart is not the seat of feeling as distinct from thought. It is the place where they have not yet been divided. When Pascal wrote that the heart has its reasons, of which reason knows nothing, he was not defending sentiment against intellect. He was a mathematician, and he meant that the heart has reasons: that there is an order of knowing — he says elsewhere that we know first principles, like space and time and number, by the heart — which is immediate, certain, and prior to proof.

The heart in the laboratory

All this might be put down to pre-scientific anatomy, a mistake about where the thinking is done, preserved in idiom. The file would be inclined to put it down that way, were it not for what the physiologists have since found. Four findings, stated at the strength they can bear.

The heart has a nervous system of its own. In 1991 the Canadian neurocardiologist J. Andrew Armour described what he called the intrinsic cardiac nervous system — a network of some tens of thousands of neurons embedded in the heart itself, with sensory neurons, local-circuit neurons and motor neurons, capable of processing information and regulating the heart's activity without instruction from the brain. He nicknamed it the "little brain on the heart." The nickname has been carried by enthusiasts far beyond the evidence — the intrinsic cardiac neurons do not think, remember your childhood, or fall in love. But the sober finding stands: the heart is not a passive pump on the end of a wire. It is a sensing and integrating organ.

The traffic runs mostly upward. The vagus nerve, the great wandering trunk that connects the brain with heart, lungs and gut, is by the usual estimate about four-fifths afferent: most of its fibres carry signals from the body to the brain. The heart, on every beat, reports to the brainstem the pressure and timing of its own contraction, and these reports are relayed upward to regions — the insula, the anterior cingulate, the amygdala — that are central to emotion and to the sense of self.

The brain's processing is timed to the heartbeat. Each heartbeat evokes a small, measurable electrical response in the cortex. More remarkably, what a person perceives depends on when in the cardiac cycle the stimulus arrives. In a line of work associated with Sarah Garfinkel and Hugo Critchley, fearful faces flashed at systole — the moment the heart contracts — were detected more readily and judged more intense than the same faces at diastole. The heart is not merely informing the brain of its condition. Its rhythm is a gate through which the world is perceived, and the gate opens and closes once a beat.

People differ in how well they can feel their own heart, and the difference matters. Interoception — the sensing of the body's interior — can be tested by asking people to count their heartbeats without touching their pulse. Some are good at it; many are poor. Accuracy is related, in a tangle of findings not all of which have replicated cleanly, to the intensity with which emotions are experienced, to intuitive decision-making, and to the capacity to recognise what others are feeling.

Put the four together and the old languages look less like error and more like report. Emotion is, in substantial part, the brain's reading of the body, and the heart is the body's loudest instrument. A feeling is not first computed in the head and then expressed in the chest. The chest is in the loop from the beginning. Antonio Damasio's phrase for this was that the body is the theatre of the emotions. The Psalmist's phrase was that the heart knows.

The finding the file most wants the reader to keep is the third. What you can perceive depends on the phase of your heart. That is a laboratory result, about faces on a screen and intervals of a few hundred milliseconds, and it must not be inflated. But let its form be noticed. It says that perception is not continuous; that it has a pulse; that the organ in the chest is setting a rhythm of openness and closure to the world. Wertheimer found that a crossing happens only in the right interval between two events. Here is a second interval, inside the perceiver — the perceiver's own beat. A crossing between two people requires, perhaps, that these intervals fall right: that the look arrive while the gate is open.

Why the organisation should care

Because organisations have, for a century, been built on Harvey's demotion.

The formal organisation is a cerebral fantasy: it imagines itself as a brain — strategy at the top, information flowing up, instructions flowing down — operating a body of hands. In this picture what people feel is, at best, a variable to be managed in the service of what they are to do, and what they feel in their chests in a meeting is not data at all. It is noise, to be mastered by professionalism.

If the physiology is even roughly right, this is not merely inhumane. It is bad epistemics. A room full of people is a room full of hearts reporting upward, and those reports carry information that has not reached and may never reach the level of the sayable. The tightness three people felt when the acquisition was announced. The drop in the stomach at a certain name. The warmth, unaccountable on the numbers, toward one bidder and not another. Organisations that have no way of making such sensation figure — to use the Gestalt word — are throwing away the output of their most sensitive instrument, and then commissioning consultants to find out what everyone in the building already knew.

The Quakers have a method for this, three and a half centuries old: a meeting for business conducted out of silence, in which a decision is taken not by vote but when the clerk discerns "the sense of the meeting" — and in which a single Friend with a "stop in the mind" can hold the matter until the unease has been heard. It has been used to run schools, banks and chocolate manufacturers. Whatever else it is, it is a technology for letting the heart report.

THE HEART HAS REASONS. THE ORGANISATION HAS NOWHERE TO FILE THEM.

What is measured. The heart's own neurons; the predominance of upward traffic in the vagus; cortical responses timed to the heartbeat; stronger perception of fearful faces at systole. The interoception literature is real and under methodological dispute, especially the heartbeat-counting task.

What is argued. That Hebrew, Greek and Chinese usage was reporting something about the heart and not merely misplacing the mind.

What is conjecture. That whether something crosses between two people depends on cardiac phase. Nobody has shown this.

8Affective-Cognitive: Love as a Way of Knowing

The proposition's first adjective is a hyphen. Affective-cognitive. The hyphen is doing the work that a paragraph of philosophy would otherwise have to do, and it is making a claim that most of modern thought has denied: that there is a state which is at once a being-moved and a knowing, and that it is one state, not two in close succession.

The denial has two forms, and they are mirror images. The first says that love is a feeling, and feelings are not about anything; they are internal weather. One may have reasons for acting on a feeling, but the feeling itself is neither true nor false — it just occurs, like a headache. The second says that love is, underneath, a judgement — an appraisal that this person is valuable, good for me, worthy — and the feeling is the bodily noise the appraisal makes. On the first view love knows nothing. On the second, love knows only what a cool judgement could know without it, and adds heat.

Against both, a long counter-tradition, which the file now calls as a sequence of witnesses.

Augustine: love as weight

Late in the Confessions, Augustine writes a sentence of four words: pondus meum amor meus — my weight is my love. He is using the physics of his day, in which each element has a natural place and moves toward it by its own weight: fire upward, stone downward. A body is carried by its weight to where it belongs. By my love, he says, I am carried wherever I am carried.

This is love as neither weather nor verdict. It is a direction: the fundamental tilt of a person, prior to their particular feelings and judgements, which determines what they will move toward and therefore what they will come to know. It is Lewin's valence, fifteen centuries early and at the scale of a whole life. And Augustine drew the consequence in another phrase which Max Scheler would later take as a title: virtue is ordo amoris, the right ordering of love. A person is not, most deeply, what they think or what they will. They are the order of what they love.

Scheler: the loving being

Scheler, writing in the years when the Berlin psychologists were writing, pushed this to its limit. Before the human being is an ens cogitans, a thinking thing, or an ens volens, a willing thing, it is an ens amans — a loving being. Love is not a response to values already perceived. It is the movement that opens the eye to values not yet seen. The lover does not first observe that the beloved is good and then love; in loving, they discover in the beloved a height of value that was invisible to the indifferent, and which is there.

Scheler also gave the distinction that every later chapter on organisations will need. In The Nature of Sympathy he separated things that the word "empathy" now blurs. There is emotional infection — catching a mood, as one catches the gaiety of a bar or the panic of a crowd, without any awareness of the other as other. There is emotional identification — losing oneself in another, or absorbing them into oneself. And there is genuine fellow-feeling, which is intentional: it is directed at the other's joy or sorrow as theirs, across a distance that is preserved. Only the last is a way of knowing a person. Infection knows no one; it is a transfer of state. And love, for Scheler, is something else again — not a feeling-with at all but a movement toward the other's highest possibility.

Set that beside the contact boundary. Infection and identification are confluence. Fellow-feeling is contact. The distinction was found twice, by a phenomenologist in Cologne and by a psychoanalyst and a poet in New York, and both times it turned on the same thing: THE OTHER MUST REMAIN OTHER FOR THE KNOWING TO BE KNOWING.

Murdoch and Weil: attention

Iris Murdoch put it in thirteen words that have not been bettered: love is "the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real." The difficulty she had in mind was specific. The mind, left alone, is a machine for producing a comfortable picture with itself at the centre — fantasy, in her strict sense. Other people appear in the picture as supporting cast. To love is to have that picture broken by the sheer independent existence of someone else.

Her example is domestic and exact. A mother-in-law privately regards her son's wife as common and juvenile. She behaves impeccably; nothing shows. But she is troubled by her own view, and she sets herself — nothing outward changing — to look again. Over time she comes to see the girl as not vulgar but refreshingly simple, not undignified but spontaneous. Murdoch insists this is not self-deception. It is the mother-in-law becoming more just, and justice here is a matter of the quality of her attention. Something has been learned — and the instrument of learning was love.

Murdoch took the word attention from Simone Weil, who used it with a severity that still shocks. Attention, for Weil, is the suspension of one's own thought, leaving it detached, empty, ready to be penetrated by the object. She called it the rarest and purest form of generosity. In the essay on school studies she says the capacity to give one's attention to a sufferer is a very rare and difficult thing, almost a miracle; nearly all who think they have it do not. The love of the neighbour, in its fullness, is simply being able to say: What are you going through?

Note what kind of sentence that is. It is not an expression of feeling. It is a question — a cognitive act, a request for knowledge. And it can only be sincerely asked by someone who has, for the moment, got themselves out of the way. The affect and the cognition are not two components. The love is the quality of the asking.

The scholastic formula

The medievals had a formula for this, traced back to Gregory the Great: amor ipse notitia est — love itself is knowledge. William of St Thierry sharpened it: amor ipse intellectus est — love itself is understanding. And Thomas Aquinas, who is supposed to be the dry one, distinguished the knowledge one has of a thing by studying it from the knowledge one has by connaturality — by being, oneself, attuned to it. The chaste person, he says, judges rightly about chastity not by having read the treatise but by inclination; the person who loves judges of the beloved from within, by a kind of kinship.

This is the proposition's noetic. The word comes from nous — in Greek philosophy, the faculty of direct intellectual sight, as distinct from dianoia, reasoning step by step. Noetic knowledge is not inferred; it is beheld. The claim that love is noetic is the claim that the lover sees something — immediately, as a whole, with certainty — which is really there and which cannot be reached by going round the long way. It is Wertheimer's point about phi and Balthasar's point about the form, now made about persons.

What exactly is known?

A sceptic is entitled to ask: known what? If love is a kind of cognition, what are its objects? Three answers, in ascending order of ambition.

The particular. Love knows this one. Science knows the general — the kind, the law, the type. The loving eye knows the individual as individual: not "a mid-career analyst with development needs" but Anjali, who goes quiet before she says the thing that matters. Duns Scotus coined a word for what makes a thing this thing and no other — haecceitas, thisness. Thisness is not available to classification. It is available only to attention sustained by something very like love.

The possible. Love knows what the other could be. The Gestalt law of closure, as applied in chapter two: the lover sees the circle the fragments belong to. This is knowledge of something real — the possibility is really a possibility of this person — but it is knowledge of the not-yet. And it is partly self-fulfilling in a way that does not make it less true: people rise toward the form in which they are steadily beheld. The research on teachers' expectations and on leaders' expectations points, with all its replication quarrels, in this direction. Scheler said it more exactly than the experimenters: love is a movement in which the object's higher value flashes up.

The real as good. Love knows that being is gift. That is Balthasar's smile. In being loved the infant learns — before it can learn anything else, and as the condition of learning anything else — that the world it has arrived in can be trusted. This is a metaphysical claim and the file marks it as such. But notice that organisations, too, run on some answer to it. A workforce that has learned, in its collective infancy, that the place can be trusted will read an ambiguous memo generously. One that has learned otherwise will read the same memo as a threat. The memo is the same. What differs is a prior knowledge, laid down by how they have been smiled at or not.

The cognitive cost of lovelessness

It follows that an organisation without love is not merely unpleasant. It is stupid — in a precise sense: it is deprived of a class of knowledge.

It does not know its people in the particular; it knows them as roles, grades, headcount. So it is perpetually surprised: by the resignation of the person everyone depended on, by the collapse of the team that looked fine on the dashboard.

It does not know its people in the possible; it knows them as their last appraisal. So it systematically under-uses what it has and buys in from outside what was sitting two desks away.

It does not know its customers, its borrowers, its patients as real others. It knows them as segments and exposures. So it designs for an average who does not exist, and is baffled when actual persons behave as actual persons do.

And it does not know itself, because self-knowledge in a collective depends on people telling each other the truth, and people tell the truth where the life space is round. The loveless organisation's picture of itself is assembled from reports written in combat landscape — which is to say, from documents whose first purpose was the protection of their authors.

None of this is a moral point. It is an epistemic one. THE LOVELESS ORGANISATION IS RUNNING ON LOW RESOLUTION. It has discarded an instrument and then wonders why it cannot see.

ATTENTION IS THE FORM LOVE TAKES WHEN IT WANTS TO KNOW.

9The Torus: A Shape for What Goes Out and Returns

Of all the words in the proposition, toroidal is the one most likely to make a careful reader wince. It has a reputation. It appears on websites that also sell crystals; it comes attached to diagrams of the human body sitting inside a luminous doughnut. The file's first instinct was to quarantine it.

The instinct was wrong. The torus is the best word in the proposition, and the reason it is the best is geometrical and has nothing to do with crystals. It is the simplest shape there is for a flow that goes out from a centre and returns through that same centre. It is the exact figure of circulation-with-a-source. And circulation, as Davies's Signature has it, is the whole matter.

What a torus is

Take a circle and sweep it round an axis that lies in its plane but does not cut it: the surface traced is a torus, the shape of a ring or a tyre's inner tube. So much for the surface. What makes the shape interesting is what can flow on and through it.

There are two independent ways of going round a torus. One goes the long way round the ring — the toroidal direction. The other goes the short way, through the hole and back over the outside — the poloidal direction. A flow that runs poloidally everywhere does this: it rises up through the central hole, fountains outward over the top, descends round the outside, curls under the bottom, and is drawn back up through the centre. Every streamline leaves the axis and returns to it. Nothing is lost at an edge, because there is no edge.

Nature is fond of this form. A smoke ring is a toroidal vortex: the air in it rolls continuously, out over the front and back through the middle, which is why a smoke ring holds together and travels while a mere puff disperses. The magnetic field of a bar magnet, or of a loop of current, or of the Earth, has the same plan: the lines leave one pole, arc round through the surrounding space, re-enter at the other pole, and run back through the body to where they began. They are closed loops — it is a law of electromagnetism that magnetic field lines have no beginnings or ends — and their family, taken together, is a nest of tori about the axis.

Now the cardiology. The heart is an electrical organ: each beat is a wave of depolarisation sweeping through the muscle, which amounts to a moving current, and a current makes a magnetic field. To a first approximation the heart is a current dipole, and the field of a dipole is the nested-torus form just described. So when the proposition says cardial-toroidal, it is, at the first level, simply correct. The magnetic field of the beating heart has a toroidal geometry, as does that of any current loop, and it does not stop at the skin. The level at which it becomes contestable is not the geometry. It is the magnitude and the meaning, and those are for chapter twelve.

Why the shape matters more than the field

Leave the magnetism aside. The file wants the torus for a different reason: as the gestalt — the form, transposable to any medium — of a certain kind of life.

Consider the alternatives.

A flow that only goes out is a jet. It has a source and no return. It is impressive and it is doomed: whatever feeds it is being emptied. The person who gives and gives and receives nothing back is a jet, and the trajectory of a jet is known.

A flow that only comes in is a sink. Everything nearby is drawn toward it and nothing emerges. Every organisation has one or two: the people after whose meetings everyone needs a coffee.

A flow that goes round and round without passing through any centre is a closed loop — the clique, the mutual-admiration circuit, the leadership team that energises itself beautifully and touches no one else. It circulates. It does not emanate.

A flow that goes out, disperses, and never returns is radiation into the void: broadcast. The all-staff email. The values on the wall.

The torus is none of these. It is the form in which a centre gives itself out into the surrounding space and receives itself back through its own heart, continuously, so that the giving is fed by the returning and the returning is the fruit of the giving. Source and sink are the same place. It is a self-sustaining emanation. A smoke ring travels across a room, intact, where a puff would have died in a foot.

LOVE IS THE ONLY GIVING THAT COMES BACK THROUGH THE GIVER. This is not a pious hope; it is close to a definition. An "outflow" that is not open to receiving back — that gives from above, from surplus, armoured against any return — is not love but patronage, and its recipients know the difference at once. And a "love" that goes out in order to get back is not love but investment. In the torus the return is neither refused nor demanded. It is simply how the form is built.

The torus and the cycle

Recall the Gestalt cycle of experience: sensation, awareness, mobilisation, action, contact, resolution, withdrawal. It is drawn, in the textbooks, as a wave or a circle. It should be drawn as a poloidal circuit of a torus. Mobilisation rises through the centre; action and contact fountain outward into the environment; resolution curves round the far side; withdrawal returns, underneath, back toward the centre, where — after a rest that is part of the form — sensation stirs again.

Drawn like that, the withdrawal phase stops looking like an absence of contact and starts looking like half of it. The return path is as much the torus as the outward path. A person, a team, an institution that has only the outward half is not "more generous" than one with both. It is a broken form, and it will fail the way jets fail.

The torus and the gyre

Davies's master-figure is the Gyre, taken from Yeats: the widening spiral — or, in Yeats's developed system, two interpenetrating cones, the apex of each at the centre of the other's base, so that as one widens the other narrows, each living the other's death.

The torus is what the gyre becomes when it is allowed to close. Follow a spiral outward on the upper surface of a torus: it widens, as Yeats's gyre widens. But on a torus the widening does not go on until the centre cannot hold. It reaches the outer rim, turns under, and begins to narrow on the lower surface, spiralling inward, until it passes through the hole and emerges, widening again, on top. The falcon can hear the falconer, because the path leads back. Davies's own formulation — meaning returns, not to confirm itself, but to be reworked under changed conditions — is a description of flow on a torus that is itself moving: each circuit comes back through the centre, but the centre is no longer where it was.

Yeats saw the widening and prophesied anarchy. The proposition sees the return and names it love. They are looking at the same geometry.

The oldest torus

The Greek Fathers, when they wanted a word for the inner life of the Trinity, chose perichoresis: a mutual indwelling, a moving-around-and-through, in which each of the three is wholly in the others and receives itself from them. The Latin West translated it circumincessio. It is a doctrine about a love that is perfectly given, perfectly received, and perfectly returned, such that the giving and the returning are not episodes but what the lovers are.

The file is not competent to do Trinitarian theology and will not try. It records only the structural fact: when the Christian tradition sought to say what love is at its source, it reached for a figure of circulation through a common centre. And Balthasar, the proposition's own witness, built his later work on it: the world's drama takes place inside an eternal exchange of self-giving, and every finite love is a participation in that prior circulation. If one wanted a diagram of his claim that one can become love, it would be this: to become love is not to turn oneself into a source. It is to be taken up into a circulation that was already running.

The organisational torus

Now to the claim that this is an organisational phenomenon. Three applications.

The person. A leader, a nurse, a teacher, a receiver in a workout: anyone whose work is to be for others is, energetically, one of the four broken forms or the whole one. The diagnostic question is plain: where does what you give come back to you from, and does it come back through the same place it left? Those in whom it does are the people who seem inexhaustible, and their secret is not stamina. It is circuit. What they give returns to them — in the faces of the people they serve, in the work visibly done, in a source beyond themselves from which they understand the giving to have come. Those in whom it does not are running on capital.

The team. A team is toroidal when the energy its members put into the common centre — the task, the patient, the client — returns to the members through that centre, and not round it. In the closed-loop team, people energise one another directly: they like each other, they have fun, and the task is a pretext. In the jet team, everything goes into the task and nothing comes back: the deal closes and the team is ash. In the toroidal team, the route by which members reach one another runs through the work: I am for you by being wholly for what we are both for. This is why the deepest working friendships are so often side-by-side and not face-to-face — C. S. Lewis's remark that friends are absorbed not in each other but in some common interest. The common interest is the hole in the torus. It is what the love goes through.

The institution. Here the torus is Davies's Circulatory Energy at its proper scale. An institution emanates — services, products, judgements, care — and something returns: revenue, certainly, but also trust, reputation, the willingness of good people to join, the stories told about it. An institution is healthy when the return passes back through its centre — through the purpose that generated the emanation — and renews that purpose. It is sick when the return bypasses the centre: when revenue comes back to a part of the organisation that has no contact with what was given, so that those who give never feel the return and those who receive the return never see the giving. A great deal of what is called loss of purpose in large organisations is just this: the torus has been cut, the outward flow and the inward flow run through different buildings, and nobody stands at the place where they would meet.

The remedy is not a purpose statement. It is plumbing. BRING THE RETURN BACK THROUGH THE CENTRE: let the people who did the work see the face of the person it was for.

A JET IS EMPTYING. A TORUS IS FED BY WHAT IT GIVES.

10Heart-Burst: The Witnesses

Love literally is a heart-burst. So the proposition; and the word literally has been promised strict handling. The handling begins by calling witnesses — people, across eight centuries, who reported that something happened in the chest, and who were not confused about the difference between a figure of speech and a physical event. The file lays the reports side by side, and then asks what the cardiologists have to say.

Richard Rolle, Yorkshire, c. 1340

Richard Rolle was a hermit, an Oxford drop-out, and the most widely read English spiritual writer of the late Middle Ages. His best-known book is called Incendium Amoris — The Fire of Love — and its prologue opens with a report so careful that it reads like a clinical note.

He was sitting in a chapel, he says, taking pleasure in prayer, when he felt in himself an unaccustomed and pleasant heat. He was astonished. He did not, at first, know what it was. And — this is the detail that makes him a witness and not a poet — he put his hand to his chest to find out whether the burning had some outward bodily cause. He says he kept feeling his breast to see if there was some physical reason for it. Only when he had satisfied himself that the heat was within and had no external source did he conclude that it was a gift. He adds that he would never have believed, had he not felt it, that such warmth could be experienced in this exile; and he is explicit that he means real heat — that his heart was kindled not in imagination but as if with sensible fire.

Rolle systematised his experience into three: calor, canor, dulcor — heat, song, sweetness. The heat came first. The song came some months later: an interior sound, a melody into which his prayer turned, as though thought itself had become music. The file notes, without yet making anything of it, that the second stage of the heart-burst was acoustic: a pattern, a wave.

Philip Neri, Rome, 1544

Philip Neri was a Florentine layman of twenty-nine who had been living in Rome for some years, praying at night in the catacombs of San Sebastiano. On the vigil of Pentecost 1544, by the account he gave late in life to those close to him, he was praying for the gifts of the Spirit when he saw a globe of fire, which entered his mouth and lodged in his breast. He was seized with such heat that he threw himself on the ground and bared his chest to cool it. When he rose, he found a swelling over his heart the size of a fist.

For the fifty years he had left, the witnesses agree on the sequel. His heart beat with a violence that shook his chair, his bed, sometimes the room. He radiated heat: he went about with his cassock unbuttoned in the Roman winter. People who were pressed against his chest — he had a way of pulling a troubled penitent's head to his heart — reported extraordinary consolation. He became the most sought-after confessor in the city, the founder of the Oratory, a man whose defining traits were gaiety and a refusal to be solemn.

When he died in 1595 the surgeons opened the body. They recorded that two of the ribs over the heart were broken and arched outward, and had never rejoined; and that the heart and the great vessel leaving it were enlarged. The physicians who examined the findings — among them Andrea Cesalpino, one of the foremost anatomists of the age and a forerunner of Harvey on the circulation — treated the condition as beyond natural explanation. A modern physician would wish to see the notes. The file records what the sixteenth century recorded: a man who said fire had entered his heart, who behaved for half a century as though it had, and whose chest, when it was opened, had made room.

Teresa, Pascal, Wesley

More briefly, three further depositions.

Teresa of Ávila, around 1559, describes in her Life a recurring experience: an angel with a long golden spear, its tip seemingly of fire, plunged into her heart several times, leaving her wholly on fire with love. She is careful: the pain, she says, is not bodily but spiritual — though the body has its share in it, even a large one. She will not say it is physical and she will not say it is not.

Blaise Pascal, on the night of 23 November 1654, between about half past ten and half past twelve, underwent something he never spoke of. He wrote an account on a sheet of paper, copied it onto parchment, and sewed both into the lining of his coat, where a servant found them after his death. The document is called the Memorial. Under the date and the time stands one word, alone on its line, in capitals: FEU. Fire. Then: certainty; feeling; joy; peace. The mathematician who would write that the heart has its reasons had dated the reason and timed it.

John Wesley, on 24 May 1738, went "very unwillingly" to a society meeting in Aldersgate Street in London, where someone was reading Luther's preface to Romans. About a quarter before nine, he wrote in his journal, I felt my heart strangely warmed. He was an Oxford don of thirty-four, methodical to a fault. He notes the time. He uses a thermal word. The movement that came out of that quarter of an hour would reorganise the religious life of the English-speaking working class and would be, among other things, one of the most formidable feats of organisation of the eighteenth century — classes, bands, circuits, conferences. It began with a temperature change in one chest in a room in the City of London.

What the witnesses agree on

Five things recur, and the file lists them because agreement among independent witnesses is its form of evidence.

It is located. In the chest; left of centre; in the heart. Not in the head, not diffusely.

It is thermal. Heat, fire, burning, warmth. The vocabulary is of temperature before it is of anything else.

It is sudden and datable. A vigil, a night in November, a quarter before nine. There is a before and an after. The proposition's word burst is right.

It is noetic. With the heat comes certainty — Pascal's word. Something is known that was not known before. Not a doctrine; a presence.

And it is expansive, then emissive. Something enlarges — Philip's ribs are the emblem — and then goes out. None of these people became more inward as a result. Rolle wrote for the unlettered in their own English. Philip turned Rome's confessional into a place of laughter. Teresa founded seventeen convents on bad roads. Wesley rode a quarter of a million miles. THE HEART-BURST IS FOLLOWED BY ORGANISATION. That is perhaps the least noticed fact about it.

What the cardiologists say

Is there anything in medicine that answers to this? There is one thing, and it is startling enough that the file will state it carefully.

In 1990 Japanese cardiologists described a syndrome in which a patient, usually an older woman, arrives with all the signs of a heart attack — chest pain, the electrocardiogram, the enzymes — and is found to have clean coronary arteries. What she has instead is a left ventricle that has changed shape. Its apex has ballooned outward and stopped contracting, while the base squeezes normally, so that on the angiogram the chamber has the form of a round-bottomed, narrow-necked pot. The Japanese named it for the octopus trap of that shape: takotsubo. The usual trigger is a violent emotion — a bereavement, a shock — and the press named it broken-heart syndrome. It is thought to be mediated by a surge of stress hormones acting on the heart muscle. Most patients recover completely within weeks.

So this much is literal, with no inverted commas: an emotion can, within minutes, alter the physical shape of the human heart so that part of it bulges outward.

And there is a rider. A minority of cases, a few in every hundred in the large registries, are triggered not by grief but by joy — a wedding, a birthday party, the birth of a grandchild, a favourite team's win. The registry investigators called it happy-heart syndrome.

The file must not overreach. Takotsubo is an injury. It is not the mystics' fire. Nothing licenses the claim that Philip Neri had a stress cardiomyopathy on the eve of Pentecost. What the syndrome establishes is narrower and still considerable: the proposition's literally is not absurd. The heart is an organ whose physical form answers to the passions, and can answer abruptly, by distension. Language in every tongue had said so. In 1990 it was put on film.

There is also a quieter physiology that needs no syndrome. A sudden strong emotion alters the heart's rhythm and force at once, through the autonomic nerves; the chest wall has sensory nerves; the sensations of warmth, fullness and pressure behind the breastbone, in moments of being moved, are real perceptions of real changes in a real organ. When someone says their heart swelled, they are reporting interoception, not composing verse.

The organisational heart-burst

Has this anything to do with institutions? The Wesley example says that it has, and that the connection is causal.

Organisations do not begin in strategy. Look back along the line of almost any institution that has lasted and has mattered, and at the start there is someone — or two or three — to whom something happened. Not an idea; an idea is cool and can be had by anyone. An ignition. Florence Nightingale's "call" of 1837, which she dated. The founders of the hospice movement at a particular bedside. The parent who starts the charity the week after the diagnosis. Bill Wilson and Dr Bob in Akron. It is datable, it is felt in the body, it brings certainty, and it is followed by an extraordinary outpouring of organising energy that those around the founder find at once exhausting and impossible to refuse.

Max Weber called the phenomenon charisma — a word he took from Paul, where it means a gift of grace — and he saw with great clarity what follows: the gift must be routinised if it is to outlast the gifted. Rules replace inspiration; offices replace the circle of disciples; a salary replaces the shared purse. The institution is the heart-burst's survival and also its cooling. A later chapter will ask whether the cooling is as inevitable as Weber thought, or whether an institution can be built as a hearth and not as an urn.

Here, the simpler point. If organisations begin in heart-burst — if that is, as a matter of history, where a great many of the enduring ones came from — then the proposition is not importing an alien category into organisational life. It is naming the organisation's own origin: the thing every founder's-day speech gestures toward and every strategy document is too well-bred to mention.

FIRST THE FIRE. THEN THE COMMITTEE STRUCTURE.

ExcursusA Spear in the Chest

The witnesses of the last chapter were hermits and saints, and the claim that institutions begin in such events was supported from Wesley and from the general run of founders. A reader may fairly ask whether anything of the kind happens to people who run companies. One of the three books laid on this file supplies cases, and the first of them reads as though it had been written for this chapter.

The carpet manufacturer

Aidan McQuade, assembling narratives of moral choice for his study of ethical leadership, begins with Ray Anderson. Anderson had founded a company in Georgia in 1973 to make carpet tiles; by the 1990s it was the largest such manufacturer in the world, an enterprise wholly dependent on petroleum for its materials and its energy. In 1994, at the age of sixty, he was asked to give a talk to a company task force on the firm's environmental vision. He had none. Casting about for something to say, he read a book on the ecology of commerce that someone had sent him.

He later described what happened as he read it. McQuade quotes the phrase and builds his analysis on it: Anderson said that the realisation of what his business was doing came as "a spear in the chest."

Located; sudden; noetic; in the chest. A mid-century American industrialist, with no vocabulary of mysticism and no interest in acquiring one, reached for Teresa's image.

McQuade's comment is that here a leadership choice emerged not from a coolly rational appraisal of interests but from a visceral impulse arising from personal values. In his Cruciform: the vertical axis broke through the horizontal. Everything in the situation's past and momentum — the industry's practice, the firm's success, the plain fact that carpet was made from oil — pointed one way. Something from the Me and the You rose against it.

And then — the fifth mark of chapter ten — it was followed by organisation. Anderson set his company the aim of taking nothing from the earth that the earth could not renew, and spent the remaining seventeen years of his life on it. The figures McQuade records are of water use, emissions and energy cut by large fractions, and of recycled content multiplied many times. Anderson claimed that it paid — in customers' loyalty, in the spirit of employees, and in cash.

McQuade notes two further things, and they bear on the argument of this work.

The first is that Anderson had advantages: he was chief executive and controlled most of the voting stock. He could act on what had struck him. McQuade's phrase for what he then did is that he opened discursive space — room, within the firm and then within the industry, in which others could take up the question and find answers he had not thought of. In the language of this file, he changed the slope; and then each point reached became a source. The heart-burst was his. The seventeen years of re-engineering were several thousand people's.

The second is a sentence the file finds as sobering as any in the three books. Ethical leadership, McQuade writes, means turning in a life-affirming direction the same social processes that elsewhere produced atrocity: legitimate authority, the wish to conform, the validation of results. The wavefront does not care what it carries.

The prosecutor

McQuade's second case is of a different kind, and it shows the crossing more starkly because it cost more.

Stuart Couch was a lieutenant colonel in the United States Marine Corps, a pilot and a lawyer, assigned after 2001 to prosecute detainees held at Guantánamo Bay. He had a personal stake: a friend from his flying days had been the co-pilot of one of the aircraft flown into the World Trade Center. He wanted, as he told a newspaper later, a crack at the men who had done it. He was given the case of a Mauritanian prisoner said to have been a significant figure in the plot, and expected to seek the death penalty.

The prisoner had denied everything for two years and then, abruptly, had confessed at length. Couch set himself to find out why. What he found, by McQuade's account of the published record, was that the confession had followed a sustained course of treatment authorised at the highest level — isolation, extremes of temperature, beatings, humiliation, mock drowning — which Couch concluded was torture.

He refused to prosecute. He told his superiors that he could not, in conscience and in law, proceed on evidence so obtained. He was a serving officer in wartime, declining a case which the entire chain of command above him wished to see brought, on behalf of a man he believed might well be guilty and whose associates had killed his friend.

Lay the Cruciform over it. The horizontal axis could hardly be stronger: an institution with a clear demand, at war, and his own grief aligned with it. On the vertical: a lawyer's formation, and — by his own later account — a Christian's. It has been reported that the turning point came at a church service, a baptism, during which the congregation was asked to affirm that they would respect the dignity of every human being; and that he found he could not say the words and go on as he was.

If so, it is McQuade's third dimension in pure form: a second social situation — a congregation, a liturgy — intersecting the first and supplying a place from which the first could be judged. And it is this file's cavity: a rite which returned to him, in the form of a question to be answered aloud, what he had long ago said he was.

Note the object of his refusal. Not a friend. A prisoner; an alleged enemy; a man with no power to reward him. Chapter forty will argue that an institution's credibility is established at its margins and nowhere else. A legal system's credibility was, for a moment, located in one officer's inability to say a sentence in church.

The politician

The third case need only be touched. John Hume, of Derry, spent thirty years working for a settlement in Northern Ireland that would give both identities a place — at the cost of his health and, for long periods, of his standing with his own side. McQuade traces it to a moment in Hume's boyhood: his father, an unemployed man, at a political meeting where flags were being waved, telling the child that you cannot eat a flag. One sentence, from a father, on a street; and sixty years later a peace.

McQuade's word for what Hume built is again discursive space: room in which people who had been killing one another could, as he drily puts it, replace bloody conflict with ill-tempered disputation, as in most other places. The file's word would be Arendt's: he rebuilt the table, the in-between, that relates and separates. It is not what one usually thinks of as love's work. On the argument of chapter five it is exactly that: the making of a boundary at which contact can happen.

What the cases add

Four things, for the argument.

The phenomenology is not confined to the devout. An industrialist said spear in the chest. The proposition's heart-burst is a fair name for something that befalls chief executives and marines.

It is aimed. In each case the visceral event was about something: the earth; a prisoner's dignity; people's need to eat. Love, said chapter eight, is noetic. The spear carried information.

It is tested by what it costs and by whom it is for. Anderson risked a prosperous company. Couch risked his career for a man he had every reason to hate. Hume gave his health. Each is Balthasar's inexplicable act.

And it is not enough. McQuade does not let the heart-burst stand alone. Each of his exemplars went on to years of appraisal, structure, persuasion and compromise — the three disciplines of chapter twenty-nine. Anderson needed engineers. Couch needed the law. Hume needed a framework, and patience on a scale hard to imagine. The spear begins it. Then the committee structure.

11Entrainment: Hearts in Step Across a Room

So far the heart has been one heart. The proposition's claim is about what passes between. Is there any evidence that hearts — the organs, on the monitor — do anything in concert across a space?

There is, and some of it is very good.

San Pedro Manrique

Every year on the night of 23 June, in a village in the Spanish province of Soria, a bed of oak is burned down to coals in a small amphitheatre, and at midnight, before three thousand spectators, a succession of local men and women walk barefoot across it — seven metres of embers at something over six hundred degrees — most of them carrying a relative on their backs.

In 2008 a team led by Ivana Konvalinka and Dimitris Xygalatas put heart-rate monitors on thirty-eight people at this ritual: twelve fire-walkers; nine spectators who were relatives or friends of a walker; and seventeen spectators who were visitors with no tie to anyone taking part. They recorded continuously through the half-hour of the event and then analysed the data with methods taken from the mathematics of nonlinear systems, which look for shared structure in two fluctuating signals.

The result was published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2011. The heart-rate dynamics of the fire-walkers and of their related spectators showed fine-grained similarities throughout the ritual. The hearts of the unrelated spectators — who were sitting in the same amphitheatre, watching the same walkers cross the same coals — showed nothing of the kind. Shown the traces blind, one could pick out who belonged to whom.

Three features of this finding deserve to be dwelt on.

The synchrony was not produced by shared movement. The walkers were walking on fire; the relatives were sitting on stone benches. Their bodies were doing entirely different things. The authors concluded that the mediating mechanism must be informational — carried by sight and sound — and not a matter of matched motion.

The synchrony was not produced by shared stimulus alone. Everyone in the arena received the same sights and sounds. Only those who were bound to a walker were entrained. The coupling was conditional on relationship.

The investigators framed their question with Durkheim. They set out to find whether his "collective effervescence" — the theoretical force that seizes a gathered people — had a physiological signature. They found one. And they found that it was not collective in the undifferentiated sense: it ran along the lines of love.

That last point is the one the file wishes to underline. The proposition says that love creates a field which extends beyond the body. Here is a measured instance of something extending beyond the body — one heart's dynamics patterned with another's across a crowded arena — and what determined whether it extended to a given person was not distance, not line of sight, not the intensity of the spectacle. It was whether that person loved the one on the coals. HEARTS SYNCHRONISE ALONG BONDS, NOT ACROSS SPACE.

The wider literature

The fire-walk is the most dramatic study. It is not alone. Over the last two decades a literature on interpersonal physiological synchrony has grown large enough to have its own systematic reviews. A few of its landmarks:

Mothers and infants. Ruth Feldman and colleagues have shown that during face-to-face interaction a mother's and her three-month-old's heart rhythms coordinate, with lags of under a second, and that the coordination tightens in moments when their gaze, affect and vocalisation are in step. Feldman's term is bio-behavioural synchrony, and she treats it as the template upon which later capacities for attachment are built. Balthasar's smile, on the monitor.

Choirs. A Swedish group led by Björn Vickhoff recorded singers' heart-rate variability and found that when a choir sings in unison with a regular phrase structure the singers' hearts accelerate and decelerate together. Here the mechanism is clear and almost mechanical — breathing is coupled to heart rate, and a hymn imposes a common breath. Human beings discovered a very long time ago that if you want a group of bodies in one rhythm, you have them sing.

Couples. Partners sitting quietly in the same room, not touching or speaking, show coupling of heart rate and respiration that strangers do not. In one notable experiment by Pavel Goldstein and colleagues, a woman received a painful heat stimulus while her partner either held her hand or sat by; with hand-holding, the coupling of their brain rhythms increased, and the more it increased, the less pain she reported.

Therapy. Several studies find that physiological concordance between therapist and client tracks the client's ratings of the therapist's empathy.

Speaker and listener. Uri Hasson's laboratory recorded brain activity from a woman telling an unrehearsed story and then from people listening to the recording. The listeners' brain activity mirrored the speaker's, with a delay — and the closer the coupling, the better they understood. In the listeners who understood best, some regions ran ahead of the speaker: anticipating.

The honest summary is this. In many settings, the physiological rhythms of people in interaction become coupled. The coupling is stronger between people who are bonded, is stronger at moments of real engagement, and is associated — in many but not all studies — with good outcomes: understanding, empathy, the easing of pain. The field has replication problems like every other; synchrony can be found in conflict as well as in concord; and the direction of causation is often unclear. But the base phenomenon is not in doubt. Bodies in relation do not keep their rhythms to themselves.

By what channel?

By what does one heart reach another across a room? This is the question on which the proposition and the sciences part company, and the file will state the divergence without softening it.

The proposition's implied answer is: directly, by a field — the heart's own, electromagnetic or luminous — radiating through space and received by the other heart.

The sciences' answer is: through the ordinary senses, which are far more capable than "ordinary" suggests. The fire-walker's relative sees the beloved face set itself at the edge of the coals, sees the first step, hears the crowd. Her nervous system, which holds a detailed model of this particular person built over years, runs that model at full power; her autonomic system follows. The lovers in the quiet room hear each other's breathing — without knowing that they hear it — and see the tiny movements that accompany it. The infant watches the mother's face at a distance at which every micro-expression is legible. No exotic channel is required. Light reflected from faces and sound from throats, falling on nervous systems tuned by attachment, are sufficient to carry the coupling.

The file accepts the sciences' answer as the best-supported one. But two things should be said about it, in fairness to the proposition.

First, the sciences' answer is already an answer in terms of light. The principal channel by which one person's state reaches another's heart across a room is the reflection of photons from a face. This is not what the proposition meant — it meant emission, not reflection — and the file will not pretend otherwise. But it is worth pausing over. A human face has more than forty muscles capable of producing thousands of configurations; the observer's visual system parses them in a fraction of a second; the result goes to the heart. When the corridor says she lit up the room, the physics of what occurred is that room light fell on a face which shaped it and sent it on, patterned, to eleven retinas. The face is a modulator of light. The proposition's phrase light becomes a photonic language is, read at this level, a sober description of how faces work.

Second, the sciences' answer explains the channel and leaves the selectivity as a wonder. Why were the unrelated spectators not entrained? They had the same photons. The answer — that only the related spectators had the internal model, the history, the stake — is correct, and what it says is that the receiver must be tuned. A signal crosses a room to everyone. It is received only by those in a particular relation to its source. The physicists have a word for a system that responds strongly to a signal at its own frequency and hardly at all to others. The word is resonance — and it is one of the three words on Davies's title page.

Resonance, strictly

Resonance has become a soft word. It should be a hard one.

Strike a tuning fork and hold it near a second fork of the same pitch: the second begins to sound. Hold it near a fork of a different pitch: nothing. The first fork radiates the same sound in both cases. The difference is entirely in the receiver — in whether its own natural frequency matches. A resonant system is one that can be driven to large response by a very small input of the right kind, and is deaf to everything else.

Four consequences for the proposition.

Small causes, large effects. The energy of a look is negligible. If rooms can be changed by looks — and they can — it is not because the look carries much energy but because it arrives at systems poised to respond to exactly that. The power is in the receiver. This will let the next chapter be honest about how weak the heart's physical field is without giving up the experience.

Specificity. Not everyone in a room receives what crosses it. Some are tuned and some are not; the same event is a blaze to one and nothing to their neighbour. This is not a failure of the phenomenon. It is the phenomenon.

The receiver is changed by sounding. A fork that has been set ringing is now itself a source. The related spectator's heart, entrained, alters her face, her breath, her grip on the arm of the person beside her. Reception becomes emission. Hold that thought for the chapter on wavefronts.

Tuning has a history. A fork is tuned at the foundry. A human being is tuned by having been loved. Feldman's longitudinal work indicates that infants who had more synchrony with their mothers become children, and then adults, with greater capacity for empathy and for synchrony with others. The capacity to receive what crosses a room was installed by its having once crossed a very small room, from one face to another, at a distance of about twenty centimetres.

The German sociologist Hartmut Rosa has built a whole theory of the good life on this word. Resonance, for Rosa, is a mode of relation to the world with four marks: one is affected — touched, called; one responds with one's own voice — he likes the etymology of e-motion, a moving-outward; both parties are transformed; and the whole thing is uncontrollable — it cannot be manufactured, guaranteed or stockpiled. Its opposite is alienation: a relation of relationlessness, in which the world is available, manageable, and mute. A resonant relation, he insists, is not an echo. An echo returns only one's own voice. Resonance requires that the other speak with a voice of its own.

Affection, outward movement, transformation, a responding other who remains other, a circuit that cannot be commanded: it is the torus again, and the contact boundary again, arrived at from sociology.

The organisational finding

What does all this say about a meeting? Something quite specific, which can be tested with equipment that now costs less than a team lunch.

In a room where the state the proposition describes is present, the autonomic rhythms of the people in it should be more coupled than in a room where it is absent — and the coupling should run along bonds: strongest between those who are, in the old plain word, for each other. A team in which no one's heart moves when another member steps onto the coals is not a team in any sense that matters, whatever the chart says. And the fire-walk gives a diagnostic of almost brutal simplicity. When a colleague is exposed — presenting to the board, receiving a hard verdict, delivering the bad account — WHO IN THE ROOM IS A RELATED SPECTATOR?

Whose pulse goes with theirs? And who is a visitor from out of town, watching a man walk on fire with the detached interest of a tourist?

That is a question about love, and it has a physiological answer.

THE SIGNAL REACHES EVERYONE. IT IS RECEIVED BY THE TUNED.

12What the Instruments Say

The proposition makes claims that touch physics. A work that calls itself experimental owes those claims a hearing at the bench, conducted without piety in either direction — neither the piety of the believer who wants the instruments to confirm the experience, nor the piety of the sceptic who wants the instruments to abolish it. This chapter is the ledger. It takes each physical clause and asks: what is measured, at what magnitude, and what follows?

"The energetic field extends beyond the human body"

The heart's magnetic field. It is real and it extends beyond the skin. It was first detected in 1963 by Gerhard Baule and Richard McFee, with two coils of two million turns each, set up in a field outside Syracuse to escape the electrical noise of the city. Routine measurement had to wait for the superconducting sensor, with which David Cohen and colleagues recorded clean magnetocardiograms inside a shielded room at MIT around 1970. Magnetocardiography is today an established, if specialised, clinical method.

Its magnitude: at the surface of the chest, the peak field of a healthy heart is of the order of fifty to a hundred picotesla. A picotesla is a millionth of a millionth of a tesla. For comparison: the Earth's magnetic field, in which every heart beats, is around fifty microtesla — about a million times stronger. The magnetic noise in an ordinary office, from wiring and lifts and passing traffic, exceeds the heart's field by several orders of magnitude; that is why Baule and McFee went out to a field and Cohen built a room of nested metal shells.

It is nonetheless true, and it is the fact from which the popular claim derives, that the heart's is the strongest rhythmic field the body makes: on the order of a hundred times stronger than the brain's, whose signals are measured in femtotesla.

Its reach: the field of a dipole falls away, at distances large compared with the source, as the cube of the distance. Double the distance and the field is an eighth. At a metre from the chest it is some hundreds of times weaker than at the chest wall — down among the femtotesla. Sensitive magnetometers in shielded conditions can still pick it up at a few tens of centimetres. So the statement "the heart's field can be detected several feet from the body" is defensible in the sense that an extraordinarily sensitive instrument in an extraordinarily quiet room can do it.

Can another human being detect it? There is no established mechanism by which they could, and no robust evidence that they do. Humans are not known to possess a magnetic sense of anything approaching the required sensitivity. One careful 2019 study reported that human brain rhythms respond to rotations of an Earth-strength field; that is a million-fold stronger stimulus, the finding awaits replication, and it concerned no conscious perception. The claims, associated chiefly with the HeartMath Institute, that one person's cardiac field registers in another's brain waves at conversational distance rest on small studies, largely unreplicated by independent groups, and are not accepted in mainstream physiology.

Verdict. The heart generates a field of toroidal geometry that extends beyond the body: true. That field is the carrier by which love crosses a room: unsupported, and — given a signal a million times below the ambient field and no known receptor — improbable. The file sets it down as it finds it.

"You become light-emitting"

Infrared. Every human being is, at every moment, emitting light — if "light" is allowed its full physical meaning of electromagnetic radiation. A body at skin temperature radiates in the far infrared, with a peak wavelength around nine or ten micrometres. The gross power is large, several hundred watts; because the surroundings radiate back, the net loss for a clothed person at rest indoors is of the order of a hundred watts. A thermal camera shows people as what, in that band, they are: lamps. And the glow is not uniform or constant. Blood flow to the face changes with emotional state; the thermal signature of a blush, or of the cooling of the nose under stress, is measurable at a distance.

So: you are already light-emitting, in a band your eyes cannot see, at about the power of an old-fashioned bulb, and the emission is modulated by what you feel. This is undergraduate physics. Whether human skin can sense another person's radiant heat across a room is a different matter; at arm's length, a warm body in a cool room can be felt, as anyone knows who has sat beside one. At five metres, no.

Visible light. Here the finding is stranger. In 2009 Masaki Kobayashi and colleagues placed volunteers in total darkness in front of a cryogenically cooled camera capable of registering single photons, and imaged them at intervals through the day. Their paper opens with a sentence one does not often meet in a scientific journal: "The human body literally glimmers." Living tissue emits visible light — ultraweak photon emission, a by-product of oxidative metabolism. The emission was strongest from the face. It followed a daily rhythm, low in the morning and peaking in the late afternoon. And its intensity, the authors report, is about a thousand times below what the naked eye can detect.

There is a fringe around this finding, associated with the German biophysicist Fritz-Albert Popp, which holds that these "biophotons" are coherent and constitute a signalling system between cells and perhaps between organisms. The emission is well established. The coherence and the signalling are not; the mainstream view is that this light is metabolic exhaust.

Verdict. The human body emits light, in the infrared powerfully and in the visible faintly; the face emits most; the emission varies with physiological state: true, and the word "literally" has a peer-reviewed warrant. That this emission increases in love so as to become perceptible, or carries meaning between persons: no evidence. The gap between what is emitted in the visible and what an eye could see is three orders of magnitude.

"In a super-luminous way"

If the word means faster than light, the verdict is short. Nothing that carries information travels faster than light in a vacuum. There are things in physics that outrun light in a carefully limited sense — the phase velocity of certain waves; the spot of a lighthouse beam sweeping a distant shore; the correlations between entangled particles — and in every case it has been shown that no signal, no energy, no message can be sent that way. A communicative field propagating faster than light would overturn relativity.

If the word means something else — beyond light and not faster — then it is not a claim in physics at all and the instruments have nothing to say. The file believes this is what the word means, and that it has an exact and ancient pedigree. That is for chapter fifteen.

Verdict. As physics: false. As a word reaching for something else: reserved.

"As a wavefront"

Unproblematic, and more interesting than it looks. Everything that actually carries one person's state to another across a room — light from the face, sound from the voice — is a wave, and propagates as a wavefront. The proposition's intuition that the thing has wave character is, at the level of its carriers, simply right. A whole chapter is reserved for what follows from it.

"Has real substance and you can feel it crossing the room"

Two claims. That one feels it cross: this is experiential report, and the file takes it as data of the first rank. It is, besides, very widely shared; it is the corridor's testimony. No instrument can contradict a report of experience; it can only bear on the interpretation.

That it has real substance: this depends on what "substance" is being asked to mean. If it means that a detectable quantity of matter or energy, specific to love, traverses the room — there is no evidence for that. If it means that what crosses is not nothing: not a projection, not a fancy, but something with causal power, which does work at the far end, which arrives whether or not it is expected, and which resists being redescribed as something else — then the evidence is abundant. The fire-walk is evidence. The pain eased by a held hand is evidence. The speaker's brain pattern reappearing in the listener's is evidence. What crosses a room when love is present changes heart rhythms at a distance, in the people tuned to receive it. That is real, and it is substantial in the sense that matters: it stands in being; it makes a difference.

The ledger, summed

Set out plainly:

That field carries love to othersNo receptor known; signal about a million times below ambientUnsupported

What follows

Two wrong conclusions are available.

The first is the debunker's: the heart's field is too weak, the biophotons too faint, therefore the proposition is an illusion and nothing crosses the room. But this confuses the refutation of a mechanism with the refutation of a phenomenon. The crossing is as well attested as anything in social physiology. What the bench has shown is only that it does not ride on the particular carriers the proposition's vocabulary suggested.

The second is the enthusiast's: the heart does have a field, the body does emit light, therefore the proposition is confirmed by science. But a field a million times below background and a glow a thousand times below vision do not confirm an experience of radiance filling a room. To quote the measurements without their magnitudes is to borrow the authority of physics while declining its discipline.

The file takes a third position and holds to it for the rest of the work. It is Wertheimer's.

THE CROSSING IS REAL. THE CARRIER IS ORDINARY. THE FORM IS NOT.

What travels across the room is light reflected from a face and sound shaped by a breath — the most ordinary physical carriers there are. What they carry is a form: a gestalt, a pattern of timing and attention and openness which is a whole and is received as a whole, by those who are tuned, and which re-forms the field they stand in. That the form is borne by ordinary photons no more makes it ordinary than the fact that a late quartet is borne by ordinary air. And when someone who has received it says that she radiated, that he glowed, that it came across like a wave — they are not reporting a magnetometer reading. They are reporting, with considerable accuracy, the structure of what happened: a source; an emanation; a propagation with a front; an arrival; and, at the arrival, the receiver becoming a source in turn.

The proposition asked to be filed as experiential. As experience, it stands. Its physics were always scaffolding around a perception, and the perception was sound.

There remains, however, a tradition that would not be content with that settlement — which insists, soberly and after centuries of dispute, that the light in question is neither a metaphor nor an electromagnetic wave, but a third thing, seen with bodily eyes by people in a particular state. Before that tradition is heard, the file must learn how its own civilisation once thought about light.

DO NOT QUOTE THE MEASUREMENT WITHOUT THE MAGNITUDE.
