Movement III

PHOS

Light

Before light was a wave it was the first form of everything. A bishop of Lincoln; a mountain in Galilee; a word that will not hold still; Huygens's principle as a theory of how love spreads; the face as modulator; and the laser, in which a crowd of independent emitters becomes one.

13Grosseteste's Light

Around the year 1225, a scholar of the young university at Oxford, a man of obscure Suffolk birth who would end his life as Bishop of Lincoln, wrote a treatise of a few pages called De Luce — On Light. Robert Grosseteste's little work has been called the only scientific cosmogony between the Timaeus and the eighteenth century. In the last decade it has been translated into mathematical form by a collaboration of medievalists and physicists at Durham, who put its propositions on a computer and found that, given its premises, it holds together.

Its interest for this file lies less in whether it is true than in what it lets us remember: that for most of the history of the West, light was not one physical phenomenon among others. It was the form of forms.

The argument of De Luce

Grosseteste begins with a problem. Matter, considered in itself, has no dimensions; form, considered in itself, has none either. How then is there extension — a world with size, spread out in three directions? Something must be capable, of its own nature, of extending itself.

That something, he says, is light. Light — lux — has a property nothing else has: it multiplies itself. From a single point it spreads instantly and equally in every direction, generating itself outward into a sphere of any size, unless something opaque stands in the way. It is not pushed. Self-diffusion is what light is.

So in the beginning, he proposes, there was a single point of light, bound up with first matter. Light did what light does: it multiplied itself, infinitely, in all directions at once, and in doing so drew matter out with it — stretching the dimensionless into dimension, to the limit at which matter could be rarefied no further. That limit is the outermost sphere. From it, light turns and radiates back inward — this returning light he calls lumen — compressing the matter within, and at successive stages of the inward journey the further spheres are formed, each less rarefied than the last, down to the dense and troubled sphere of the elements at the centre. The cosmos is one expansion and one return. A point that bursts; a boundary; a reflux toward the centre.

A modern reader thinks of the Big Bang, and the Durham team have been properly stern about the anachronism. The file notices a different resemblance. From a centre, outward to a limit, and back to the centre: Grosseteste's universe is breathing in the form of chapter nine.

Light as first form

What Grosseteste did with this was more than cosmogony. He drew from it a general philosophy of nature.

Light, he held, is the first corporeal form — the form by which a body is a body. Everything bodily is therefore, at root, a kind and degree of light. And every natural agent acts as light acts: by sending out from itself, in all directions, along straight lines, a likeness of itself. This he called the multiplication of species — "species" meaning not a class but an appearance, an emanated likeness. A fire multiplies its species: that is how it warms you at a distance. A colour multiplies its species: that is how you see it. Every agent is a little sun, continuously radiating its own form into the space around it; and what it means to be acted upon is to receive, and be assimilated by, the species of another.

His pupil in spirit, Roger Bacon, turned this into a programme: the science that studies how species multiply — optics, with its rays and reflections and refractions — is the key to all the others. Grosseteste had already said that the whole of natural philosophy cannot be known without lines, angles and figures. The mathematical physics of the seventeenth century had an ancestor in a bishop's meditation on light.

This is what the proposition's phrase photonic language would have meant to the thirteenth century, and they would not have found it odd. All action at a distance was photonic. Every thing was, by being what it was, speaking itself outward in a language of rays, and to be in the presence of a thing was to be bathed in its self-communication.

The light of the mind, the light of love

There was a second side to the medieval metaphysics of light, older than Grosseteste, to which he was heir: Augustine's doctrine of illumination. As the eye cannot see without the sun, so the mind cannot understand without an interior light, which is not itself any of the things understood but that in which they are understood. To know anything truly is to see it in a light one did not make.

And there was a third side, which Bonaventure, a generation after Grosseteste, developed in Paris: light as the most fitting bodily name for goodness, because of all bodily things it is the most self-giving. The scholastic axiom ran: bonum est diffusivum sui — the good is diffusive of itself. It pours out. It cannot keep itself to itself; to be good is to communicate goodness. The sun does not deliberate before it shines. Dionysius, the mysterious sixth-century writer on whom all the medievals drew, had made the comparison canonical: as the sun, by simply being what it is, sends its rays to everything able to receive them, so the Good, by simply being, extends goodness to all that is.

Put the three together — light as the self-multiplying first form; light as that in which the mind knows; light as the image of self-diffusing good — and one has the thought-world in which a sentence like the proposition's is not strange at all. Love is a state in which a field emanates from the heart as light. A scholar of 1250 would have replied: naturally. Love is the highest form of the good; the good is diffusive of itself; light is what self-diffusion looks like in bodies; therefore the lover shines. Dante, a century later, built the whole Paradiso on precisely this optics: the blessed appear as lights, they brighten as their love increases, and the pilgrim's ascent is a progressive strengthening of the eye to bear more radiance, until at the summit he looks into a point of light and sees, bound by love in one volume, all that is scattered through the universe as leaves. The poem's last line names what turns the sun and the other stars. It is not gravity.

What was lost and what was gained

Then light was secularised. Huygens made it a wave; Newton a stream of corpuscles; Maxwell an electromagnetic oscillation; Einstein and his successors a quantum field whose excitations are photons. Each step was a triumph, and each took light further from goodness and knowledge and nearer to being one phenomenon among others, with a speed, a spectrum and a set of equations.

The gain is beyond calculation. The loss is that we no longer have a way of saying, within our official picture of the world, what every language still says in its idioms: that understanding is illumination, that a face can be radiant, that a person can brighten a room, that some people are luminous and that we are enlightened by them. These have become, officially, metaphors — figures transferred from the real (physical) light to something that is not really light at all.

Grosseteste would have reversed the direction of the transfer. For him the light of a candle is the lowest and most external instance of something whose fuller instances are the light of the understanding and the light of love. The candle is the metaphor. The face is the thing.

The file does not ask the reader to return to the thirteenth century. It asks only that they notice which way their own assumption runs, and that it is an assumption. The proposition's language of light feels like a category mistake only to someone certain that the physicist's light is light in the proper sense and all other uses derivative. That certainty is about three hundred years old. The contrary view is about three thousand.

The organisational residue

A last observation before the file climbs a mountain.

Grosseteste's principle — every agent acts by multiplying its species, sending out its likeness in all directions — is, whatever its fate as physics, an excellent account of how persons act in organisations. A person in a role does not chiefly affect others by what they decide. They affect others by what they are, continuously, in every direction, whether they intend it or not. The anxious director multiplies anxiety. The contemptuous partner multiplies contempt — downward, through tiers of people who never met him and yet have, unmistakably, his manner with a junior. The species is received and re-radiated.

And the principle carries a corollary Grosseteste would have taken for granted: one cannot multiply a species one does not have. An agent can only radiate its own form. A leader cannot emanate trust while being suspicious, nor calm while being afraid, by any technique of communication whatever. What goes out is what is there. Communications departments exist, in large part, to manage the consequences of this law without acknowledging it.

It also has a hopeful form. If every agent radiates its form, then one person in the state the proposition describes is, simply by being in it, a source. They need no platform and no permission. The species multiplies itself. LIGHT DOES NOT ASK LEAVE TO SPREAD.

THE CANDLE IS THE METAPHOR. THE FACE IS THE THING.

14Tabor: The Light That Was Seen

On a hillside in Galilee which tradition identifies as Mount Tabor, three men — Peter, James and John — saw their teacher's face shine like the sun and his clothing become white as the light. So the Gospels. One of the three, John, is the disciple for whom Balthasar's community is named, and the author of the letter that says in its first chapter that God is light and in its fourth that God is love. The file has now arrived at the tradition that took that vision with complete seriousness as a datum about what human beings can become, and which argued out, over a thousand years, exactly what kind of light it was.

Symeon

Symeon the New Theologian was a Byzantine abbot who lived around the turn of the first millennium and who is one of only three people on whom the Orthodox Church has conferred the title "Theologian." He earned it by an insistence that scandalised his contemporaries: that the conscious experience of God as light is not a privilege of the apostolic age but the normal vocation of every Christian, and that someone who has not had it has no business teaching.

His own accounts, placed discreetly in the third person in some texts and blazingly in the first in his hymns, describe a young man at prayer who was suddenly flooded by a light that filled the room, so that he lost awareness of walls and roof and whether he was standing on the ground. Later visions were more interior: light in the heart, a light that is personal and speaks. He is emphatic that this is not imagination and not a figure of speech; equally emphatic that it is not sensible light of the lamp-and-sun kind. It is seen. It is not that.

Palamas

Three centuries on, the question was forced. The monks of Mount Athos practised a discipline they called hesychia, stillness: the continual repetition of a short prayer, with attention gathered — the phrase is theirs — in the heart, sometimes with a regulated breath and a bowed posture, the gaze toward the chest. Some of them reported that in this prayer they saw light, and they identified it with the light the apostles had seen on Tabor.

A learned Calabrian, Barlaam, heard of this and was appalled. God, he argued, is unknowable in essence; any light that is seen must be a created thing, a product of the imagination or the atmosphere; and men who sat staring at their own midriffs expecting to behold the uncreated were deluded. He called them omphalopsychoi — navel-souls.

The reply was written by Gregory Palamas, an Athonite monk and later Archbishop of Thessalonica, in a work called the Triads in Defence of the Holy Hesychasts. Its argument turned on a distinction with deep patristic roots. God's essence — what God is in himself — is and will forever remain beyond all participation and all knowledge. But God is not only essence. God also acts, shines, goes forth, and these goings-forth — Palamas called them the divine energies, energeiai, activities — are not created effects standing between God and us. They are God himself, as he gives himself to be shared. The light on Tabor was such an energy. It was uncreated. It was truly seen. And it is seen still.

Two features of the Palamite position bear directly on the proposition.

The light is seen with the body. Palamas would not say that the vision was purely intellectual. The apostles saw it with their eyes — but with eyes that had been changed, opened by the Spirit to perceive what was always there. On Tabor, the tradition says, it was not Christ who changed. He had always shone. It was the disciples whose eyes were for a moment made adequate. The hesychast likewise sees with the whole person, body included; that is why the body is given a posture and the prayer is brought down into the heart. Palamas defended the physical method against Barlaam's ridicule precisely because the human being is not a mind using a body but one thing, and it is the one thing that is to be illumined.

The one who sees becomes what he sees. The purpose of the vision is not information. It is theosis, deification — becoming by grace what God is by nature, as the Fathers put it with a boldness that still unnerves Western readers. The saint does not merely look at the light. The saint is penetrated by it and begins to shine with it. The Byzantine councils of 1341 and 1351 upheld Palamas. The Orthodox Church keeps his memory on the second Sunday of Lent, and regards this teaching as its own.

Energeia. The reader will have registered the word. The proposition speaks of an "energetic field"; Davies's entire book is called We Are Energy. The word they use is, by direct descent through Aristotle, the word Palamas used for the uncreated radiance. The Greek means being-at-work: the activity in which a thing is fully what it is. Before energy was a quantity conserved in physical systems — a meaning it acquired in the nineteenth century — it was the shining-forth of a nature in act. When the proposition calls love an energetic state it is using the word, knowingly or not, in the older sense, and in that sense there is nothing figurative about it.

Motovilov's snow

The most circumstantial account in the whole tradition is modern. It comes from the notes of Nikolai Motovilov, a provincial Russian landowner, describing a conversation with the hermit Seraphim of Sarov on an overcast morning in November 1831, in a forest clearing, in the snow.

Motovilov had asked how one could know that one was in the Spirit. Seraphim, having explained at length, took him by the shoulders and said: we are both in the Spirit now; why do you not look at me? Motovilov answered that he could not look, because lightning was flashing from the old man's eyes, his face had become brighter than the sun, and it hurt to see it. Seraphim replied: do not be afraid; you have become as bright as I am, or you could not see me so.

Motovilov's description of what he then saw is exact. Imagine, he says, in the centre of the sun, in the dazzling brilliance of its midday rays, the face of the man who is talking to you. You see the movement of his lips and the changing expression of his eyes; you hear his voice; you feel that someone is holding your shoulders. Yet you do not see his hands, nor yourself, nor his body — only a blinding light spreading for several yards around and lighting up the snow on the clearing and the snowflakes falling on both of them.

Seraphim then questioned him like a physician. What do you feel? — An extraordinary quiet and peace. — What else? — Sweetness. — What else? — Joy. — What else? — Warmth. — How warmth? It is late November; there is snow under our feet and on our heads. — Warmth as in a bath-house. — And the smell? — A fragrance like nothing on earth.

Calm, sweetness, joy, warmth without external cause, in a man who could report the time of year and the snow on his shoulders. Lay it beside Rolle with his hand on his chest: calor, dulcor. Lay it beside Pascal: certainty, joy, peace. The depositions concur across five centuries, three languages and the breach between the Eastern and Western churches.

And note the sentence that has no parallel in the Western witnesses: you have become as bright as I am, or you could not see me so. Here is resonance stated as a law of spiritual optics. The light is visible only to one who is, at that moment, emitting it. The tuned fork again. The proposition's you become light-emitting is not, in this tradition, the exotic climax of the experience. It is the condition of having the experience at all.

What the file may and may not conclude

The file is not in a position to say what Motovilov saw. A sceptic has explanations to hand — suggestion, the effect of sun breaking on snow, the writing-up of a memory by a devout and excitable man many years afterwards. The manuscript surfaced only at the beginning of the twentieth century. These cautions are legitimate.

What the file may say is this. There exists a disciplined tradition — not a scatter of enthusiasts but a church, with councils — that has maintained for at least a millennium, against powerful internal opposition and with full awareness of the alternatives, the following: that there is a light which is neither metaphorical nor the light of physics; that it is seen by human beings with their bodily eyes when those eyes have been made able; that it is associated with a prayer deliberately located in the heart; that those who see it become radiant with it; that it is perceived by others who are in the same state; and that it is love — for the same tradition, reading its patron evangelist, never separated the light from the charity.

The proposition, written by someone without a steady language, in the vocabulary of fields and photons that the twentieth century leaves lying about, says the same seven things. The file's ledger in chapter twelve showed that the proposition's physics could not carry its experience. The hesychasts would not have been surprised. They never thought the light was electromagnetic. They thought the experience was true and that it needed a third category — uncreated energy — because neither "symbol" nor "physical light" would do. That third category is not available to a file that has undertaken to stay with what can be argued and tried. But it is on the table, it has a pedigree, and it is the nearest thing in the record to what the proposition's author is reaching for.

Transfiguration as an organisational category

One last move, to bring the mountain down to the meeting.

The event on Tabor is called, in Greek, metamorphosis: a change of form. Nothing was added to the figure the disciples had been walking with for three years. What changed was that what he was became visible — the form became transparent to its own depth. It is Balthasar's doctrine exactly: Gestalt, and through it, Glanz.

There is an ordinary version of this, and everyone has seen it. A colleague one has worked beside for years, competent and unremarkable, is at some moment — speaking of the thing they care most about; defending someone who cannot defend themselves; simply doing, with complete absorption, what they are best at — transfigured. One sees, for an instant, who they are. They have not changed. They have become visible. And those who see it do not afterwards see that person the same way; nor are they, themselves, quite the same.

Organisations have no name for these moments and no place to keep them, but they are remembered longer than any strategy. An institution's real history — the one told at leaving parties — is a sequence of transfigurations: that was the day we saw what she was made of. And an institution's health might be gauged by a question no survey asks: HOW OFTEN, HERE, DOES SOMEONE BECOME VISIBLE?

For visibility of that kind has conditions, and they are the conditions this work has been assembling. It requires a round life space, for no one is transfigured in a combat landscape; the form stays hidden behind the position. It requires contact at a boundary. And it requires a beholder who is, at that moment, capable of seeing — which means, on Seraphim's law, a beholder who is in some measure shining too.

HE HAD ALWAYS SHONE. IT WAS THEIR EYES THAT CHANGED.

15Super-Luminous: On a Word That Will Not Hold Still

The proposition says the field extends beyond the body "in a super-luminous way." The ledger has already disposed of one reading. If the word is the physicist's superluminal, faster than light, the claim is false, and no amount of goodwill can make it otherwise.

But the proposition does not say superluminal. It says super-luminous, with a hyphen, and the hyphen opens onto one of the strangest and most consequential passages in the whole of Western spiritual writing. The author of the proposition says they have no steady language. In this instance they reached, without knowing it, for a word that is fifteen hundred years old.

The word in Greek

At some time around the year 500, probably in Syria, an unknown writer composed a small body of treatises and issued them under the name of Dionysius, the Athenian whom Paul converted on the Areopagus. The pseudonym held for a thousand years and gave these works an authority second only to Scripture. The shortest of them, the Mystical Theology, is barely five pages long, and it opens with a prayer that the Trinity would lead us up to the highest peak of the mystical oracles —

where, in the Victorian translation of John Parker, the mysteries of theology "lie hidden within the super-luminous gloom of the silence."

The Greek is hyperphōtos gnophos. Gnophos is darkness, the thick cloud into which Moses went on Sinai. Hyperphōtos is a word Dionysius seems to have made for the occasion: hyper, over, beyond, above — and phōs, light. Beyond-light. Over-light. In Latin, superlucens; in English, from the first translators onward, super-luminous. Dionysius's prose is thick with such coinages; the prefix hyper occurs in his few hundred pages with an insistence no translation can reproduce. God is not good but hyper-good, not being but hyper-being, not divine but hyper-divine. It is not hyperbole. It is a method.

What the prefix does

The method is this. Every name we give to the highest reality is taken from created things, and is therefore both true and false: true, because the creature really does reflect its source; false, because the source infinitely exceeds the reflection. So theology proceeds in three movements. First, affirmation: God is light. Then negation: God is not light — not the light we know, not any light we can conceive. And then a third movement, which is not a return to the first and not a resting in the second, and for which the Greek has only the prefix: God is hyper-light. The negation was not because the name said too much. It was because it said too little.

Hence the paradox on which the Mystical Theology opens. The super-luminous is a darkness — a gloom, a cloud. Not because light is absent but because it is present in an excess the eye cannot register. One who looks at the sun sees a black disc. The darkness on the mountain is, in Dionysius's phrase, a darkness that outshines all brilliance; the seventeenth-century poet Henry Vaughan, who had read him, wrote of a deep but dazzling darkness in God. Super-luminous means: more than light, in the direction of light, to the point where "light" fails as a description and its opposite becomes the nearer word.

This is the lineage in which Symeon and Palamas stand. When they insisted that the light of Tabor was truly seen and yet was not sensible light, they were not being evasive. They were using the third movement. It is light — affirmation. It is not what a lamp gives — negation. It is beyond-light, of which lamplight is the faint and outermost echo.

The proposition, re-read

Read with this key, the hardest sentence in the proposition comes clear, and — the file thinks — comes right.

The field extends beyond the human body in a super-luminous way. Not: faster than light. But: in a manner for which "light" is the nearest available word and is not enough. The author felt something cross a room. The only category to hand for what radiates from a source, travels across space, arrives, and illumines, was light. And at the same time the author knew that it was not the light that comes through the window — it was warmer than that, it carried meaning, it was personal, it knew one. So the word was reached for and overreached in the same breath: luminous, and beyond-luminous.

That is exactly Dionysius's procedure, performed without the training, by someone trying to tell the truth about an experience. And the file's own ledger performed the middle movement. Chapter twelve was the negation: it is not light — not electromagnetic, not biophotonic, not at any magnitude an eye could catch. The debunker stops there. But negation is the second movement, not the last. The experience that survives the negation is not thereby shown to be nothing. It is shown to have been under-described by the affirmation.

So the file proposes a repair to the proposition's language, and it is the smallest repair possible. Keep the word. Keep the hyphen. Understand the prefix as Dionysius understood it. LOVE IS NOT FASTER THAN LIGHT. IT IS MORE THAN LIGHT, IN THE SAME DIRECTION.

The dazzling dark, at work

Does a sixth-century apophatic prefix have any purchase on an organisation? It has more than might be thought, because it names something every person who has been truly met has experienced and could not account for.

The experience of being loved — the real thing, in the Overture's sense — is not an experience of being shown something. Nothing in particular is illuminated. The woman's look conveyed no information; if the man had been asked what he had learned from it he could have named nothing. And yet he could suddenly see: his own situation, what he needed to say, the faces round the table as faces. The light was not on any object. It was that by which objects became visible. This is Augustine's illumination, and it is why being-loved is so hard to report: one reports the things one sees by a light, never the light.

There is a corresponding organisational phenomenon which the literature has circled without landing on. The best leaders are, very often, hard to describe. Ask their people what exactly this person does, and the answers are thin — "she listens," "he's just straight with you," "you feel you can do anything" — and wholly inadequate to the magnitude of the effect. Ask the same people to describe a merely charismatic leader and the answers are vivid: the speeches, the presence, the lines one remembers. The charismatic leader is luminous: he is an object one sees, brilliantly lit. The other kind is super-luminous: one does not so much see her as see by her. She is dark with excess of bright; attention passes through her to the work, to one another, to oneself. The Chinese tradition has a phrase for it — 和光同塵, hé guāng tóng chén: to soften one's glare and merge with the dust — and the Dao De Jing says of the best rulers that when their work is done the people say, we did it ourselves.

This gives the file a first diagnostic for the movement on counterfeits. If, in a person's presence, one's attention is drawn to that person — to their brilliance, their warmth, their specialness — one is in the presence of something luminous, and should be on guard. If, in a person's presence, one finds one can see everything else more clearly, and afterwards has trouble recalling what they did, one has probably met the real thing.

A caution about the caution

The file has been stern with physics and is about to be generous with apophatic theology, and the reader is entitled to ask whether a thumb is on the scale. Is "beyond-light" simply an unfalsifiable retreat — a way of saving the proposition from the magnetometer by removing it to a place where no instrument can follow?

The danger is real. A claim that is true "in a higher sense" whenever it is false in the ordinary one is not a claim. So let the file say what would count against the reading given here. It would count against it if the experience the proposition reports had no stable structure — if those who claim it described it in ways that had nothing in common. It has a structure, and chapters ten and fourteen set the depositions side by side. It would count against it if the experience had no effects in the ordinary world, checkable by ordinary means. It has effects: chapter eleven measured some, and the movement on the organisation will measure others. And it would count against it if the "more than light" turned out to be distinguishable from less than light — from mere warm feeling, suggestion, the glow of being liked — by nothing at all. That last test is the serious one. The whole of the sixth movement is given to it, for the tradition that speaks of super-luminous darkness also warns, in a sentence of Paul's, that the adversary himself is transformed into an angel of light.

THE NEGATION WAS NOT BECAUSE THE WORD SAID TOO MUCH. IT SAID TOO LITTLE.

16Wavefront: How Love Spreads

As a wavefront. Of all the proposition's physical words this is the one the ledger passed without objection, since everything that does carry a person's state across a room is a wave. But the word deserves more than a pass. A wavefront is a very particular kind of thing, and a great deal follows from saying that love propagates as one and not as, say, a transfer of parcels.

Christiaan Huygens, twice

In 1678 the Dutch polymath Christiaan Huygens presented to the Académie in Paris a theory of light, published twelve years later as the Traité de la Lumière. Light, he proposed, is not a stream of particles shot from the source. It is a disturbance spreading through a medium, as rings spread on a pond. And he gave a principle for how the spreading works, which still carries his name and is still taught in the first year of every physics course.

Every point on a wavefront is itself the source of a new spherical wavelet. The wavefront a moment later is the common surface — the envelope — of all those wavelets.

Consider what this says. The original source emits once. After that it is, in a sense, out of the picture. The wave goes forward not because the source keeps pushing but because each point the wave reaches becomes a source in its turn. The front advances by continual re-emission. A wave is a relay in which every runner is also a starter.

Thirteen years earlier, ill in bed in The Hague, the same man had noticed something else. He had hung two of his new pendulum clocks from a common wooden beam, and he observed that within half an hour, however he started them, the two pendulums fell into exact opposite swing and stayed so. He disturbed them; they returned. He called it, in a letter to his father, an odd kind of sympathy. He correctly guessed the cause: imperceptible movements of the beam, by which each clock infinitesimally nudged the other. It was the first recorded observation of the spontaneous synchronisation of coupled oscillators, and the file will come back to it under the heading of complexity. For now it is enough to note that the man who gave us the wavefront also gave us sympathy between clocks — and that he found the second lying in bed, watching.

The four properties of a wave

Take Huygens's principle and the general physics of waves, and set them against the alternative picture of how something spreads between people: the parcel model. On the parcel model, influence is a thing that A has and gives to B — a quantity of motivation, a dose of confidence, a piece of information. A has less; B has more; the parcel has moved. Most of what organisations do in the name of communication, engagement and culture assumes parcels. The proposition says: wave. The differences are four.

A wave moves through a medium without carrying the medium with it. When a ring spreads on a pond, the water does not travel outward; a cork on the surface bobs up and down and stays where it is. What travels is the form. This is Wertheimer's point again, from physics: the crossing is real and no stuff makes the journey. Love that propagates as a wave does not deplete its source by propagating — the source has not shipped anything. This is the fundamental reason the "energy" of love does not obey the arithmetic of a budget, in which what I give you I no longer have. A form is not used up by being transmitted. A flame is not diminished by lighting another.

Each point reached becomes a source. This is Huygens's principle proper and it is the heart of the matter. On the parcel model, the recipient is a terminus: the parcel arrives and the transaction is closed. On the wave model, there are no termini. To receive the wave is to re-emit it. The man in the Overture, having been met, said the true thing; and his saying it was a new wavelet, which reached the finance director, who had been sitting on a doubt of her own, and who now voiced it. Nobody "cascaded" anything. Each person the front reached became a point of emission, and the front went on.

It follows that the reach of love in an organisation has almost nothing to do with the power of the original source and almost everything to do with whether the points it reaches re-emit. One absorber — one person who receives and does not pass on — is of no account; the front heals round a small obstacle, as waves do. A layer of absorbers stops it dead. This is why love so often fails to cross a level of hierarchy: the board is warm with one another and with the executive; the executive is warm with their own reports; and then, somewhere about two levels down, there is a stratum of managers who receive what comes from above and transmit downward only its content, without its form. Below that stratum the organisation is in shadow, and the people at the top, bathed in what they themselves emit, cannot understand why the survey scores are what they are.

Waves superpose. Two parcels arriving at once make two parcels. Two waves arriving at once add — and how they add depends on their timing. Crest on crest, they reinforce: the result is not double but, in terms of energy, fourfold. Crest on trough, they cancel: two real waves, and flat water. This is interference, and it has no analogue in the world of parcels.

It explains two of the commonest puzzles of organisational life. The first: why a group of individually warm, decent people can make a cold room. They are all emitting; they are out of phase; each one's gesture arrives as the other's is withdrawn; the sum is nil. The second: why, on certain rare occasions, a group catches fire in a way no one member could account for. They have fallen into phase. Nothing was added. The same amplitudes, differently timed. COHERENCE IS NOT MORE ENERGY. IT IS THE SAME ENERGY IN STEP. The chapter after next is about what that looks like when it is pushed to the limit.

A wavefront has a shape, and the shape depends on the sources. A single point source gives an expanding sphere, weakening as it goes: the intensity falls with the square of the distance. But many sources, emitting in step along a line, combine into a plane wave that travels a great distance without spreading. One loving person in an organisation is a point source: vivid nearby, faint at thirty metres, gone by the next floor. A community of them, in phase, is a different object in kind. It does not fade with distance in the same way. It can cross a whole institution. And since by Huygens's principle every point reached is a new source, a front that starts from one person can become a plane wave, if enough of those it reaches re-emit in step. That transition — from a point that radiates to a front that travels — is, the file suggests, the difference between a good manager and a culture.

Ripples

The file is not the first to describe moral action in an organisation or a society as a matter of wavelets and their envelope. Among the three books laid on this file after its drafting had begun — volumes in a De Gruyter series on the transformation of leadership, of which more in the fifth movement — is Aidan McQuade's Ethical Leadership: Moral Decision-making Under Pressure. McQuade spent years as the director of Anti-Slavery International, and before that in humanitarian operations in places where the room had a front in Lewin's most literal sense. He opens his book with a passage from the speech Robert Kennedy gave in Cape Town in 1966: that each time someone stands up for an ideal they send out a tiny ripple of hope, and that these ripples, crossing one another from a million different centres of energy and daring, build a current that can sweep down the mightiest walls.

It is Huygens's principle as political ethics, and Kennedy's physics is sound. A million different centres: every point a source. Crossing each other: superposition. Build a current: constructive interference, the envelope of the wavelets becoming a front. McQuade's whole book is, in a sense, an inquiry into the one question the principle leaves open — what determines whether a given person, at the moment the front reaches them, re-emits or absorbs. The social psychologists he reviews, Milgram and Zimbardo and Darley and Latané, give the sobering base rate: most people, most of the time, conform to what those around them are doing. They absorb. His interest is in the minority who do not, and in the inner structure of the moment at which they decide. The file will take up his account of that structure — a figure he calls the Cruciform of Agency — when it comes to love and judgement. Here it wants only his starting point, which is also the proposition's: that the unit of moral change is not the programme. It is the wavelet.

Diffraction, or how love gets round corners

One last property of waves, with an odd dignity.

A stream of particles, meeting a wall with a gap in it, passes through the gap in a straight beam and leaves a sharp shadow. A wave does not. A wave, passing through an opening, spreads out again on the far side, bending into the region that geometry says should be dark. Each point in the gap is a Huygens source, and it radiates in all directions, including sideways. This is diffraction. It is why one can hear a voice round a corner.

Organisations are full of walls: between functions, between sites, between the firm and its contractors, between those inside the meeting and those outside it. The parcel model says that what passes a wall is exactly what is sent through the door, in a straight line, to the addressee. The wave model says that anything which gets through an opening at all will spread on the far side into places it was never sent. One person who carries the form through the gap — one transferred manager, one secondee, one member of the closed meeting who walks out of it the same person who walked in — is a new source on the far side, radiating in every direction.

The practical corollary is one of the most hopeful in the whole work, and experienced reformers of institutions know it. One does not need to take down the walls. One needs a gap, and someone standing in it.

NO ONE IS A TERMINUS. TO RECEIVE IS TO RE-EMIT.

17Photonic Language: The Face

Light becomes a photonic language. The ledger found a sober sense in which this is true: the principal carrier of one person's state to another, across a room, is light reflected from a face, and a face is a modulator of light of extraordinary bandwidth. This chapter takes that sober sense and asks how far down it goes.

What a face does to light

The human face is, by a wide margin, the most finely controllable surface in nature. Some twenty pairs of muscles, uniquely attached to skin and not to bone, can produce thousands of visibly distinct configurations; the anatomist's coding system needs forty-odd elementary "action units" to describe them, and they combine. Changes in blood flow alter the colour and — in the infrared — the temperature of particular regions within seconds. The eyes add a second instrument: the whites of human eyes are far more exposed than those of any other primate, so that the direction of a human gaze can be read across a room, and the pupil dilates and contracts with arousal and interest in a way an observer registers without knowing that they do.

On the receiving side there is dedicated machinery. A region of the temporal lobe responds selectively to faces. Newborn infants, minutes old, turn preferentially toward face-like patterns. Expressions shown for a few hundredths of a second — too briefly to be consciously seen — produce measurable changes in the viewer's own facial muscles, skin conductance and heart rate. One's body has answered a face before one knows there was a face to answer.

So the phrase photonic language is less fanciful than it sounds. There is a code; there is a transmitter of high resolution; there is a receiver specialised for the code, operating largely beneath awareness and wired to the heart. The medium is visible light. The room is full of it. And the "language" is not mainly about propositions. What a face says, continuously, is what the file earlier called readiness: open or guarded, approaching or withdrawing, with you or against you or absent.

Duchenne's distinction

In the 1860s the French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne, stimulating the facial muscles of his patients with electrodes and photographing the results, made a discovery about the smile. The mouth is drawn up by a muscle one can contract at will. But a smile of real enjoyment also involves the muscle that rings the eye, lifting the cheek and gathering the skin at the outer corner — and this, Duchenne found, most people cannot contract on demand. It obeys, he wrote, only the sweet emotions of the soul. Its inertness in a smile unmasks a false friend.

The detail has been refined since — some people can produce the eye movement voluntarily, and context matters a great deal. But the core finding has lasted a century and a half and it is of the first importance for this file. The photonic language has a grammar that is hard to counterfeit. Its truest marks are precisely those not under voluntary command: the muscle round the eye, the timing of onset and fading, the pupil, the colour of the skin. One can decide to smile. One cannot, by deciding, produce the form.

This is the physiological root of the corridor's infallibility. When an organisation performs the behaviours of care without the thing — chapter one's fruit and wellbeing weeks — people do not need to reason their way to the conclusion that it is hollow. They see it, in a hundred faces arranged from the mouth down. And it is the root of Grosseteste's corollary, that an agent can multiply only the species it has. What the face transmits is not what its owner intends to convey. It is what is the case.

Levinas: the face as command

Thus far the face has been treated as a signal. There is a philosophical tradition that says this is already to have missed it.

Emmanuel Levinas — a Lithuanian Jew, a prisoner of war whose family was murdered — spent his life arguing that the encounter with another person's face is not a species of perception at all. To perceive is to take the thing in, to make it mine, to fit it to my categories. The face resists this. It presents itself as that which I cannot possess: as an other who looks back, who exceeds whatever I make of them, and who by sheer presence addresses me. The first thing the face says, Levinas insists, is a prohibition — you shall not kill — and an appeal. Before I have chosen anything, I have been made responsible.

Two points from this difficult thinker belong in the file.

First, the face speaks. Levinas is emphatic that the relation to the face is discourse, not vision. This is the strong sense of "photonic language": not that light carries data about someone's mood, but that in the light from a face one is spoken to, and the address is prior to anything said.

Second, the face signifies from height and from destitution at once. The other is above me — I am answerable — and is naked, exposed, in need. Recall Köhler's conductor, on which the charge crowds at the points. The one giving the bad account in the Overture's meeting was, at that moment, pure face in Levinas's sense: exposed, and by his exposure commanding. Ten people managed not to hear the command. One did.

Marion: the look that crosses

Levinas's pupil Jean-Luc Marion carried the analysis into love, in a book called The Erotic Phenomenon. Its argument starts from a displacement of Descartes. The question that really grips a human being, Marion says, is not am I certain? but does anyone love me? Certainty about my own existence is cold comfort if that existence is of no account to anyone. And the question cannot be answered from within. It can be met only by a reversal: I must cease asking whether I am loved and ask instead can I love first? — make the advance without guarantee of return.

What then occurs between lovers Marion describes in terms of crossed gazes. I do not see the other's gaze, as I see an object; the pupil of an eye is the one place on a face where there is, strictly, nothing to see — a small black emptiness. I feel it resting on me. And the other feels mine. Two aims cross in a space neither occupies, and each receives itself from the other's regard. The phenomenon of love is this crossing: it belongs to neither and is given to both.

Marion's name for phenomena of this kind is saturated. Kant had taught that experience is the meeting of intuition — what is given — with a concept that masters it. In ordinary experience the concept is adequate, or more than adequate. But there are phenomena, Marion argues, in which intuition overflows every concept: there is more given than can be thought, and the mind is dazzled. He means the word precisely. A saturated phenomenon bedazzles as too much light bedazzles the eye. One does not constitute it. One is constituted by it — as its witness.

This is hyperphōtos transposed into phenomenology, and it is as near as contemporary philosophy comes to stating the proposition's fifth claim in an idiom a seminar room will accept. What crosses the room in love is a saturated phenomenon: given directly, in excess of what the receiver can conceptualise, experienced as a kind of light because of the excess, and constituting the receiver as one who has been met.

The first face

Now Balthasar's image can be given its full weight.

The newborn's eyes focus best at about the distance from the breast to the mother's face. For weeks the infant gazes at that face, which gazes back, and smiles, and speaks, and waits. Then, at around six weeks, the infant smiles in return.

Balthasar's claim is that this is the event by which a human being becomes a subject at all. The "I" does not awaken by reflecting upon itself. It is awakened from outside, by a "Thou" — by love directed at it, in a face. And what the child takes in, in that first exchange, is not a fact among facts but the shape of reality as such: that it is welcomed; that being is not a bare thereness but a being-given; that there is another, that the other is good, and that the child, as the one smiled at, is good too. Everything the scholastics distinguished as the transcendentals — that being is one, true, good and beautiful — arrives in a single undivided moment, he says, in the light of a face.

The developmental psychologists say something close to this, in their own idiom. The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott asked what the baby sees when it looks at the mother's face, and answered: itself. The mother is looking at the baby, and what she looks like is related to what she sees there. The infant learns what it is by reading it in the face that beholds it. And the psychologist Edward Tronick showed what happens when the photonic language is switched off. In his "still face" procedure a mother, after some minutes of ordinary play, is asked to keep looking at her infant with a face that is entirely unresponsive. Within seconds the infant registers that something is wrong. It smiles, points, vocalises — it works to bring her back. When that fails, it turns away, slumps, and dissolves into distress. The episode lasts two minutes. It is painful to watch on film, and the mother is always permitted to repair it.

Tronick's finding about ordinary life is as important as the experiment. Even in good-enough pairs, mother and infant are in matched, coordinated states only about a third of the time. The rest is mismatch and repair. What predicts a child's security is not the absence of mismatch. It is the reliability of repair.

The still-faced organisation

This matters for organisations at once.

A great many of them present to the people who work in them a still face. Not hostile: unresponsive. One speaks, and nothing in the institutional countenance moves. The suggestion is logged. The grievance enters a process. The appraisal is delivered from a form by a manager whose face has been schooled to give nothing away. The all-hands message arrives in prose from which every mark of a particular human being addressing particular others has been removed by three rounds of review.

People in such organisations go through Tronick's sequence, on a timescale of months instead of seconds. First they work to elicit a response: they volunteer, propose, raise matters, perform. When that fails they protest — or, more often, the protest takes the retroflected forms of cynicism and gossip. And at last they turn away: they are present in body, they do what is asked, and they have withdrawn the thing the organisation most needed and did not know how to ask for. The engagement literature calls this disengagement and treats it as a deficit in the employee. On Tronick's film it is perfectly clear in whom the deficit first arose.

And the remedy the film shows is the remedy here. The infant does not need the mother's face to be perfectly attuned. It needs her to come back. An organisation need not be continuously warm — a thing which, attempted, produces only the fixed smile of the counterfeit. It needs to be capable of repair: when it has gone still on someone, to return, visibly, in a face, and to say what happened. THE MEASURE OF A LOVING INSTITUTION IS NOT THE RATE OF MISMATCH. IT IS THE RELIABILITY OF REPAIR.

One of the three books lately laid on the file sharpens this. Kirstie Papworth, in Compassionate Leadership, builds her model of compassion on four steps — awareness, feeling, appraisal, responding — and she is careful to choose the word awareness over noticing. Noticing is the registering of what has caught one's attention. Awareness is a standing alertness to oneself, to others and to nuance, which takes in what she calls the white space: what is unarticulated, absent, not yet observable. She observes that one need not behave with malice to harm someone; sometimes not noticing their suffering is enough; and that for a person in pain, being seen and heard is very often itself the most influential response. That is the still face and its repair, set down by a practitioner for leaders. The first act of compassion is a face that moves.

WHAT THE FACE TRANSMITS IS NOT WHAT ITS OWNER INTENDS. IT IS WHAT IS THE CASE.

18Becoming Light-Emitting: The Laser and the Saint

You become light-emitting. The ledger granted this in two senses the proposition did not intend — everyone glows in the infrared, and faintly in the visible — and denied it in the sense intended. The tradition of Tabor affirmed it in a third sense which the file cannot test. This chapter adds a fourth, and it is the one the file can stand behind without reserve. It comes from the physics of the only device human beings have ever built whose entire purpose is to become light-emitting in a new way.

What a lamp does

Consider an ordinary source of light: a filament, a gas tube, a candle. It contains an immense number of atoms. Energy is fed in — heat, a current — and lifts electrons in the atoms into excited states. An excited atom sooner or later drops back, and in dropping it emits a little wave-train of light.

Each atom does this on its own, at a moment of its own, in a direction of its own, with a phase bearing no relation to its neighbours'. The light of a lamp is therefore a vast superposition of unrelated wavelets: every direction, a spread of colours, the crests of one arriving at random against the troughs of another. Physicists call such light incoherent. It is, quite strictly, noise — optical noise. It spreads in all directions and weakens with the square of the distance. It can warm a room. It cannot be made to do anything precise.

What a laser does

Now arrange the same kind of atoms differently. Place them between two mirrors facing one another, so that light emitted along the axis is sent back through the atoms again and again. And keep feeding energy in.

At low rates of feeding, nothing remarkable occurs. The atoms emit at random; the device is a rather poor lamp.

But there is a second way an excited atom can emit. If a light wave of the right frequency passes an atom that is already excited, it can induce the atom to drop — and the wave the atom then gives out is an exact copy of the wave that induced it: the same frequency, the same direction, the same phase, crest on crest. Einstein predicted this in 1917 and called it stimulated emission. The passing wave is not absorbed. It is doubled.

So between the mirrors there is a competition. Many possible waves are present, each recruiting excited atoms to itself by stimulation, each leaking away at the mirrors. As the feeding is increased, a point arrives — a sharp, definite threshold — at which one wave begins to recruit faster than it leaks. It grows. Growing, it recruits faster still. In an instant it has captured essentially all the excited atoms; the other waves, starved, die. Every atom is now emitting in step with every other, into a single wave of extraordinary purity.

The light that emerges is coherent. It is one colour. It travels as a beam that hardly spreads: laser light sent to the Moon returns from reflectors left there by astronauts. It can be focused to a point fine enough to weld a retina. And — this is the fact the file wants above all — no additional energy was required. Just below threshold and just above it, the power fed in is almost the same. The difference is not in how much the atoms emit. It is that they have stopped emitting separately.

Haken's reading

In the 1960s the German physicist Hermann Haken worked out the theory of that threshold, and saw in it something much larger than a result about lasers. Here was matter passing, by itself, from disorder to order — not by being cooled into a crystal but by being driven, by a through-flow of energy, far from equilibrium. No one tells the atoms what to do. No atom is in charge. Yet above threshold they act as one. He called the general study of such transitions synergetics — the science of working together — and he took the laser as its paradigm case.

His analysis introduced two ideas that will be developed in the next movement and should be met here, at their source.

The first is the order parameter. Above threshold, one need not follow each of the billions of atoms. The state of the whole is captured by a single quantity — the amplitude of the winning wave. Know that, and one knows what every atom is doing.

The second he called, in an unlovely word, the slaving principle: the order parameter "enslaves" the individual atoms, which fall in with it. But he at once added that the wave is nothing other than the atoms' own combined emission. The atoms generate the wave; the wave orders the atoms. Neither comes first. Haken's term for this was circular causality, and it is the precise point at which a whole and its parts stop being separable into cause and effect.

The fourth sense

Now the proposition. You become light-emitting.

Think of a human being as a great population of emitters: every gesture, word, glance, hesitation, tone and act is a small wave-train sent into the shared field. In most of us, most of the time, these are incoherent. The mouth says welcome and the shoulders say go away. Monday's decision contradicts Friday's speech. One is kind to this person and cutting to that, generous in public and mean in private, for one's stated values on the slide and for one's interests in the vote. Each emission is real. They do not add. To those nearby the result is what a lamp's output is to a physicist: warmth, perhaps, and noise. Nothing that carries, nothing that could be focused to a point.

The saints, and the people the corridor calls luminous, are not people who emit more. They are often quiet, even plain. They are people in whom the emitters have fallen into phase. Word and face and act and absence say one thing. The scholastic name for this was simplicity — not naivety but being un-folded, one-fold. Kierkegaard's was purity of heart, which he defined as to will one thing. The Hebrew is lev shalem, a whole heart; the Sermon on the Mount speaks of the single eye by which the whole body is full of light. The plain modern word is integrity, and its root is the integer: the undivided.

A person in that condition is coherent in the physicist's sense, and has a laser's properties. What they emit carries: a few words from such a person travel across an organisation, and across decades, without spreading into vagueness. It focuses: their attention, resting on one, is felt as a point of extraordinary intensity, because all of it is there. And it recruits: this is stimulated emission. In their presence one's own excited and disordered states are induced to drop into step — one finds oneself, to one's surprise, saying what one means. They do not transmit their content into others. They induce coherence in others' own emission. LOVE DOES NOT ADD ENERGY TO A PERSON. IT BRINGS THE ENERGY THEY HAVE INTO PHASE.

And that, the file proposes, is what the order parameter is. The proposition calls love a state — and a state of a whole person, affective and cognitive and cardial at once. Love is not one of the emissions. It is the wave that, above a threshold, captures all of them: the one thing willed, of which every act is then an expression. Augustine's sentence, love, and do what you will, is not a relaxation of the moral law. It is a statement about order parameters. Where love is the governing wave, the individual acts need no separate supervision, because they are all already its.

The threshold, and the mirrors

Two features of the laser have precise bearing on what the proposition calls heart-burst.

The onset is sudden. Below threshold, increasing the pump yields a slightly brighter lamp. At threshold the character of the output changes in kind, discontinuously. The witnesses of chapter ten said the same of themselves. Pascal could give the hour. Wesley could give the quarter-hour. Years of pumping — reading, praying, failing, wanting — and then, on a date, coherence. The long preparation was not coherence in small quantities. It was sub-threshold. It looked like nothing, and it was the whole precondition.

There must be mirrors. The atoms cannot reach coherence in the open. The emitted light must be returned through the medium, again and again, for one wave to build. Take the mirrors away and one has a lamp, however hard one pumps.

What are a person's mirrors? Whatever returns their own emission to them, faithfully, so that it passes again through the heart. A spiritual director. A real friend — the Celtic tradition's anam cara, the soul-friend. A rule of life, which brings one back daily to the same few acts. A community that remembers what one said one was for. The examination of conscience at the day's end, which is nothing but the day's emissions returned for a second pass. Solitary seekers are heavily pumped and unmirrored, and they shine like lamps: brightly, incoherently, briefly. The traditions that have reliably produced luminous persons — the monastery, the Oratory, the Methodist class meeting, the Quaker meeting — are, structurally, cavities. And this is the torus again. The outward path must return through the centre. A laser is a torus for light.

The organisational laser

All of it transfers, and here the transfer is not analogy but the same mathematics; the next movement will set out why.

An organisation is a population of emitters. Below threshold, it is a lamp: people working hard, each emitting, the sum incoherent; great expenditure of energy, modest light, nothing that carries. Leaders in such organisations respond by pumping harder — more initiatives, more communication, more hours — and get a hotter lamp.

Above threshold it is something else. The same people, the same effort, and the emissions are in step. Decisions made in different rooms agree without having been coordinated. A customer meets the same organisation at every point of contact. Its word travels without diverging.

What does the lasing transition need? Pumping — energy, real commitment, flowing through. An order parameter able to win the competition — something that can actually be willed as one thing; and the difficulty with most corporate purposes is that they cannot, being lists. And a cavity: mirrors by which the organisation's emission is returned to it and passed again through its centre — rituals of review that are truthful, people empowered to say this is not who we said we were, customers and patients and borrowers brought face to face with those who serve them. Most organisations pump heavily and have removed their mirrors, experiencing them as criticism.

One caution, which the sixth movement will make into a chapter. Coherence is not goodness. A laser can cut as well as heal. An organisation can lase around fear, or greed, or contempt for an out-group, and the result will be as coherent, as far-carrying, and as recruiting as one that lases around love. The physics does not tell them apart. Something else must.

THE SAINT DOES NOT EMIT MORE. THE SAINT EMITS IN PHASE.

InterludeThe Screen

A movement on light as the carrier of love cannot end without facing the fact that a large part of organisational life is now conducted through a device which converts faces into light and sends them elsewhere. If the photonic language is real, the video call is the most literal experiment on it ever run, with several hundred million subjects, and the results are in. The Danish authors list it among their ten leadership paradoxes — physical and virtual presence, each with goods the other lacks — and the file agrees that it is one. But the earlier chapters allow something more exact to be said about what is lost and what, surprisingly, is not.

What the screen does to the interval

Wertheimer found that the crossing lives in a window of timing. Conversation has such a window, and it is narrow. Studies of turn-taking across many languages find that the gap between one speaker stopping and the next starting clusters around a fifth of a second — shorter than the time it takes to plan a word, which means listeners are predicting the end of the turn and launching their reply before it arrives. A gap of half a second is already felt as hesitation; a second, as trouble.

A video call inserts a transmission delay which is seldom less than a tenth of a second and, over ordinary connections, often a quarter or more, and it varies. This falls squarely across the window. The result everyone knows: people talk over one another, stop, apologise, wait, both start again. Experimental work has shown that delays of this size cause listeners to judge the speaker as less attentive and less friendly, without knowing why. Nothing is wrong with anyone's goodwill. Both lamps are flashing. The timing at which phi appears has been taken away.

What it does to the gaze

Marion said that love is two gazes crossing. On a screen they cannot. To appear to look into your eyes I must look at my camera, in which case I am not seeing your eyes; if I look at your eyes on my screen, you see me looking slightly down. The geometry forbids mutual gaze. Each party sees a face that is almost, and never quite, looking at them — which is, for a primate, a strange and tiring signal.

At the same time the faces are too many and too near. Jeremy Bailenson's analysis of what came to be called videoconference fatigue names four causes, and two concern gaze: a grid of faces at close range all appearing to stare, which in life occurs only in confrontation or intimacy; and one's own face in the corner, an all-day mirror. The others are the loss of bodily movement, and the extra work of sending and reading signals through a narrow channel — the exaggerated nod, the thumbs-up held to the lens.

What it does to the field

Köhler's field was the web of mutual perception: each perceiving each perceiving. In a room this web is complete; I see you see her. On a call it is cut to a set of spokes. I cannot tell whom you are looking at. I cannot catch a third person's eye when a fourth says something foolish. The sideways glance, by which a room continually checks and tunes itself, is gone. A call is not a room. It is a set of simultaneous broadcasts.

And the body is cropped. The felt body's narrowing and widening shows in the shoulders, the hands, the lean, the breath — below the frame. The chest, the proposition's organ, is out of shot.

What survives

Given all this, the surprise is how much gets through. People do feel met on calls. Hard conversations are held. Therapists who moved online, expecting the alliance to fail, mostly found it did not. What explains this?

The earlier chapters suggest three things. The voice. It was never only the face; prosody — the music of speech — carries readiness with great fidelity, and audio is far less damaged by the medium than video. Many people find a telephone call more intimate than a video call, and they are not imagining it: with the eyes freed from a degraded visual signal, attention goes to an undegraded acoustic one. The tuned receiver. The fire-walk showed that coupling runs along bonds and depends on the receiver's internal model. Where two people already know one another well, a poor signal suffices to drive a rich model; the screen is a reminder and not a source. That is why remote work is sustained by relationships formed in person, and why teams that have never met find it so much harder. Attention as such. Weil's question can be asked through any channel. What it needs is that the one asking has got themselves out of the way, and that needs no bandwidth.

The navigation

If this is a paradox and not a problem, there is no solution; there is practice.

Meet in the body to build the model; use the screen to refresh it. The value of gathering is not information transfer, which the screen does better. It is tuning. Organisations that bring people together and then sit them in rows before slides have spent the fare and thrown away the purpose.

Protect the interval. Smaller calls. Slower pace. An explicit round in place of a free-for-all, so that no one must fight the lag for a turn.

Hide the mirror. Turn off self-view. Attention on oneself is the one thing certain to prevent a crossing.

Prefer the voice for what matters. The call that begins "have you five minutes — don't bother with the camera" is often the one in which something is said.

Do not mistake the grid for the room. The decisive loss is the mutual web. What needs a room — a real disagreement, a grief, a first meeting, the making of a decision that people must own together — should have one.

And watch the still face. A muted grid of motionless tiles is Tronick's experiment run on the speaker. The junior analyst presenting to twelve black rectangles is an infant working to elicit a response. The simplest loving act available on a video call is to leave one's camera on and let one's face move.

A note on the written word

One further carrier, older than any screen. Most organisational communication is neither face nor voice but text, and text has no photonic language at all: no timing, no gaze, no prosody. Everything this movement has described must be reconstructed by the reader from black marks. The well-attested result is that messages are read as colder and more hostile than they were meant, and that senders greatly overestimate how well their tone has carried.

Yet the letter is the oldest technology for love across distance, and its masters show what it requires. Paul's letters were written to be read aloud in a gathered room. Seneca's, Héloïse's, Bonhoeffer's from prison: what they have in common is that the writer has imagined the reader's face while writing, and has written to it. The reader feels the address. A form has been encoded in syntax and rhythm, and is re-emitted, on reading, across twenty centuries.

That is Davies's Signature exactly: the humanities as the field in which a form survives its moment and can be received again. The email dictated between meetings and the letter that someone keeps for forty years are made of the same marks. The difference is whether a face was present to the one who wrote.

THE SCREEN CUTS THE WEB TO SPOKES. LEAVE YOUR CAMERA ON AND LET YOUR FACE MOVE.
