Movement IV

COMPLEXITY

Order Without a Designer

The proposition rebuilt in the language of thresholds, flows and synchrony. Love as a structure that exists only while energy passes through it; the order parameter; the critical coupling at which a crowd falls into step; Ralph Stacey's objection to the whole idea of a field; constraint in place of cause; and the adjacent possible of the heart.

19Love Far From Equilibrium

The gestalt tradition said that wholes are real and primary. It did not say how a whole comes to be where there was none. That is the question the sciences of complexity were invented to ask, and their first great answer was given by a Russian-born Belgian chemist, Ilya Prigogine, who received the Nobel Prize in 1977 for the theory of what he named dissipative structures.

Two kinds of order

There are, Prigogine pointed out, two entirely different kinds of order in the physical world, and nineteenth-century thermodynamics had recognised only one.

The first is the order of equilibrium. A crystal is ordered. Its atoms sit in a regular lattice, and they do so because that arrangement has the lowest energy; left to itself, with nothing flowing in or out, the system settles there and stays. A crystal is ordered because nothing is happening. It is the order of rest; in a manner of speaking, the order of the grave.

The second is order far from equilibrium. Take a shallow pan of liquid and heat it gently from below. At first the heat simply conducts upward; the liquid is still. Increase the heating. At a critical value of the temperature difference, the liquid abruptly organises itself: it breaks into a regular array of cells, in each of which fluid rises at the centre, spreads across the top, sinks at the edges and returns along the bottom. Seen from above it is a honeycomb. Millions of millions of molecules, each of which a moment before was jostling at random, are now moving in concert over distances vastly greater than the range of any force between them. These are Bénard cells.

Nobody arranged them. And — the decisive point — they exist only so long as the heat flows. Turn off the burner and the pattern vanishes; the liquid returns to featureless rest. The structure is not maintained in spite of the flow of energy through it. It is maintained by that flow. It is a pattern in a throughput. It persists by continuously dissipating energy — hence the name. A flame is a dissipative structure. So is a whirlpool, a hurricane, a cell, an organism, a city.

And note the form of the Bénard cell: fluid rising through the centre, spreading out across the top, descending round the outside, returning underneath to the centre. Each cell is a torus. Far-from-equilibrium order, in its simplest laboratory instance, takes the shape the proposition named.

Love is the second kind

The file now makes one of its central claims. LOVE IS A DISSIPATIVE STRUCTURE. It is order of the second kind, and nearly every mistake that persons and organisations make about it comes from treating it as order of the first.

The crystalline picture of love is very widespread. On it, love is a state one arrives at and then has: a bond formed, a commitment made, a culture built, values embedded. Once achieved it is a possession; it should hold unless something breaks it. This is the picture behind the couple who say, puzzled, "but we were in love"; behind the chief executive who says, "we did the culture work two years ago"; behind every institution that points to its founding charism as though it were an endowment.

If love is a dissipative structure, all of that is confused in a precise way. The pattern exists only while something is flowing. There is no storing it. A marriage is not a crystal that formed at the wedding; it is a cell pattern in a convection that must be driven today. A culture of care is not installed; it is the current form of a through-flow of attention, time and truthfulness, and when the flow drops below the critical value the pattern does not degrade gracefully. It disappears, as the Bénard cells disappear — at a threshold, and all at once. People then say that the culture "suddenly" went wrong. It did not. The heat had been turned down for years, and the pattern held until the moment it could not.

Three consequences.

Love requires a gradient. The cells form only when there is a difference across the system, hot below and cool above, steep enough to drive the flow. Remove the difference and there is nothing to dissipate. This is the thermodynamic face of what the Gestalt therapists found at the contact boundary: no difference, no contact. A relationship or a team in which all difference has been smoothed away — everyone agreeable, everyone aligned — has no gradient. It will be calm. It will be an equilibrium. And nothing will circulate in it. The paradox of the confluent group is that it is the most "harmonious" and the least alive, and thermodynamics says why.

Love produces entropy elsewhere. A dissipative structure maintains its internal order by exporting disorder to its surroundings. Order of this kind is never free. In human terms: love costs, and the cost is real — time that could have gone elsewhere, attention that is finite, energy that must be replenished. Any account of love in organisations which presents it as a costless multiplier — more engagement, more productivity, and nothing given up — is describing a perpetual-motion machine. This is why the later chapters on burnout are not a pessimistic appendix to the work but a structural part of it. And it is one reason why Kirstie Papworth, in the model of compassion the file has begun to draw on, inserts between feeling and responding a step she calls appraisal — one of whose four parts is a deliberate reckoning of one's own resources. On her arithmetic, a response to suffering that takes no account of the responder's capacity is not compassion at all but what she calls altruism, and it does not last. The thermodynamics is on her side. A dissipative structure with no intake is a description of a fire going out.

Love needs an open system. A closed system runs down to equilibrium; that is the second law. Only a system open to a flow from beyond itself can sustain order. The couple that closes upon itself, the team that becomes its own world, the institution that exists to perpetuate itself: each has cut off the through-flow, and each will crystallise or decay. The traditions which speak of love as received from a source beyond the lovers — and Balthasar's is one — are making, whatever else they are making, a sound thermodynamic point. The heart is a pump in a circuit. It is not a reservoir.

Bifurcation

Prigogine's second great theme was what happens at the threshold. As a system is driven further from equilibrium it reaches points — bifurcations — at which its former state becomes unstable and two or more new states become available. Which it takes is not determined by its prior condition. At the bifurcation the system is exquisitely sensitive: a fluctuation that would ordinarily be damped out in an instant is instead amplified, and carries the whole into one branch or the other. In the Bénard pan, adjacent cells rotate in opposite senses, and whether a given cell turns clockwise or anticlockwise is settled by a chance flutter at the critical moment.

He drew the lesson that near equilibrium the world is lawful and dull, and fluctuations do not matter; far from equilibrium, at a bifurcation, the individual fluctuation becomes the author of the new order. He called it order through fluctuation.

This is the physics of the Overture. A meeting in its third hour, strained to the limit, is a system at a bifurcation. The existing pattern — defended, deflecting — has become unstable; it cannot go on. Two branches are open: collapse into blame, or a break into candour. Which is taken is not determined by the agenda, the numbers, or the personalities. It will be decided by a fluctuation. A woman sits down and looks at a man. In the first ten minutes of the same meeting that look would have been damped out: noticed, perhaps, and absorbed. At the bifurcation it is amplified and it selects the branch.

So the timing which Wertheimer found at the scale of milliseconds recurs at the scale of hours. There are moments at which a room, a team, an organisation, is at a bifurcation, and at those moments — only at those — a single small act of love has consequences out of all proportion. The art, which cannot be reduced to rule, is to feel when the system is near its threshold. People who have it are called wise, or lucky. It may be chiefly a kind of interoception: sensing, in one's own chest, that the room cannot continue as it is.

It also follows that crisis is not the enemy of love in organisations. Equilibrium is. An organisation at comfortable equilibrium damps out every fluctuation, the loving ones included: the kind word is nice and changes nothing. It is when the old pattern is breaking — the failed strategy, the insolvency, the scandal, the merger — that the system becomes sensitive to what a single person does. Those who work with organisations in distress know that there is a window in every failure in which one honest and generous act will be amplified into a new order, and that when the window closes it will not open again for years.

Irreversibility

A last note from Prigogine, who was a philosopher of time as much as a chemist. Equilibrium physics is reversible: run the film backward and nothing looks wrong. Dissipative structures have histories. Which branch was taken at the last bifurcation determines which bifurcations are available next. The system is its past.

Love has that kind of time. The mended relationship is not the one that existed before the breach; it is a new structure which contains the breach as part of its history. Tronick's repair is not a return. And an organisation's acts of love or of betrayal at its bifurcations are not episodes laid upon a stable underlying culture. They are the culture. The branch taken in the redundancy round of ten years ago is still determining what is possible today. This is Lewin's contemporaneity and Zeigarnik's charge, restated as physics: the past is present as the shape of the present.

A CULTURE IS NOT A CRYSTAL. TURN OFF THE HEAT AND IT IS GONE.

20The Order Parameter

The laser introduced an idea the file now needs to make fully explicit, because it supplies the most exact meaning available for the proposition's opening words: love is a … state.

What Haken found

Hermann Haken's question was how to describe a system of very many interacting parts as it passes through a transition from disorder to order. The laser has some ten-to-the-eighteenth atoms. Below threshold, a description of what it is doing would need, in principle, the state of every one. Above threshold the same system can be described by a single number.

His analysis showed why. Near a transition, the many possible collective motions of the system divide into two classes. Almost all are stable: disturb them and they die away quickly. One, or a very few, become unstable: disturbed, they grow, and grow slowly. Now the fast, stable modes, because they relax so quickly, simply follow whatever the slow, growing modes are doing — adjusting to them instant by instant, as a boat's attitude follows the swell. The slow modes therefore set the terms for everything else. Haken called them order parameters. To know them is to know the system.

This is an enormous compression of information, and it is not something the observer imposes for convenience. It is something the system does to itself. Out of a near-infinity of possibilities it selects a handful of collective variables, and thereafter it is those variables, with the rest in train.

He gave the relation between the order parameter and the parts the name circular causality. The parts, by their interaction, produce the order parameter. The order parameter, once present, governs the behaviour of the parts. Ask which is cause and which is effect and there is no answer; the question assumes a line where there is a circle.

Haken liked a homely illustration. Think of a language. It exists only in and through the speech of its speakers; with no speakers there is no language. Yet every child born among them is "enslaved" by it — learns it, thinks in it, cannot do otherwise — and by speaking sustains it for the next child. The language is an order parameter. The speakers make it; it makes the speakers.

Love as order parameter

The file now offers its most technical formulation. In a person, in a dyad, in a room, in an institution: love is an order parameter.

That is a claim about what kind of thing love is, and it resolves at a stroke several old puzzles.

Is love a feeling, a judgement, an act of will, or a pattern of behaviour? The question supposes that love must be one of the parts. An order parameter is not one of the parts. It is the slow collective variable to which feelings, judgements, volitions and behaviours all conform. This is why love can persist through wide fluctuations in every one of them — a long marriage has days without warm feeling, days of poor judgement, days of feeble will, days of bad behaviour — and why, conversely, any of them can be present where love is not. The proposition's hyphenated affective-cognitive was reaching for exactly this: a state that is neither affect nor cognition but that which orders both.

Why can love not be produced by producing its components? Because of the direction of dependence at a transition. The fast variables follow the slow one. Engineering the fast variables — the behaviours, the expressed sentiments — leaves the slow one untouched, and when the engineering stops they relax to whatever the actual order parameter dictates. This is the precise mechanics of every failed culture programme: the behaviours were pushed; the order parameter of the organisation was fear, or indifference, or the share price; the behaviours decayed back to what that parameter commanded.

Why does love feel like being governed? Lovers in every literature say they were taken, seized; that they fell; that they could do no other. The moderns suspect this of bad faith. Haken would recognise it as plain report. The order parameter does "enslave" the parts. The phenomenology of love as a sweet compulsion — Augustine's weight — is what it is like, from inside, to be a system whose fast variables are being ordered by a slow one which those same variables are sustaining.

And why does it also feel like the freest thing one has ever done? Because the order parameter is not imposed from without. It is the system's own; the parts make it. Circular causality is the dynamical form of an old theological claim: that in love, necessity and freedom coincide.

Many possible order parameters

Haken's laser, at threshold, contains many competing waves, and one wins. A person, a team, an institution, is likewise a system in which many would-be order parameters compete, and the one that recruits fastest governs. This is Augustine's ordo amoris — one's deepest love orders all the rest — restated as dynamics. It is also McQuade's Dark Side and Light Side: the same people, the same creed, the same organisational chart, ordered by different parameters.

In organisations, the usual contenders are few and they can be named. Fear: the governing variable is the avoidance of blame, and every behaviour — the passive voice, the long email chain copied to seven people, the decision deferred upward — is its expression. Status: the governing variable is relative standing, and meetings are tournaments. The number: a target has become the thing itself, and all else follows it, sometimes over a cliff. The founder: the governing variable is one person's regard. The work: what is being made or done has itself become what everyone serves. The person served: the patient, the pupil, the client, in the concrete.

Only the last two are forms of love, and they are the two that pass through a centre beyond the organisation's own membership. It is a useful and somewhat frightening exercise to sit in an organisation's meetings for a week and ask, not what the stated values are, but: to what variable does everything here actually relax? When a disturbance arrives — bad news, a conflict, a surprise — and the fast behaviours scatter and then settle, what do they settle around? That is the order parameter. It can be read off in an afternoon, and almost never from the wall.

Changing the order parameter

How does a system move from one to another? Not gradually. Haken's theory and Prigogine's agree: by a transition at a threshold, in which the old order parameter loses stability and another, hitherto a suppressed fluctuation, grows and captures the modes. Between the two there is a passage of instability in which the system is noisy, disordered, and exquisitely sensitive — critical fluctuations, in the physicists' phrase, and they are observed in real systems as a great increase in variability just before the new order sets in.

Anyone who has lived through a real change in an organisation's character — as distinct from a reorganisation — knows the passage. Things get worse. Behaviour becomes erratic; old certainties fail; people who were steady become volatile; there is more conflict, not less. The managerial reflex reads this as the change failing and reaches to restore control, which means restoring the old order parameter. In the theory, the noise is the sign that the old order has lost its grip and that a new one is competing for the modes. It is the most hopeful and most dangerous moment.

Here the third book laid on the file gives a practitioner's confirmation from another direction. Rikke Kristine Nielsen and her colleagues, in Navigating Leadership Paradox, report from a Danish research programme with managers in a number of companies, and one of their recurring observations concerns what they call thresholds in the work — points at which the managers, and the facilitators too, were tempted to simplify a tension out of existence because staying in it was so uncomfortable. One facilitator is quoted describing the sensation of being, when deep in the work, at the cusp of something almost spiritual, and losing the thread moments later. The authors' counsel at that point is the fifth of their thresholds: staying with the paradox. In Haken's language: do not damp the critical fluctuations. The discomfort is the transition.

The slow variable

One more property, of great practical weight. The order parameter is the slow variable. It changes on a timescale much longer than that of the parts it governs.

This sets what can and cannot be asked of love in an institution. Feelings change in seconds; behaviours in days; the order parameter in years. An organisation whose governing variable is love will still have bad meetings, cruel remarks, quarters in which everyone behaves abominably — fast fluctuations about a slow mean. One reads the order parameter not from a day but from where the system returns to after disturbance. The loving institution is not the one in which no harm is done. It is the one that, disturbed, comes back to care — Tronick's reliability of repair, now at the scale of a firm.

And an organisation whose governing variable is not love will not be changed by a month of excellent behaviour. Leaders who have "tried being more caring" for a quarter and concluded that it does not work have measured a fast variable and drawn a conclusion about a slow one.

There is, finally, an arresting corollary about leadership, which Haken's own homely example makes vivid. If the order parameter is like a language, then it does not reside in the leader. The leader may have been the fluctuation that seeded it. But once it has captured the modes, it lives in the circular causality of the whole, and the leader is as much governed by it as anyone. This is the criterion by which to tell an institution that loves from one that merely contains a loving person: REMOVE THE PERSON AND SEE WHAT THE SYSTEM RELAXES TO.

ASK NOT WHAT THE VALUES ARE. ASK TO WHAT EVERYTHING HERE RELAXES.

21Sync: The Critical Coupling

Huygens's two clocks fell into step. The seventeenth century found it charming and let it be. Three hundred years on, the question of how a great population of independent rhythms comes spontaneously to beat as one became one of the central problems of the mathematics of complexity — and its solution yields a result about love and organisations that is precise enough to be alarming.

The fireflies and the bridge

Along tidal rivers in Thailand and Malaysia, at nightfall, male fireflies of certain species gather in the mangroves in their thousands. Each flashes with a rhythm of its own. For the first minutes the trees glitter at random. Then patches begin to flash together; the patches grow; and within the half-hour whole trees, and then whole stretches of bank, are pulsing in perfect unison — on, off, on, off, like one great lamp. Early Western travellers who reported it were disbelieved. There is no conductor. Each insect sees its neighbours' flashes and makes a small adjustment to the timing of its own next one, and that is all.

On 10 June 2000 the Millennium Bridge opened across the Thames between St Paul's and Bankside. Within minutes of the first crowds stepping onto it, it began to sway from side to side, and the people on it found themselves walking in a strange, wide-legged, lurching gait — all together. It was closed two days later and stayed closed for nearly two years. What had happened was worked out by the engineers and later modelled by the mathematician Steven Strogatz and colleagues. Any crowd, by chance, has a slight excess of people stepping in time. That excess gave the bridge a tiny sideways motion. A person on a surface that is moving sideways instinctively adjusts their step to it, to keep their balance. So the motion recruited more walkers to its rhythm; more walkers in step made more motion; more motion recruited more walkers. The engineers' tests showed that with a hundred and fifty people on the central span nothing much happened. At about a hundred and sixty-six the bridge began to move.

That number is the point of the story. Below a threshold, nothing. At it, abruptly, everything.

Kuramoto's result

In 1975 the Japanese physicist Yoshiki Kuramoto wrote down the simplest model he could of this class of phenomena. Take a large population of oscillators. Give each its own natural frequency — the pace at which it would run if left alone — and let these differ, spread around some average. Couple them: let each feel a weak pull toward the phase of the others, with a strength governed by a single number, the coupling. Then ask what the population does as the coupling is turned up.

One might expect that synchrony would increase smoothly: a little coupling, a little order. It does not. For weak coupling there is no synchrony at all; the differences in natural frequency win, and every oscillator runs at its own pace as though the others were not there. This remains so as the coupling is raised — until it reaches a definite critical value. There, a small cluster of oscillators whose natural frequencies lie nearest the average lock together. And once that cluster exists, it exerts a combined pull on the rest much stronger than any single oscillator could; it captures those next nearest, which strengthens it further. Beyond the critical coupling, synchrony grows rapidly, and the population passes from incoherence to a state in which a large fraction beat as one.

The transition has an order parameter in exactly Haken's sense: a single number between nought and one measuring how nearly the phases coincide. Below the critical coupling it is nought. Above, it rises from nought.

And the critical value is fixed by one thing: the ratio of the coupling to the spread of natural frequencies. A population of very similar oscillators synchronises at weak coupling. A population of very diverse ones needs strong coupling to synchronise at all.

Four results for the proposition

There is a threshold, and below it effort is invisible. This is the hardest thing for anyone trying to bring love into an organisation to accept. For a long time, raising the coupling — more real attention to one another, more truthful meetings, more presence — produces no visible result whatever. Not a small result. None. The order parameter stays at nought; the room looks as it always did. Then, at a value that cannot be known in advance, a first cluster locks, and things move with a speed that astonishes everyone, including those who had been doing the work.

Those who gave up at a hundred and fifty walkers concluded that it does not work.

The first cluster forms near the middle. Not at the edges: synchrony nucleates among those whose natural frequencies are closest to the mean, and spreads outward from them. In an organisation, that is not the enthusiasts, whose pace is far from everyone's, and it is certainly not the resistant. It is a handful of people of ordinary standing and ordinary temperament who find themselves, with each other, in step. The lesson for anyone seeding a change is against instinct. Do not begin with the evangelists; they are outliers, and outliers lock last or not at all. Find the few near the centre who can lock with one another. Every later recruitment will be to that cluster.

Diversity raises the threshold; it does not forbid the transition. A team of very different people requires stronger coupling to cohere than a team of similar ones. That is a theorem, and it is a comfort to no one's ideology. Homogeneous groups synchronise cheaply — which is exactly why they are tempting, and why the easy coherence of the like-minded proves nothing about the presence of love. Diverse groups must be coupled far more strongly: more time, more contact, more willingness to be affected. But if they are, they reach a synchrony the homogeneous group cannot match in richness, since what locks is a population that still contains its differences. This is, in mathematics, the contact boundary once more: the difference kept, the coupling made strong enough to cross it.

Synchrony is of phase, not of nature. In the Kuramoto state the oscillators do not become identical. Each keeps its own natural frequency as a disposition; they agree in timing. Remove the coupling and each returns to its own pace. This distinguishes the proposition's state from its fused counterfeit with real precision. In confluence the members become the same. In synchrony they remain themselves and move together. A choir is not thirty people with one voice. It is thirty voices in time.

What is the coupling?

The model has one free parameter and the application turns on naming it. What, between human beings, is the coupling?

It is the degree to which each allows their own state to be shifted by the state of the others: the readiness to adjust one's timing to another's. The firefly that did not look at its neighbours would never synchronise, however brightly it flashed. The walker on the bridge was coupled to the deck because he had to keep his balance; he could not not respond.

In human terms that is being affectable. And here the model delivers something that is nearly a definition. A person's coupling strength is the measure of how far they let others move them — how much of what the other is doing actually gets in and alters what they do next. It is not warmth of feeling. It is not goodwill. A person can wish others well with great intensity and be, dynamically, uncoupled: flashing at their own rhythm, admirable and alone.

LOVE IS HIGH COUPLING WITH DIFFERENCE RETAINED. It is the willingness to be moved by the other, held together with the continuing reality of one's own frequency. Low coupling with difference retained is the ordinary organisation: a set of professionals, each on their own clock. High coupling with difference abolished is the cult. High coupling with difference retained is the thing itself, and it is hard, because each condition, alone, is easy and each makes the other harder.

This is also why hierarchy tends to lower the coupling at exactly the place where it matters most. Power is, among other things, the capacity not to be affected: the powerful can afford to ignore the timing of others, and the experimental literature on power suggests, with the usual caveats, that they do — less perspective-taking, less mimicry, less attention to those below. Papworth, summarising the same body of research for her readers, notes that the higher a leader stands the more likely they are to overestimate their own self-awareness and empathy. The senior person in a room is therefore, very often, the oscillator with the weakest coupling and the strongest signal: everyone adjusts to them and they adjust to no one. That produces synchrony of a kind. It is entrainment to a pacemaker — a different dynamical state, in which the population follows one driven rhythm and has no order of its own. Switch the pacemaker off and it falls at once to incoherence. The test of the previous chapter again: remove the person and see.

A leader who wishes for the other kind of order must do the one thing power makes unnecessary. They must let themselves be moved, visibly, by people who have no power to compel it.

The bridge, again

The Millennium Bridge was mended with dampers, and it is worth saying what a damper is. It is a device that dissipates energy at the frequency of the unwanted motion, raising the threshold above any crowd that will ever stand there. The bridge's fault was not that it synchronised. It was that it synchronised around a motion nobody had chosen, by a feedback nobody could see, at a threshold nobody knew was there.

Organisations have their dampers too, and most were fitted for good reason: procedures that stop a mood from sweeping the firm, committees that slow a decision, separations of duties that prevent one enthusiasm from capturing everything. An institution with no damping is a mob. But dampers do not discriminate. Tuned to prevent panic, they prevent ignition; installed against the wobble of the crowd, they also raise the threshold for love beyond anything the organisation's members can reach. A great part of the art of institutional design, on this view, is damping the frequencies of fear while leaving those of care free to build. No one, so far as the file knows, has ever specified a governance structure in those terms. It might be worth trying.

BELOW THE THRESHOLD NOTHING SHOWS. THEN A HUNDRED AND SIXTY-SIX PEOPLE STEP ONTO THE BRIDGE.

InterludeBelow the Threshold

The mathematics of the last chapter says that for a long time nothing shows. It is one thing to be told this and another to live in it. What follows is a composed record — a notebook such as a manager might keep — of eleven months in which the coupling was being raised and the order parameter stayed at nought. No such person exists. The pattern is one that many who have tried it will know.

January. New in post. Fourteen in the team, three sites. Inherited a weekly meeting that is forty minutes of people reading out what is already in the tracker. Nobody looks at anybody. I have decided to do two things and nothing else: start the meeting with one sentence each on what people are carrying, and have a proper half-hour with each of them once a month in which I do not talk about targets. I have told no one that this is a plan.

February. The opening round is excruciating. "Fine." "Busy." "Fine." R. said "Nothing to report" as though I had asked for a status. The one-to-ones are courteous and empty. They are waiting to find out what I want.

March. No change. I catch myself filling the silences in the round. Stopped doing that. The silences are worse. M. asked me in the kitchen whether the round was "an HR thing".

April. Bad month. We missed the quarter. I was sharp with T. in front of the others about the forecast and saw the room close — you could have photographed it. Went to see him afterwards and said I had been out of order and that the forecast problem was at least half mine. He said, "It's fine." It was not fine. But I notice he has stopped copying his manager's manager on emails to me.

May. Nothing. The round still produces "fine". I have begun to dread it. Considered dropping it; nobody would object. Did not drop it — chiefly because I could not think what I would be telling them by doing so.

June. One thing. In the round, J. said, "My dad's in hospital." Then looked as if she wished she hadn't. Nobody said anything. I said, "Thank you for telling us," and we went on. Afterwards two people stopped at her desk. I did not arrange that.

July. Back to "fine". Holidays. Half the team missing each week.

August. D. disagreed with me in the meeting about the rota — properly, with reasons. First time anyone has. He was right. I said so, and changed it, and said it was because of what he had said. Felt the room notice. Then nothing; no one else followed.

September. Still measuring badly. My own boss asked what I had "done with the team" since January. I had no answer he would have recognised. I said we were getting the basics right. He looked unconvinced, and he is entitled to be: on every number he has, nothing has happened.

I do not, on the evidence, know that anything has. Three small incidents in nine months. One might be making it up.

October. R. — "nothing to report" — came to his one-to-one and, twenty minutes in, said that he has been covering for an error in the reconciliation process since before I arrived. He found it in the spring of last year. He did not make it. He has been quietly correcting its effects by hand every month because the last person who raised a process fault here was made to feel it was his own. He said, "I thought you should probably know." He was grey.

I thanked him. I meant it, and I think he could see that I did. We spent the rest of the time on how to put it right and who needs telling. I asked if he would say something at the meeting. He said he would rather not. I said that was up to him.

November. He said it at the meeting. In the round. "I've been carrying the recs thing since last year and I'm glad it's out." There was a pause of perhaps three seconds.

Then T. said that while we were at it there was something about the forecast model he had been meaning to raise. Then M. Then two I had barely heard speak. It took fifty minutes. We came out with a list of eleven things, seven of which I had not known, three of which were serious, and one of which explains April.

Nobody read from the tracker.

In the kitchen afterwards they were all in there at once, talking over one another. I stayed out.

Later. What strikes me, reading back: there is no moment in the first ten months at which I could have shown anyone that it was working. There were three or four small fluctuations, each of which died away. On the day before R.'s one-to-one the team was, by any measure available, exactly as I had found it.

And yet it was not. Something had been going up the whole time that had no gauge. Each "fine" in the round was a person finding out that the round would be there again next week whatever they said. April — the afternoon I thought I had wrecked it — may have mattered more than anything else, since it was the first time they saw what I do when I am wrong.

I do not know which week it crossed. I think R. had been deciding since June.

I also think that if I had been moved in September — and I nearly was — my successor would have inherited a team with a reputation for being closed, would have been right to say so, and would have been told that I had tried all that and it made no difference.

What the notebook shows, in the terms of the chapter before it: coupling raised at a steady cost for ten months with the order parameter at nought. Three fluctuations damped out. A repair in April that reset the slope. Then a first lock — and it came, as the theory says, not from an enthusiast but from the man nearest the middle, whose natural frequency was "nothing to report". Once he and the manager were in step, the pull on the rest was of a different order, and the room synchronised in fifty minutes.

And one thing the theory does not say but which the notebook's author half-sees. What he was doing all those months was not a technique for producing November. Had it been — had he kept the round in order to get the disclosure — the faces would have shown it, and R. would have gone on correcting the figures by hand. He kept it, by his own account, because he could not think what dropping it would tell them. The pumping was real; the mirrors were in place; he did not know the threshold existed. That is the ordinary condition of anyone who loves in an organisation. THE WORK IS DONE WITHOUT A GAUGE.

ON THE DAY BEFORE IT CHANGED, NOTHING HAD CHANGED.

22Stacey's Objection: There Is No Field

The file has now spent many chapters speaking of fields, wholes, order parameters and systems that do things. It is time to let the most formidable critic of that entire way of speaking have the floor. He would have regarded most of the foregoing as a sophisticated mistake, and he was a complexity theorist.

The objection

Ralph Stacey began as an economist and a corporate planner, became one of the first writers to bring chaos and complexity theory into management, and then — this is what makes him interesting — turned upon his own earlier work. With Douglas Griffin, Patricia Shaw and later Chris Mowles at the University of Hertfordshire, he developed through the late 1990s and after a position they called complex responsive processes of relating. It is built from the social behaviourism of George Herbert Mead, the process sociology of Norbert Elias, and an analogy — he insisted it was only that — with the complexity sciences. And it contains a sustained attack on what he called systems thinking.

The attack runs as follows. To speak of an organisation as a system, or a field, or a whole, is to speak as if there were a something, over and above the people, with properties and tendencies of its own, which acts back upon them. But there is no such something. Nobody has ever met an organisation. One meets persons, interacting. "The organisation," "the culture," "the field" are patterns in that interaction — and a pattern in an interaction is not an entity standing outside it that could cause it. To treat it as one is to reify: to turn a process into a thing.

And the reification has consequences, intellectual and ethical. Intellectually it smuggles in what Stacey, following Kant, called a "both… and" doubling of causality: individuals are taken as autonomous agents choosing their acts, and as parts shaped by a whole — and theorists slide between the two as convenient. Ethically it permits an evasion. If "the system" or "the culture" does things, then no one does them. And it flatters the manager, who is pictured as standing outside the system, diagnosing it and designing its improvement — a position that does not exist, since the manager is one more participant in the interaction, with more power than most and no more outsideness than any.

What he puts in its place

From Mead, Stacey takes the conversation of gestures. One person makes a gesture — a word, a look, a movement. Another responds. And the meaning of the gesture is not in the gesture, nor in the intention behind it. It arises in the response. Gesture and response together constitute one social act, and the meaning of what I did is not available to me until you have answered. Since I cannot know how you will answer, I cannot know, when I act, what my act will turn out to have been.

Mead adds that human beings have the peculiar capacity to call out in themselves the response their gesture calls out in the other; that is what consciousness is. And they can take the attitude not only of a particular other but of the group — the "generalised other." The self is this process turned upon itself: a silent conversation, formed by the social process while forming it.

From Elias, Stacey takes the game. Elias observed that when many people each pursue their own plans, their intentions interweave, and what results is an order "that no individual person has planned or created." He called these patterns figurations and studied them over centuries. The players are not free of the game, and they are not determined by a game existing apart from them. They are the game, each constraining and enabling the others — which is what Elias meant by power: not a possession but a feature of every relation, in which each needs something of the other.

So the Stacey picture: an organisation is nothing but the ongoing local interaction of persons — gesture and response, in the living present — in which population-wide patterns emerge without blueprint. He called the patterns themes organising the experience of being together. They are not stored anywhere. They exist only in their continual re-enactment, and in re-enactment they are both sustained and potentially transformed, because no repetition is exact, and small differences can amplify. He was fond of the phrase "the paradox of the known-unknown": at every moment we are forming the future while being formed by a past, and it is at once predictable and unpredictable.

There is no outside. There is no whole acting on the parts. There is no field.

The force of it

The file takes this with full seriousness, and concedes three things at once.

It concedes the danger of reification. The proposition says love "creates and emanates" a field which "extends" and "has real substance." Every one of those verbs makes love a thing: a stuff, emitted, spreading. The file's own ledger found no such stuff. Stacey explains why one keeps looking for it: grammar. English wants a subject for its verbs; "love crosses the room" needs a something that crosses. The need is syntactic and the file must not mistake it for a discovery.

It concedes the ethical point. Talk of fields can be an evasion. "The energy in the room was bad" is a sentence without an agent; nobody did it. "The culture here doesn't allow candour" — but cultures do not allow or forbid. You did not speak, and he punished the last person who did. Stacey's insistence on local interaction is an insistence on responsibility, and a work on love cannot do without that.

It concedes the point about the leader. There is no place outside the interaction from which love can be installed. The leader who sets out to "create a loving culture" has imagined themselves a designer standing over a system. They are a participant making gestures whose meaning will be decided by the responses.

The reply

And yet the file does not think Stacey has abolished what the proposition reports. It thinks he has relocated it — and to a better address.

Consider what Mead's account says about the Overture. The woman looks at the man. That is a gesture. Its meaning, on Mead's own terms, is not in her — it is not her "love," sitting in her chest and radiating. Its meaning arises in his response: he begins again, in the active voice. The love was in the social act. It existed in the completed circuit of gesture and response and nowhere else. Had he responded otherwise — bridled, performed, ignored it — the same look would have been another act: a failed overture, a piece of pity, nothing.

That is no refutation of the proposition. It is its best statement. For what was the proposition insisting on, with its language of fields extending beyond the body? That love is not a private interior state. That it exists in the space between. That it is there, across the room. Mead and Stacey say precisely this, more rigorously than the field-language can: LOVE IS NOT IN THE GESTURE. IT IS IN THE GESTURE-AND-RESPONSE. It is "beyond the body" not as an emanation is beyond its source, but as a conversation is beyond either speaker.

Take the file's other key terms in turn.

The crossing. Wertheimer had already said that nothing travels. Stacey says why: there is no gap to cross, because gesture and response were never two things. They are phases of one act.

The whole. The gestaltists said the whole is other than the sum. Stacey denies there is a whole apart from the interacting. But the pattern which emerges in interaction is other than anything in any participant's intention — Elias's order that none of them planned. What Stacey refuses is only the further step of setting the pattern up as an agent. The file, having followed Haken into circular causality, had already half-refused it: the order parameter is nothing but the atoms' own combined emission.

The order parameter. Here the two views grind against each other and the file will not paper it over. Haken says the order parameter "enslaves" the parts; Stacey would call that sentence a paradigm of the error, a pattern promoted into a cause. But Haken's mathematics does not need the slave-talk. What it describes is each atom responding to the waves of its neighbours — local interaction — and a population-wide pattern arising in that. One can state every result of the last two chapters in Stacey's grammar. It is longer. It is also, the file admits, cleaner.

Resonance and the torus. What goes out returns through the centre. In Mead's terms: the gesture returns to the gesturer as the other's response, and — because we call out in ourselves what we call out in others — is received as the meaning of what one did. The torus is the social act.

What Stacey adds that the field-language cannot

Something positive comes out of the encounter, and it bears on the practical question of how love comes about in organisations.

On the field picture, the route is: get into the state, and emanate. That places the whole weight on the lover's interior. It is also faintly grandiose — the leader as radiator.

On Stacey's picture, love is something we do together and cannot do alone, and no one controls whether it happens. I can make the gesture. I cannot make it love; that takes your response, which I cannot command. This is humbler and it is truer to experience. It explains why love cannot be planned — the meaning of the plan lies in responses not yet given. It explains why the same person, with the same presence, is received as love in one room and as intrusion in the next. And it relocates the practical task. The question is no longer how do I become a source? It is: WHAT GESTURE IS MINE TO MAKE NOW, AND AM I PREPARED TO DISCOVER FROM YOUR RESPONSE WHAT IT WAS?

It also yields a severe and useful test of anyone's claim to love those they lead. The claim is not established by the leader's sincerity. It is established, or not, in the responses. If they do not respond as people who are loved — if they manage upward, withhold bad news, perform — then, whatever was felt in the leader's chest, the social act was not love. Mead's principle bars the oldest consolation of the failed leader: but I really did care about them. The meaning of the gesture was in the response.

Stacey's colleague Chris Mowles has insisted that this view is not a counsel of helplessness. To say that no one stands outside is to say that everyone is inside, and that what each does matters. Patricia Shaw gave the practice a title that would serve as an epigraph for half of this work: changing conversations in organisations. Not designing a field. Changing a conversation — this one, now — by taking part in it differently.

The settlement

Two idioms, then, and the file's terms for using them.

It will go on saying "field," because the proposition does, because the gestalt and energy traditions do, and because the word catches a real feature of the experience: love is met as something already there, into which one walks, larger than oneself. The phenomenology is field-like.

But it reads every such sentence under Stacey's correction. The field is not a stuff and not an agent. It is the pattern of gesture and response among these people, here, now — sustained only in being re-enacted, changeable at any moment by a different gesture or a different response, and the responsibility of each of them. When the file says "love crossed the room," the reader should hear: she made a gesture; he completed it; and the nine others, by what they then did, made it the act of a room.

This is, as it happens, the oldest formula in the tradition: where two or three are gathered. Not where one is radiant. Where two or three are gathered, there is something in the midst of them.

THE MEANING OF THE GESTURE IS IN THE RESPONSE. SO IS THE LOVE.

23Constraint, Not Cause

There is an objection to the proposition which is more basic than any yet considered, and it arises just when the work has begun to sound confident. How can a state — a pattern, a form, an order parameter, a theme in a conversation — do anything? Forces do things. Molecules do things. A pattern is just the arrangement that the things doing things happen to have. To say that love "re-forms the field" or "orders the emissions" seems to credit a description with causal power. Stacey's worry about reification was a special case of this one.

The philosopher who has done most to answer it is Alicia Juarrero, in Dynamics in Action and, more recently, Context Changes Everything. Her answer supplies the file with the one concept it has so far been using without having named.

The trouble with causes

The modern picture of causation is the billiard ball: one thing strikes another and makes it move. It is efficient causation, in Aristotle's old scheme, and from the seventeenth century it was taken to be the only real kind. On that picture a whole can do nothing its parts are not already doing, and the idea that it might act back upon its parts is either a mystification or a violation of physics — the parts would be pushed twice, once by each other and once by the whole.

But this makes human action unintelligible. When I raise my arm in order to vote, what distinguishes that from the same arm rising in a spasm? Not the physiology, which may be identical. The difference is that the vote is about something — it is shaped, throughout, by an intention and a situation. An intention is not a little push at the start, after which the arm travels on its own. It is something that keeps the movement on course, correcting as it goes. That is not a billiard-ball relation.

Constraints

Juarrero's proposal is that wholes act on their parts not as forces but as constraints. A constraint does not add energy to anything. It alters what is possible and what is probable: it changes the space of available states. A riverbank does not push the water; it shapes where the water can go. A sonnet's form does not write the poem; it makes some lines possible and others not. The rules of chess move no pieces, and no move makes sense without them.

She distinguishes kinds, and the distinctions are the valuable part.

Context-free constraints bias a system in the same way regardless of what else is going on: a gradient, a slope, a standing inequality of probabilities. They take a system away from flat randomness. A loaded die.

Context-sensitive constraints make the probability of one thing depend on another. If this, then more likely that. In English a q is nearly always followed by a u; the letters are no longer independent. This is the birth of relation, and with it of information. It is context-sensitive constraint that knits separate things into an interdependent whole. A catalyst is one. So is a feedback loop. So is the rule that makes my turn depend on your move.

Then the crucial pair. Once context-sensitive constraints have closed into a coherent whole, the whole has properties the parts lacked, and those properties operate as enabling constraints, which create new possibilities — the grammar that lets infinitely many sentences be said — and as governing constraints, by which the whole regulates and stabilises its parts. Neither is a force. Both are real, since both make a difference to what happens.

Her summary of how wholes act: they do not push. They shape the landscape over which the parts move. Mereological causation — whole to part, part to whole — is constraint all the way round. And with that the "pushed twice" objection dissolves. The whole is not an additional force; it is the structure of possibility within which the forces operate.

Love as constraint

Now the proposition can be restated a final time in the idiom of complexity, and the restatement removes the last suspicion that it requires anything occult.

Love is not a force. It does not push anyone. No energy passes from lover to beloved to make them do anything. LOVE IS A CONSTRAINT: IT CHANGES WHAT IS POSSIBLE.

This is Lewin's point about the life space, now with its philosophy of causation attached. The woman's look did not cause the man to speak truthfully, as one ball causes another to roll. It altered the probability distribution over what he might do next. An instant before, "say plainly what went wrong" had a probability close to nil — not forbidden, but hemmed about by every context-sensitive constraint in the room, each expected response making candour less likely. Her look was one new context-sensitive constraint: given that she is here and for me, the probabilities shift. The landscape tilted. He did the rest, with his own energy, as a stone rolls downhill by its own weight once the slope is changed.

This explains with some exactness why love is experienced as freeing and not as being pushed. A force overrides: where I am forced, the act is not mine. A change of constraint does not override: I do what I do, out of what I have, but in a space with more room in it. And it explains why love has such large effects with such small energies. A constraint needs no power proportional to its consequences. A hand on the points of a railway does not move the train.

Enabling and governing

Juarrero's last distinction permits a more discriminating account of how love works in an institution than is usually given.

Organisations are thick with governing constraints: rules, procedures, hierarchies, targets. They stabilise; they make behaviour dependable; they cut down the space of possibility to a manageable region. They are indispensable. An organisation without them is not free. It is formless.

Love in an organisation is in the first place an enabling constraint: it adds possibilities. In a team where people are for one another, things can be said, tried, admitted and risked that are simply not in the repertoire elsewhere. The empirical literature the file will review in the next movement — on psychological safety, on high-quality connections, on companionate culture — is, read with Juarrero, a literature about enabling constraints. Amy Edmondson's well-known finding, that the better hospital teams reported more errors because they were the ones in which an error could be spoken of, is a finding about an enlarged possibility space.

But this must not be sentimentalised. Love is also a governing constraint, and a strict one. Where love is the order parameter, certain things become very nearly impossible: to humiliate, to abandon, to lie to someone "for their own good," to treat a person as a line item. Not prohibited — no rule need be written. They drop out of the space of live options, as it drops out of the space of live options to strike one's own child. Augustine's love, and do what you will is misread as licence. It is the observation that love, as governing constraint, has so shaped the landscape that what one then wills lies within it.

The two functions give a test for distinguishing love from its nearest neighbours. Mere niceness is all enabling and no governing: everything is permitted, nothing is required, and the space is so open that nothing in it has any shape. Mere discipline is all governing and no enabling: the space is narrow and safe and nothing new can happen. Love does both at once. It widens the space of what one may be and narrows the space of what one may do to others. The scholastics called it vis unitiva, a unifying power. Juarrero would call it the constraint that closes a set of persons into a coherent whole — whose coherence then opens to them what none of them had alone.

Constraint and the absent

A companion thought comes from the biological anthropologist Terrence Deacon, who has argued that the most distinctive features of life and mind — function, purpose, meaning, value — are all defined by something that is not there. A function is for an end not yet achieved. A meaning is about a thing that may be absent. A purpose aims at what does not yet exist. He calls these absential features, and he argues that they are causally efficacious because constraint is: a constraint is defined by what is not allowed to happen, and what is thus excluded does real work. The hole in the hub is what makes the wheel useful; the emptiness in the vessel, as the Dao De Jing says in almost the same words, is where its use lies.

Love is thick with the absential. It is directed at a person's possibility — what they are not yet. It works by what it refrains from. Attention, in Weil's account, is a making-empty. And the torus has a hole in the middle through which everything passes.

There is here a rather exact answer to the proposition's phrase real substance. If "substance" must mean stuff, then love has none, and the ledger was right. But if Deacon and Juarrero are right, the insistence that only stuff is real is the error. Constraints are real. Absences that constrain are real. They make differences; they can be studied; they persist; they have conditions and consequences. Love has real substance in the only sense in which a form, a meaning, a purpose or a law has it — and since those are the things that distinguish a living world from a dead one, that is no second-class reality.

What a leader can and cannot do

The practical upshot is the most useful single shift of posture the file has to offer.

A leader who thinks causally asks: what must I do to people to get the behaviour I want? That is a question about forces, and its instruments are incentive, instruction and pressure. It works, within limits, for behaviour that can be specified beforehand. It cannot produce love, candour, initiative or care, because a pushed act of that kind is not one.

A leader who thinks in constraints asks: what, in the space these people move in, is making the thing I hope for improbable — and which of those constraints are mine? That is a question about the landscape. Its instruments are of another sort: removing a barrier, changing who is in the room, altering what follows when someone tells the truth, being a different context for others' acts. Above all it means attending to oneself as a constraint. A senior person is, for those around them, one of the heaviest context-sensitive constraints in their world: given that she reacts so to bad news, the probability that she hears any is thus. She need exert no force. She simply is the slope.

YOU ARE NOT A CAUSE OF WHAT YOUR PEOPLE DO. YOU ARE PART OF THE SHAPE OF THE SPACE THEY DO IT IN.

A FORCE OVERRIDES. A CONSTRAINT MAKES ROOM.

24The Adjacent Possible of the Heart

The complexity movement has been, so far, about how order arises and holds. It ends with the question of how anything new arises — and with a thinker of complexity who actually wrote about love.

Kauffman's idea

Stuart Kauffman, a theoretical biologist long associated with the Santa Fe Institute, introduced a phrase that has travelled far beyond biology: the adjacent possible.

Consider the set of all the kinds of molecule present on the early Earth. From them, by a single reaction step, certain new molecules could be formed which did not yet exist. Call those the adjacent possible: one step from the actual. Now suppose some of them form. The actual is larger — and so is the adjacent possible, because the new molecules can react with the old and with each other to make things that were not one step away before. Each realised possibility opens further possibilities which did not exist, even as possibilities, until it was realised.

He drew two conclusions. First, the biosphere — and, he argued, the economy, technology and culture — advances into its adjacent possible, and by doing so expands it; the space of the possible is not fixed in advance but grows with each step. Second, and more radical: we cannot state beforehand what the adjacent possible contains. Before the swim bladder there was no way to list "worm that lives only in swim bladders" among the possible niches. The possibilities are not merely unknown. They are unprestatable. No finite list, and so no probability calculation over the list.

The universe, on this view, is not working through a menu. It is cooking, and the dishes make new ingredients.

Love and the possible

Now put this beside what the tradition says love knows. Chapter eight claimed that love knows the possible: it sees what the beloved could be. Kauffman lets that be said with more exactness and more wonder.

A person's adjacent possible is the set of things they could become or do from where they are, in one step. It is not fixed by their nature. It depends on their situation — on what is actual around them with which they can combine. Lewin: the life space. Juarrero: enabling constraint. And Kauffman adds: it depends above all on relation, since relation is what creates combinatorial possibilities that did not exist. A molecule alone has few adjacent possibles. In the presence of a catalyst it has many.

LOVE IS CATALYTIC. In the chemist's sense: a catalyst is not consumed in the reaction, supplies none of its energy, and makes possible a transformation that would otherwise be so improbable as never to occur. The lover does not transform the beloved. The lover's presence lowers the barrier to a transformation the beloved carries out with their own energies. And afterwards the catalyst is still there, available for the next.

More: what love makes possible is frequently something that was not on any list. The man in the Overture did not have "tell the unprotected truth in front of the board" as a live but unlikely option which her look made likelier. In the room as it was, it was not among his possibilities. Her look did not select from his menu. It added to it. Every teacher worth the name has had the experience from the other side: a pupil does, in their presence, a thing which the pupil had no idea they could do, and which the teacher also had not foreseen — which neither could have foreseen, since it came into being as a possibility only in the relation.

That is why love cannot be merely a means to an outcome specified beforehand, and why its instrumental capture by management — love your people and they will hit the target — is not only distasteful but incoherent. To love someone is to enter with them an adjacent possible that cannot be prestated. One does not know what they will become. One knows only that the space of what they might become has just enlarged. The manager who "loves" as a way of obtaining a known result has, by fixing the result, closed the very space love opens.

Autocatalytic sets

Kauffman's earliest and most celebrated work concerned the origin of life. Take a soup of molecules, some of which catalyse the formation of others. If the variety is low, each reaction needs a catalyst that is probably not present; nothing much occurs. But as variety increases, a threshold is crossed — he showed it mathematically — at which a set of molecules appears in which every member's formation is catalysed by some other member. The set as a whole catalyses its own production. He called it collectively autocatalytic, and proposed that life began not with a single self-copying molecule but with such a set: a web of mutual making which, above a critical diversity, crystallises abruptly out of chemistry.

No member makes itself. Each is made by others, and makes others. The set is self-making; the members are not.

This may be the most exact formal image the file can offer of a loving community, and of the proposition's claim that one can become love. For a set of persons in which each one's flourishing is catalysed by some other's, and each catalyses another's, is collectively autocatalytic with respect to flourishing. It produces more of itself. It requires no external supplier of motivation, which is why communities of this kind — a good monastery, a great teaching hospital at its best, a regiment, a theatre company in a good year — have a self-sustaining vitality that outsiders find uncanny and executives long to bottle. And it has Kauffman's threshold: below a certain density of mutual catalysis there are only individuals, each waiting for an enabling that is not there. Above it, the web closes, and the thing is alive.

It is also the torus, at the scale of a community: what each gives returns — not from the one to whom it was given, necessarily, but through the web, from somewhere — and passes through each again.

Note the property that matters most for the last movement. In an autocatalytic set, to be a member is to be a catalyst. One does not first belong and then, perhaps, contribute. One's place in the set simply is one's catalytic relation to the others. That is the structural meaning of becoming love: not being an individual who has love or does loving things, but being a node whose entire function in the web is that others are made possible by it.

Morin: the complexity of love

Edgar Morin, the French philosopher of la pensée complexe, who lived past a hundred and wrote more than sixty books in the attempt to think the world without mutilating it, is the one major complexity thinker to have addressed love directly — in the lectures gathered as Amour, poésie, sagesse.

His principles of complex thought are three. The dialogic: two logics, complementary and antagonistic, held together without one absorbing the other — order and disorder, autonomy and dependence. The recursive: products that are necessary to their own production — individuals make the society that makes individuals. The hologrammatic: the part is in the whole and the whole is in the part, as the whole organism's genetic information is in each cell.

Love, for Morin, is the pre-eminent complex phenomenon, since it exhibits all three at full strength. It is dialogic to the root: it unites what he calls homo sapiens and homo demens — reason and delirium, the wisest and the maddest in us — and cannot be had with either alone. A love entirely wise is not love; a love entirely mad destroys. It is the union of the mythological and the physical: a love is at once a bodily fact and an idea of extraordinary cultural elaboration, and each feeds the other. It is recursive: the lovers make the love that makes them. And it is hologrammatic: in one love the whole of a life, and in a sense the whole of a culture's imagination of what life is for, is present.

Morin adds something no physicist would. Human beings, he says, live in two registers, the prosaic and the poetic. The prosaic is the state of utility, function and calculation: what we do to stay alive. The poetic is the state of fervour, wonder, communion and intensity: what we stay alive for. And love is the summit of the poetic state. He does not mean the prosaic can be dispensed with. He means that a life, or a society, wholly given to prose has secured the conditions of living and lost the living.

It is the most direct challenge a complexity thinker has put to organisations, which are the supreme institutions of prose. They exist for utility, function and calculation, and they are right to. Morin's dialogic says that they need the poetic as well — not as relief, not as the away-day, but as the complementary and antagonistic logic without which the prose goes dead. And he says it cannot be folded in. If the poetic is made useful — if the fervour is harnessed for the quarter — it has become prose. The two must be held as two.

The third book: tensions that will not be dissolved

Morin's dialogic has an exact practical counterpart in the third of the volumes recently laid on this file, and the correspondence is close enough that it should be introduced here, where its theoretical ground is being laid, before the fifth movement puts it to work.

Navigating Leadership Paradox, by Rikke Kristine Nielsen, Frans Bévort, Thomas Duus Henriksen and their colleagues, begins by separating three kinds of difficulty which managers habitually run together. A problem is an unsettled matter that can be solved, and once solved stays solved. A dilemma is a choice between alternatives — between a rock and a hard place, or between two attractive options — and it calls for prioritising: one chooses and bears the cost. A paradox is a different creature. Its poles are in conflict and bound to one another, so that choosing one gives only temporary relief; the tension comes back up, in the authors' homely image, like a cork pushed under water. The poles, they say, are as yin and yang: each contains the other and depends on it. A paradox is not to be solved or decided but navigated, continuingly, with no final resting place.

That is Morin's dialogic, word for word, transposed from epistemology to the manager's desk. And it is the dissipative structure of chapter nineteen as lived from within: an order that exists only while a tension is kept and worked, and that collapses to dead equilibrium the moment one pole is allowed to win.

Their principal instrument is a simple four-box figure which they call the Paradox Quadrant, adapted from Barry Johnson's polarity mapping. One writes the two poles at either end of a horizontal line; above the line the benefits of each; below, what goes wrong when each is over-emphasised. Then one reads it three ways, of which the most revealing is the diagonal: the dark side of one pole is commonly the mirror of the bright side of the other, and what a person fears in the opposite pole is usually the shadow of what they prize in their own.

The file will fill in such a quadrant for love in its fifth movement. Here it records the theoretical point. Almost everything this work has said about love has had the form of a paradox in their strict sense — contact and boundary; coupling and retained difference; enabling and governing; going out and returning; the poetic and the prosaic. In no case can one pole be chosen. In every case, to choose is to lose both. The Danish authors have a blunt and valuable name for what happens when a facilitator, to spare managers the discomfort, quietly turns a paradox into a problem with a solution: they call it deparadoxification, and they warn that it defuses precisely the energy the paradox held.

LOVE DEPARADOXIFIED IS SENTIMENT ON ONE SIDE AND CONTROL ON THE OTHER. The whole of the corruption movement will turn out to be a catalogue of what follows when one pole of love is permitted to win.

LOVE DOES NOT CHOOSE FROM YOUR MENU. IT ADDS TO IT.

InterludeSorokin's Forgotten Laboratory

Before the file carries the proposition into the organisation, it should record that this has been attempted before — that a major sociologist once set out to study love as a form of energy in social life, built an institute to do it, and was almost entirely forgotten. The proposition's author is not the first to file under this heading.

The man

Pitirim Sorokin was born in 1889 in a village in the far north of Russia, the son of an itinerant craftsman. He was imprisoned three times by the Tsar's government and three times by the Bolsheviks, was condemned to death in 1918 and reprieved, was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1922, and in 1930 became the founding chairman of the department of sociology at Harvard. He was, by mid-century, one of the most eminent social scientists in the world — and then did something his profession could not forgive. In 1949, with money from the pharmaceutical philanthropist Eli Lilly, he founded the Harvard Research Center in Creative Altruism, and announced that he would devote the rest of his life to the scientific study of love.

His colleagues were embarrassed. Talcott Parsons, his junior, who had displaced him from the chair, was building a sociology on quite other lines. The Center was treated as an old man's eccentricity. It closed when the money ran out. Sorokin's principal work from it, The Ways and Power of Love, published in 1954 — the same year as Tillich's book — went out of print and stayed there for nearly half a century.

The argument

Sorokin's reasoning was that of a man who had watched two revolutions and two world wars at close quarters. Humanity, he observed, had learned to release the energy of the atom and knew almost nothing about the energy that might stop it from using that knowledge on itself. The sciences had studied hatred, aggression, crime and madness in vast detail. On what he called the production, accumulation and distribution of love energy there was, he said, practically no science at all.

He meant the phrase. Love, for Sorokin, is a real force in social life — measurable in its effects, variable in quantity, capable of being generated, stored in persons and in institutions, and transmitted. He proposed that societies possess mechanisms for each, mostly unstudied. Its producers are, chiefly, certain persons: the great altruists, the saints, the ordinary good neighbours, each of whom he regarded as a kind of generator. Its accumulators are cultural: the scriptures, the music, the rituals, the exemplary lives remembered, in which love once produced is held for later release. Its distribution runs through families, communities and institutions that either conduct it or resist it.

Read this beside Davies's Signature and the kinship is plain: stored energies persisting across generations, awaiting activation; the humanities as the medium in which they are kept. Sorokin said it in 1954, about love by name.

The five dimensions

His most useful contribution was an attempt to say along what dimensions love varies, so that it might be compared and, roughly, measured. He gave five.

Intensity. From the trifling — giving up a seat — to the giving of one's life.

Extensity. From love of oneself alone, through family and nation, to all humankind and all that lives.

Duration. From a moment to a lifetime.

Purity. From love mixed with motives of advantage, pleasure or reputation, to love for its own sake.

Adequacy. The fit between what love intends and what it brings about. A love may be genuine and blind: the parent who smothers, the helper who harms. And conduct may be beneficial in effect with no love in it at all.

He then made an observation which the present work has reached by another road. The dimensions do not rise together. Love of great intensity tends to be of small extensity: one will die for one's child, and not for humanity. Love of wide extensity tends to be thin: goodwill toward all mankind costs little and does little. The rarest thing is love high on all five at once, and those who attain it, he argued from several hundred biographies, are the figures whose influence has outlasted every empire of their day.

What the file takes

Three things.

The dimension of adequacy is Papworth's appraisal, thirty years early. Sorokin saw that love's intention and love's effect can come apart, and that a science of love has to study the difference. A warm impulse that entrenches a victim scores high on intensity and purity and low on adequacy. His fifth dimension is the reason the proposition's state needs the disciplines of chapter twenty-nine.

The trade-off between intensity and extensity is the Contra's third objection, stated as an empirical regularity. Love is naturally partial. Extending it without thinning it is the problem — Mozi against the Confucians, agape against philia, Weber's clerk and the widow. Sorokin did not solve it. He documented that it had occasionally been solved, in persons, and thought the question of how was the most important one social science could ask.

The concept of accumulation gives the institution its function. If love can be held in cultural forms and released later, then an institution's stories, rituals, places and elders are capacitors, and the question to put to an institution is the engineer's: what is its capacitance, and what is its leakage?

Why he was forgotten, and why it matters

Sorokin's programme failed for reasons that bear directly on the present work.

Some were his own. His methods were loose; his biographies of saints took hagiography at its word; he moved without warning between measurement and exhortation. The energy language, in his hands, never became more than a suggestive analogy — he had no mathematics of thresholds, coupling or order parameters with which to give it structure. The sciences of complexity that might have supplied one were twenty years off.

But the larger reason was the taboo. Mid-century social science was establishing its credentials as a science, and love was the paradigm of what a science did not touch. A colleague of Sorokin's is said to have remarked that the trouble with the Center was that one could not tell whether it was a laboratory or a chapel.

The remark is fair to Sorokin and it is fair to this file. A work on love that draws on physics and on the Fathers of the Church is open to the same doubt. The file's defence is the one it has been making throughout: that the FILE NOTES say at each point which room one is standing in. But it records Sorokin here as a warning from a predecessor. He was right about the gap in the sciences; right that it mattered more than almost anything else they were doing; right in several of his particular claims — the literature of chapter twenty-six is in large part his programme carried out by people who had never heard of it. And he was forgotten, because he let his argument's evidential standards slip beneath its ambition. The proposition's author asked for this to be filed as experimental. Sorokin's fate is the reason to hold to the word.

WE CAN RELEASE THE ENERGY OF THE ATOM. OF THE PRODUCTION AND STORAGE OF LOVE WE KNOW ALMOST NOTHING.
