Movement V

THE ORGANISATION

Where It Must Be Tried

The word that cannot be said at work, and the evidence that the thing is there anyway. The room as atmosphere; the leader as source and as slope; three disciplines for love under pressure — compassion, agency, paradox; love and power; love and judgement; holding; and the institution that remembers.

25The Taboo Word

In a lifetime of board papers, strategy documents, credit submissions, annual reports and performance reviews, a diligent reader will meet the word love perhaps twice: once in a retail slogan and once in a leaving speech. It is the best-enforced silence in organisational life. People who will discuss, in a meeting, their redundancy, their cancer and their divorce will not use that word about their work or their colleagues, and if a chief executive were to say plainly that she loved her staff, the room would wonder what was coming.

The silence has reasons. They are good reasons, and a work proposing to break it owes them a hearing.

Weber's reason

The modern organisation was built to exclude love, and the exclusion was a moral achievement.

Max Weber's account of bureaucracy is commonly read as an indictment. It is closer to a eulogy. The bureaucratic official, he wrote, discharges his office sine ira et studio — without anger and without partiality; without hatred or passion, and therefore without affection or enthusiasm. The rule applies to the case, whoever the case may be. The office is separate from the person; the files from the household; the public purse from the private pocket. Appointment is by competence and not by kinship.

What this replaced was government by love — in the precise sense that under patrimonial rule everything went by personal attachment. The lord favoured those he was fond of. Office went to nephews. Justice depended on who one was to the judge. Weber's impersonality is the invention that allows a stranger to get a fair hearing: the widow with no connections receives her pension on the same terms as the minister's cousin, because the clerk does not care who she is. Every anti-corruption statute, every procurement rule, every conflict-of-interest register and every equal-opportunities policy is a monument to the proposition that love, at work, is what is to be kept out. The English words for love in the wrong place at work are nepotism, cronyism and favouritism, and they are terms of abuse.

So the first reason for the taboo is that love is partial, and organisations are obliged to be fair. A manager who loves some of her people more than others — and if love is a matter of particular attachment, how could she not? — and acts upon it is doing wrong, however warm it feels.

Arendt's reason

Hannah Arendt gave a deeper version of the objection in The Human Condition. Love, she argued, is by its very nature unworldly. What it does is abolish the in-between — the space of the common world which relates people to one another and at the same moment separates them. Lovers have no world between them; that is the bliss of it. But the public realm consists of the in-between: a table round which people sit, which relates and separates them at once. Take the table away and they are no longer a public; they are a huddle or a crowd. Love is therefore, she concluded, not only apolitical but antipolitical — perhaps the most powerful of all antipolitical forces. What can legitimately bind people in public is not love but respect: a regard for the person from the distance the world's space puts between us, a kind of friendship without intimacy.

She was writing with her century in view. The movements that had promised brotherhood, that had sought to make the nation one loving body with one heart and one will, had been the murderous ones. A politics of love slides toward the demand for unanimity, and from there to the identification of those who spoil it.

So the second reason: love collapses distance, and institutions need distance in order to hold plurality. The file's own sixth movement will show Arendt's fear realised in corporate form — the firm that is "a family," the team that is so close no one can disagree.

The third reason: instrumentalisation

There is a newer reason, and it is felt by precisely the people most drawn to the proposition. An employment relation is a power relation and an economic one. For an employer to speak of love within it risks two things together: demanding an affective performance from people who are not free to decline it, and wrapping an exchange of labour for wages in a language that makes its terms harder to contest. "We love our people" has been said by firms on the eve of dismissing them by video call. Arlie Hochschild's study of airline cabin crew, to which the file will return, showed what it costs a person when feeling itself becomes part of the job.

So the third reason: love at work may be extracted or faked, and to name it is to invite both.

The fourth reason: sex

And a plain one. In English the word unqualified suggests the erotic. Workplaces have had cause enough to learn that the erotic combined with power does harm, and the word is avoided partly from elementary prudence.

What the reasons establish

Taken together these are a strong case. The file accepts every one of them — and observes that not one is a case against what the proposition describes. Each is a case against a deformation which the work has already distinguished from it.

Weber's objection is to love as partiality: preferential attachment that bends judgement. The state the proposition names is a quality of presence to whoever is before one — Weil's what are you going through? — which can in principle be extended to the stranger and the widow as readily as to the favourite. The Greeks had different words: philia for the love of friends, erōs for desire, storgē for family affection — and, in the New Testament, agapē, a word chosen exactly because it carried little prior freight, for a love directed at the other's good which does not depend on the other's being attractive, or kin, or one's own. Weber's clerk, who gives the widow her due without caring who she is, is not agape's opposite. He may be its humblest instance — or its absence, according to what is in his face when he does it. The file's question is what difference that face makes.

Arendt's objection is to love as fusion. The Gestalt tradition has given a name to love that abolishes the in-between: confluence, which is not contact. The whole argument of chapter five was that love requires the boundary, and of chapter twenty-one that synchrony keeps the differing natural frequencies. Arendt's respect — regard across a distance kept — comes very close to what the file means by contact. She took fusion for love's essence. It is its commonest failure.

It should be added that Arendt was a more complicated witness than this one passage suggests. Her doctoral dissertation was on love in Augustine. And at the centre of her mature thought is a concept which she herself linked to love's one worldly product: natality — the fact that human beings are born, each a new beginning, and that because of this, action can start something that did not exist. She wrote that the miracle that saves the world from its ordinary ruin is at root the fact of birth; and the faculty she paired with it, as the only remedy for the irreversibility of what has been done, is forgiveness — which, she says, only love has the power to accomplish, though respect may do duty for it in the public realm. So even Arendt, having put love out at the door of the polis, found she needed two of its children indoors: the capacity to begin again, and the capacity to release each other from what we have done.

The instrumentalisation objection is to love commanded or counterfeited. If love is an order parameter that cannot be produced by producing its behaviours, and a social act whose meaning lies in the response, then it cannot be commanded and its counterfeits will be detected. That is an objection to bad practice, and the sixth movement is given to it.

The prudential objection is answered by vocabulary. The file says love and means what the tradition calls agape and Sigal Barsade called companionate love.

What the silence costs

If the reasons do not tell against the thing, then the taboo is suppressing something real for fear of its deformations. That has costs, and they are of a specific kind: what cannot be named cannot be noticed, protected, taught, or mourned.

It cannot be noticed. A hospital has a dozen measures of what its nurses do and none for the thing patients remember. When that thing declines, no indicator moves. The first sign is an inquiry.

It cannot be protected. A restructuring removes "duplication." What it removed was the two people who had worked side by side for nineteen years and between whom the unit's whole capacity for repair was carried. The business case had no line for that.

It cannot be taught. The partner whose teams would follow her anywhere retires. The firm has captured her client list and her precedents. What she actually did — which was to love her juniors, in the strict sense of chapter eight: to see each in the particular and in the possible — was never described and so is not passed on.

It cannot be mourned. When a workplace that had it is closed or merged or "transformed," people grieve with an intensity that mystifies those who did the arithmetic. They are told that change is always hard. No one says: you have lost a place where you were loved. And so the grief has no object, and turns to bitterness.

And there is a cost in honesty. People in organisations do love: their work, their colleagues, their patients, the craft, the place. It is frequently the truest thing about why they stay, and why they are good. Required to translate it into engagement, commitment and discretionary effort, they are required to misdescribe their own lives in a vocabulary invented to measure them. The corridor keeps the true account. The official record keeps the translation. This work has been, from its first page, an attempt to read the corridor's account into the record.

THE REASONS FOR THE SILENCE ARE REASONS AGAINST THE COUNTERFEITS.

26The Evidence That It Is There

The taboo has not kept researchers from finding the thing. It has made them find it under other names. This chapter collects what has been found, at the strength it can bear. The file's promise was that a doctrine of love must be able to be tried on a Tuesday afternoon; here are the people who have tried.

Barsade and O'Neill: the word, used

In 2014 Sigal Barsade of Wharton and Olivia O'Neill of George Mason University published a paper in Administrative Science Quarterly — the discipline's most demanding journal — whose title put the forbidden word in a question: "What's Love Got to Do with It?" They defined a culture of companionate love as one marked by the expression of affection, caring, compassion and tenderness among colleagues, and they set out to learn whether it mattered.

The setting was a large long-term care facility and hospital in the north-eastern United States, studied over sixteen months: a hundred and eighty-five employees, over a hundred residents, forty-two family members. The culture of each unit was assessed not only by asking staff but by outside raters, by family members, and by cultural artefacts.

Units with a stronger culture of companionate love had employees with higher satisfaction and better teamwork, less emotional exhaustion and lower absenteeism. And the effect reached those the organisation was for: patients in those units were in better mood, reported better quality of life and satisfaction, and made fewer trips to the emergency room.

Lest it be thought a peculiarity of caring work, they then surveyed three thousand two hundred and one employees in seven industries — among them biopharmaceuticals, engineering, financial services, higher education, real estate, travel and utilities. Companionate love in the culture was associated with greater satisfaction, commitment and personal accountability. Barsade reported afterwards that levels varied as much within industries as between them. Sector is not destiny; there are loving teams in finance and loveless ones in hospices.

Three observations.

It is the culture, not the trait, that is measured. The variable was a property of the unit, assessed from several vantage points. That is a field-level variable, in the language of this work; an order parameter read from outside.

The effect crosses the organisational boundary. The love was among the staff; the benefit appeared in the patients. This is the wavefront: Huygens's principle on a hospital ward. The nurses were not instructed to pass it on. Each point reached became a source.

The limits should be stated. The main study was of a single organisation; the cross-industry extension was a correlational survey; the association with the hard clinical outcomes was weaker than with mood and satisfaction; and the authors found the benefit was greater for employees of sunnier disposition. It is a strong first study and not the last word.

Dutton: connection and compassion

At the University of Michigan, Jane Dutton and a circle of colleagues spent two decades studying what they chose to call positive organisational scholarship. Two strands matter here.

The first is the high-quality connection. Dutton and Emily Heaphy argued that the basic unit of organisational life is not the role or the relationship but the connection — which may be momentary: a thirty-second exchange in a corridor. A high-quality connection has three structural marks: it can bear a greater range and intensity of emotion; it has tensility — it bends under strain and springs back; and it is generative. And it has three subjective marks: a sense of vitality, of positive regard, and of mutuality. They gathered evidence that such connections have immediate physiological effects — on cardiovascular reactivity, on immune function — and they proposed a phrase the proposition's author will recognise: that connections are life-giving or life-depleting, like the vessels of a body.

A moment; felt in the body; enlivening; mutual; recoverable under strain. It is the proposition's state, given in the idiom of the business school — with vitality doing duty for energy, positive regard for the form perceived under the law of closure, and tensility for the reliability of repair.

The second strand is compassion organising. Dutton, Monica Worline, Peter Frost and Jacoba Lilius studied what happened in a university when three students lost everything in a fire. Within days, with no central direction, money, clothes, housing, books and replacement coursework had been assembled. The paper anatomised how one person's noticing became an organisation's response: the process ran through existing structures put to a new use — routines, networks, the values people could appeal to — and through the emergence of roles no one had assigned. Their finding is, in the terms of chapter twenty-three, about enabling constraints: the organisation already possessed the channels; what the fire did was to send something else along them.

Worline and Dutton later condensed the work into a four-part account of compassion at work: noticing suffering; interpreting it generously; feeling empathic concern; and acting to alleviate. They stressed how easily the sequence breaks at its first step — how much suffering in organisations is simply not seen.

Papworth: the appraisal step

It is on that four-part sequence that Kirstie Papworth's Compassionate Leadership, the first of the three De Gruyter volumes laid on this file, makes its distinctive intervention, and the file wants to give it with some care because it corrects a tendency in the present work.

Papworth reviews the earlier models and proposes a construct of her own in four steps: awareness, feeling, appraisal, responding. The first, second and fourth have ancestors. The third is her addition, and it has four parts.

One appraises safety and intention: is it safe to act, and what am I actually after in acting? One appraises patterns of behaviour — here she draws on transactional analysis, on Eric Berne's psychological games and Stephen Karpman's Drama Triangle of victim, persecutor and rescuer — asking whether one's impulse to help is a move in a familiar game that will leave the sufferer more fixed in the victim's place and oneself gratified in the rescuer's. One appraises resources: have I the capacity for this, and if not, what must I do first? And one appraises role: is this mine to do, in the position I occupy — bearing in mind that a leader's acts, and a leader's omissions, are amplified.

She then states what she calls compassion maths. All four steps are required. Without awareness, the suffering goes unseen. Without feeling, the response is robotic. Without appraisal, action may deplete the actor, exceed the role, serve a Machiavellian end, or entrench a victim. And — the sentence the file most wants from her — "Without action, the response is empathy, not compassion." Action with no thought for oneself she calls altruism, and distinguishes it firmly.

Why does this correct the present work? Because the file has, so far, leaned heavily on the immediacy of love: the look, the crossing, the direct perception of form, the heart that knows before the head. All true. But a work that stopped there would license something dangerous — the belief that because love is immediate, the immediate impulse is love. Papworth's appraisal step is the place where the warm impulse is examined before it is acted upon. It is a practitioner's version of the scholastic doctrine that charity is the form of the virtues and prudence their charioteer: love supplies the end; practical wisdom must still find the act. It is also, exactly, the contact boundary. The rescuer in Karpman's triangle is confluent: he has merged with the victim's helplessness and needs it. Appraisal is how the boundary is kept in the moment of being moved.

There is a correspondence here with the Gestalt cycle that deserves to be set down. Awareness is sensation become figure. Feeling is the mobilisation of energy. Responding is action and contact. Papworth has inserted, between mobilisation and action, a moment the Cleveland cycle does not mark and that every experienced practitioner knows: the breath in which the mobilised energy is aimed. On the torus it is the point of emergence from the centre, where the upward flow turns outward and takes its direction. A fountain with no nozzle is a flood.

She also reviews what she frankly calls compassion's dubious reputation: that it is weak, that it tires people out, that it is a vice dressed as a virtue. On fatigue she follows the neuroscientists Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki, whose work the file will need in the sixth movement, and reports their conclusion that what exhausts carers is not compassion but empathic distress — the unregulated sharing of another's pain — and that compassion, which is other-directed and moves toward action, activates different neural systems and is associated with positive affect. And on the organisation she insists, with the philosopher Gregory Pence, that compassion cannot rest on a few admirable individuals: it must be built into four layers of the institution — the strategic, the structural, the behavioural and the cultural. The file will draw on that in the chapter on the institution that remembers.

Energy, measured

The proposition's word is energetic, and there is an empirical literature that uses the word without embarrassment.

Rob Cross, Wayne Baker and Andrew Parker, mapping the informal networks of large firms, added to their surveys a question about each colleague: when you interact with this person, how does it typically affect your energy? The answers yield a map of energisers and de-energisers which is not the map of friendship or of information flow. Their reports are consistent: people identified as energisers are higher performers, and so are those connected to them; ideas proposed by energisers are more likely to be taken up; and de-energisers do damage out of proportion to their number, with people going to considerable lengths to route round them. What energisers do, on their interview evidence, is unglamorous. They are fully present in the conversation. They create a sense of real possibility. They allow others to contribute. They engage with integrity between word and deed — the coherence of chapter eighteen.

Bradley Owens, Wayne Baker, Dana Sumpter and Kim Cameron gave this a formal construct, relational energy — the heightened psychological resourcefulness generated from interaction with another, which enhances one's capacity to work — and showed across several studies that relational energy with one's leader predicts engagement and, through it, performance, over and above other well-established measures of the relationship.

And Ryan Quinn and Jane Dutton made the theoretical statement nearest to this file's own: that energy is not merely an input or an outcome of coordination but its very texture. In each conversational turn, they argued, people read whether the exchange is raising or lowering their autonomy, competence and relatedness; their energy rises or falls accordingly; and that energy shapes the next turn. Coordination is energy-in-conversation. That is Stacey's gesture and response, with a gauge fitted.

The sociologist Randall Collins had built a general theory on the same foundation. Interaction rituals — any occasion on which people are bodily co-present, share a focus of attention and a common mood, and fall into rhythmic entrainment — generate what he called emotional energy: confidence, enthusiasm, initiative. People are, in his view, seekers of emotional energy; they move toward the encounters that charge them and away from those that drain. A person's biography is a chain of such rituals. Collins drew this from Durkheim's collective effervescence; and the fire-walking study of chapter eleven found that effervescence on a heart monitor.

Fredrickson: love as a micro-moment

The psychologist Barbara Fredrickson has offered the most direct scientific redefinition. In Love 2.0 she proposed that love, considered as an emotion, is not a lasting bond but a momentary event — she calls it positivity resonance — with three woven strands: a sharing of positive emotion between two or more people; a synchrony of their biochemistry and behaviour; and a reflected motive of mutual care. It may last seconds. It may occur between strangers. Lasting bonds are what accumulate from many such moments.

She has reported that such moments are associated with the tone of the vagus nerve — the heart's brake — and that the relation runs in both directions, in what she calls an upward spiral; the specific longitudinal claims have had a contested history, and one prominent mathematical claim from her earlier work was withdrawn after critique. The file notes both and holds to the conceptual point, which survives: that a leading emotion scientist, asked what love is at the level of the body, answered — a brief, shared, synchronised, mutual state, of which the heart's regulation is part. It is not the proposition's vocabulary. It is the proposition's object.

Edmondson: the space that allows truth

And the finding that has travelled furthest. In the 1990s Amy Edmondson, studying drug errors in hospital teams, expected the better-led teams to make fewer. Her data showed them making more. It took her some time to see that they were not making more errors; they were reporting more, because in those teams an error could be spoken of. She named the variable psychological safety — a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — and three decades of work have tied it to learning, to quality, and to performance.

Edmondson is careful that this is not niceness, not comfort, not a lowering of standards. It is the condition under which candour is possible. In the vocabulary of this work it is Lewin's round life space, measured: a room without a front.

What it comes to

Laid side by side, these literatures triangulate something. There is a property of working groups — not of individuals — which is experienced as energy, warmth and safety; which arises in moments of contact and builds over time; which is bodily and involves physiological coupling; which spreads beyond its origin to third parties; which increases what people can do, say and learn; and which has measurable consequences for the people served. It has been called companionate love, high-quality connection, compassion, relational energy, emotional energy, positivity resonance and psychological safety, by people working mostly without reference to one another.

The file's contention is that these are seven names for the aspects of one thing; that the one thing is what the proposition, in its unsteady language, was describing whole; and that the reason the literature has seven names and no account of their unity is the taboo. Each team of researchers found the part that could be published under the word it could get past the reviewers.

SEVEN LITERATURES. ONE PHENOMENON. THE WORD NONE OF THEM COULD USE.

27The Room: Atmosphere

The Overture began in a room that had a temperature and no thermometer. Seven literatures have now been reviewed which measure what people in rooms do. It remains to say what the room is — what kind of thing has a temperature of that sort.

Böhme and Schmitz

The German philosopher Gernot Böhme made atmosphere the central concept of a new aesthetics. An atmosphere, he argued, is what one meets on entering a space, before noticing any object in it: the tense air of a meeting, the hush of a church, the cheer of a kitchen. It is grasped at once and as a whole. And it has a peculiar ontological standing. It is not a property of the things in the room — one can list every object and miss it. It is not a mere projection of the visitor's mood either — a cheerful person walking into a room of mourners does not find it cheerful; they find their cheer jarring against something that is there. Atmospheres are in between. Böhme calls them quasi-objective: spatially poured out, without edges, not locatable, and yet encountered as real. He describes a space so qualified as tuned, and the things and persons within it as contributing to its tuning by their "ecstasies" — the ways they go out from themselves into the space.

He took the concept from Hermann Schmitz, founder of what he called the New Phenomenology, who made a still stronger claim: that feelings are atmospheres. Western thought since Plato, Schmitz argued, has made a mistake he named introjection — locating feelings inside a private container called the soul. In experience they are not found there. Grief, joy, shame, the solemnity of an occasion: these are encountered as spatially extended powers which seize a person in what he calls the felt body — the Leib, the body as lived from within, as distinct from the body the anatomist dissects. One does not have a feeling and then express it into the room. One is gripped by a feeling that is in the room.

Readers will see how this meets the proposition. The field it creates and emanates extends beyond the human body: Schmitz would say that puts the matter the wrong way round, though in the right direction. The feeling was never inside the body to extend out of it. Love is an atmosphere; atmospheres are where feelings live; the lover is one whom it has seized and who, by her "ecstasies", contributes to its tuning.

Schmitz's concept of the felt body gives the proposition's cardial a philosophical home besides. The felt body is not laid out like the anatomical one; it is organised by what he calls corporeal islands — regions of felt presence that come and go — and by a fundamental rhythm of narrowing and widening. Fear, pain and shame narrow: one is pressed in upon oneself. Joy and relief widen: the chest opens, one expands into the space. And the chest region is the principal island where this is felt. Heart-burst, in his vocabulary, is the extreme of widening: the abrupt release of a felt body from constriction into expanse. Any person can verify the general phenomenon by attending to their sternum while receiving first bad news and then its retraction.

The room as an instrument

If atmospheres are real in this sense, then a room is an instrument which is tuned, and a great part of organisational life consists in the tuning — unintended, unexamined, done by nobody in particular.

The physical tuning. The long table with a head. The glass wall through which a meeting is watched by those excluded from it. The reception desk raised eighteen inches above the visitor. The call-centre floor on which a supervisor's screen shows who has been in the lavatory more than four minutes. These are Böhme's "generators" of atmosphere, and architects have always known it; the Cistercians understood exactly what a cloister does to a quarrel. Open-plan offices were introduced in the name of communication, and the studies that followed, tracking people with sensors before and after, found face-to-face interaction falling sharply and electronic messaging rising. Remove every boundary and nobody can make contact; they put on headphones.

The temporal tuning. What happens in the first ninety seconds. Does the meeting open with the agenda, or does anything human occur first? Is there a silence? Who speaks first, and to whom do eyes go when anyone else has finished? Collins's ingredients of an interaction ritual — co-presence, a barrier to outsiders, a shared focus, a common mood — are either assembled in those seconds or not, and the emotional energy that the meeting will generate or consume is largely settled before the first item.

The personal tuning. Each person entering carries an atmosphere and is met by one. Böhme's point about the cheerful visitor among mourners describes the collision. Whose prevails? Usually the room's, which has the inertia of numbers. But not always: there are persons whose atmosphere re-tunes rooms. The Overture described one. And there are persons, likewise, who can lower the temperature of any gathering by entering it. The network analysts' energisers and de-energisers are the measurable shadows of this.

Reading the room

The ability to perceive atmospheres accurately — the corridor says to read the room — is among the most valuable capacities anyone in an organisation can have and it is nowhere taught. It is not the reading of individual faces. It is the perception of a gestalt, a whole, a tuning; it is done by the felt body, as narrowing or widening in oneself; and it is quicker than thought.

Three practical notes.

The instrument is oneself. One reads the room by what it does to one's own chest, breath, shoulders. This was the Gestalt consultant's method, the use of self as instrument, and it is Schmitz's point about the felt body. Hence the importance of interoception: someone who cannot feel their own narrowing has no gauge. The executive who "didn't see it coming" was very often in a room whose atmosphere everyone else was registering in the sternum, with an instrument he had trained himself not to consult.

The reading must be distinguished from the reader. The cheerful visitor knows the difference between his mood and the room's because they jar. When they do not jar the two are easily confused. An anxious chair experiences an anxious meeting — and cannot tell whether she is reading it or tuning it. Probably both; it is circular causality. The discipline is to ask: what was I carrying when I came in?

The reading should sometimes be said. The most powerful single intervention available in a mis-tuned room is to name the atmosphere, without blame, as one's own perception: "I notice we've all gone very careful. I have, anyway." This is Beisser's paradox at work — contact with what is. It is Papworth's awareness, spoken; and it honours her observation that being seen is itself a response. Very often the naming discharges the thing, as the charge at a conductor's point discharges with a glow. Sometimes it does not, and the namer is left standing alone in a silence. That risk is what makes it an act of love and not a technique.

Love as an atmosphere

What is the atmosphere of a room in which the proposition's state is present? The file risks a description, drawn from the convergences so far, as a set of marks one could look for.

It is wide. Felt bodies are expanded, not contracted. People take up their natural space. Breathing is low and slow.

It is round. In Lewin's sense: it has no front. Nobody is positioned. One could say anything from anywhere.

It is unhurried without being slow. Much may be going on; the interval is right. Turns are taken in time. A silence can occur and is not rushed to be filled.

It is bright, in the corridor's word: things are distinct. People see one another and the matter in hand with a certain sharpness — the higher resolution of chapter eight. It is not a haze of goodwill. Disagreements are clearer in it, not blurrier.

It is warm and not hot. Motovilov said warmth as in a bath-house, while the snow fell. There is energy and it is not agitation. Excitement with breath, in the Gestalt phrase.

It is directed beyond itself. Attention goes through the group to what the group is for. The atmosphere is not about how well everyone is getting on; a room that is enjoying its own warmth is already a closed loop.

And it is uncontrollable. Rosa's fourth mark of resonance. It was not produced by anyone and cannot be produced again by repeating what was done. It can be made room for. It can be destroyed in a sentence.

This last property is why organisations, which exist to make outcomes reliable, find the phenomenon so difficult to hold. An atmosphere of love cannot be specified, procured, guaranteed or scaled. It can only be hoped for, prepared for, recognised, and protected. The verbs available to management do not include the right ones. One hosts it.

YOU DO NOT HAVE A FEELING AND PUT IT IN THE ROOM. THE FEELING IS IN THE ROOM AND HAS YOU.

InterludeA Ward at Handover

A second scene, composed like the last. The argument of the preceding chapter was that a room is an instrument which is tuned. Here is one being tuned, at seven in the morning, by nobody in particular.

The ward has twenty-eight beds and this morning twenty-nine patients, one of them on a trolley by the linen cupboard. The night staff have been on for twelve and a half hours. The day staff are coming in with wet coats. Handover is in the office, which was built for four and holds eleven, standing.

The nurse in charge overnight reads from the sheet. Bed one, bed two. She reads fast and flat, because she is tired and because the day staff have heard a thousand of these. Bed six, a fall at three; not hurt; the form is done. Bed nine. She stops.

"Bed nine died at ten past five."

Nobody says anything. It was expected. He was ninety-one. The sheet has the time and the name of the doctor who certified.

There are two ways this goes, and the ward has had mornings of both kinds.

In the first, she reads on. Bed ten. The day staff write. A healthcare assistant near the door, who sat with him through most of the small hours because the family could not get there, looks at the floor. Bed eleven. In four minutes they are finished and the night staff go home. The assistant gets into her car and sits a while before she starts it. Nobody did anything wrong. Tomorrow night she will be a degree more careful about how long she sits with anyone.

This is the other morning.

The sister coming on for the day — fifty, brisk, not a sentimental woman, known for sending students home to iron their uniforms — puts her pen down on the desk. That is all. She puts her pen down, and looks at the night nurse, and waits.

The night nurse looks up from the sheet. Something in her face alters.

"Dawn was with him," she says. "She held his hand from about two. His daughter rang at four and Dawn held the phone to his ear." She turns to the door. "She was brilliant."

The assistant by the door says, "He was all right. He wasn't frightened." Her voice goes on the last word.

The sister says, "Thank you, Dawn." It is not said warmly. It is said the way she says everything — as a fact which is to be recorded. Then: "Did the daughter get here?"

"Half past six. She's in the relatives' room."

"Has she had a cup of tea?"

No one knows.

"Right. I'll go in after this. Dawn, before you go — would you come in with me for two minutes? She'll want to meet whoever was with him." The assistant nods. She is crying, quite quietly, and no one is embarrassed by it, and a staff nurse beside her has put a hand flat between her shoulder blades without looking at her.

"Bed ten," says the sister.

The night nurse reads on. But she is reading differently — slower; she looks up between beds. At bed fourteen a student who has not opened her mouth all week says that she thinks the lady in fourteen is more confused than yesterday, and she is not sure, but. In the first kind of morning she would not have said it. The sister says, "Good. Go and look at her obs chart with Priya straight after and tell me what you find."

It takes six minutes instead of four.

What happened? A pen was put down.

In the vocabulary this work has been assembling: the handover was a ritual being run as a procedure — bodies co-present, no shared focus, no common mood; a still face, eleven of them. The report of a death came to a bifurcation. One small fluctuation selected the branch. The sister made a gesture, and its meaning was not in it; had the night nurse read on, the pen would have been a pen. The night nurse completed it. Then the wavelet went on: the assistant spoke; a hand was laid on a back; a student found that the room was round and said a thing she was unsure of — which may, this afternoon, turn out to have mattered to the lady in fourteen.

The return path was restored: the one who gave, through the night, was shown to the one it was for. In two minutes' time a daughter will meet the woman who held the telephone to her father's ear, and both will be changed by it, and the assistant will drive home having set something down.

The sister appraised her role. She did not make a speech about valuing staff. She did not hug anyone; she is not that sort and the ward would have been alarmed. She was aware — of what was unsaid on the sheet, the white space; she weighed, in the time it takes to put down a pen, what was hers to do; and she did the least that would do it. Then she said "bed ten," because twenty-eight other people need the ward to work.

And nobody in that office, asked at half past seven what had occurred at handover, would say that anything had. Bed nine died. Sister was all right about it. It was a good handover.

By such things a ward is tuned. They are not in the nursing strategy. When this sister retires, in four years, the ward's sickness rate will rise by a third, and a review will be commissioned to find out why.

A PEN WAS PUT DOWN. THAT WAS THE INTERVENTION.

How to check it. Ask a ward nurse.

A caution. The scene makes its point with a sympathetic sister and a happy sequel. Real handovers are noisier, and a pen put down is often just a pen. The meaning, as chapter 22 insists, was in the response.

Registers used here
  • E Experiential. Reported from the first person, by the author of the proposition or by a witness in the tradition. True as experience; open as to cause.

28The Leader: Source and Slope

The literature on leadership is the largest in management and the least cumulative, and this file does not propose to add a theory to it. It proposes to collect what the foregoing chapters imply about one question: if love is what this work has said it is, what is a leader in relation to it?

Four things, and they are in tension.

The leader as point source

By Grosseteste's principle, every agent multiplies its species; by Huygens's, every point reached is a source. A leader is a point from which a form radiates, and the form is not what they say. It is what they are in the moment of saying it.

The evidence is unambiguous that this propagation is real. Barsade and O'Neill observed that the chief determinant of the companionate love in a manager's group is the companionate love the manager shows. Barsade's earlier experimental work on what she called the ripple effect had planted a trained confederate in small groups and shown that his enacted mood spread to the others and altered how they cooperated and how they judged their own performance — and that they did not know it had happened. Papworth, for her part, makes it a formal element of appraisal: a leader must weigh their role precisely because leadership amplifies actions and their absence. The leader who fails to notice has not done nothing. They have broadcast non-noticing.

This is the simplest and most uncomfortable of the four. A leader cannot have a private mood. And since, by Duchenne, the true marks of the photonic language are not under voluntary control, a leader cannot reliably perform one they do not have. The only way to emanate a thing is to be in it.

The leader as slope

By Lewin and Juarrero, a leader is a heavy constraint on the life spaces of others: part of the shape of the landscape across which they move. This has nothing to do with emanation. It concerns consequences: what happens, here, to someone who brings bad news, admits ignorance, disagrees, asks for help.

A leader may be personally warm and still be a steep slope away from candour — because of what happened to the last person who spoke up, or what is known to have befallen someone three years ago under a predecessor, or simply because they hold the power of appointment and nobody yet knows how they use it. Warmth is felt in the room; slope is known from history. A new leader inherits a landscape cut by others, and discovers that their own good intentions do not alter it. Only acts alter it — and, in particular, the first few occasions on which someone tests the ground. Every organisation watches those occasions with total attention. What the leader does when first contradicted in public reshapes the life space of several hundred people in an afternoon.

The leader as weakly coupled oscillator

By Kuramoto, the order that matters arises from mutual coupling, and power tends to reduce a person's coupling: everyone attends to the leader's timing and the leader need attend to no one's. The result is pacemaker entrainment — an order that depends on the driver and vanishes with it.

So here is the first tension. The leader's signal is the strongest in the room; and the stronger it is, the more the room organises round them and the less round one another. The emanation that the first heading commended can, by its very success, prevent the mutual synchrony which is the thing itself. A brilliant, warm, coherent leader may produce a group in which every member is coupled to the leader and no member is coupled to any other. It feels wonderful. It is a hub and spokes, and the measure of it is what happens on the day the leader leaves.

The remedy is not to shine less. It is to be affected more — to raise one's own coupling — and to turn the room's attention from oneself to one another and to the work. This was the point of chapter fifteen's distinction between the luminous and the super-luminous: the leader by whose light one sees, and who is herself hardly seen.

The leader as participant

And by Stacey and Mead, the leader is none of the above from any vantage outside the interaction. They make gestures. What the gestures mean is settled by responses they do not command. The leader "as source" is a description after the event of social acts that happened to complete.

Here is the second tension, and it is with the whole notion of leadership development as the acquisition of a capacity to emanate. No one becomes a source by resolving to. The woman in the Overture did not come in meaning to transform a meeting. She came in and paid attention to a man. Had she come in intending to radiate, she would have been attending to herself, and nothing would have crossed.

What follows: four disciplines

From the four descriptions, four disciplines. None of them is a technique.

Be in what you would have spread. One cannot emanate what one is not in. The interior work — whatever form it takes for a given person: prayer, therapy, friendship, a rule of life, plain honesty with oneself — is not preparation for leadership. It is the thing, since the form one is in is the form that propagates. Papworth devotes a full chapter to self-compassion for leaders, and positions it not as indulgence but as resourcing; her review of the research distinguishes it from self-pity, self-esteem and self-criticism, and reports its association with resilience and with better, not worse, acceptance of responsibility for one's mistakes. The file would put it in terms of the cavity: a leader without mirrors cannot lase. And it adds a gloss from the same author which is salutary. She cites research that people who introspect by asking why tend to be less self-aware and less content than those who ask what — what am I feeling, what is the pattern, what will I do. The mirror must show the emission, not explain it.

Attend to the first tests. The slope is changed by acts, at bifurcations. When the first person brings the first piece of truly unwelcome news, what the leader does in the following four seconds — with their face, before a word — will be known to everyone by evening.

Be moved, visibly, by those with no power to compel it. Raise the coupling. Change one's mind in public because of something a junior said, and say that that is why. Ask the question to which one does not know the answer and wait for it. Let the room see that what they do alters what you do. Nothing else brings a leader into the mutual order as one of its members instead of as its pacemaker.

Make the gesture and wait for its meaning. Give up the fantasy of the designer. The practice is to make the next gesture one honestly can, and then attend with complete seriousness to the response, since that is where one will learn what one did.

Greenleaf and the test

Robert Greenleaf, an AT&T executive who retired to write, published in 1970 an essay called "The Servant as Leader". Its seed was Hermann Hesse's story of a band of travellers sustained by their cheerful servant Leo, which falls apart when he disappears — and which learns, long after, that Leo had been the head of the order that sponsored the journey. Greenleaf's thesis was that the great leader is servant first, and he offered a test which may be the best single criterion in the literature:

Do those served grow as persons? Do they, while being served, become healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous, more likely themselves to become servants?

Read through this work, that test is asking of a leader: are you a point source or a wavefront? A sink, a jet, a closed loop — or a torus? Does what crosses from you make new sources? It applies Huygens's principle to persons, and it has the merit of being checkable over time by looking at who the leader's people have become.

One of Papworth's citations bears on the mechanism. She draws attention to research on what its authors call elevation: the uplifted, prosocial state that people enter on witnessing an act of moral excellence. Leaders who are visibly given to the common good, and who treat people exceptionally well, are reported to induce it in those who watch, with measurable gains in consideration for others and in commitment. Elevation is a wavelet. It is what Huygens's principle feels like from the inside of the point being reached — the warmth and widening in the chest on seeing someone do a beautiful thing, followed by the wish to do likewise. And the wish to do likewise is the re-emission.

Charisma, distinguished

The reader may think the file has simply been describing charisma. It has not, and the difference decides everything in the sixth movement.

Weber's charismatic leader is set apart: endowed, in the eyes of followers, with extraordinary powers. Attention flows to him. The bond is of each follower to the leader. It is intense, unstable, dependent on continual proof, and it does not survive him without being turned into something else. In the terms of this work: luminous, not super-luminous; a pacemaker, not a coupling; a hub. And very often a sink presenting as a source — for the charismatic commonly draws energy from the adoration of the following, and gives back a reflected version of what they gave him.

The leader in whom the proposition's state is present has opposite marks at each point. Attention flows through her to the work and to one another. The bonds she fosters are among the others. She is frequently unremarkable to meet. What she leaves is a population of sources.

There is a short test, usable on any leader in any organisation, and the reader may care to run it on those they have worked for. AFTER AN HOUR WITH THIS PERSON, DO YOU THINK MORE HIGHLY OF THEM — OR OF YOURSELF, YOUR COLLEAGUES AND THE WORK?

THE CHARISMATIC LEADER IS SEEN. THE LOVING ONE IS SEEN BY.

29Three Disciplines for Love Under Pressure

Part-way through its drafting, three books were laid on this file with an instruction to analyse, synthesise, distil and apply them. All three belong to one series — De Gruyter's Transformative Thinking and Practice of Leadership and Its Development, edited by Bernd Vogel of Henley — and none is about love. One is about compassion. One is about ethical choice. One is about paradox. They have been cited in passing where their matter touched the argument. This chapter treats them together, because together they supply what the proposition most conspicuously lacks.

The proposition describes a state: sudden, luminous, whole. It says nothing about what one is to do in that state on a Wednesday, when the person in front of one is suffering and also underperforming; when what the organisation asks conflicts with what one believes; when two goods pull apart and both are owed. A state is not yet a practice. These three volumes are, each of them, an account of the practice — of what the heart must learn in order to act well under pressure, which is the only condition in which organisations ever act. The file takes them as three disciplines and argues that they are three because love under pressure meets three different resistances.

The first resistance: suffering. The discipline of compassion

Kirstie Drummond Papworth, Compassionate Leadership: For Individual and Organisational Change (2023).

When love meets suffering it is called compassion; and Papworth's concern is with what must happen between meeting it and helping. Her four steps have been set out: awareness, feeling, appraisal — of safety and intention, of patterns, of resources, of role — and responding. The distillation is her own arithmetic: remove any one step and what remains is something else. Remove awareness, and nothing is seen. Remove feeling, and the help is cold. Remove appraisal, and the help may be a rescuer's game, an overreach of role, or a self-emptying that cannot last. Remove response, and one has only empathy.

She adds a chapter the file commends to anyone inclined to think their own compassion is beyond examination: on cognitive bias. Confirmation bias, self-serving bias, the fundamental attribution error, availability, inattentional blindness, in-group favouritism, the just-world hypothesis, naïve cynicism, negativity, the bystander effect — she takes each in turn and shows at which of her four steps it interferes. Inattentional blindness defeats awareness. In-group favouritism narrows feeling to those like oneself. The just-world hypothesis corrupts appraisal with the thought that the sufferer must have earned it. The bystander effect halts response while everyone waits for someone else. The heart has reasons; it also has habits, and some of them are prejudices.

Applied to the proposition. The proposition's state is, in her terms, an intense form of the first two steps: awareness so full that the other is perceived whole, feeling so strong it is felt in the chest. Her construct says that this is half. And it names the specific ways in which the luminous half goes wrong when the other half is wanting. The person seized by a great warmth toward another, who acts on it at once and without appraisal, may be playing rescuer; may be exceeding what their role permits; may be spending what they have not got; may be favouring one of their own. The heart-burst needs a nozzle. Her appraisal step is the organ of prudence in love — and it answers Weber's objection from within, since the appraisal of role is exactly the question of whether this warmth is mine to act on, here, in this office, toward this person and not that one.

The second resistance: the system. The discipline of agency

Aidan McQuade, Ethical Leadership: Moral Decision-making Under Pressure (2022).

When love meets an organisation that requires what love cannot do, it must become choice; and McQuade's concern is with how an individual chooses rightly when everyone around them is choosing otherwise. He writes from a working life in humanitarian relief and then at the head of the world's oldest human-rights organisation, and the examples he reasons from are forced labour in supply chains, child marriage, a coup.

He begins from the finding that should trouble anyone who thinks goodness comes naturally: the experiments of Milgram, of Zimbardo, of Darley and Latané. Most people, most of the time, go along. Determinism has a good deal to be said for it. And yet some do not go along. To explain the some, he builds a model out of two sociological accounts of agency — Margaret Archer's "internal conversation" and the temporal analysis of Mustafa Emirbayer and Ann Mische — and gives it a memorable form.

Draw a horizontal line. It is the social situation one is in, which has a past — its taken-for-granted practices, how things are done here — a present, and a future toward which it is tending. Draw a vertical line through its centre. It is the person: below, the Me — the values and beliefs one's life has laid down; above, the You — who one hopes to become; and at the crossing, the I, now. He calls the figure the Cruciform of Agency. A choice is made at the crossing: the present self, deliberating between what the situation presses for and what its own biography and hope require.

Most of the time the two axes agree, or the horizontal one simply prevails; the past of the situation is carried forward into its future through a person who has not consulted the vertical at all. But sometimes the pressure of the situation sets up a dissonance with the Me and the You — and the person, finding the dissonance intolerable, dissents. That, McQuade argues, is what the refusers in the experiments were doing, and what his own gallery of moral exemplars did: they assessed the choice before them against cherished values and not merely against their interests in the situation. And he adds a third dimension that enlarges freedom: one is always in several social situations at once, and may judge a demand made in one from the standpoint of another. The man pressed toward corruption at work asks what the woman he loves would think of him.

For the harder cases — and he devotes a chapter to doctors facing end-of-life decisions, abortion and treatment against a patient's will — he coins a second term. Where the crossing yields not a clear clash with one's values but a grey uncertainty about which course is the most life-affirming, because goods conflict with goods, he calls the condition assonance: moral doubt. He holds that it is not a defect. It keeps the decision-maker aware that they may be wrong, open to new information, ready to correct. He draws on Martha Nussbaum for the tragic point that human beings often do wrong not by breaking their moral code but by privileging one code, or one reading of it, over another that also binds them. From all this he derives a code of six elements — three of process: appreciate complexity, take responsibility, reflect and learn; three of substance: attend to financial sustainability, operate within social and planetary limits, and, for the grey cases, choose life: judge which course does most good to the lives and livelihoods of others.

He closes with advice he once gave young engineers bound for disaster zones. Of everything he might have told them, he chose four words: "Don't be an arsehole." The reason he gives is the gravest thing in the book. They were going out to do good; and "good," he observes, has been the most seductive excuse for some of the most shameful things human beings have done. Every creed has its dark side and its light side, and they are the same creed.

Applied to the proposition. Three things.

First, the Cruciform gives the proposition a geometry for the moment of choice which its torus does not supply. The torus says how love circulates. The cross says where it is tested: at the intersection of what the room demands and what the heart holds. And the file cannot but notice — McQuade, an Irishman writing on moral courage, will not have been unaware — that the figure is a cross with a self at the centre of it. The heart sits where the beams meet. A heart-burst, in an organisation, is very often the moment at which the vertical axis reasserts itself against the horizontal: when someone, in a room carrying its past forward by sheer momentum, consults the Me and the You and says no, or not like this.

Second, it re-reads the Overture. The man giving his account in the passive voice was all horizontal: the situation's past practice of self-protection flowing through him into its future. The woman's look did something that the Cruciform lets us name. She was, for him, a second social situation intersecting the first — a relation in which another answer made sense. From within it he could judge what the first was making of him. Love, on this model, enlarges agency by supplying another axis to stand on. It is the reason the solitary seldom dissent, and the reason every one of McQuade's exemplars, examined closely, had someone.

Third, his warning about good is the most important corrective a work on love can receive, and it will govern the sixth movement. Love is the creed with the brightest light side and therefore the darkest dark one. What has been done to people for love — of God, of country, of the family, of the firm, of the people themselves and for their own good — fills the histories. A proposition that says you can become Love needs a guard at its elbow saying four plain words. The file adopts them. The most elementary test of whether what has crossed the room is love is whether the person from whom it came is, in McQuade's exact sense, behaving decently to whoever is in front of them — particularly to those who can do nothing for them.

The third resistance: contradiction. The discipline of paradox

Rikke Kristine Nielsen, Frans Bévort, Thomas Duus Henriksen and colleagues, Navigating Leadership Paradox: Engaging Paradoxical Thinking in Practice (2023).

When love meets two goods that pull apart and are both owed, it must learn to hold; and this book's concern is how a manager acts on a tension that will not go away. It reports a research programme with managers in Danish companies, and its temper is that of the workshop: five phases, ten common paradoxes, fifteen tools, twenty cases.

The distinction between problem, dilemma and paradox was introduced in chapter twenty-four, with the cork that comes back up. The five phases are: choose one's paradox, and check that it is one; investigate it — chiefly with the Paradox Quadrant, mapping the bright and dark side of each pole and reading it vertically and diagonally to find one's own favoured pole and blind spot; chart a course of action; act; and evaluate — after which the round begins again, since the navigation has no end.

Four of their observations carry particular weight for this file.

Not everyone is energised. They are candid that paradox is an energiser to some and a stressor to others, and they quote a distinguished scholar of the subject confessing that in practice, as distinct from theory, large tensions make her very uncomfortable. They ask their reader for three things before beginning — a wish to change something, curiosity, and a concrete challenge of one's own — and warn that paradox-talk kept general becomes a refined way of avoiding the thing.

We each have a knee-jerk. They offer a gallery of nine caricatures of the ways managers habitually meet a tension, running from the ostrich, who waits with head down for it to pass, to the action hero, who must do something at once. The purpose is self-recognition with a laugh: under pressure one does not choose a response, one emits one's habit.

Do not deparadoxify. Of the thresholds they identify in helping others, the third is the temptation to make a paradox comfortable by dissolving it, and the fifth is the difficulty of staying.

Communicate consistently inconsistently. Their most counter-intuitive counsel concerns what a manager should say. Leaders are schooled in clarity and consistency. But a manager truly navigating a paradox must, at different moments, emphasise different poles, and must admit to uncertainty; a message that honoured both poles would, by ordinary standards, be mixed. They defend this, following Eisenberg on strategic ambiguity, while setting out its dark side with equal care: paradoxical talk can be impression management, a defensive routine, a way of prolonging indecision, a badge of honour, or a means of silencing those who are being asked to "live with the tension" of an arrangement that suits the powerful. One of their sources supplies the right name for the corrupt form: complexity washing.

Applied to the proposition. The proposition speaks of love as a single state. The file has found, chapter by chapter, that the state is structured as a set of paradoxes in the Danish authors' strict sense — poles in conflict and interdependent, neither to be chosen. It is time to fill in their quadrant.

Take the paradox on which the next two chapters turn. One pole: mercy — being for this person, as they are, in their need. The other: truth — being for what is the case, what was promised, what is owed to the others. Call them, in organisational dress, care and accountability.

Mercy (care)Truth (accountability)
Bright sideThe person is seen whole; they can admit, learn, recover; the room is round; energy is releasedStandards mean something; others are treated fairly; reality is faced early; trust in the institution's word
Dark side, when over-emphasisedCollusion; the avoided conversation; rescuers and victims; resentment of those who carry the load; driftFear; the passive voice; concealment; the combat landscape; people as line items

Now read it their three ways. Vertically: can one honestly fill both boxes for each pole? Most people find one of the four very hard to write, and that is their blind spot. The warm-hearted cannot easily write the dark side of mercy; the rigorous cannot write the dark side of truth. Horizontally: the two bright sides are both goods; the two dark sides both harms; neither pole is the virtuous one. Diagonally — and here is the thing worth the price of the book: the dark side of truth is the mirror of the bright side of mercy, and conversely. What the rigorous manager fears in mercy (drift, unfairness) is the shadow of what she prizes (standards, fairness). What the kind manager fears in accountability (fear, concealment) is the shadow of what he prizes (safety, candour). Each is right about the other's dark side and blind to their own.

The proposition's state, the file submits, is the upper row held at once. And it is the only thing that can hold it — because, as chapter two argued from the law of closure, love sees the gap as a gap in a circle. It is merciful and truthful in one perception. Deparadoxified to the left, it is sentimentality. Deparadoxified to the right, it is severity. The Psalmist put the upper row in a single line, in which mercy and truth are met together and righteousness and peace have kissed.

The three together

Set side by side, the three disciplines make a shape.

Love meets…It must learn to…The instrumentThe failure it guards against
Papworthsufferingappraise before respondingthe four steps; the four appraisalsrescue, overreach, self-emptying, bias
McQuadethe systemchoose at the crossingthe Cruciform; assonance; the six-part codeconformity; and the tyranny of one's own good
Nielsen et al.contradictionhold both poles and keep movingthe Quadrant; the five phaseschoosing a pole; and complexity washing

And they need each other. Compassion without the Cruciform is kindness within whatever the system allows — and McQuade's field is full of kindly people in exploitative supply chains. The Cruciform without the Quadrant is a hero's ethic of dissent, which in the grey cases — his own assonance — has nothing to dissent to, since both courses are goods. The Quadrant without compassion is a manager's balancing act with nobody's face in it; and without the Cruciform it is exposed to the abuse its own authors name, in which "holding the tension" becomes the alibi for never choosing when choice is owed.

There is a temporal order among them, and it is the order of a single act. In the instant: awareness, feeling. In the breath: appraisal. At the crossing: choice, with doubt kept. And through the long sequel: the navigation of what the choice did not and could not resolve. See; weigh; choose; hold. It is as near to a rule of life for the proposition's state as the file can distil from three books that never mention it.

THE STATE IS GIVEN. THE PRACTICE IS LEARNED: SEE, WEIGH, CHOOSE, HOLD.

30Love and Power

A proposition about love that says nothing of power describes a world without organisations. Every relation in an institution is a relation of power — the capacity to affect another's situation, whether or not they consent — and the proposition's state, if it is real, has to exist there.

Tillich's definitions

In 1954 Paul Tillich published a short book called Love, Power, and Justice, which undertook to rescue all three words from the sentimentality and cynicism that had overtaken them, by defining them ontologically — as features of being itself.

Love, he said, is the drive toward the reunion of the separated. It presupposes a prior belonging-together: one can be reunited only with what one was never wholly estranged from. Power is the possibility of self-affirmation in spite of internal and external negation — the capacity of a being to actualise itself against what resists it. And justice is the form in which power actualises itself: the shape that being must take if it is to be affirmed in encounter with other beings.

From these he drew a conclusion that cut across his century's assumption that love and power are opposites. They cannot be. Love is the drive to reunite the separated; to accomplish that against resistance requires power; so power is love's instrument and love is power's meaning. Love that renounces power is, he said, a chaotic surrender, destroying both the one who loves and the one who accepts it. Power that renounces love has denied its own foundation, since the being that affirms itself by destroying what it is bound to is destroying itself.

King's sentence

Thirteen years later, Martin Luther King — who had written his doctoral dissertation partly on Tillich — condensed this into the form in which it entered the world. In his last presidential address to the Southern Christian Leadership Conference he said that one of the great problems of history was that the concepts of love and power had usually been contrasted as polar opposites, love identified with a resignation of power and power with a denial of love. And he set them right in a pair of perfectly balanced clauses: power that lacks love turns reckless and abusive, while love that lacks power turns sentimental and thin. At its best, he went on, power is love carrying out what justice demands, and justice is power setting right whatever stands against love.

He was speaking to a movement tempted to divide between those who would keep love and give up power and those who would take power and give up love. He told them it was the collision of immoral power with powerless morality that made the crisis of the age.

The paradox, mapped

Adam Kahane, who spent his working life facilitating intractable multi-party conflicts — in South Africa at the transition, in Guatemala, in Colombia — took King's sentence as the title and frame of a book, and described from experience what each pole does when it works alone. Power alone — the drive to get one's job done, to realise oneself — becomes, unchecked, the steamroller. Love alone — the drive to unite — becomes, unchecked, a smothering that suppresses every difference for the sake of harmony. His conclusion was that one cannot choose, and that one cannot quite do both at once either: one walks, he said, on two legs, shifting weight from one to the other, always slightly off balance.

That is a paradox in the Danish authors' strict sense, and Kahane's two legs are their navigation. The file sets it out in their quadrant.

Love (the drive to unite)Power (the drive to realise)
Bright sideConnection, inclusion, the whole kept in view; people are for one anotherThings get done; each can become what they are; wrongs can be stopped
Dark side, aloneSmothering; false harmony; nothing is decided; the strong need not listen because nobody presses themSteamrolling; winners and losers; fear; the whole torn for a part

The diagonal reading again gives the insight. What the advocates of love fear in power — domination — is the shadow of what they value: that no one be overridden. What the advocates of power fear in love — paralysis — is the shadow of what they value: that something be accomplished. And an organisation's history can very often be told as an oscillation between the lower two boxes: a period of consensual drift, ended by a strong hand; a period of the strong hand, ended by exhaustion and a wish for peace.

Two kinds of power

It helps to distinguish, as political philosophy long has, two things the one word covers. Latin kept them apart, and Spinoza made a system of the difference. Potestas is power over: command, authority, the capacity to determine what another shall do. Potentia is power to: capacity, the strength of a thing to exist and act, the force of its own nature.

Mary Parker Follett, the Boston social worker who became in the 1920s the most original thinker on organisations of her day and was then forgotten for half a century, drew the same line in plain English: power-over and power-with. Power-with is jointly developed; it is co-active and not coercive; it is not a quantity to be divided but one that grows by being exercised together. She thought the whole task of organisation was to find ways of increasing power-with and reducing the need for power-over. She also taught that the three ways of dealing with a conflict are domination, compromise and integration — in which neither side gives way and neither is split down the middle, because a third course is found in which both desires have a place. Integration, she said, requires bringing the differences fully into the open. It is the paradox navigator's both-and, sixty years ahead; and it is the Gestalt contact boundary as a method of management.

In the terms of this work: love increases potentia. That was Spinoza's own definition of joy — the passage to a greater power of acting — and love, for him, is joy accompanied by the idea of its cause. What the lover does to the beloved is, exactly, to empower: to enlarge their adjacent possible. And love is power-with; it is Kauffman's autocatalytic set, in which each member's capacity is produced by the others.

Toward potestas love's relation is harder, and here the easy answers are false.

Love in the seat of power-over

The easy answer says that love has no dealings with power-over: the loving leader persuades, includes, empowers, and does not command. This is love without power, and King gave its adjectives.

Institutions require potestas. Someone must decide which of two good people gets the post. Someone must close the unit. Someone must tell the borrower that the facility will not be renewed. Someone must stop the bully — and that means overriding the bully's will. These are acts of power-over, performed on people who have not agreed, and no amount of process makes them otherwise.

What does love do there? It does not abstain; abstention merely hands the decision to someone who does not love, or to drift, the cruellest decider. Papworth's appraisal of role is in point: one asks whether this is mine to do, and if it is, the compassionate course is to do it. Love exercises power-over, and is recognisable in how — by four marks.

It keeps the other in view as a person while overriding them. The decision is against you; I am not. This is contact without confluence in its severest application. The receiver who must enforce security against a family firm, the manager who must dismiss, the examiner who must fail a candidate: each can do it to a case or to a person, and the person on the other end knows in the first seconds which it is. The file has not found this better put than in a remark attributed to several good judges: one can take from a man his liberty or his property, if the law requires it; one may never take his dignity, and the law never requires it.

It takes the cost upon itself and does not hide. The loveless exercise of power-over arranges not to be present: the letter, the intermediary, the Friday afternoon. Love delivers its own hard decisions in person, stays for the response, and bears being hated. McQuade's second processual rule — take responsibility — is this, set down as professional conduct: an ethical leader takes personal responsibility for the consequences of their choices. Stacey's ethics said the same: no one may hide in a system.

It uses the least power-over that will do, and gives back what it can. Having decided the thing that must be decided, it opens everything else: how, when, with what help, with what said to others. The space of the other's agency is narrowed only so far as the decision requires.

It tells the truth about its being power. It does not dress command as consultation, nor a decision already made as an open question. Nothing corrodes trust faster than power-over in the costume of power-with — the "conversation" whose outcome was fixed. People can bear to be overruled. They do not forgive being managed. This is where the Danish authors' warning about complexity washing bites: a leader who answers a matter that calls for decision with talk of "holding the tension" is exercising power by declining to, and concealing it.

Kenosis

The Christian tradition has a word for the relation of love to its own power which belongs here, since Balthasar made it the centre of his theology. In the letter to the Philippians, Paul cites what is probably an older hymn: Christ, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be clung to, but emptied himself — ekenōsen — taking the form of a servant. Kenosis: self-emptying.

It is constantly misread as the renunciation of power — as though the lesson were that love has none. The text says otherwise. It is the one who has the form of God who empties himself. Kenosis is not powerlessness. It is what power does when its order parameter is love: it does not clutch itself; it puts itself at the disposal of the other's good; it goes down. And Balthasar's most audacious claim was that this is no exception to what divine power is, a temporary disguise, but its revelation: that the power which made the stars is in itself a self-giving, and that the self-emptying shows what omnipotence was all along.

One need not share the theology to take the organisational point, and experienced people do take it. There is a difference, visible at once, between those who hold authority as a possession and those who hold it as a trust. The first use the office to affirm themselves; every exercise of it is, at some level, about them. The second have, in a way hard to describe and unmistakable to meet, got themselves out of the way. They use every ounce of the office's power when it is needed, without apology — and it is plainly not theirs. They can be contradicted without injury. They can lay the office down. Chinese political thought drew a near line between 德, dé — the moral force of a person, which draws others without coercion, as the pole star keeps its place and the other stars turn toward it — and 勢, shì, positional advantage, the power that belongs to the seat whoever sits in it. Confucius held that governing by dé was the only kind that lasted. The Legalists replied that shì was all there was. Every organisation re-runs the quarrel daily.

KENOSIS IS NOT THE ABSENCE OF POWER. IT IS POWER THAT IS NOT ABOUT ITSELF.

LOVE WITHOUT POWER ABANDONS THE WEAK TO WHOEVER HAS IT.
