ExcursusTen Tensions, Read for Love

The Danish volume sets out ten paradoxical tensions which its authors found recurring in the managers they worked with. They offer them as a starting inventory, not a complete list. The file takes each in turn and asks one question of it: what does the proposition's state do here? — on the hypothesis that if love is the capacity to hold the bright sides of two poles in one perception, it should have something particular to say at every one. The entries are brief by design. Each could be worked through with the Quadrant.

1. Leadership and management. Inspiring and enabling, on the one hand; planning, controlling, administering on the other. Read for love: Morin's poetic and prosaic. The temptation is to think love lives at the leadership pole and that management is its absence. The Rule of Benedict says otherwise: most of its chapters are about rotas and portions. Administration done for someone — the rota that lets a tired person rest; the budget that is honest — is love in its prosaic form. The test is whether the manager can see a face on the far side of the spreadsheet.

2. Individual and collective leadership. The one who leads, and leadership as something a group does together. Read for love: the pacemaker and the mutual coupling of chapter twenty-one. A leader who is the only source has a hub and spokes. The proposition's state, by Huygens, makes every point a source — so it tends by its nature toward the collective pole; but someone must be willing to go first. Marion's question: can I love first?

3. Matrix and function. Flexibility across boundaries against depth within a specialism. Read for love: a matrix multiplies the number of people to whom each is answerable and thins each tie; it is extensity bought with intensity, in Sorokin's terms. Its characteristic injury is that no one holds anyone. The question to ask of a matrix is Kahn's: trace the chain of holding and find where it breaks.

4. Purpose, passion and performance. Meaning and commitment against measurable results. Read for love: this is the tension the Danish authors use for their worked example of the Quadrant, and it is the paradox of chapter thirty-five: the thing matters for results and dies when sought for them. Passion harnessed to the quarter has become prose. The navigation is to serve the work and the person served, let performance follow, and to measure performance honestly as its own thing.

5. Mobility and permanence. People moving on, and people staying. Read for love: tuning has a history; synchrony takes time below threshold; the elders are the institution's memory. High turnover resets the coupling to nought with each departure. Yet a place no one may leave is Arendt's huddle, and the test of the exit applies. A loving institution keeps people long enough to be known and lets them go with a blessing — and its former members remain, in some sense, its own.

6. Physical and virtual presence. Read for love: the Interlude on the screen. Meet in the body to tune; use the screen to refresh.

7. Local and global. Differentiation for each place against integration across all. Read for love: the particular and the fair. Love knows this one; justice treats like cases alike. Contra III. The local manager who bends the global rule for someone she knows is being loving and unjust in one act; the head office that will not bend is being just and blind. Follett's integration, where it can be found: a rule whose own terms provide for the particular case.

8. Innovation from outside and from inside. Open co-creation with strangers against development within. Read for love: the closed loop and the torus. An organisation that draws only on itself has no gradient. One that draws only from outside has no centre. The adjacent possible is enlarged by relation with what is other — which is the reason for the stranger at Benedict's gate.

9. Human and non-human resources. People, and the digital systems that increasingly do or direct the work. Read for love: the still face, industrialised. An algorithm that allocates shifts, scores calls or screens applications is a face that cannot move. The paradox is real — such systems can be fairer than a prejudiced manager, Weber's impartial clerk perfected. What they cannot do is repair. The navigation: wherever a system decides about a person, a human being who can be reached, who has the power to look again, and whose face moves.

10. Profit, people and planet. The several sustainabilities. Read for love: McQuade's fourth and fifth code elements, and the objection this work does not meet. It is unethical, he says, to bust one's own organisation; and unethical to keep it solvent by exporting harm to those who cannot object — the far end of the supply chain, the generation not yet born. A torus whose return is fed by a sink somewhere out of sight is not a torus. This tension marks the outer edge of the present work: love that stays within the room.

Run the eye down the ten and a pattern shows. In each, one pole is the particular, present, warm, near and the other the general, structural, fair, far. Leadership and management; individual and collective; passion and performance; local and global; people and systems. The proposition, with its heart-burst and its crossing of rooms, speaks from the first pole every time. The books laid on the file speak for the second: Papworth's appraisal of role, McQuade's stakeholders at the far end of the chain, the Danish authors' refusal to let either pole win.

That is the correction this file has had to make to the proposition it set out to serve, and it should be stated once without softening. THE HEART-BURST IS HALF. The other half is the rota, the rule, the stranger one will never meet, and the question of what is owed to those who are not in the room.

ExcursusThe Cross and the Torus

Two figures have governed this work. One was in the proposition: the torus. The other arrived with McQuade's book: the cross. They are not rivals, and when they are drawn together each explains what the other leaves obscure.

The construction

Draw the torus as chapter nine described it: a flow that rises through a central axis, fountains outward over the top, descends round the outside, and returns beneath to the centre.

Now draw McQuade's Cruciform upon it. His vertical axis runs from Me — what one's life has laid down — up through I, the present self, to You — who one hopes to become. Set that along the axis of the torus. It is the direction of the central flow: up out of one's history, through the present, toward one's possibility.

His horizontal axis is the social situation: its past practice, its present demand, its tendency. Set that in the equatorial plane — the plane in which the torus spreads outward and comes back. It is the world into which one emanates and from which one receives.

The two axes cross at the centre of the hole. McQuade puts the I, the present, there, and calls it the place of choice. The proposition puts the heart there, and calls it the source. They are the same point.

What the cross adds to the torus

The torus, alone, is too smooth. It shows love circulating as water circulates in a fountain — beautifully, and with no one deciding anything. It has no place for refusal, for doubt, for the moment at which the outward flow meets a situation that demands what it cannot give.

The cross supplies that. Everything which rises through the centre must pass the crossing. At that point the vertical — what I hold and hope — meets the horizontal — what this room, with its history and momentum, is pressing for. Three things can happen there.

The horizontal may simply prevail. The situation's past flows through the person into its future; nothing rises; the fountain is dry, and what moves in the plane is only the room's own inertia. That is conformity, and McQuade's reading of the experiments is that it is the ordinary case.

The vertical may meet the horizontal in dissonance and break through: the flow rises against the pressure and enters the plane as something the situation did not contain. That is dissent; it is also the heart-burst — the moment in chapter ten at which something entered a room in Aldersgate Street that the room had not been tending toward.

Or the crossing may be grey: assonance. Then what rises is slowed and weighed. Papworth's four appraisals are made exactly here, in the throat of the fountain, before the flow turns outward and takes a direction. This is the nozzle of chapter twenty-six.

So the cross gives the torus its moral structure: a point through which everything must pass and at which it may be stopped, turned or aimed.

What the torus adds to the cross

The cross, alone, is too stark. It shows a solitary self at an intersection, choosing. Where does the Me get its values, and what feeds the You? Why do some have a vertical axis strong enough to stand against the horizontal and most do not? The Cruciform says that this depends on what a life has laid down. It does not say how it is laid down, or kept supplied.

The torus answers. What rises through the centre is what has returned. The outward flow curves round, passes through the world, and comes back underneath — into the Me. One's accrued values are not a private store. They are the return path of every earlier giving and receiving: the faces that once smiled, the people who held, the stories heard on the stairs, the times one was met at a bifurcation. The Me is the sediment of the circulation. And the You — the hoped-for self — is drawn upward by the same thing: by having seen, in some person or some transfigured moment, what one might become.

So the torus gives the cross its supply. A person stands at the crossing with whatever has come back to them. The solitary seldom dissent because the solitary have no return. McQuade's third dimension — the other social situation from which one can judge this one — is, on the figure, a second torus linked through the same centre: another circulation, in which one is also held.

Where the paradox lies

And the Danish authors? Their poles sit at the two ends of the horizontal: the pull toward one good and the pull toward its opposite, within the plane. A paradox is felt as being drawn both ways at the crossing. Deparadoxification is the collapse of the flow to one side — a jet toward a single pole. Navigation is the continued circulation that goes out toward both and returns through the centre from both: now leaning one way, now the other, never ceasing to pass the crossing. Their five phases, drawn as a wheel with no last spoke, are one turn of the torus.

The figure as a rule

Reduced to an instruction, the combined figure says four things, and they are the four words of chapter twenty-nine set on a diagram.

Rise — bring what you hold and hope up into the present. See.

Pass the crossing — let it meet what the situation presses for, and appraise. Weigh.

Turn outward — commit to a direction in the plane, knowing it leans toward one pole. Choose.

Return — let what comes back, including what you got wrong, come back through the centre, and go round again. Hold.

The cross without the torus is heroism without supply. The torus without the cross is warmth without judgement. Together they are a picture of what the proposition's author saw and of what the three books say must be learned: A HEART THAT GIVES ITSELF OUT, IS TESTED AT THE CROSSING, AND IS FED BY WHAT RETURNS.

The cross does not say where a person's values come from or what keeps them supplied; the torus says they are what has returned.

31Love and Judgement

The hardest test of the proposition in an organisation is not whether love can coexist with power in general. It is whether it can coexist with judgement — the daily, unavoidable business of assessing, ranking, refusing, correcting and deciding against. Organisations are machines for judgement. Is the state the proposition describes suspended while the appraisal is written?

The false opposition

The common view holds that love and judgement are opposed: love accepts, judgement evaluates; love is warm, judgement cold; one should be loving or rigorous, or mix them in prudent proportion — a little less truth for the sake of kindness, a little less kindness for the sake of truth.

Chapter twenty-nine filled in the quadrant and showed why the mixing model is wrong: mercy and truth are not quantities on one scale, so that more of one means less of the other. They are two poles, each with its own bright and dark side, and the state to be sought is the two bright sides together.

The first movement gave the ground for thinking this possible. Love is a way of knowing. It perceives under the law of closure: it sees the gap as a gap in a circle. That is to say, love is already a judgement — the most exact one. It sees precisely what is wrong, because it sees what the thing is meant to be. Indifference does not judge more accurately than love; it judges less, having no perception of the form against which the defect is a defect. The indifferent manager's assessment of a struggling subordinate is typically both harsher and vaguer than the loving one's: "not performing," where the other would say, "he has stopped asking questions since the reorganisation, and he was the one who always asked."

So the first thing to say is that the opposite of loving judgement is not rigorous judgement. It is lazy judgement — categorical, fixed on the gap, unable to say what the circle would be.

Radical candour, and before

A good deal of the management literature has been circling this. Kim Scott's two-by-two has had wide circulation: one axis is care personally, the other challenge directly. Both together she calls radical candour. Challenge without care is obnoxious aggression. Care without challenge she named, memorably, ruinous empathy — and she reported that it was by far the commonest failing of the managers she coached: people too kind to tell someone the thing they most needed to hear. Neither is manipulative insincerity.

It is the Paradox Quadrant, and it carries the same lesson in a form managers will take from an executive who has run teams at scale. The scholastic tradition had the lesson eight centuries earlier. Among the spiritual works of mercy — alongside instructing, counselling, comforting, forgiving — it listed fraternal correction: to admonish the one in error. Aquinas treats it under charity. It is an act of love; to omit it from fear or from a wish to be liked is a sin against love. And he adds at once the conditions that make it love and not its counterfeit: it must aim at the other's amendment, not at their humiliation; it should be private before it is public; and it must be done in a manner that gives it the best chance of being received. A correction that does not care whether it lands is not correction. It is discharge.

The Cruciform at the appraisal

McQuade's figure can be laid over the moment of judging, and it exposes what usually happens there.

The horizontal axis is the situation: the appraisal cycle, with its past (how ratings have always been distributed here, what was said last year, what it is safe to write) and its tendency (the forced curve, the calibration meeting, the bonus pool). The vertical is the manager: what their life has taught them to value, and who they hope to be. At the crossing sits the choice of what to write and what to say.

Almost always the horizontal runs straight through. The rating is whatever the situation's past makes easiest: in a lenient culture, a "meets expectations" which neither party believes; in a harsh one, a mark on a curve that has to be filled from somewhere. No judgement in the proper sense has occurred — nobody has looked at this person and asked what is true. The form has been carried forward.

A real judgement requires the vertical axis: the manager consulting what they actually believe about truth-telling and about this person, and who they would be if they signed the easy thing. McQuade's dissonance is the discomfort of noticing that the easy rating is a lie. His assonance is the more common and more honourable discomfort of not knowing: is he failing, or is the role impossible? Is the kindest thing a hard message now or another quarter's patience? It is grey. McQuade's counsel for that condition is that the doubt is to be kept and not suppressed, since it holds the judge open to being wrong; that the complexity is to be appreciated by considering every party the decision touches; that responsibility is to be taken personally; that one should look back later and ask whether one would do the same again; and, where the considerations are evenly matched, that one choose the course most favourable to life — the person's, and the others'.

That is no formula. It is a posture. And it is what distinguishes a judge from a clerk.

Judgement in the particular

Three situations, each a commonplace of organisational life, and what the foregoing implies for them.

The hard feedback. Someone must be told that their work is not good enough. Love's contribution is not to soften the content. It is, first, resolution: the message is specific, because the judge has looked. Second, the circle: it is delivered from within a perception of what this person can be, and that perception is communicated — not as a compliment sandwich, which everyone sees through, but in the quality of attention. The message is: I am telling you this because I take you seriously. Third, the interval: it is said at the time it can be used, not saved for the annual review. Fourth, the response awaited: by Mead's principle the meaning of the feedback is in what the other does with it, so the giver stays to find out, and is prepared to learn that it was heard as something quite other than was meant. Fifth — Papworth's appraisal — the giver has checked their intention. A piece of hard feedback can be given for the other's amendment or for the relief of one's own irritation, and the words may be identical. The face will not be.

The dismissal. Sometimes a person must go. A whole vocabulary exists to make this unsayable — letting go, exiting, managing out, transitioning — and each euphemism is a small still face. What does love do? It decides clearly, since prolonged ambiguity is the cruellest course. It tells the person itself, in a room, truthfully, with the reasons. It does not pretend the decision is the person's own. It does not rewrite their history to justify the outcome; the tendency, once someone is to be dismissed, to discover that they were never any good is one of the meanest reflexes of institutional life, and exists to spare the deciders the pain of harming someone of worth. Love bears that pain. It attends to how the person leaves — what is said to colleagues, whether there is a farewell, whether they go by the front door. And it remembers that the rest of the organisation is watching with complete attention, since each of them is learning what will be done to them.

The decision against a party one is bound to serve. The lender who must call the loan; the receiver appointed over the family's property; the regulator who must refuse the licence; the doctor who must decline the treatment the family begs for. Here the one who judges stands in an office with duties that run to others — to the creditor, to the public, to the patient's own interest — and those duties cannot be set aside for the suffering of the person present. Papworth's appraisal of role is exactly this. McQuade's doctors describe exactly this assonance, in which a personal value is set aside, with discomfort, for a deeper professional one.

It is the Weberian case, and it is where the proposition is most severely tried. The answer is the first mark of the previous chapter. The office decides the what. Love governs the how, and the how is not a small thing. People on the wrong end of such decisions report, with great consistency, that what they remember — what determined whether they came through as themselves — was not the decision, which they often understood, but whether the person who carried it out treated them as a human being: explained, listened, did not hurry, did not lie, did not gloat, did not hide. A receiver can sell a man's property over his head in a manner that leaves him his standing as a man. That is not a soft addition to the office. The file is inclined to say that it is the office's true test, and the place where Weber's sine ira et studio is fulfilled and not contradicted: without anger, without favouritism — and with the face.

Forgiveness

Judgement looks back at what was done. An institution that could only judge would be a tribunal. Arendt, who put love outside the public realm, saw that action needs a remedy for its own irreversibility. What is done cannot be undone; its consequences run on; and the doer would be fixed for ever to a single deed were it not for the faculty of forgiving, which releases both parties from it. Without forgiveness, she wrote, our capacity to act would be confined to one deed from which we could never recover.

Organisations forgive badly. They have two modes, which are forgiveness's two counterfeits. One is amnesia: the error is not mentioned; nothing was learned; it will recur. The other is the permanent record: the error is never released; ten years on the person is still "the one who lost the Henderson account." What they lack is the real thing, which has three parts and requires all of them. The wrong is named as a wrong — without that there is nothing to forgive. The person is distinguished from the deed: you did this; you are not this. And the future is reopened: we go on, and this will not be held against you.

The safety literature rediscovered the structure under the name of just culture. In aviation and, later, medicine it was found that punishing those who report their errors produces concealment, and that concealment kills; and equally that a blanket no-blame rule is unjust, since it fails to distinguish the honest slip from recklessness. A just culture names the act accurately, treats the honest error as information and the reckless choice as a matter for consequences, and keeps the person who erred in good standing where they acted in good faith. It is a system of institutional forgiveness that does not abolish judgement. It is mercy and truth in a procedure, and it measurably saves lives.

INDIFFERENCE DOES NOT JUDGE MORE ACCURATELY THAN LOVE. IT JUDGES LESS.

32Holding

Love under pressure has a temporal form, and its name in the clinical literature is holding. The fourth resistance which chapter twenty-nine left open — time — is met here.

Winnicott

Donald Winnicott, the paediatrician and psychoanalyst who watched something like sixty thousand mothers and babies over four decades at a London children's hospital, held that there is no such thing as a baby. He meant that wherever one finds an infant one finds maternal care, and without the care there would be no infant; the unit is the pair. What the care consists in, at the start, he called holding: literally, the way a baby is held, and by extension the whole provision of an environment in which the infant's "going on being" is not interrupted.

A held infant is not aware of being held. It simply exists, and its existing has continuity. An infant not held — dropped, impinged upon, left too long — is forced to react, and reacting breaks the line of its being. Winnicott thought the consequence of repeated breaks was the formation of a false self: a compliant surface organised around the environment's demands, behind which the true self — the source of spontaneity and the feeling of being real — goes into hiding.

Two of his further ideas complete the picture. The mother must be, in his famous phrase, good enough — not perfect. A perfect mother, anticipating every need, would give the infant no experience of a world beyond its wishes. The good-enough mother fails, in small and tolerable ways, and repairs; and it is through that graduated failure that the child comes to discover a reality outside itself and the capacity to bear it. This is Tronick's finding in the language of the clinic. And the mature fruit of having been held is what he called the capacity to be alone — which, paradoxically, is first acquired in the presence of someone: the small child playing absorbed while the mother is nearby and not attending. Because she is reliably there, the child can forget her and be wholly in its own activity.

Bion

Wilfred Bion, who had commanded a tank at Cambrai at nineteen and later worked with groups of soldiers who had broken down, described the same function from the side of thought. The infant has experiences it cannot bear — raw dread, without name or shape. It expels them; it screams. The mother who is able to receive this, to take the dread into herself without being overwhelmed by it or pushing it away, to feel it, think about it, and return it in a form that can be borne — "you're hungry, yes, here" — has performed what he called containment. The state of mind in which she can do it he called reverie. Over thousands of repetitions the infant takes in not only the detoxified experience but the function itself, and becomes able to think its own thoughts.

If the mother cannot contain — if she is too anxious, or absent, or herself overwhelmed — the dread comes back to the infant not made tolerable but stripped of meaning: Bion's phrase was nameless dread.

His earlier work with groups supplied a companion idea. A group that cannot contain its anxieties, he observed, stops doing its work and begins instead to behave as if it had met for another purpose altogether — as if to be looked after by an all-providing leader (dependency), as if to fight or flee an enemy (fight-flight), or as if two of its members would produce a saviour (pairing). He called these basic assumptions. They are, in the language of chapter twenty, alternative order parameters which capture a group when the one called the work loses its hold.

What holding is, in an organisation

William Kahn, the organisational psychologist who gave the field the concept of engagement, carried Winnicott's term across. In a study of a social-work agency published under the title "Caring for the Caregivers," he traced how care moved — or failed to move — through the organisation: whether the social workers who spent their days absorbing the distress of clients were themselves held by supervisors, and the supervisors by the director. Where they were, the caregivers could go on giving. Where the flow was blocked — where those above took care from those below, or gave nothing — the caregivers burned out or hardened. He later defined holding environments at work as relationships in which people can safely express and make sense of difficult experience, and he was specific about what the holder does: makes themselves available; attends; inquires; receives what comes without judgement or panic; helps the person find words; and conveys, throughout, that they will not be dropped.

It is containment, set down as a list of behaviours, and its place in this work's geometry is clear. Kahn's flow of caregiving is the return path of the torus. The frontline worker gives out; something must come back, through the centre, or the form is a jet.

A leader, a team, an institution holds when it does for its members what the mother does for the infant in distress. It receives the anxiety — of the restructuring, the bad quarter, the investigation, the death. It is not swamped by it, and does not pass it on amplified. It does not bat it away with reassurance: "there's nothing to worry about" is a refusal to receive. It metabolises the anxiety: thinks about it, finds its true shape, separates what is known from what is feared. And it returns it in a form that can be thought about: here is what has happened; here is what we know and do not know; here is what will happen next; here is what does not change.

Organisations characteristically fail at this in the infant's two directions. The swamped organisation takes in the anxiety and amplifies it: the leadership panics; the panic runs down the hierarchy gathering speed; every level adds its own. The deflecting organisation will not take it in: communications are bland; questions are answered with slogans; the anxiety, unreceived, returns to its owners as nameless dread and becomes rumour. In both the work stops, and the basic assumptions take over. One can observe a whole division slide into fight-flight inside a week.

Holding through time

Holding is the form love takes when what is called for is not an act but a duration. Much of what is asked of people in organisations is to stay in something unresolved: the eighteen months of a turnaround whose outcome is unknown; the long illness of a colleague; the investigation that will take a year; the paradox that — the Danish authors insist — never ends. The human reflex under such strain is premature closure: to make it stop by deciding something, blaming someone, declaring victory or defeat. Most bad decisions in organisations are taken to relieve the deciders.

The poet Keats, in a letter of 1817, named the opposite capacity. He called it negative capability: being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason. Bion took the phrase over for the analyst's stance. Stacey and his colleagues took it for the manager's. The Danish authors, without using it, describe it as their fifth threshold. McQuade's assonance is its moral form: doubt carried, not discharged.

But negative capability is not a talent of solitary strong minds. Winnicott's capacity to be alone is acquired in someone's presence, and so is this. A person can stay in what is unresolved if they are held while they do so. The practical question about any leader asked to hold a long uncertainty for others is therefore: WHO IS HOLDING THE HOLDER? Kahn's finding was that the chain may not break anywhere. Papworth's third appraisal — of resources — puts the question to the leader as a duty: before turning to others, see to it that you are yourself supplied; and her suggestions span the physical, social, emotional, mental and spiritual. An executive at the top of a troubled organisation with no one above, no peer who can be told the truth, and no source beyond the organisation is an unheld holder. The form is a jet, and the trajectory of jets is known.

The toxin handlers

Peter Frost, a Canadian scholar of organisations who wrote out of his own experience of cancer, gave a name to a role that appears on no chart. In every organisation, he observed, there are people to whom others bring their pain: who listen after the brutal meeting, who intervene quietly with a harsh boss, who translate a wounding instruction into something bearable. He called them toxin handlers. They are seldom senior. Their work is invisible and unrewarded. And it keeps the organisation functioning, by absorbing emotional poison which would otherwise disable people.

His sombre finding was what it does to them. They carry what they absorb. Often they have nowhere to put it down. They become ill — he was not speaking in metaphor — and they burn out, and the organisation, never having known what they did, does not understand what it has lost. A ward loses its ability to survive bad days and no one links it to the retirement, six months before, of a healthcare assistant.

The toxin handler is the unheld container: Bion's mother with no one for her reverie. And she is the proposition's state in its most common organisational disguise — an unremarkable person to whom, for some reason nobody examines, everyone goes. If the file had one piece of advice for an incoming chief executive it would be: FIND OUT, IN YOUR FIRST MONTH, WHO THESE PEOPLE ARE. Then discover who holds them. Then make sure that someone does.

MOST BAD DECISIONS ARE MADE TO RELIEVE THE DECIDERS.

33The Institution That Remembers

An order parameter lives only in its continual re-enactment; a dissipative structure exists only while the energy flows. How, then, does love outlast the people in whom it began? Davies's Signature makes circulation across generations the heart of the matter, and this chapter asks what an institution must be for the proposition's state to circulate through it over decades.

Weber's pessimism

Weber's answer was that it cannot — not as itself. Charisma is by its nature extraordinary and personal. When the founder dies, the community faces a problem of succession, and of providing for its own ordinary needs: income, property, discipline, the training of the next generation. In solving these it turns the original gift into one or both of the two stable forms of authority: tradition (we do it thus because it has always been done) or legal-rational rule (we do it thus because the regulations say so). He called this routinisation. The disciples become officials. The message becomes doctrine. The shared purse becomes a salary scale. What was fire is now the tending of a grate.

The history of religious orders, of reforming movements, of mission-led companies, is very largely as he said. Founders' generations glow; third generations administer. The rule of St Francis, who wished his brothers to own nothing, was being revised to permit the use of property before he was dead.

What the rule is for

But one may look at the same history differently, and ask what the founders who wrote rules thought they were doing. They were not naive about cooling. Benedict of Nursia, composing his Rule about the year 530 for a community which he expected to outlive him by generations, called it a little rule for beginners, and its prologue speaks of establishing "a school of the Lord's service." Its seventy-three short chapters hardly mention exalted states. They deal with the hours of prayer, the measure of food and drink, who serves in the kitchen, how the porter is to answer the door, what is to be done with a monk who is late.

What Benedict understood, in the terms of this work, is that the state cannot be stored; the conditions can. A rule is a set of governing and enabling constraints designed so that when the fire comes there is somewhere for it to burn — and when it is absent, as it will be for long stretches, the form persists in a condition from which it can be relit. The rule is not the love. It is the hearth. And he was explicit about what the hearth was for: he says that as one advances in this way of life the heart is enlarged — the Latin is dilatato corde — and one runs the way of God's commandments in an unspeakable sweetness of love. The enlargement of the heart is named, in the sixth century, as the purpose of an organisational design.

Four features of a rule of that kind explain its durability, and each has a secular equivalent.

It specifies rhythm, not feeling. The community stops and gathers seven times a day whether or not anyone is in the mood. This is the choir of chapter eleven: a shared breath imposed by a shared practice, which brings bodies into step and keeps them near the threshold at which mutual synchrony can occur. An organisation's equivalents are its real rituals — the morning huddle, the ward handover, the weekly meeting at which the same questions are asked — where they are kept with enough seriousness to entrain.

It builds in the mirrors. There is a daily chapter at which faults are acknowledged. The abbot is to take counsel of the whole community on weighty matters — Benedict adds, strikingly, that the Lord often reveals what is better to the youngest. There is mutual obedience among the brothers. This is the laser's cavity: the community's emission returned through its centre.

It binds the powerful. A long chapter instructs the abbot, and it is mostly warning. He is to remember that he will give account for every soul; to adapt himself to many dispositions; to be loved rather than feared; not to be turbulent or anxious, excessive or obstinate, jealous or suspicious, for then he will never be at rest. And there is the image the file would hang in every boardroom: he is so to arrange everything that the strong have something to strive after and the weak are not driven to flight.

It is about the stranger. Guests are to be received as Christ; the porter is to answer every knock with a blessing. The centre of the torus lies outside the membership.

The four layers

The secular literature on how an organisation carries compassion beyond individuals is thin, and the best of it is a practical chapter in Papworth's book. Having argued that no organisation can be compassionate on the strength of its leaders alone — such a structure, in her image, would teeter — she sets out four areas in which compassion has to be built in, and the file translates them into its own terms.

Strategic. Whether care for people is part of what the organisation takes itself to be for, and so enters the decisions that matter; she connects it to the research on affective commitment — the attachment of those who stay because they want to, as distinct from those who stay because they must. In this work's terms: the candidate order parameter.

Structural. HR policy across the whole employee lifecycle — how people are recruited, inducted, appraised, supported in illness and bereavement, and how they leave — and the organisation's standing arrangements for responding to suffering, including resources and recognition. In this work's terms: governing and enabling constraints; the shape of the landscape; also the dampers, which should be examined for what frequencies they suppress.

Behavioural. The small, repeated acts; she draws on the behavioural-science literature on nudges, and insists that opportunities for compassionate leadership belong to everyone and not only to those with titles. In this work's terms: Huygens's principle, in which every point is a source.

Cultural. Psychological safety, trust, and the continual creation and reinforcement of culture by what leaders do, attend to and reward. In this work's terms: the atmosphere; the slope; the order parameter as actually enacted.

She adds a section on measurement, under a heading with a wry parenthesis: what gets measured (sometimes) gets done. The file endorses the parenthesis. Measures of an order parameter are fast-variable proxies for a slow variable, and when the proxy becomes the target the order parameter has changed — to the number.

Her insistence that all four layers be worked together is correct, and the complexity movement has shown why: these are not four levers. They are four descriptions of one circular causality, and an intervention in any which is contradicted by the others will be relaxed away.

Memory

Davies writes of stored energies awaiting activation, and of the humanities as the medium in which a culture keeps what it cannot presently use. An institution has its humanities also — the forms in which it remembers what it is for. They are of four kinds, and their condition is a fair index of the institution's.

Stories. Every institution has a canon: the tales told to newcomers, at leaving parties, in the bar after the conference. They are the form in which transfigurations are kept. The night the whole firm came in to help when the warehouse flooded. The partner who gave her bonus to the trainee whose mother was dying. The time the chairman told the bank the truth and it nearly finished us. Their content matters less than their existence, and less than who tells them. When the stories are of triumphs over rivals, or of what one could get away with, the order parameter is known. When no stories are told at all, the institution has no memory and is merely a set of contracts.

Rituals. The handover, the welcome, the farewell, the marking of a death. A ritual is a practice that brings bodies into shared attention and rhythm, and so, by Collins and by the choir, into the vicinity of the threshold. Institutions in decline hollow theirs out before they abolish them: the leaving do moves from the pub to a card left on a desk to an email.

Places. The spot where the thing happened; the room that has always been used for this; the photograph on the stairs. Atmospheres attach to places and are found there by people who never knew their origin.

Persons. The elders, the long-serving, the ones who "have always been here." They are the institution's living memory of its own form, and the only fully adequate one, since a form is transmitted whole only by a person in whom it lives. Redundancy programmes that remove everyone over fifty-five in the name of cost have been found afterwards, with some surprise, to have removed something that the balance sheet did not carry.

All four are means by which a form is held in latency — in Davies's capacitance — across the stretches in which no one is enacting it. A newcomer in a dry season, hearing the story in the room where it happened from someone who was there, at the annual occasion on which it is always told, may be reached by a wavelet emitted forty years ago.

The humanities of an organisation

Davies's title for his ninth Signature is "The Humanities as a Living Field", and he means literature, philosophy, history, art, music and ritual as the medium through which a civilisation keeps its meanings in circulation. The four kinds of memory just listed are the same thing at the scale of a firm, a hospital or a school. Every institution has its humanities. Its literature is its stories. Its history is what the elders remember and the minutes leave out. Its ritual is the handover and the farewell. Its art is whatever in its buildings and its made things was done better than it had to be. Its philosophy is the argument, renewed in every generation, about what the place is for. Its music is harder to name and unmistakable when met: the pace and pitch at which people there speak to one another.

Institutions also have, in Davies's sense, a relation to their humanities which may be living or dead. A firm can keep its founder's portrait on the stairs and its values on the wall as a museum keeps artefacts — collected, labelled, and out of circulation. Or the same stories can be told because they have not finished speaking: because someone, this year, facing this difficulty, needs to know what was done the last time. His distinction between storing meaning and circulating it is exact. A story that is only ever told at the anniversary dinner is stored. A story that a ward sister tells a frightened student at two in the morning is in circulation.

It follows that those who tend an institution's humanities — who remember, who tell, who keep the rituals with enough seriousness that they still do their work, who notice when a thing was done beautifully and say so — are performing a function as necessary as finance and far less often thought of as work. Nobody is appointed to it. In most places it is done by a few long-serving people of no great rank, in the margins of their real jobs, and it is what Davies says the humanities do for a society: they keep shared life capable of remembering, questioning, and becoming otherwise. When a restructuring describes such people as resistant to change, it has usually mistaken the organisation's memory for an obstacle to its future.

Relighting

This is the answer to Weber. He was right that the state cannot be institutionalised. He was wrong that this leaves only ash. An institution can be a hearth: a structure which does not burn, and in which fire can be kept and relit.

The history of the orders bears it out. Each long-lived one shows the same rhythm: foundation, cooling, and then — unpredictably, from within, usually from the margins and usually by someone who goes back to the rule and the stories and takes them at their word — reform. Cîteaux out of Cluny. The Carmelites under Teresa. The reformer does not invent. The reformer is someone in whom the stored form, meeting a prepared heart, crosses threshold again. Without the hearth there would have been nothing to ignite and nowhere for the flame to go. Davies's gyre has exactly this shape: meaning returns, not to confirm itself, but to be reworked under changed conditions.

So of an institution one should ask not is it on fire? — it will not be, most of the time — but could it be relit? Are the stories still told? Are the rituals kept, even thinly? Are there still persons in whom the form lives? Is the rule — the charter, the founding purpose — still there to be gone back to and taken at its word? And when someone does go back to it and take it at its word — which will be inconvenient, since it will indict present practice — is that person heard, or managed out?

AN INSTITUTION CANNOT STORE LOVE. IT CAN KEEP THE HEARTH.

THE RULE IS NOT THE FIRE. IT IS WHERE THE FIRE CAN BE RELIT.

Movement VI

PHTHORA

The Corruptions

Every word in the proposition has a dark twin. The light that draws attention to itself; love taken as labour; the boundary dissolved; the wavefront of fear; and the burning-out of those who shine. If the file cannot tell these from the real thing, nothing it has said is safe to use.

34Counterfeit Light

Paul, writing to a community he feared was being taken in, remarks that it is no marvel that false apostles should pass for true ones — for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. The older name of that figure in Latin Christendom was Lucifer: light-bearer. The tradition which gave the West its language of love as radiance placed at the root of all evil a being who is luminous.

That is not decoration. It is a structural warning, and it applies with full force to everything this work has said. McQuade made the same point in the idiom of the cinema: the adversary and the hero follow the same religion. If love is recognised by a certain radiance, warmth, energy and coherence, then whatever can produce radiance, warmth, energy and coherence without love will be mistaken for it. The better the description of the real thing, the more exact the specification handed to the forger.

Love-bombing

The phrase was coined inside a religious movement of the 1970s, as the approving name for its own practice of surrounding a potential recruit with concentrated, orchestrated affection: constant company, flattery, touch, the sense of having at last been found by people who understood. Those who studied such movements took the term over as the name of a technique. The recruit's experience is, by the marks so far given, indistinguishable from the proposition's state. Something crosses the room. It is warm. One feels seen, energised, larger. The life space re-forms: one's former life looks grey; the group is where the light is.

What distinguishes it emerges only over time, and can then be stated exactly. The warmth is contingent: it is withdrawn the moment the recruit hesitates, questions, or looks toward the door. It is instrumental: it has a purpose beyond the recruit, and the recruit is its means. It narrows rather than widens: the adjacent possible contracts to what the group permits, and ties to the world outside are cut. And its geometry is a sink presenting as a source: energy flows from members to the centre.

Organisations do it. The lavish recruitment process, the offsite, the founder's embrace, the language of family and mission, the perks that make it unnecessary ever to go home. And then, at the first missed quarter, the first sign of doubt, the first refusal to work the weekend, the temperature falls thirty degrees and the person finds that the love was a credit facility, callable on demand.

"We are a family"

The commonest corporate form of counterfeit deserves a paragraph to itself, because it is usually sincere.

A firm is not a family, and those who say it is are generally aware of the differences that matter. A family does not dismiss its members for under-performance or when revenues fall. The firm reserves both rights. So the statement cannot mean what it says. What it does, functionally, is import the obligations of family — loyalty beyond contract, availability without limit, the unsayability of the word "no" — without the security that makes those obligations reasonable. Membership in a family is unconditional; that is why one owes it so much. To ask the owing while keeping the membership conditional is to take on credit what will not be repaid.

Arendt's objection, deferred from chapter twenty-five, is vindicated here. The family metaphor abolishes the in-between — the space of contract, role and respect that lets people be related and separate — and what rushes into the vacated space is not love but an unlimited claim.

The marks of the counterfeit

Since the forgery matches the original in every feature that can be felt in the first hour, the tests are of another kind. The file has been gathering them as it went. Collected:

The test of direction (chapter fifteen). Does attention flow to the source or through it? The counterfeit is luminous — one sees it, is dazzled by it. The real thing is super-luminous: by it, one sees everything else. After the encounter, is one thinking about the person, or about one's own life and work with new clarity?

The test of difference (chapters five and twenty-one). Can one disagree? The counterfeit is confluent: it needs sameness, and the first real no reveals it. Love is contact at a boundary, and is not threatened by the boundary's assertion. The quickest diagnostic of any warm group is to differ with it about something that matters and observe the temperature.

The test of the exit. What happens when one leaves, or wants to? Love's regard survives the leaving. The counterfeit's turns to coldness, injury, or pursuit.

The test of the third party (chapters nine and twenty-eight). Does the warmth extend to those outside — to the stranger, the competitor, the one who has left, the one who cannot be of use? The counterfeit is a closed loop; its warmth is the obverse of a coldness toward the out-group, and often depends on having one. Papworth's bias chapter names the mechanism — in-group favouritism — and her appraisal of role sets the corrective: the task is to extend compassion beyond the known and the like, to dissenters and awkward non-conformists not least. McQuade's four words are the same test in monosyllables. Watch how the person treats the waiter.

The test of time (chapters nineteen and twenty). The counterfeit is a fast variable performed; love is a slow one enacted. Under disturbance — a bad quarter, a conflict, a real cost — to what does the system relax?

The test of fruit (chapter twenty-eight). Greenleaf's. Do those in its field become freer, wiser, more themselves, more able to stand alone and to become sources — or more dependent, narrower, more like the leader, less able to imagine a life outside?

The test of truth (chapter thirty-one). Can it tell one something unwelcome? The counterfeit flatters, since its purpose requires that one stay. Love corrects.

The test of cost. Who pays? In love, the lover bears cost for the beloved's sake. In the counterfeit, examined closely, the "beloved" is paying — in time, money, labour, independence — and the "lover" receives.

None of these can be administered in the first hour. That is the forger's advantage and there is no removing it. The defence is not to distrust warmth. It is to let time, difference and cost do their work before giving what cannot be got back.

The dimmed light

The Dao De Jing offers the counter-image, twice, in the same four characters met earlier: 和光同塵 — soften the glare, be one with the dust. The sage's light does not dazzle. It may be the best single pointer to the real thing: it is not trying to be seen. The counterfeit must be noticed, for it wants something. Love has no such need, and is therefore commonly found in people one overlooked.

Motovilov could not look at Seraphim's face for brightness. But the same Seraphim, for the fifteen years before, had been a silent recluse whom the monks of his own house thought eccentric at best. Philip Neri went about Rome performing absurdities — half his beard shaved, a cushion on his head — lest anyone take him for a saint. The light-emitting, in the tradition's own records, spend much effort on not being luminous.

THE COUNTERFEIT MUST BE SEEN. THE REAL THING HAS NO SUCH NEED.

35Love Extracted: Emotional Labour

In the early 1980s the sociologist Arlie Hochschild attended the training school of a large American airline. The recruits — almost all women — were being taught to smile. Not merely to smile: to mean it. They were told to think of the cabin as their living room and the passengers as guests in their home; faced with an abusive passenger, to imagine that he had perhaps just suffered some bereavement, so that sympathy and not anger would arise. The company was not purchasing a facial expression. It had grasped Duchenne's point, that a painted smile is seen through. It was purchasing the feeling.

Hochschild called what was being sold emotional labour: the management of one's own feeling to create a publicly observable display, as a requirement of the job, for a wage. Her book, The Managed Heart, became one of the founding texts of the sociology of emotion. Its title could stand as the epigraph of this chapter — the proposition says cardial, and here was the heart, managed.

Surface and depth

She distinguished two ways of doing it, borrowing from the theatre. In surface acting one changes the display and leaves the feeling: the smile goes on and the irritation remains beneath. In deep acting one works upon the feeling itself, by techniques of imagination and memory, so that the display is "genuine": one actually summons warmth toward the passenger. The airline trained deep acting.

Both, she found, exact a price, and they are different prices. Surface acting produces dissonance — a standing gap between what is shown and what is felt — and forty years of subsequent research have confirmed its association with exhaustion, cynicism and ill health. It is the more plainly harmful. Deep acting is subtler, and the later research has been less uniformly negative about it. But Hochschild's original worry concerned what it does over years. A person whose capacity for warmth is hired out by the shift, summoned at will and directed at whoever management names, may come to lose the sense of which feelings are theirs. Her cabin crew described going home and not knowing how to stop — or else going numb; not being able to tell a real smile from the company's; feeling fraudulent in their own marriages. She called it estrangement from one's own heart. What is alienated in the factory is the worker's body. What is alienated in the service economy is the signal function of feeling — the faculty by which one knows what one cares about.

The proposition, extracted

Now read the proposition as a job description.

An affective-cognitive cardial state… creating a field that extends beyond the body… felt crossing the room… light-emitting. This is what the airline wanted to hire. It is what every "customer experience" strategy, every nursing competency framework that specifies compassion, every leadership model listing warmth and presence, is trying to specify. The service economy has understood perfectly well that the proposition's state is valuable — that customers return for it, that patients get better in it, that teams perform in it. And it has drawn what looks like the reasonable conclusion: it should be recruited for, trained, required, measured and rewarded.

The file has to say with some force that this conclusion is where the phenomenon dies; and since it spent the last movement arguing for love's organisational reality and worth, it must say just why this is not a contradiction.

Four reasons, each from the earlier chapters.

The order parameter cannot be commanded. Engineering the fast variables leaves the slow one where it was. When warmth is required, what one gets is surface acting — the display without the state — and Duchenne's muscle gives it away. Or one gets deep acting: a state manufactured by technique for an external end.

The return path is cut. Hochschild's cabin crew were jets. They emitted, by the shift, toward three hundred strangers, under instruction, to a script, with their supervisors timing them. What returned through the centre? The passengers' gratitude went to the airline. The wage came for hours and not for hearts. And the company's own regard for them was — it was the early 1980s, an age of speed-up — conditional and falling. The form was broken by design: outward flow required, inward flow diverted. A torus cut in that way is the precise structure of exhaustion.

A constraint has been turned into a force. Love works by changing what is possible. The employer who demands it is applying a force — do this or lose your job — to produce an act whose whole nature is that it is not forced. The act is destroyed by its mode of production, as a gift is destroyed by being invoiced.

The purpose has been prestated. Love opens an adjacent possible that cannot be listed in advance. The service script specifies the outcome: the customer is to feel valued and buy again. What is produced under that specification is a simulation of love with the open end closed.

Papworth's appraisal step supplies a fifth, from within. One of its four parts is intention: before responding, ask what one is really after. She names the Machiavellian use of compassionate behaviour explicitly among the things that are not compassion. An organisation that cultivates the appearance of care in order to raise retention, when it would drop the care tomorrow if retention could be had otherwise, has failed its own appraisal at the level of the institution.

The paradox of saying so

Here the file must turn upon itself. It has argued that love is real in organisations, that it is valuable, that its absence is costly. It has cited studies showing that it improves patients' outcomes and employees' commitment. A manager reading the fifth movement might reasonably conclude: then I should get more of it. And the present chapter says that the attempt to get it destroys it.

That is a paradox in the strict sense of the Danish volume — two poles, in conflict and interdependent — and it will not be dissolved. One pole: the thing matters, and an institution that is indifferent to whether its people are loved and loving is negligent. The other: the thing cannot be made a target without ceasing to be itself. What can be done is to navigate, and the navigation has a recognisable shape.

One can remove what prevents it. The quotas that leave a nurse four minutes for each patient. The script. The surveillance. The forced ranking that sets colleagues against one another. Juarrero's question: what constraints are making it improbable, and which of them are ours?

One can restore the return path. Let those who serve see the faces of those they served. Let the gratitude go to the person who earned it. See that those who give are held.

One can be in it. A leader may neither require the state nor produce it. They can be in it themselves, and let Huygens do the rest.

One can protect it where it arises. Notice it; name it — carefully, since the naming easily becomes the targeting; do not restructure it away.

And one can refuse to measure it into a target. Papworth's parenthesis: what gets measured (sometimes) gets done. And sometimes what gets measured gets performed, which is the death of this.

It is, the file concedes, a modest programme. It is the gardener's and not the engineer's. Organisations which have the thing have, in general, not tried to produce it. They have attended passionately to something else — the patient, the craft, the truth — and have treated one another decently on the way, and the thing arose and was not interfered with.

Who does the work

A last observation from Hochschild, with a sharp edge. Emotional labour is unequally distributed. It falls most heavily on women, on those in low-status service roles, and on members of minorities who are expected to manage the comfort of majorities. Frost's toxin handlers of chapter thirty-two were disproportionately women and seldom senior. In many organisations the warmth that makes the place bearable is produced by its least-paid members for the benefit of its best-paid, who experience it as "our lovely culture."

The torus, there, is a class structure. An honest inquiry into love in an organisation has to ask not only whether it is present but who is giving it, who is receiving it, and whether those are the same people. Where they are not, what is being called love is a transfer.

A GIFT IS DESTROYED BY BEING INVOICED.

36Fusion: The Boundary Dissolved

The second corruption has been named several times already. It is what Arendt took for love itself, what the Gestalt therapists called confluence, what Scheler called identification, and what the Kuramoto model distinguishes from synchrony by a single property. It is love with the boundary gone.

The appeal

Fusion feels like the fulfilment of everything this work has commended. The room is one. Everyone is in step. There is no friction, no dissent, no awkwardness of difference. Decisions are made easily, since everybody agrees. Energy is high. People speak of how close the team is, of finishing one another's sentences, of never having worked anywhere like it. An observer applying the seven marks of chapter twenty-seven hastily would tick most of them.

Three would fail, and they are the diagnostic ones. A fused room is not bright: things are not distinct in it; they are blurred in a general warmth, and disagreements are not clearer but invisible. It is not directed beyond itself: its attention is on its own cohesion. And it is not round: it has a hidden front — an edge, at the limit of what may be said, with a strong negative valence beyond.

Groupthink

The psychologist Irving Janis, studying American foreign-policy disasters — the Bay of Pigs above all — asked how groups of exceptionally able people had arrived at decisions which any one of them, alone, would have seen to be foolish. His answer was a syndrome he called groupthink, and his finding was that it arises not in groups that are divided but in groups that are cohesive: where members like and esteem one another, value their membership highly, and are under stress.

Its symptoms he listed: an illusion of invulnerability; an unquestioned belief in the group's own morality; collective rationalisation; stereotyped views of outsiders; self-censorship of doubt; an illusion of unanimity, silence being read as consent; direct pressure on any who dissent; and the appearance of self-appointed "mindguards" who shield the group and its leader from disturbing information.

Each is a boundary dissolved or a difference suppressed for the sake of the warmth. Self-censorship is retroflection. The stereotyped out-group is projection. The mindguard is the damper fitted to the wrong frequency. And the ground condition — cohesion — is what the incautious reader of this work might think it had been advocating.

It has not. Janis's remedy, and the remedy adopted by the same President after the fiasco, to good effect, in the missile crisis eighteen months later, was to reintroduce difference deliberately: assign someone to argue the contrary; bring in outsiders; have the leader withhold his view; divide into sub-groups and compare. That is, raise the diversity of natural frequencies and require the coupling to work across it. In Follett's terms: bring the differences into the open so that integration, and not mere agreement, becomes possible.

Why fusion is not love

The earlier chapters permit a rigorous statement.

Contact requires a boundary. Where there is no difference there is nothing to meet. The fused group does not have closer contact than others; it has none. Its members relate to an image of the group, not to one another.

A dissipative structure requires a gradient. The fused group has eliminated the differences that drive circulation. It is at equilibrium. Its "energy" is the pleasant hum of people confirming one another; nothing new can come of it, since nothing differs from anything.

Synchrony keeps the natural frequencies. In fusion, members become alike: they converge on one view, one manner, one taste, often the leader's. Remove the coupling from a synchronised group and each returns to their own rhythm. Remove it from a fused group and its members find they have no rhythm of their own to return to.

The meaning of a gesture lies in the response of an other. If there is no other — if you will respond as I would — then my gesture returns to me unchanged. This is Rosa's distinction between resonance and echo. The fused group is an echo chamber in the exact sense: what comes back is one's own voice, and it is mistaken for confirmation.

Love knows the other as other. Murdoch's realisation that something other than oneself is real. In fusion, the other's otherness is the one thing that cannot be borne.

The codependent helper

Fusion has a form at the scale of two, and in organisations it tends to wear the dress of compassion. Papworth devotes part of her appraisal step to it by way of Karpman's Drama Triangle, and the file wishes to set it out because it is the characteristic corruption of the very people most drawn to this work.

The triangle has three positions. The victim is helpless, done-to. The persecutor blames and attacks. The rescuer helps — helps unasked, helps more than is wanted, helps in a way that keeps the victim helpless. The positions are roles in a game, in Berne's sense: a repeated pattern of transactions with a concealed payoff. And the players rotate. The rescuer whose help goes unappreciated turns persecutor ("after all I've done"); or collapses into victim ("nobody looks after me"). The victim who is over-helped turns on the helper.

The rescuer experiences themselves as loving, and from outside can look like the proposition's state: warm, attentive, always available, moved by others' suffering. What marks the difference is the hidden payoff. The rescuer needs the victim to stay a victim, because the rescuer's worth is drawn from being needed. This is a sink presenting as a source: under the outward flow of help there is a stronger inward flow of significance. And it fails Greenleaf's test at once — those served do not grow.

Her appraisal questions are the antidote, and they are worth giving as questions. Is it safe, and what is my intention? Am I helping for their sake, or to be someone who helps? What is the pattern? Have I been here before, with this person or others like them, and how did it end? Have I the resources? Or am I giving what I have not got and will come to resent? Is it my role? Is this mine to do — or am I doing it because I cannot bear to watch them do it themselves, and struggle?

Many leaders with a reputation for caring are rescuers, and their teams are full of capable people who have been kept, tenderly, from growing up.

Boundaries as love

The practical upshot can be put shortly, and it is counter to sentiment. The boundary is not the limit of love. It is its organ. To say no; to disagree; to decline to carry what is another's to carry; to end a conversation; to go home; to keep one's own counsel; to let someone fail at a thing they must learn: none of these is a withdrawal of love. Each is the maintenance of the surface at which love occurs.

It follows that organisations wishing to be places where the proposition's state can arise should be more interested in the health of their boundaries than in the warmth of their climate. Can people here say no? Do meetings end? Is the working day finite? Is disagreement with the leader survivable, and has anyone lately survived it? Do people have lives the organisation knows nothing about? Where the answers are yes, warmth, if it comes, will be the real thing. Where they are no, warmth is to be feared.

THE FUSED GROUP DOES NOT HAVE CLOSER CONTACT. IT HAS NONE.

37The Dark Field: Fear's Wavefront

Everything this work has said about how love propagates is equally true of fear. That sentence is the most sobering in the file and it follows from the file's own method: the mechanisms described were mechanisms, and mechanisms have no preference.

The symmetry

Run down the list.

Gestalt. Fear is perceived as a whole, directly, not inferred. It crosses the gap between two people in the right interval, exactly as phi does. It re-forms the life space — Lewin's first example was a battlefield. It has its own closure: the frightened eye completes ambiguous figures in the direction of threat.

Kardia. Fear is cardial. It is in the chest, and the work on cardiac timing was a study of fear: faces seen at the heart's contraction look more frightening. Hearts synchronise in dread as well as in love; the fire-walk was an ordeal.

Phos. The face is a modulator of light, and it transmits terror, contempt and disgust as efficiently as tenderness — more so, since vigilance for threat is the older system. Papworth lists negativity bias among the obstacles to compassion: the bad registers more strongly than the good.

Wavefront. Each person fear reaches becomes a source of it. Panics, bank runs and rumours are Huygens's principle in its purest social form.

Laser. A population can lase around fear. The coherence is as complete, the beam as far-carrying, the recruitment as strong. The twentieth century supplied the demonstrations, and they looked — the photographs are unbearable for this reason — like joy.

Order parameter. Fear is the commonest order parameter of organisations: the variable to which everything relaxes.

Kuramoto. And it has the lower threshold. This is the decisive asymmetry and needs explaining.

Why fear wins by default

Coupling was identified, in chapter twenty-one, with affectability: the degree to which each lets their state be shifted by others'. For love, the coupling must be chosen — one has to consent to be affected, lower one's guard, attend. That is costly and it is voluntary.

For fear, the coupling is obligatory. The nervous system does not ask leave to respond to a frightened face; the response is underway before one knows there was a face. A walker on a swaying bridge must adjust. So the coupling for fear is high in every population without anyone doing anything, while the coupling for love is whatever people have made it. Given the mathematics, a group will synchronise around fear at a density of frightened members far below the density of loving ones needed to synchronise it around love.

That is why, left alone, organisations drift toward fear. No malice is needed. It is the default attractor, the downhill direction. Love in an institution is an achievement held against a gradient — a far-from-equilibrium structure; fear is where the system goes when the heat is turned off.

It is also why one frightened leader does more harm than one loving leader does good, and faster. The asymmetry is in the physics, not in the persons.

The combat landscape, institutionalised

What does an organisation look like whose order parameter is fear? Lewin gave the outline: the landscape has a front. In detail:

Information travels upward slowly and arrives distorted, since each level edits what it passes on in the interest of its own safety. The top therefore knows least, and knows it last. Most great organisational failures on record have this signature: the facts were known, in the building, by people who did not say or who said and were not heard.

Decisions migrate upward, since deciding is exposure. Senior people are swamped with matters that should have been settled three levels below, and complain that nobody takes responsibility.

Documentation swells. Its function has ceased to be record and become defence.

Language shifts into the passive and the abstract. Mistakes were made. Learnings will be taken forward. The agent disappears from the sentence.

Scapegoats are needed, periodically, and found. René Girard's account of the mechanism fits the organisational case closely: a community whose internal tensions have risen to the breaking point recovers its unity by loading them onto a single member and expelling that member. The peace that follows is real, and brief, and it proves to everyone that the victim was guilty. The departure of a "difficult" executive is followed by a few weeks in which everyone remarks how much better the atmosphere is. Then the tension rises again, having had nothing to do with him.

And — the cruellest feature — a fear-ordered organisation can display, at its upper levels, considerable warmth. Those at the top are safe with one another. They experience the place as collegiate, and are sincerely puzzled by the survey.

Contempt

A word on a second dark order parameter, less remarked than fear and arguably worse. The psychologist John Gottman, who for decades observed married couples in a laboratory flat and predicted with unsettling accuracy which would divorce, found that the single strongest predictor was not anger and not even hostility. It was contempt: the communication, by a rolled eye, a curled lip, a tone, that the other is beneath one.

Contempt is love's exact inverse on every axis of this work. Love perceives under the law of closure; contempt perceives the gap as the whole. Love knows the particular; contempt knows the type. Love enlarges the adjacent possible; contempt fixes the other as what they are and will always be. Love is the realisation that something other than oneself is real; contempt, that the other is not quite. And it propagates as love does. A contemptuous senior partner multiplies his species down through four grades, and one meets his curl of the lip on the face of a trainee who has never spoken to him.

Organisations tolerate contempt in high performers to a remarkable degree. The file suggests that this is the most expensive toleration there is, and that McQuade's four words are, among other things, the most compact anti-contempt policy yet composed.

What can be done

If fear is the default and love the achievement, what follows practically? Not that fear can be abolished — it is a proper response to real danger, and an organisation with none of it would be reckless. What follows is a set of asymmetric disciplines.

Damp fear at its points. The field is changed at its points: fear concentrates at the exposed — the bearer of bad news, the newest, the one who erred. What is done to that person, in view of the rest, sets the coupling for all. Thank the messenger where the room can hear.

Do not transmit one's own. A leader's first duty under threat is containment: to receive the fear, metabolise it, and return something that can be thought about. Not to conceal it — the still face frightens more than the worried one — but not to pass it on raw. Bion's reverie, in a crisis meeting.

Name it. Fear is strongest unnamed, as nameless dread. Said aloud, as a fact about the room — "I think we're all frightened of what this means for our jobs, and I am too" — it becomes something a group can hold together and not something each must manage alone.

Shorten the distance to the truth. Fear thrives on ambiguity. Tell people what is known, what is not, and when they will hear more. Then keep the appointment.

Refuse the scapegoat. When a group's tension is seeking a victim, the leader who declines to supply one — who says, this failure was the system's and I am responsible for the system — breaks the mechanism, at personal cost. McQuade's take responsibility is this in his code; and the cost is what makes it credible.

And raise the other coupling, patiently, below threshold. Since love's coupling is voluntary and costly it must be built deliberately, over a long time, with nothing to show: the hundred and fifty walkers on the bridge.

FEAR'S COUPLING IS FREE. LOVE'S MUST BE CHOSEN. THAT IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY.
