38The Burning-Out of the Luminous

The last corruption is not a counterfeit. It is what happens to the real thing when its form is broken. Those in whom the proposition's state is actually present — the nurse the patients ask for, the teacher who stays behind, the manager everyone goes to, the toxin handler — are the people most at risk of a particular destruction, and the name for it is taken, fittingly, from combustion.

Burnout

The term was introduced in the 1970s by the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger, who had observed it in volunteers at a free clinic — and in himself. Christina Maslach gave it its research form, and her three dimensions remain the standard. Exhaustion: the sense of having nothing left. Depersonalisation, or cynicism: a detached, callous, even dehumanising attitude toward the people one serves — the patient becomes "the gallbladder in bed four." And a reduced sense of accomplishment: the conviction that nothing one does makes any difference.

Read through this work, the three dimensions are the three parts of a broken torus. Exhaustion is the centre emptied: outward flow with no return. Depersonalisation is the defensive closing of the contact boundary: unable to bear the contact, the person ceases to make it, and the other becomes an object. Reduced accomplishment is the severed return path felt from within: what goes out vanishes; nothing comes back to say it arrived.

And the second dimension is the grievous one. The burned-out carer does not just stop loving. She starts — against her nature and to her own horror — to feel something near contempt for those she serves. The luminous goes not merely dark but cold. Maslach's research made a point which organisations have been slow to hear: burnout is not chiefly a property of the person. It arises from a mismatch between person and setting, and she listed where to look — workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values. The remedy most commonly offered, resilience training, addresses the one party who is not the cause.

Empathic distress and compassion

For a long time what befell carers was called compassion fatigue, as though compassion were a reservoir that ran dry. The phrase encodes a theory — the budget theory, parcels and not waves — and the theory appears to be wrong in an instructive way.

Tania Singer and Olga Klimecki, whose work Papworth reports at some length, set out to separate two things the word "empathy" confuses. In one series of studies they trained volunteers first in empathy — resonating with another's suffering, feeling it with them — and then showed them film of people in distress. Negative emotion rose, and the brain regions active were those associated with experiencing pain oneself. They then trained the same volunteers in compassion — a practice, taken from contemplative traditions, of extending warmth and care toward the sufferer. Shown the same kind of film, the volunteers now reported positive feeling alongside their recognition of the suffering, and the brain activity shifted to networks associated with affiliation, reward and love.

Their conclusion: what exhausts is not compassion. It is empathic distress — sharing the other's pain in a way that becomes one's own pain, self-oriented and aversive, issuing in withdrawal. Compassion — other-oriented, warm, moving toward the sufferer — is not depleting; it is, if anything, restorative. They proposed that "compassion fatigue" be renamed empathic distress fatigue, and Papworth endorses the suggestion, observing that the older phrase has done compassion's reputation undeserved harm.

Set this beside the earlier chapters and it locks into place.

Empathic distress is confluence: the boundary has gone; the other's pain is in me as mine. It is Scheler's emotional infection, not his fellow-feeling. It is Bion's mother overwhelmed and unable to contain. It is coupling with the difference lost.

Compassion is contact: I am with you in your pain, and I am not you. Your suffering is recognised as yours, across a boundary which is kept, and what arises in me is not your pain reproduced but warmth and the wish to help. The healthcare maxim which Papworth takes from Stephen Post's work on compassionate care states it with clinical bluntness: be empathic, but the patient's suffering is not your suffering.

So the neuroscience, as far as it goes, confirms the structural claim made in chapter nine from pure geometry. LOVE DOES NOT DEPLETE. FUSION DEPLETES, AND SO DOES A CUT CIRCUIT. A wave is not used up by propagating. What exhausts people is something else that travels with love and is mistaken for it — the unbounded taking-in of another's pain — together with the organisational severing of the return.

Kenosis and depletion

This permits a distinction the tradition has always needed and seldom drawn clearly: between self-emptying and being emptied.

Kenosis, as chapter thirty read it, is power putting itself at the other's disposal. It is a giving from fullness, and — in the theology Balthasar inherited — it is fed: the Son who empties himself receives himself eternally from the Father. Kenosis is the outward half of a torus whose return is assured.

Depletion is being drained. It is giving from an emptiness which the giving deepens. It commonly has an anxious, driven quality, a note of must, and that is the diagnostic: there is, beneath, something the giver needs to get from giving — worth, safety, the avoidance of guilt — and never gets. It is the rescuer's position, and Papworth's name for it, altruism in her technical sense of care for others to one's own detriment, is not a compliment.

Religious cultures and caring professions have often confused the two, and praised depletion as kenosis: the priest who never rests, the nurse who never goes home, the founder who gives everything. The saints the file called as witnesses are worth looking at once more in this light. Philip Neri's defining trait was hilarity. Teresa is the funniest writer among the doctors of the Church. Seraphim greeted every visitor, in every season, with the same two words: my joy. They gave everything, and they were not depleted, and the marks of depletion — grimness, resentment, the sense of being owed — are absent from the record. Whatever they were doing was not what the exhausted helper is doing. Joy is the sign of the intact circuit.

Acedia

The desert monks of the fourth century had a name for a condition which resembles burnout closely and which they regarded as the most dangerous of the monastic temptations. Evagrius of Pontus called it akēdia — literally, not-caring — and the "noonday demon," since it struck in the long dead middle of the day. Its marks: the sun seems not to move; the cell becomes hateful; the work pointless; the brothers irritating; one thinks constantly of other places where one might serve God so much better. It is a slackening of the soul, a loss of all taste for the very thing one gave one's life to.

Their remedy was neither rest nor a change of scene. Evagrius is firm: do not leave the cell. It was stabilitas — to stay; to keep the small, regular acts of the rule: the next psalm, the next basket woven. And it was to confess the condition to an elder. That is: keep the rhythm, and restore the mirror.

It would be glib to prescribe this to an exhausted clinician in an understaffed hospital. Maslach is right that the setting is commonly the cause, and the first duty is to mend the setting. But the desert has something for the part of burnout that is not about workload — the loss of meaning in those whose work has become an unreturned outward flow. The monks did not say: try harder. They said: do the next small thing, and do not carry this alone.

What the institution owes

If the luminous are the institution's most valuable members and the most exposed, its duties to them are plain, and they are duties of plumbing.

Restore the return path. See that those who give see the fruit. The surgeon meets the patient at follow-up; the ward nurse seldom learns what became of anyone. Mend that.

Hold the holders. Supervision, in the clinical sense — a regular, protected hour in which the one who contains others is contained — is standard in psychotherapy and social work and nearly unknown in management and in medicine. It is cheap. It is Kahn's finding made into a practice.

Legitimise the boundary. Make it honourable to go home, to say "not today," to hand over. Institutions that celebrate the one who never stops are celebrating a jet.

Fix the setting before the person. Workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values. Papworth's structural layer.

Teach the difference. Singer and Klimecki's finding is teachable: the difference between drowning in another's pain and being warmly present to it. It ought to be part of the formation of everyone whose work is other people — which is to say, of everyone who manages anyone.

JOY IS THE SIGN OF THE INTACT CIRCUIT.

Movement VII

BECOMING LOVE

The Seventh Claim

The proposition's last sentence leaves psychology behind. One can become Love; a Swiss theologian saw it and said that love alone is credible; and he would not bargain. What the claim means, what the book says, what the record shows — then a rule for trying it, and a room.

39You Can Become Love

You can become Love. The capital letter is the proposition's own. Six claims described a state one may be in. The seventh says the state is not the end of the matter: that there is a transformation in which a person does not have love, or feel it, or do it, but is it.

A work that calls itself experimental should say plainly that it has reached the limit of what it can test. No instrument will show whether a human being has become love. What the file can do is ask what the claim means — what is being asserted, and by whom — and whether it can be given a sense that does not dissolve into piety or inflation.

Three weak readings and a strong one

The claim may be read weakly in three ways, and each is true and insufficient.

Dispositionally: by long practice a person can become reliably loving — love can become a stable trait. Aristotle's account of virtue as a hexis, a settled state acquired by repeated acts, covers this. True; and it is not what the proposition means. One can have a kindly disposition and not be what the witnesses of chapter ten became.

Dynamically: love can become a person's order parameter — the slow variable to which all else in them relaxes. This is chapter twenty's claim and the file stands by it. It is nearer. But an order parameter is still a property of a system.

Relationally: by Mead and Stacey, the self is constituted in gesture and response; a person whose every gesture is completed as love is, in the only sense in which a self is anything, love. Nearer still. And Kauffman's image: in an autocatalytic set, to be a member is to be a catalyst — one's place is one's making-possible of others.

The strong reading is the one the tradition actually makes, and it is ontological. It says that Love — with the capital — is not a state of human beings at all in the first place. It is what is ultimately real. God is love: the sentence is in the first letter of John, and the grammar is identity, not attribution. And human beings can, by gift, come to participate in that reality so fully that it becomes the truth of what they are. The Greek Fathers' word was theosis. Athanasius's formula was that God became human so that the human might become God. Peter's second letter speaks of becoming partakers of the divine nature. Catherine of Genoa, a fifteenth-century hospital administrator — she ran the largest hospital in the city through an outbreak of plague, and is as hard-headed a witness as the tradition affords — put it in a sentence that shocked her confessors: my Me is God, nor do I recognise any other Me except my God himself.

The file cannot adjudicate the strong reading. It observes three things about it.

First: it reverses the direction of becoming

On the weak readings, becoming love is a human achievement: one builds the disposition, attains the coherence. On the strong reading it is the reverse. Love is prior. It is already there, already circulating — the perichoresis of chapter nine — and what happens to a person is that they are taken up into it. One does not become a source. One is joined to the source.

This is why every witness in chapter ten uses the passive voice. A globe of fire entered. My heart was strangely warmed. Rolle put his hand to his chest because the heat was not his doing. And it is why Beisser's paradoxical theory — change comes not by striving to be what one is not — proved the first qualification of the seventh claim. The traditions that know most about becoming love are unanimous that it cannot be done. It can be undergone. What is in one's power is the removal of obstacles and the giving of consent: the sub-threshold pumping, and the mirrors.

For organisations the point is not small. It is the difference between a programme and a hospitality. No organisation can make itself loving, as no person can. It can become a place where love, should it come, would not be turned away.

Second: it does not abolish the self

The obvious fear about "becoming Love" is that it means dissolution: the drop into the ocean, the self gone. That would be fusion, and the sixth movement has said what fusion is.

The Christian tradition, at its most careful, denies it and offers images to mark the difference. The favourite is iron in fire. Iron left in a furnace becomes fire: it glows, it burns, it does all that fire does. And it remains iron — it has not turned into something else, and taken out it is iron still, though it will not be quite as it was. Bernard of Clairvaux used it, with two others: a drop of water in a great quantity of wine, taking the wine's taste and colour; and air flooded with sunlight, so transfigured that it seems to be not so much lit as light itself.

You become light-emitting. The proposition's sixth claim is the classical image for its seventh. The iron glows with a light that is the fire's, and it is the iron that glows. Participation without confusion. And the hesychasts' essence–energies distinction existed to protect exactly this: one becomes by grace all that God is — in the energies, the shining-forth — while the essence remains for ever other. Contact without confluence, at the highest level at which anyone has tried to state it.

There is a Chinese parallel that should be on the file, though it is a parallel and not an identity. Wang Yangming, the Ming-dynasty general and philosopher, taught in his Inquiry on the Great Learning that the great person regards Heaven, Earth and the myriad things as one body — 以天地萬物為一體. Not as a doctrine to be held: as a perception. On seeing a child about to fall into a well one feels alarm, and this shows that one's 仁 — rén, humaneness, the character composed of "person" and "two" — forms one body with the child. One feels something at the cry of a bird, the breaking of a plant, even the shattering of a tile. That humaneness is the original nature of the heart-mind; it is obscured by selfish desire; and learning is nothing but the clearing away of what obscures it. The classic on which he was commenting begins with the phrase 明明德 — to make bright one's bright virtue. The radiance is already there. One does not acquire it. One un-dims it.

Third: it has an organisational form

This is the unexpected thing, and the reason the seventh claim belongs in a work about organisations.

In every tradition that makes the strong claim, becoming love is not a private attainment. It is incorporation — being made a member of a body. Paul's image for those who have been taken up into love is literally organisational: a body with many members, differing in function, each needing the others, the eye unable to say to the hand I have no need of thee, the less honourable parts given the more abundant honour, and when one member suffers all suffering with it. It is the most influential piece of organisation theory ever written, and it occurs immediately before, and as the setup for, the most famous chapter on love in any literature. The order is not accidental. First the body; then, a more excellent way; then the hymn to charity. Love is what a body of that kind runs on.

So the strong reading does not say that an individual can become a luminous monad. It says that a person becomes love by becoming a member — a node in an autocatalytic set, a point on a wavefront, a voice in a choir — of a circulation greater than themselves. Kauffman's formal image and Paul's theological one coincide: to be a member is to be a catalyst.

Translated out of theology into what the file can stand behind: no one becomes love alone. The state the proposition describes, if it is to be more than an episode, needs a body — a community with a centre beyond itself, a rhythm, mirrors, and a place for the weak — in which it is received, returned and kept. Heart-burst is followed by organisation; that was the least-noticed fact of chapter ten. It can now be said why. It is not that the fire needs administering. It is that the fire is a circulation, and a circulation needs members to circulate through.

THE IRON BECOMES FIRE. IT DOES NOT CEASE TO BE IRON.

40Love Alone Is Credible

The proposition cites a book by its title. Chapter six gave its argument in a page. The file now returns to it to ask what the title means, and what it would mean for an organisation to take it as a criterion.

The claim, more exactly

Glaubhaft ist nur Liebe. The German adjective is the telling word: glaubhaft — believable, worthy of belief, such as can be given credence. Balthasar's question is not whether Christianity is true. It is under what aspect it can show itself as worthy of being believed — what it must look like for a human being to be right to stake their life on it.

His answer proceeds by eliminating the two aspects under which it had mostly been commended. If it shows itself as the completion of the world's order, it is credible to the extent that the world's order is, and falls when cosmologies change. If it shows itself as the fulfilment of human need, it is credible to the extent that one's needs are a reliable guide, and it has made the human subject the measure of the divine. In both it is believed for the sake of something else.

What remains is the aspect of love. And his point about love is that it is credible only as itself. If someone loves me, there is no further fact on which I could ground my belief that they do. I cannot deduce it from their interests — if it followed from their interests it would not be love. I cannot deduce it from my deserts — if I had earned it, it would be wages. Love appears as groundless, in the precise sense of having no ground outside itself; that is exactly what makes it love; and its only evidence is its own form. It is perceived — Schau der Gestalt — or not at all.

Hence the form it must take in order to be seen. A love that could be accounted for — that stopped where prudence stops — would always be open to another explanation. Only love that goes beyond every explicable limit shows itself unambiguously as love. For Balthasar that is the meaning of the cross and of the descent into hell which so preoccupied him: love going to the uttermost point of lostness, where nothing could possibly be gained. It is credible because it is, by every other measure, absurd.

And the response which that form calls for is not assent to a proposition. It is being taken: the rapture which is the other half of seeing the form. One does not conclude that love is credible. One finds that one has believed it.

Credibility in institutions

Chapter six made the first application: institutions commend themselves cosmologically (we are sound) or anthropologically (we meet your needs), and neither is a reason to trust. The file can now press it further, with the intervening chapters in hand.

What trust is. The standard account in the organisational literature — Mayer, Davis and Schoorman's — defines trust as the willingness to be vulnerable to another on the expectation that they will act as one hopes, irrespective of one's ability to monitor or control them; and it names three grounds on which someone is judged trustworthy: ability, integrity, and benevolence. Ability is competence. Integrity is adherence to principles one accepts. Benevolence is the extent to which the other is believed to want to do one good apart from any egocentric profit motive.

Put that beside Balthasar. Ability is the cosmological commendation: we function; we fit. Integrity is near to it: we follow the rules. Benevolence — a wish for my good not explicable by the other's interest — is love, in his exact sense, and under its sober management-science name. And the research that followed the model has found, on the whole, what he would have predicted: ability and integrity make one reliable; benevolence is what makes one trusted, especially as a relationship deepens and especially by those in the weaker position.

How benevolence is known. Not by assertion. An organisation's declaration that it cares is, at best, uninformative, since both a caring and an uncaring one would make it. It is known the only way love is known: by acts that cannot be otherwise explained. The economists have a concept that fits — the costly signal: a signal is credible to the degree that it would be too expensive to send if it were false. Balthasar's theology of the cross is a theology of costly signalling carried to infinity. Its institutional version is finite and observable: the act for which the organisation paid, and which it had no interest in performing.

Everyone who has worked for long can name such acts, and they are how institutions are actually judged. The employer who kept paying a man through two years of his wife's dying. The bank that told the customer about the cheaper product. The firm that reported itself. The receiver who found the tenant somewhere to go when nothing in the appointment required it. These are recounted for decades; they are the canon of chapter thirty-three. And they do more for the institution's standing than all its communications together — on the strict condition that they were not done for that reason. The moment the generous act is seen to have been reputational investment it becomes explicable, and what is explicable is not credible as love.

So here is a paradox, in the Danish authors' strict sense, at the heart of institutional trust, and Balthasar's title names it. THE ONLY THING THAT MAKES AN INSTITUTION CREDIBLE IS WHAT IT DOES WITH NO VIEW TO ITS CREDIBILITY.

The asymmetry of the test. Love shows itself as love where it could have got away with not loving. So the test of an institution is not how it treats those who can reward or punish it — its large customers, its regulators, its stars. That is prudence. The test is how it treats those who cannot: the junior, the leaver, the small supplier, the borrower in default, the complainant with no lawyer, the patient with no family. McQuade's four words mark the floor; his book as a whole — forced labour at the far end of a supply chain, where no customer will ever look — marks how far down the test reaches. Benedict's Rule makes the same test its measure: the guest, the poor man at the gate, the sick brother, the boy. The cross is the limit case: love toward those in the act of killing it.

An institution's credibility is established at its margins and nowhere else.

The corollary for the proposition

And now a thing about the proposition itself. Its first six claims were, in Balthasar's terms, reductions. They commended love cosmologically: it has a field, a geometry, a physics; it fits the order of nature. And anthropologically: it is a state, it fulfils, it energises. This file has followed and extended both — it has spent six movements showing that love fits what gestalt psychology, physiology, optics and complexity science know, and that it answers to what people and organisations need.

Balthasar's title says that none of this is why love is to be believed. If love were credible because it is toroidal, it would be only as credible as toroids. If it were credible because it lowers absenteeism in long-term care, it would be as credible as the next study. The whole apparatus is, by his measure, scaffolding — worth erecting, since it removes false obstacles and shows that nothing known forbids the thing. But the thing is credible only by itself, in a form, in a face, crossing a room.

The proposition's author saw this. It is why the proposition, having given a physics, ends not with a further fact but with a title and a refusal. Love alone is credible. The seventh claim is not a seventh item of evidence. It is the statement that the first six were not the reason.

WHAT IS EXPLICABLE IS NOT CREDIBLE AS LOVE.

41The Man Who Would Not Bargain

The proposition closes on a biographical claim: that Balthasar saw one could become Love, said that love alone is credible, and that this is why he stopped negotiating to rejoin the Jesuits. The file owes the claim two things: the record, as far as it is known; and an honest marking of where the record ends and reading begins.

The record

Hans Urs von Balthasar was born at Lucerne in 1905, of a patrician family. He took his doctorate at Zurich in German literature. At a retreat in the Black Forest in 1927 he experienced what he later described as a sudden and wholly unexpected call — he said he could, decades on, still find the tree beneath which it struck him — and in 1929 he entered the Society of Jesus. He studied under Erich Przywara and, at Lyon, alongside Henri de Lubac; he detested the dry scholasticism of his formal training and read the Fathers of the Church under the desk. Ordained in 1936, he was sent in 1940 to Basel as chaplain to the university's Catholic students.

There, the same year, he met Adrienne von Speyr: a physician, one of the first women in Switzerland to qualify, a Protestant of difficult temperament and intense interior life, married to a professor of history. He received her into the Catholic Church that November. Almost at once there began in her a flood of mystical experience, which she reported to him and which he came to regard as authentic. Over the following twenty-seven years he took down, from her dictation, some sixty volumes. He said repeatedly, and with force, that her work and his were not to be separated — two halves of one whole — and that the greater part of what was thought his own came from her.

In 1945 they founded together a secular institute: the Community of Saint John, for laypeople and diocesan priests who would take the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and remain in their ordinary occupations in the world. Its patron is the disciple whom Jesus loved. The community's own statement of its purpose, published today, is that God needs more love, and man needs more love, and it wishes to stand in the midst of that double need.

The Society of Jesus could not accept the arrangement. A Jesuit under obedience could not be the head of a separate institute outside the order's authority; nor were his superiors, or the local bishop, persuaded of the mission. There was a long discernment and an interview with the Father General. Balthasar was offered, in effect, a choice. In February 1950 he left the Society. He explained it as obedience — to a God who has the right, at any time, to call a man out of the home he chose in a religious order and use him as he will. He renewed his vows privately at the abbey of Maria Laach. He is reported to have regarded the Society, to the end, as his dearest and most natural home.

The cost was real. He had no ecclesiastical standing: for six years no bishop would have him, and he could not lawfully exercise a ministry until the diocese of Chur took him in. He had no post and no income but lecturing and a small publishing house. He was not invited to the Second Vatican Council, in whose aftermath he would be recognised as one of the century's major theologians. Herrlichkeit was begun in those years; Love Alone Is Credible appeared in 1963. Adrienne von Speyr died in 1967, after long illness, blind. He stayed in Basel, led the community, and published her.

And at the end: by the account of the Dominican scholar Aidan Nichols, drawing on the biographical sketch by Balthasar's cousin, the Jesuit bishop Peter Henrici, Balthasar shortly before his death asked the then Father General, Peter-Hans Kolvenbach, to receive him back into the Society. The negotiation foundered — once more — on the question of the Community of Saint John. He died on 26 June 1988, two days before he was to have been made a cardinal.

Where the record ends

That is what the sources the file has been able to consult establish. They establish that he sought readmission; that there was a negotiation; and that it failed over the community. They do not say, in so many words, that he broke it off, nor do they give his reasons in his own voice. The proposition's wording — he stopped negotiating — is a reading, and the causal clause — because of what he had seen about love — is a reading of the reading. The file marks it so. Archives which would settle the matter are, by the testimony of those who have written on him, not yet fully open.

But it is not an arbitrary reading. The file sets down why.

The reading

Consider the structure of what happened, twice.

In 1950 he was offered a choice between two goods. One was the home he loved, the order of Ignatius to whom he was devoted until his death, with everything it gave: standing, livelihood, companions, a platform. The other was a small, uncertain community of a few laypeople, founded with a woman whose visions his superiors doubted, with no recognition and no future anyone could see. Either could have been defended. He might have told himself that obedience to superiors was obedience to God; most would have. He chose the community, and paid.

In his last years he sought to come home. And the same condition met him. One may suppose — it would be the natural supposition — that some formula was available: that the community could have been placed under other care, or allowed to lapse, or its tie to him loosened, and an old man of eighty, about to be made a cardinal, could have died a Jesuit. He did not die a Jesuit.

What was it that he would not put on the table, twice, thirty-eight years apart? Not a doctrine. Not a position. A community — a body of persons, bound together under the sign of the beloved disciple, which he and Adrienne von Speyr had been given to found. By his own account, the centre of his work. A thing that love had made.

Now set against this the argument of his book. Love is credible only as itself. It cannot be grounded in anything else; and therefore — this is the step the proposition's author took — it cannot be exchanged for anything else. Whatever can be traded has a price, and whatever has a price is being valued by a standard outside itself. To negotiate away the community for readmission would have been to treat what love had made as a means to another good — a great good, his dearest home. It would have been, in his own vocabulary, a reduction.

On this reading his not-bargaining was not stubbornness, and not a low view of the Society. It was the enacted form of his title. He could negotiate about everything else — his standing, his reputation, his security had all been given up long before. He could not negotiate about that, because it was not his to trade. LOVE CHANGES WHAT CAN BE NEGOTIATED: the Overture's claim, at its source.

The file adds two cautions, in the spirit of McQuade's assonance.

First, the same facts bear another reading, and a critic could give it. A man deeply bound to a visionary woman, convinced of a private revelation which his superiors could not verify, twice put that conviction above the judgement of his order. The tradition he belonged to knows this pattern and is properly wary of it. That his was the authentic case and not the deluded one is a judgement his later standing in the Church supports, and which the facts alone do not compel. Much of the criticism of his theology has turned on his dependence on von Speyr.

Second, the Jesuits were not wrong to refuse. An order cannot have a member whose primary obedience lies elsewhere; that is what an order is. Two goods, each with its own integrity, could not both be had. This was no dilemma solved. It was a paradox carried for thirty-eight years — and the cork came up at the end exactly as the Danish authors say it does.

The Cruciform, exemplified

McQuade's figure fits the case more closely than any other in this work, and the fit is instructive.

The horizontal: the social situation of a Jesuit in 1950 — its past, four centuries of the Society's practice of obedience; its present demand; its future, a distinguished career within the order. The vertical: the Me — everything the Black Forest, the Fathers, and ten years with Adrienne von Speyr had laid down in him; the You — the man he believed he was being called to become. At the crossing: February 1950.

McQuade's account of how dissent becomes possible — that one is always in more than one social situation, and may judge the one from the other — is precisely what occurred. The community was his second situation. From within it, what the first required of him could be seen and weighed. And McQuade's observation about the cost holds: some who choose according to their deepest values against the pressure of their situation pay a high price; others change the world. Balthasar did both, in that order, with twenty years between.

Note what kind of choice it was. Not good against evil; both courses were good. It was McQuade's assonance, Nussbaum's conflict of goods — and his rule for it is to choose the more life-affirming. It may be that this is what Balthasar thought he was doing. The community's own word for its purpose is more love.

What an organisation can take from it

The story is about one man and a religious order. It generalises to a question that can be put to any person in any institution, and to any institution itself.

What will you not negotiate?

Everyone in organisational life negotiates constantly, and rightly. Compromise is the ordinary and honourable business of living with others; Follett's integration is better still. A person who can never yield is not principled but rigid, and the Danish authors have a caricature for him.

But a person — or an institution — with nothing that is off the table has no centre. Everything about them has a price; and those who deal with them know it, and deal accordingly. This is the deepest reason why merely strategic actors are not trusted, however reliable: one knows that their commitment to oneself is, like everything else, a position.

What makes a person or an institution credible is that there is something they will not trade — and that the something is for others. A fixed point of self-interest is not credibility; it is a reservation price. A fixed point of love — I will not sell these people; I will not lie to that one; I will not abandon this — is what the word integrity means when it means anything.

Such points are known only when tested, and the test is always an offer: something good, in exchange. Balthasar was offered his home. The offers made in organisations are smaller and of the same form. The promotion, if one says nothing about what one saw. The deal, if the weaker party's interest is quietly dropped. The quiet life, if the difficult colleague is left to face it alone. The merger that secures the institution's future, at the price of what it was for.

It is, the file suggests, a useful discipline for a leader to know before the offer comes — since once it has come one's reasoning is no longer to be trusted — what is not for sale. And for a board to know the same of the institution. The list should be short. If it is long, one is rigid. If it is empty, one is nothing. On Balthasar's it seems there was one item.

WHATEVER CAN BE TRADED HAS A PRICE. LOVE IS WHAT HAS NONE.

42A Rule for Trying It

The file promised experiments. A treatise on love that ended in contemplation of its own argument would be a closed loop. What follows is a short rule — in Benedict's sense, a little rule for beginners — distilled from the forty-one chapters and from the three disciplines of chapter twenty-nine: see, weigh, choose, hold. Its items are practices that a person or a team can try, with something to observe afterwards. None requires permission, budget, or the use of the word.

They are given in the order of the argument. The fuller protocols, with what to look for, are gathered in the Apparatus.

For the person

1. Find the chest. Three times a day, for a week, stop for thirty seconds and attend to the region behind the breastbone. Is it narrow or wide? Tight, warm, hollow, full? Do not change it. Note it. This is the instrument; one cannot read a room with a gauge one never looks at. (Chapters 7, 27.)

2. Ask "what", not "why". At the day's end, five minutes: what did I send out today — in the three encounters I remember best? Not what I meant: what was probably received? This is the mirror; without it there is no cavity. (Chapters 18, 28.)

3. One act of attention. Once a day, give one person two minutes of attention with nothing else in it: no device, no rehearsing of a reply, no agenda. If a question arises, let it be Weil's — what are you going through? — in whatever words are natural. Afterwards note what happened in your chest, and what they did next. (Chapters 8, 11.)

4. Appraise before you help. The next time you are moved to step in for someone, pause for one breath and put Papworth's four questions. What is my intention? Is this a pattern — am I rescuing? Have I the resources? Is it my role? Then act, or do not. Note which question changed what you did. (Chapters 26, 29, 36.)

5. Find your pole. Draw the Paradox Quadrant for mercy and truth. Fill all four boxes. The one you find hardest to fill is your blind spot. Show it to someone who is your opposite and ask them to complete it. (Chapters 24, 29, 31.)

6. Know the item. Write down what you will not negotiate. Keep the list to three lines. Check each: is it for others, or for me? (Chapter 41.)

7. Check the circuit. Where does what I give come back to me from? If the honest answer is "nowhere", that is the first thing to mend, before any of the others. Who holds me? (Chapters 9, 32, 38.)

For the room

8. The first ninety seconds. Begin one regular meeting differently for a month. Before the agenda, a round in which each person says one sentence about what they are carrying into the room. No discussion. Then begin. Observe what happens to the passive voice over the month. (Chapters 4, 27.)

9. The related spectator. When a colleague is exposed — presenting, being challenged, giving bad news — decide to be for them. Not to defend them: to attend, with your face, as someone on their side. Observe what they do. (Chapters 11, 17.)

10. Thank the messenger where the room can hear. The next time someone brings unwelcome truth, thank them specifically and publicly before responding to the content. This alters the slope for everyone watching. (Chapters 23, 28, 37.)

11. Name the atmosphere. Once, when the room is plainly mis-tuned, say what you notice as your own perception, without blame: "I've gone careful. I think we all have." Then be quiet. (Chapters 5, 27.)

12. Disagree with the warmth. In the team you think is closest, differ openly about something that matters, and watch the temperature. If it drops, the closeness was fusion. If the disagreement is met, it is the real thing. (Chapters 21, 34, 36.)

13. Be moved in public. Change your mind in a meeting because of something a junior person said, and say that that is why. (Chapters 21, 28.)

14. Complete one thing. Identify one unfinished relational act in the team's history — the unthanked, the unapologised-for, the unmourned — and finish it. Say the thing. Observe the corridor. (Chapter 4.)

For the institution

15. Read the order parameter. For one week, in every meeting you attend, ask silently: when something disturbs this room, to what does it relax? Write the answer down each time. At the week's end read the list. (Chapter 20.)

16. Find the toxin handlers. Ask ten people, separately: when things are bad here, who do people go to? The names that recur are carrying the place. Find out who holds them. (Chapter 32.)

17. Restore one return path. Pick one group that gives and never sees the result. Arrange for them to meet, once, face to face, someone their work was for. (Chapters 9, 35, 38.)

18. Test a margin. Choose the person or party with least power to reward or punish the organisation — a leaver, a small supplier, a customer in arrears. Find out, in detail, how they were last treated. That is the institution's credibility. (Chapters 40, 41.)

19. Audit the dampers. Take one procedure that slows things down. Ask what it was installed to prevent — and what else it is now preventing. (Chapter 21.)

20. Tell the story. Find the oldest person in the building. Ask them for the story of the day the place was at its best. Then ask who else knows it. If no one does, tell it. (Chapter 33.)

21. Do one inexplicable thing. One act of institutional generosity for which there is no business case and which will not be publicised. Do not announce it. (Chapter 40.)

The rule of the rule

Three warnings, which are the sixth movement in brief.

Do not turn these into a programme. The moment the first ninety seconds is rolled out across the division with a facilitator's guide, it is a fast variable being pushed. These are for a person to try, and to tell another person about if it was worth it. That is the only scaling the phenomenon allows, and it is Huygens's.

Do not measure the result into a target. Observe; note; tell. Do not score.

Expect nothing to show for a long time. A hundred and fifty walkers.

And the fourth, which is McQuade's. Whatever else: decency to whoever is in front of you. If the rule is being kept and that is not, something has gone wrong with the rule.

THE ONLY SCALING LOVE ALLOWS IS ONE PERSON TELLING ANOTHER.

How to use them. One at a time, by one person, with something noted afterwards. Apparatus IV gives what to look for in each.

What the chapter forbids. Turning them into a programme; scoring the results into a target; expecting anything to show quickly.

43Crossing the Room

A scene, to end. It is composed; no one in it is a real person. It is given because an argument about a form should finish by showing one.

It is a little after four on a Thursday in late November and already dark outside. A meeting room on the third floor of an office that has seen better decades: a long table of pale veneer, a screen, a tray with the cold remains of the two o'clock coffee. Nine people. They have been here since half past one.

The matter is a business that is going to fail. Not theirs — a customer's. A family firm, third generation, which has borrowed against everything it owns and has now, for the second time, missed what it promised. The numbers on the screen are worse than the numbers in the pack. The people round the table are the ones who must decide what happens next, and all of them know what the decision is. They have known since before lunch. What they have been doing for two and a half hours is arranging for it not to have been anyone's.

The man from credit has spoken in the passive for twenty minutes. It was felt at the time. Assurances were received. The relationship manager, who brought the firm in eleven years ago and has eaten at the family's table, has not looked up from his papers. The lawyer has said twice that she is only advising on the options. The chair — a decent man, tired — has said let's just step back three times, and each time the room has stepped back to precisely where it was.

The landscape has a front. Everyone can feel where it is. It runs just in front of the relationship manager's chair.

The door opens and a woman comes in, apologising quietly — a train. She is the one who will have to carry out whatever is decided: go to the premises, meet the family, do the thing. She has done it some hundreds of times. She is not senior to anyone here. She sits at the one empty place, which is opposite the relationship manager, and does not open her folder.

She looks at him.

It is not a sympathetic look, exactly. She is not sorry for him. She has simply seen that he is the one on the coals. She knows what it is to have sat at someone's table. Her face says, with no softness whatever about what is coming: I know. Go on.

He looks up. It takes, perhaps, a second and a half.

"I should have called it in March," he says. "I saw the stock figures and I knew. I didn't want to be the one. I told myself they'd trade through." He stops. "They won't trade through."

Nobody speaks. It is not the silence of the last two hours. It is wider.

The man from credit puts down his pen. "We approved the second extension on my recommendation," he says. "I'd like that minuted properly. I recommended it."

The chair breathes out. The lawyer, a little to her own surprise, says: "Can I say what I actually think you should do?" — and says it, in four sentences. It is what they all knew.

It is decided in ten minutes. It is the same decision. The firm will go into receivership; the property will be sold; a family will lose what three generations built. No one in the room pretends otherwise, and nothing that has happened here will make it hurt less when it comes.

But listen to what the room does now, because it is different work. The relationship manager says he will go with her on the first day — he owes them his face. The man from credit asks whether the old man's house is caught by the security, and when told that it is, asks whether it has to be, and for the first time in the afternoon three people lean forward to look for a way. The lawyer thinks there may be one. Someone says the workforce should hear it from a person and not from a notice on the gate, and the woman who came in late says that is how she does it anyway; she will be there at seven, before the shift, and she will stay until everyone who wants to has spoken to her.

The chair asks if she needs anything.

"Someone to ring afterwards," she says. "It's a long day."

"Ring me," he says, and means it, and she can see that he means it.

They gather their papers. It is ten to five. On the way out the youngest person in the room — an analyst, eight months in, who has said nothing all afternoon and has been watching as the young watch — holds the door for her, and finds he wants to say something and does not know what, and says, "Thank you for coming."

She laughs. "I was late."

"I know," he says. "But —" and he makes a small, helpless gesture at the room behind him, the table, the cold coffee, the nine chairs pushed back at angles.

She understands him perfectly. She has no word for it either. She touches his arm, briefly, as she passes, and goes down the stairs.

He stands a moment in the doorway. He will be thirty years in rooms like this one. Most of them will have a front. He does not know it yet, but he has just been shown what he will spend those years trying to do, and will sometimes, on a good day, with no idea how, manage: to come in, sit down, and look at whoever is on the coals.

The lights in the corridor are the ordinary lights. The building's heating ticks. Through the window at the stair-head the city is lit, storey upon storey, each lamp sending out its small indifferent brilliance into the dark.

He goes back to his desk. He finds that he can see it very clearly.

NOTHING WAS ADDED. THE SAME PEOPLE. THE SAME DECISION. A DIFFERENT ROOM.

File note, in fullChapter 43

What kind of thing this is. A composed scene. Nobody in it is real. It asserts nothing the preceding chapters have not argued and is there so that the argument can be checked against a room.

What to check. Whether anything in it is implausible to someone who has sat in such meetings: the passive voice, the look, the sentence begun again, the same decision reached and different work done afterwards.

The objection it invites. That the scene is about how lenders felt while a family lost everything. The Contra's fifth objection says so, and the file concedes most of it.

What the scene claims and no more. Nothing was added. The same people, the same decision, a different room.

Registers used here
  • E Experiential. Reported from the first person, by the author of the proposition or by a witness in the tradition. True as experience; open as to cause.

Contra: The Objections at Full Strength

A file kept as experimental must record what tells against it. Eight objections follow. They are stated as their best advocates would state them. Some are answered. Some are answered in part. Two are not answered, and are left standing because the file does not know how to knock them down.

I. The objection from physics

The proposition makes physical claims: a field, a wavefront, light, substance, super-luminous propagation. Your own ledger shows that each is either false or irrelevant at the magnitudes involved. You then keep the vocabulary on the plea that it is "phenomenologically apt" or "beyond-light". This is having it both ways. Either love is an electromagnetic phenomenon, in which case it is refuted, or it is not, in which case the language of fields and photons is ornament and should be dropped. A metaphor that has been shown to be a metaphor should not go on being used as though it were something more.

Reply. The objection is right about the electromagnetism, and chapter twelve said so without hedging. It is wrong that the only alternatives are literal physics and ornament. There is a third status, which the file has tried to give with some care: structural description. To say that love propagates as a wavefront is to say that it has the specific properties which distinguish waves from parcels — it does not deplete its source; each point reached re-emits; contributions superpose and can cancel or reinforce; it diffracts round obstacles. Those are checkable claims about how influence moves among people. They are true or false regardless of whether anything electromagnetic is involved. The same holds for field (interdependence of states across a group), torus (outflow that returns through its origin), coherence (emissions in phase), resonance (selective response in tuned receivers), threshold (discontinuous onset). The vocabulary is kept because, term by term, it carries structure which plain speech lacks.

Conceded. The proposition's own sentence — light has real substance — claims more than structure, and the file has not vindicated it. The hesychast tradition would; this work could only report that tradition. On substance in the sense of stuff, the objection stands.

II. The objection from reification

This is Stacey's, pressed harder than you allowed. You conceded that the field is "not a stuff and not an agent" — and then continued for twenty chapters to write sentences in which love re-forms, orders, crosses, constrains, propagates and recruits. You speak of institutions "holding" and "remembering". Every such sentence makes a pattern into a subject that acts. The concession was verbal. In practice you have written a systems-thinking book with a disclaimer in chapter twenty-two.

Reply, partial. The grammar is as charged, and the file knows of no way to write English at this length without subjects for its verbs. The defence is that each such sentence can be cashed out in terms of persons doing things to and with one another, and that at the critical points the file has done the cashing: the leader as participant, not designer; the meaning of the gesture in the response; responsibility under the Cruciform as personal and not transferable to "the culture"; the warning in the rule against programmes.

Not answered. Whether the cashing-out is always possible — whether "the institution remembers" is in every case shorthand for what named people do, or whether something really is carried by arrangements which no present person intends or understands — the file does not know. Chapter thirty-three suggested that atmospheres cling to places and are found there by those who never knew their source. If that is so, it is a fact which Stacey's ontology has trouble admitting. If it is not, chapter thirty-three is partly mystification. The matter is left open.

III. The objection from partiality

You answered Weber by separating agape from partial attachment. But a love with no preference is no love. Love is essentially of this one and not that; it singles out; you said so yourself, with your haecceitas. An impartial benevolence toward whoever happens to be in front of one is admirable, and it is not what the proposition describes — heart-burst, fire, something crossing a room to this person. Either the proposition's love is particular, and Weber's objection holds: it has no place in an office that must treat like cases alike. Or it is general, and you have changed the subject.

Reply. This is the strongest objection of the eight, and the answer is not comfortable. It is true that love is particular. The file denies that particularity is the same as preference. To attend wholly to the person before one — to see this one — is not to rank them above the next. The nurse who is fully present to the patient in bed four is not thereby less present to the patient in bed five when she reaches him. What Weber's clerk owes the widow is impartiality in the outcome: the same pension as anyone. What he may also give her — and the minister's cousin — is attention to her. Impartiality governs the decision; particularity governs the encounter. Papworth's appraisal of role exists to keep the two apart.

Conceded. In practice they leak. Attention is finite; it goes more readily to those we like; and what begins as fuller attention ends as better treatment. Papworth's bias chapter documents precisely this — in-group favouritism at the feeling step. Anyone who has managed knows that the people they find it easy to love get more of everything. The file's distinction is sound in principle and is violated daily, and an organisation which licensed its managers to love without guarding hard against that leakage would have earned every word of Weber's reproach. The procedures are not love's enemy. They are what protects those the manager does not happen to warm to.

IV. The objection from instrumentality

You spend chapter twenty-six showing that love improves outcomes and chapter thirty-five saying it must not be sought for its outcomes. The first will be read; the second will be ignored. Whatever your intent, the effect of this work is to supply management with a new and deeper resource to mine. You have told it where the gold is and then asked it to be a gardener. It will not be. The honest course was not to write the fifth movement.

Not answered. The file called this a paradox and proposed navigating it. That may be the truth of the matter. It may also be an instance of what the Danish authors themselves warn against: the language of paradox used to avoid a choice which is owed. The evidence that love benefits organisations is evidence, and to suppress it would be a dishonesty of its own. But the objection's prediction about how such evidence is used is, on the historical record of every previous humanisation of management — human relations, culture, engagement, purpose, wellbeing — accurate. Each was taken up, instrumented, and emptied. There is no reason in the argument of this file why love should fare differently, and one reason, set out in chapter thirty-five, why it will fare worse: it is the most valuable.

All the file can say is that it has put the warning in the same binding as the evidence, and at greater length.

V. The objection from power

Your scene is set in a bank. A family loses everything; and the point of the scene is that the bankers felt better about it and behaved more gracefully. This is the oldest function of love-talk in institutions: to make the exercise of power over others more comfortable for those who exercise it. Nothing changed for the family except the manner of their dispossession. You have written a hundred thousand words about the hearts of those on the strong side of the desk. McQuade, whom you cite, would ask about the political economy that put the family there.

Reply, partial. The objection is fair to the scene and the file chose the scene knowing it. Three things in mitigation. First, the manner is not nothing; those who have been on the weak side of such a desk say so with one voice, and to wave it away as cosmetic is a luxury of people who have not been there. Second, the scene shows something material changing: the house; the way the workforce hears. Rooms without a front find options that defended rooms do not look for. Third, chapter thirty argued that love without power abandons the weak, and that the question is what love does in the seat of power-over — not whether it may sit there.

Conceded. McQuade's two closing chapters are about what his title leaves out: slavery, climate, the structures within which individual choices are made. He holds that ethical leadership which stops at the leader's own decisions, and does not reach the political economy, has stopped too soon; two of his six code elements are substantive constraints on what an enterprise may do at all. This work has no equivalent. It has much to say about how the lender should treat the borrower and nothing about whether the terms of lending are just. A treatise on love in organisations that does not ask what organisations are doing to those outside them — at the far end of the supply chain, downstream, in the next generation — has answered Arendt only in part. Love that stays within the room is still worldless.

VI. The objection from testimony

Your "witnesses" are a hermit, five saints and a Russian squire, reported in hagiography and canonisation dossiers, whose agreement you treat as data. They agree because they shared a tradition which told them what to expect and how to describe it. Rolle had read the mystics on fire. Motovilov knew what a transfiguration was supposed to look like. Their concurrence is the concurrence of people using one script.

Reply. The shared-script point has force and the file accepts that it weakens the evidential value of the agreement. Three things remain. The reports include details the script does not supply and would be unlikely to invent: a hand put to the chest to check; ribs displaced; a man noting that it was a quarter before nine. They come with marked reluctance — Pascal hid his; Philip Neri played the fool to deflect attention; Symeon was exiled for his. And the experience at lower intensity is not confined to any tradition: it is the corridor's testimony. People with no script at all say that the lights came on.

Conceded. None of this establishes what the experience is of.

VII. The objection from abundance

You have explained love by gestalt psychology, field theory, Gestalt therapy, theological aesthetics, neurocardiology, toroidal geometry, medieval optics, hesychasm, apophatic theology, wave mechanics, laser physics, phenomenology of the face, dissipative structures, synergetics, coupled oscillators, complex responsive processes, constraint theory, autocatalytic sets, complex thought, atmospheres, three management books and a Rule for monks. A thing that can be explained by everything has been explained by nothing. These frameworks do not converge; you have made them rhyme. Any sufficiently rich concept — "meaning", "life", "power" — could be threaded through the same twenty literatures with the same air of discovery.

Reply. Partly just. The file was asked for an exploratory treatment and has explored; exploration is not proof, and the FILE NOTES have tried to say at each step which claims are argued and which are reaches. But the charge of mere rhyme can be tested, since convergence, where real, takes a specific form: independent traditions, without contact, drawing the same distinction. The file submits that this occurred at least four times. Contact versus confluence (Perls) is fellow-feeling versus infection (Scheler), synchrony versus identity (Kuramoto), compassion versus empathic distress (Singer and Klimecki), resonance versus echo (Rosa), respect versus fusion (Arendt), essence versus energies (Palamas). That is seven vocabularies and one line, drawn in the same place. Likewise: form perceived whole and not assembled (Wertheimer, Balthasar, Böhme). Likewise: order that exists only in throughput (Prigogine, Benedict, Tronick's repair). Likewise: the both-and that cannot be chosen between (Morin, Follett, Kahane, the Danish volume). Rhyme does not usually produce the same cut seven times.

Conceded. Where the frameworks actually conflict — Stacey against Haken; Arendt against the whole enterprise — the file has tended to reconcile where it might have had to choose.

VIII. The objection from the seventh claim

You hold the first six claims to a standard of evidence and then report the seventh — that one can become Love, capital L — as "the tradition's claim", neither asserted nor denied. That is an evasion. If it is true it is the most important thing in the work and should have governed it from the first page. If false, the last movement is edification. You cannot be agnostic about your own conclusion.

Reply. The file can be, and is; and it thinks this the honest position for a work with these terms of reference. It was asked to treat the proposition through gestalt, complexity and energy, as an organisational phenomenon, and to file it as experimental and experiential. Within those terms the seventh claim cannot be established. What could be done was to show that the first six, properly restated, point at it: that love has the structure of a participation in something prior to the lovers; that those who seem to have gone furthest say they were taken up and did not climb; that the proposition's own images are the classical images for it. Whether there is anything there to be taken up into is a question that gestalt psychology, complexity science and organisational research do not have the standing to decide.

The proposition's author did not offer it as a conjecture. They offered it as what they saw. The file has recorded that, with the capital letter.

Coda: What Circulates

The file was opened on a nine-page chapter which said that the humanities are a living field, that something circulates in it, and that the circulation renews. It did not say what. A proposition was laid beside it which said: love — an affective-cognitive, cardial, toroidal state, emanating a field, propagating as a wavefront, beyond-luminous, in which one becomes light-emitting, and which one can become. The author said they had no steady language and asked that it be filed as experimental and experiential. Three books on compassion, agency and paradox were added while the work was in hand.

What has the filing shown?

That the language was less unsteady than its author feared. Term by term it proved to have a lineage and a structure. Affective-cognitive: the unity of knowing and being-moved, from Augustine to Murdoch. Cardial: the heart as the organ where that unity is lived, in three ancient languages and a modern physiology. Toroidal: the exact form of a giving that returns through the giver. Field: a condition of the space between, in which each depends on all. Wavefront: propagation by re-emission, in which no one is a terminus. Super-luminous: Dionysius's word, for what is more than light in light's direction. Light-emitting: coherence — the same energy, in phase. Heart-burst: a threshold, crossed. Become Love: participation, not attainment.

That its physics, taken as physics, does not hold — and that this matters much less than might be thought. The crossing is real; the carrier is ordinary; the form is not.

That the thing is an organisational phenomenon in the fullest sense: it exists between people and not in them; it has thresholds, propagates, synchronises, and can be the variable to which an institution relaxes; it has been measured, under seven other names; and it is the origin of more institutions than their strategy documents admit.

That it has three disciplines when under pressure — to weigh before responding, to choose at the crossing with doubt kept, and to hold what will not resolve — and that the state without the disciplines is dangerous.

That every one of its marks can be forged; that fear travels by all the same roads, and more cheaply; and that those who carry it are destroyed when the circuit is cut.

And that its credibility does not rest on any of this.

Davies's Signature ends: nothing encountered here disappears; it continues to circulate beneath the forms that follow; the movement widens. The file can now say what it takes that to mean. What a person has once given in the state the proposition describes is not lost when the room empties. It was a wavelet. It reached someone, who became a source. It is, by now, somewhere in the envelope of a front no one can see the whole of — in the manner of a nurse who was once well taught, in the way a certain firm treats its leavers, in a story told on the stairs, in the habit of a young analyst who was shown something at ten to five on a Thursday and has been trying to do it ever since.

The gyre widens. But the figure was never only a gyre. It turns under at the rim, and comes back, altered, through the centre.

The proposition asked to be filed. It is filed — under experimental, since nearly every sentence here should be tried and many will be found wanting; and under experiential, since its ground was never an argument. Someone felt it cross a room.

So have you.

WHAT CIRCULATES IS LOVE. THE REST WAS COMMENTARY.

IN ONE SENTENCE: LOVE IS A FORM, SOURCED IN PERSONS AND EXISTING BETWEEN THEM, THAT PROPAGATES BY BEING RE-EMITTED, RETURNS THROUGH WHOEVER GIVES IT, BRINGS WHAT IT TOUCHES INTO PHASE WITHOUT MAKING IT THE SAME, MUST BE WEIGHED, CHOSEN AND HELD WHEN PRESSED, CAN BE HOSTED BY AN INSTITUTION BUT NOT STORED, AND IS BELIEVED ONLY FOR ITSELF.

Apparatus I · A Lexicon for the Unsteady Language

The author of the proposition said they had no steady language. This lexicon takes each of the proposition's terms, and the chief terms the file added, and gives for each: the sense in which the file found it to hold; the sense in which it does not; and its nearest relatives in the literatures consulted. It is meant for use — as a set of handles — and for correction.

Affective-cognitive. Holds as: a single act in which perceiving and being-moved are not yet two; Lewin's valence; Balthasar's beholding-and-rapture. Does not hold as: a mixture of two ingredients. Relatives: amor ipse notitia; knowledge by connaturality; Scheler's ens amans; the heart-mind, 心.

Appraisal. Papworth's third step: the weighing of safety and intention, patterns, resources and role between feeling and responding. The file's gloss: the nozzle on the fountain; prudence within charity; the boundary kept in the moment of being moved.

Assonance. McQuade's term for moral doubt about which course is most life-affirming, where goods conflict with goods. The file's gloss: negative capability in its ethical form; doubt carried and not discharged; the condition of anyone who judges honestly.

Atmosphere. Böhme and Schmitz: what is met on entering a space, before any object; a feeling poured out spatially. Holds as: the best phenomenological description of what the proposition calls a field. Caution: quasi-objective is not objective.

Cardial. Holds as: (i) the heart as an organ that senses, integrates and reports upward, whose rhythm gates perception; (ii) the chest as the principal region of the felt body's narrowing and widening; (iii) lev, kardia, xīn — the undivided centre. Does not hold as: a claim that the heart's magnetic field carries love to others.

Coherence. Emissions in phase. Holds as: integrity, simplicity, purity of heart; the property by which a person's or an institution's acts add and do not cancel. Caution: coherence is not goodness. One can lase around anything.

Confluence / fusion. The dissolved boundary. Love's commonest counterfeit and the thing Arendt mistook for it. Tests: can one disagree; can one leave; do members keep their own frequency.

Constraint. Juarrero: that which alters what is possible and probable without adding force. The file's central repair to the proposition: love is not a force. It is an enabling constraint (it adds possibilities) and a governing constraint (it removes some).

Contact. Meeting at a boundary that both parties keep. The file's shortest definition of love: contact without confluence.

Coupling. The degree to which each lets their state be shifted by others'. Identified with: affectability. Love is high coupling with difference retained.

Credible. Balthasar's glaubhaft: such as can rightly be believed. Holds as: the self-evidencing character of love's form; in institutions, what is shown by inexplicable costly acts toward those who cannot repay.

Cruciform of Agency. McQuade's figure: a horizontal axis of the social situation (past, present, future) crossed by a vertical axis of the person (Me, I, You). Choice is made at the crossing. The file's use: the geometry of the moment at which love is tested; the complement to the torus.

Deparadoxification. The Danish authors' term for turning a paradox into a solvable problem to relieve discomfort. The file's use: what sentimentality and severity each do to love.

Dissipative structure. Prigogine: order that exists only while energy flows through it. The file's claim: love is of this kind; it cannot be stored; cultures of care vanish at thresholds when the flow drops.

Elevation. The uplifted, prosocial state on witnessing moral beauty. The file's gloss: what a Huygens wavelet feels like at the point it reaches.

Empathic distress. Singer and Klimecki: the self-oriented, aversive sharing of another's pain. What actually exhausts carers. Distinguished from compassion, which is other-oriented, warm and not depleting.

Energetic / energy. Holds as: (i) energeia — being-at-work, the shining-forth of a nature in act; (ii) relational or emotional energy as measured by Cross, Owens, Collins and others; (iii) Davies's Circulatory Energy. Does not hold as: a conserved physical quantity specific to love. Caution: the arithmetic of budgets does not apply; a form is not used up by being transmitted.

Field. Holds as: Köhler's sense — a single extended whole in which the state at each point depends on the state at every other — applied to the web of mutual perception and readiness in a group. Under Stacey's correction: not a stuff and not an agent, but the pattern of gesture and response among these people now.

Gestalt. A whole that is other than the sum of its parts and transposable to other material. In Balthasar, the form through which splendour shines. The file's first claim: love is a gestalt; it cannot be assembled from behaviours.

Heart-burst. Holds as: (i) the phenomenology of sudden onset — located, thermal, datable, noetic, expansive — attested by the witnesses; (ii) a threshold transition after long sub-threshold preparation; (iii) the extreme of the felt body's widening. Literal warrant: the heart can change shape abruptly under emotion (takotsubo). Not established: that the mystics' experience and the cardiological syndrome are one thing.

Holding. Winnicott, Bion, Kahn: receiving another's distress, metabolising it, returning it in a form that can be borne; love's form when what is called for is duration. Rule: the chain of holding may not break anywhere.

Light-emitting. Holds as: (i) trivially — every body radiates in the infrared and glimmers faintly in the visible; (ii) the face as modulator of light; (iii) coherence, the laser's sense — a person whose emissions are in phase; (iv) in the hesychast tradition, a claim the file reports and cannot test. Does not hold as: a measurable increase of visible emission in love.

Noetic. Of nous: direct intellectual sight, not inference. Holds as: love knows the particular, the possible, and the real as gift.

Order parameter. Haken: the slow collective variable to which the fast ones conform, and which they jointly produce. The file's most technical claim: love is an order parameter of a person, a pair, a room or an institution. Diagnostic: to what does the system relax after disturbance?

Paradox. In the Danish authors' strict sense: poles in conflict and interdependent, so that choosing one gives only temporary relief. Distinguished from a problem (solvable) and a dilemma (decidable). The file's finding: love is structured as a set of such paradoxes — contact and boundary, mercy and truth, love and power, going out and returning.

Photonic language. Holds as: light reflected from faces, carrying a code with a grammar that is hard to counterfeit, received by dedicated machinery wired to the heart; in Levinas's strong sense, an address. Does not hold as: communication by emitted biophotons.

Reading the room. Perceiving an atmosphere by its effect on one's own felt body. The instrument is oneself.

Repair. Tronick: the return to coordination after mismatch. The file's measure of a loving relationship or institution: not the rate of mismatch but the reliability of repair.

Resonance. Strictly: large response in a system driven at its own natural frequency, and none otherwise. Implies: small causes can have large effects; reception is selective; receivers become sources; tuning has a history.

Super-luminous. Holds as: Dionysius's hyperphōtos — more than light, in light's direction, experienced as a dazzling dark; that by which one sees and not that which one sees. Does not hold as: faster than light.

Synchrony. Agreement in timing among members who keep their own natural frequencies. Not sameness.

Threshold. The value at which a system's behaviour changes in kind. Implies: below it, effort is invisible.

Toroidal / torus. Holds as: the simplest form of a flow that goes out from a centre and returns through it; the gestalt of self-sustaining emanation. Broken forms: the jet (outflow only), the sink (inflow only), the closed loop (no centre beyond itself), broadcast (no return). Also true: the heart's magnetic field has this geometry. Not established: that this field carries anything between persons.

Wavefront. Holds as: propagation by re-emission — every point reached becomes a source. Contrasted with the parcel model. Implies: no one is a terminus; a layer of non-re-emitters casts a shadow; contributions superpose.

Apparatus II · The Chinese Register

The proposition is written from within a Christian and a Western scientific vocabulary. The Chinese tradition was called at several points, and this note gathers those references so that the reader may see them together — and see where the register agrees with the proposition and the one place where it most instructively does not. Characters are given in traditional form.

心 xīn — heart-mind. The seat of thought and feeling as one faculty. The character is a pictograph of the organ. Mencius (6A15) says that the office of the heart is to think (思). The proposition's affective-cognitive cardial is a three-word English circumlocution for this one syllable.

仁 rén — humaneness. The central Confucian virtue. The graph combines 人 (person) with 二 (two): what a person is in relation. Not a feeling inside one. Stacey and Mead would recognise it at once.

惻隱之心 cèyǐn zhī xīn — the heart of alarm and compassion. Mencius (2A6): anyone suddenly seeing a child about to fall into a well feels it, before any calculation. It is the "sprout" (端) of rén. Mencius's point is that it is immediate and universal; Papworth's point would be that the sprout must still be tended into right action.

感應 gǎnyìng — stimulus and response; resonance. The classical cosmological concept that things of the same kind respond to one another across distance, as a string sounds when its match is plucked. The Chinese term for what chapter eleven called resonance, with two millennia of use behind it.

氣 qì — vital breath, energy-matter. That of which everything is a condensation and which circulates through all. The nearest classical Chinese term to Davies's Circulatory Energy and to the proposition's energetic — with a difference worth stating: qì is not opposed to matter. It is what bodies are made of, in rarefied and condensed states. The proposition's worry over whether love has "real substance" would be, in this register, hard to formulate.

德 dé — virtue, moral force. The power of a person of integrity to draw others without coercion. Analects 2.1: one who governs by dé is like the pole star, which keeps its place while the others turn toward it. The file's super-luminous leader. Contrasted with 勢 shì, positional power.

明明德 míng míng dé — to make bright the bright virtue. The opening phrase of the Great Learning. The first 明 is a verb. The radiance is original; the work is to un-dim it. Compare the proposition's you become light-emitting — and note the difference: here one does not become so. One is, and is obscured.

萬物一體 wànwù yītǐ — the myriad things, one body. Wang Yangming's formulation of what the great person perceives. The Neo-Confucian counterpart of the body in Paul.

兼愛 jiān'ài — inclusive care. Mozi's doctrine, against the Confucians, that one should care for others' families and states as for one's own. The Confucian reply — that love properly has gradations, beginning from kin — is the exact Chinese form of the Contra's third objection. The quarrel between Mohist impartiality and Confucian graded love is twenty-four centuries old and not settled.

慈 cí — compassion, parental tenderness. The first of the three treasures in Dao De Jing 67; the text adds that from it comes courage.

和光同塵 hé guāng tóng chén — soften the glare, be one with the dust. Dao De Jing 4 and 56. The file's test for telling the real thing from the luminous counterfeit.

The instructive difference. The proposition is dramatic: burst, wavefront, becoming. Its exemplars are seized, pierced, set on fire. The Chinese register, at its most characteristic, is undramatic. The heart-mind's humaneness is not an eruption but an original condition, recovered by steady cultivation; the sage's influence is that of the pole star, which does nothing; the highest light is dimmed. Where the proposition says heart-burst, Mencius speaks of a sprout that must be neither neglected nor pulled — he tells of the man of Song who went out and tugged at his grain to help it grow, and killed it. This does not contradict the proposition. It is a second tempo: the same thing as it appears not at the threshold but in the long sub-threshold years, and in the long years after. A work on love in organisations has more daily use for the second tempo than for the first.
