The distillation, once more. Love meets three resistances under pressure — suffering, the system, contradiction — and needs a discipline for each: to weigh (Papworth), to choose (McQuade), to hold (Nielsen and colleagues). Prefix the state the proposition describes, and the sequence is: see, weigh, choose, hold.

Apparatus IV · The Experiments, with What to Look For

The twenty-one practices of chapter forty-two are restated here as experiments: each with what to do, for how long, and what to observe. None has been trialled in this form. All are safe to try. The observations are the point; a practice that yields none should be dropped.

1. Find the chest. Do: thirty seconds, three times daily, attend to the sternum. For: one week. Observe: can you discriminate at least three states (narrow, wide, neutral)? Does the state change predictably with particular people or rooms? Sign of success: you begin to notice it unprompted.

2. What, not why. Do: five minutes at day's end: what did I send out in three encounters? For: two weeks. Observe: how often what you sent differs from what you meant. Sign: you catch one mid-encounter.

3. One act of attention. Do: two minutes of undivided attention to one person daily. For: three weeks. Observe: what they do next; whether they return; what occurs in your chest. Sign: someone tells you something they had not planned to.

4. Appraise before helping. Do: one breath and four questions before each impulse to step in. For: a month. Observe: which question most often changes your action. Sign: you help less often and it lands better.

5. Find your pole. Do: complete the mercy–truth quadrant; give it to your opposite. Once. Observe: which box they fill that you could not. Sign: discomfort.

6. Know the item. Do: write what you will not negotiate. Once; revisit yearly. Observe: whether each line is for others or for yourself. Sign: the list gets shorter.

7. Check the circuit. Do: name where what you give returns from, and who holds you. Once; act on the answer. Sign: you have an appointment in the diary with a person.

8. The first ninety seconds. Do: one sentence each, before the agenda, on what people are carrying. For: a month, one meeting. Observe: count passive constructions in the first ten minutes, first week and last. Sign: the count falls; someone objects when the round is skipped.

9. The related spectator. Do: when a colleague is exposed, attend as one on their side. Each time, for a month. Observe: what they do in the following thirty seconds. Sign: they look at you.

10. Thank the messenger. Do: thank publicly and specifically before responding to bad news. Each time. Observe: the latency of the next piece of bad news — does it come sooner? Sign: someone junior brings one.

11. Name the atmosphere. Do: once, in a mis-tuned room, say what you notice as yours. Observe: the next ten seconds. Sign: an exhalation; someone else says "me too". Risk: silence. Bear it.

12. Disagree with the warmth. Do: differ openly on something that matters in your closest team. Once. Observe: temperature, and who speaks to you afterwards. Sign of the real thing: the disagreement is engaged. Sign of fusion: it is soothed.

13. Be moved in public. Do: change your mind because of a junior's point and say so. When it truly occurs. Observe: who speaks next.

14. Complete one thing. Do: finish one unfinished relational act in the team's history. Once. Observe: whether a subject that was avoided becomes speakable. Sign: someone tells the story differently.

15. Read the order parameter. Do: after each disturbance in each meeting, note to what the room relaxes. For: one week. Observe: the list. Sign: one word recurs.

16. Find the toxin handlers. Do: ask ten people who others go to. Once. Observe: the names; their grades; who holds them. Sign: you are surprised.

17. Restore one return path. Do: bring one giving group face to face with someone their work served. Once. Observe: what they say in the week after. Sign: they ask to do it again.

18. Test a margin. Do: trace in detail how the least powerful party was last treated. Once. Observe: whether you would be content for it to be told on the stairs.

19. Audit the dampers. Do: for one slowing procedure, list what it prevents — intended and unintended. Once. Sign: a second column.

20. Tell the story. Do: collect the story of the place at its best from its longest-serving member; tell it once to someone new. Observe: whether they pass it on.

21. Do one inexplicable thing. Do: one institutional generosity with no business case and no publicity. Observe: nothing. That is the experiment.

A note on instruments. For those with the means: consumer heart-rate monitors now record at a resolution sufficient for crude measures of physiological synchrony between people in a meeting. Chapter eleven's prediction — that coupling runs along bonds, and rises in rooms where the proposition's state is present — could be examined by any team willing to wear them and to share the traces. The file would regard such a trial as the most valuable single test of its argument, and would caution that the first thing a team will learn is who, in its own room, is a visitor from out of town.

Apparatus VI · The Signature, Section by Section

The file began from Davies's ninth Signature and then travelled a long way from it. This note returns and reads the Signature's own sections in order, setting beside each what the work has found. It is meant as an answer to the chapter in its own sequence, and as a check that the answer has not lost its question.

The vignette. Davies's opening page says that within the living field no participant commands the whole, yet each may contribute to its continuing formation. The file's gloss: Elias's game, Stacey's local interaction, Huygens's wavelets. It is the sentence that most exactly forbids the designer's stance, and the file's whole account of leadership follows from it: source, slope, weakly coupled oscillator, participant — never commander of the whole.

9.0 Orientation. Three claims were drawn from this section in chapter one: propagation beyond contact, latency, and return through the Gyre. To these the file can now add a fourth which it passed over. Davies writes that what the field amplifies or marginalises shapes what a society finds thinkable, sayable and feelable; that the humanities are a subtle infrastructure of meaning. The file's gloss: this is the order parameter, at the scale of a culture. It is also the taboo of chapter twenty-five described from above. An organisational culture in which love is unsayable has an infrastructure of meaning that marginalises the thing by which it lives. And Davies's observation that the field "absorbs disruption, registers fracture, and allows contradiction to coexist without demanding premature resolution" is holding, containment and paradox navigation in one sentence — written about literature and true of any institution worth belonging to.

He speaks, too, of radiosynthesis: the continual conversion of lived complexity into circulating meaning. The file did not have that word when it wrote of metabolising anxiety, of Bion's reverie, of the toxin handler who takes in what is unbearable and returns it bearable. It is the same process. What the mother does for the infant and the humanities do for a civilisation, someone must do for a ward.

9.1 Field logic and cultural movement. Davies: meaning does not reside in single texts; it forms through interaction; ideas gain force through circulation, resonance and uptake, and lose it through neglect, challenge or saturation. Cultural change rarely follows intention alone; it arises from atmosphere, mood and shared sensibility. It is not directed from above. The file's gloss: the wave model and the parcel model; Böhme's atmospheres; the failure of culture programmes. Note his three ways in which an idea loses force. Neglect is the heat turned down on a dissipative structure. Challenge is contest among order parameters. And saturation is one the file did not treat and should have: a form repeated until it no longer registers. "Our people are our greatest asset." The word love itself, if this work were ever to succeed in making it sayable in organisations, would be worn smooth within five years. There may be a protective wisdom in the taboo after all.

9.2 Relational energy as an interpretive lens. This is the section in which Davies takes most care, and the file should be held to it. Relational energy, he says, is not scientific analogy but a way of perceiving; it does not explain society; it sensitises attention. The file's gloss: this is the standard the FILE NOTES were introduced to keep. Where the file has said C, it has been using energy as Davies's lens. Where it has said M, it has claimed more — that something is actually measured — and should be checked. The proposition's author wanted more than a lens. The file's conclusion, in chapter twelve, was that as physics the proposition does not hold, and as structure it holds very well. That puts it between Davies's caution and the proposition's boldness: more than a lens, less than a force. A structure. A form.

Davies also says here that societies appear less as fixed structures than as evolving relations, and that meaning forms through participation. The file's gloss: the dissipative structure; and Mead.

9.3 Meaning as human field dynamics. Every act of interpretation, conversation, artistic creation, ethical judgement or collective remembrance, Davies writes, contributes energy to the wider field; the energy moves through dialogue, ritual, institutions, stories, technologies, images and systems of governance; it gathers force, meets resistance, transforms and returns. The file's gloss: this is a list of carriers, and chapter thirty-three's four kinds of institutional memory — stories, rituals, places, persons — are a sub-set. He includes two the file neglected: technologies and systems of governance. The Interlude on the screen made a beginning on the first. On the second the file said only that no one has specified a governance structure in terms of which frequencies it damps. Davies, who has written five volumes on governance, is better placed than this file to say what a constitution, a board, a scheme of delegation look like when they are understood as channels for the circulation he describes — and what they look like when they are understood, as chapter twenty-one proposed, as dampers tuned to the frequencies of fear and care.

His further remark, that meaning often gathers first through atmosphere, gesture and imagination before it stabilises into doctrine, institution or formal explanation, is the history of this file's subject in one line. The corridor knew. The seven literatures of chapter twenty-six are the stabilising. And it describes the proposition itself: an atmosphere and a gesture, not yet a doctrine — which is how its author asked for it to be filed.

9.4 Closing orientation. Davies ends by looking forward to his book's turn toward reason, governance and structure, and says that the earlier movements remain active beneath what follows: rational systems emerge within human fields already shaped by imagination, memory, relation and ethical tension; what later appears as order first gathers through interpretation and shared orientation. The file's gloss: first the fire, then the committee structure. Weber's routinisation, seen without his pessimism. And it is the exact relation between the proposition's state and the three disciplines of chapter twenty-nine. The heart-burst comes first. Appraisal, the crossing, the navigation of paradox are the consolidation — the reason and structure which follow. Davies's warning applies to them: that the living field is sometimes stabilised within institutions, sometimes strained by abstraction, sometimes reawakened through disruption, critique and return. A compassion construct, a cruciform, a quadrant: each is an abstraction that can strain what it was made to serve. They are hearths. They are not the fire.

His last two sentences are: nothing encountered here disappears; the movement widens. The Coda has said what the file makes of them.

What the Signature gave the file, and what the file returns. It gave the frame: a field, circulation, latency, return. The file returns a name for what circulates; a geometry for the circulation; an account of its thresholds; a catalogue of its counterfeits; three disciplines for it under pressure; and the suggestion that an organisation, no less than a civilisation, has its humanities — the stories, rituals, places and persons in which it keeps what it cannot presently use — and lives or dies by whether they are tended.

Apparatus VII · The File Examined for Its Own Biases

Papworth gives a chapter to the cognitive biases that interfere with compassion and observes that the commonest response to the subject is: but I am not biased. A work that has cited her should submit to her list. What follows applies ten of her biases to this file's own argument. It is an exercise in her second question — what, not why.

Confirmation bias. The file was asked to develop a proposition and has found support for it in some twenty literatures. A file asked to demolish it would have found support for that. The search was for convergence; divergences — Stacey, Arendt, the magnetometer — were admitted but were treated as things to be answered. What to do: the reader should weigh the Contra more heavily than its length suggests.

Authority bias. Balthasar, Aquinas, Prigogine, Haken: the file leans on great names, and a great name makes a weak inference feel strong. That Balthasar built a theology on Gestalt does not make the Gestalt psychologists' concepts apply to love. That Haken's laser has an order parameter does not make love one. Each transfer was an argument from likeness of structure, and the authority of the source lends it nothing.

Availability. The witnesses are those the Western Christian archive makes easy to hand: a Yorkshire hermit, Counter-Reformation saints, a Methodist. The Chinese register was called and confined to an apparatus. Of Sufi, bhakti, Hasidic and Buddhist testimony — which is abundant, and in the first two cases overwhelmingly about love as fire and light — the file has said nothing. Its picture of the heart-burst is one tradition's picture.

In-group favouritism. The organisational examples are of professionals in offices and wards: people like the file's likely readers. The call-centre worker, the warehouse picker, the garment worker at the end of McQuade's supply chain appear only as objects of concern, never as those in whom the state might arise and by whom rooms are crossed. There is no reason to think love rarer on a factory floor than in a boardroom, and some to think the opposite.

Fundamental attribution error. Explaining behaviour by character and not by situation. The file condemned this, with Lewin — and then wrote of "energisers", "the luminous", "toxin handlers" and "rescuers" as kinds of person. On its own argument these are positions in a field. The woman in the Overture is not a luminous type. She was, in that room, on that afternoon, the one who looked.

Just-world hypothesis. The belief that people get what they deserve. A quieter form runs through the fifth movement: that loving organisations do better. The evidence cited supports a correlation in some settings. It does not show that love is rewarded. Balthasar was not rewarded for twenty years; many are not rewarded at all; and plenty of organisations ordered by fear are highly profitable for a long time. The file's own chapter forty says that love which is explicable by its rewards is not credible as love. The fifth movement should be read under that sentence.

Self-serving bias. Taking credit for successes and attributing failures elsewhere. In its replies to objections the file "concedes" freely on matters that leave its main line standing and replies firmly on those that would not. A hostile reader might tally the concessions and ask whether any of them cost anything.

Negativity bias. The bad registers more strongly than the good. The sixth movement is vivid; its portraits of counterfeit, fusion and fear are sharper than the fifth movement's portraits of the real thing, which keep retreating into lists of marks. This may be the subject — Tolstoy's remark about happy families — or it may be that the file knows the corruptions better.

Naïve cynicism. Expecting others to be more self-interested than they are. The file's treatment of "we are a family" and of corporate care assumes bad faith or self-deception rather readily. Some employers mean it and bear its cost.

Bystander effect. The diffusion of responsibility among many witnesses. A hundred thousand words on love is, among other things, a way of standing by. The rule of chapter forty-two has twenty-one items; the reader who has read this far and tried none of them — and the file that describes them and can try none — are bystanders at the scene described.

Papworth's remedy for bias is neither guilt nor the claim to be free of it. It is the four steps, applied to oneself: be aware; feel what it is to have been wrong; appraise; respond. The response open to a file is to say where it is most likely mistaken. It is most likely mistaken where it was most pleased with itself: in the convergences, in the saints, and in the scene.

WHAT TO DO WITH A WORK ON LOVE: TRY ONE THING ON TUESDAY.

Apparatus VIII · A Cabinet of Caricatures

The Danish authors offer managers a gallery of nine caricatures of the ways people habitually meet a paradox, from the ostrich to the action hero, on the sound principle that exaggeration helps one to see oneself and that it is easier to own a habit one has first laughed at. Under pressure, they observe, nobody chooses a response; one emits one's reflex.

The device is too good not to borrow. What follows is this file's own cabinet — nine caricatures of what people do when the situation calls for love and they reach for the nearest thing. Two are taken from the Danish gallery with thanks; the rest are drawn from the argument. Everyone is several of them. The file's author is at least four.

The Radiator. Has read that leaders should emanate warmth and is emanating it. Beams. Holds eye contact a second too long. Says "I hear you." Attention is on the quality of his own presence, which is why nothing crosses. Form: broadcast. Reflex under pressure: turn up the wattage. What would help: turn off the self-view; ask a question to which he does not know the answer; look at the work. (Chapters 15, 28.)

The Rescuer. Sees a struggle and is in it before anyone has asked. Takes the task back. Stays late to redo it. Is exhausted and faintly aggrieved. Her team are very fond of her and have not grown in years. Form: a sink presenting as a source. Reflex: help. What would help: Papworth's four questions, the second above all; and tolerating the sight of someone finding it hard. (Chapters 29, 36.)

The Clerk. Believes that feelings have no place at work and that fairness means treating everyone as a case. Is, in fact, scrupulously fair. Delivers a dismissal as he would a parking notice. Is baffled to be thought cold: he followed the procedure exactly. Form: the still face. Reflex: the process. What would help: learning that the office decides the what and he decides the how; one sentence, before the form is opened, addressed to the person. (Chapters 25, 31.)

The Family Man. "We're all family here." Means it. Hugs. Remembers birthdays. Expects weekends. Experiences a resignation as a betrayal and a disagreement as a wound. Form: the closed loop. Reflex: closeness. What would help: a boundary; discovering that people can leave and still be thought well of; Arendt. (Chapters 34, 36.)

The Thermostat. Cannot bear a drop in the room's temperature. Smooths. Jokes at the moment of tension. Says "let's take that offline" just as something true is about to be said. Runs meetings that everyone enjoys and at which nothing is decided. Form: a damper tuned to every frequency. Reflex: deflect. What would help: ten seconds of silence, endured; finding that a room can go cold and come back. (Chapters 5, 27.)

The Auditor. Agrees entirely that care matters and has therefore built a dashboard. There is a compassion index. It is green. Managers are appraised on it. Ask-about-my-weekend scores are up eleven per cent. Form: the proxy that became the target. Reflex: measure. What would help: Papworth's parenthesis; one conversation with someone on the receiving end of the index. (Chapters 33, 35.)

The Martyr. Gives everything. First in, last out. Has not taken leave in two years and mentions it. Underneath the giving is something that needs to be seen giving, and which is never satisfied. Form: the jet. Reflex: more. What would help: the question "who is holding you?", asked by someone who will wait for an answer; the observation that the saints were cheerful. (Chapters 9, 32, 38.)

The Ostrich (from the Danish gallery). Knows that something is wrong between two colleagues, or with one of them, and is waiting for it to pass. Has been waiting since spring. Tells himself that it is not his place, that they are adults, that raising it would make it worse. Form: absorption — a point that does not re-emit. Reflex: wait. What would help: knowing that not noticing is itself a broadcast, and that being seen is very often the whole of what was needed. (Chapters 16, 17.)

The Action Hero (from the Danish gallery). Hears of a difficulty at ten and has fixed it by noon: a reorganisation, a new policy, a difficult conversation had briskly and ticked off. Mistakes a paradox for a problem and a grief for a task. Leaves behind a number of people who were solved before they had finished speaking. Form: feeling to response with no appraisal. Reflex: act. What would help: asking whether this is a problem, a dilemma or a paradox before touching it; Weil's question, and then silence. (Chapters 24, 29, 32.)

Reading the cabinet. Lay the nine on the Quadrant of mercy and truth and they sort themselves. The Rescuer, the Family Man, the Thermostat and the Martyr have collapsed toward mercy and live in its dark side: collusion, fusion, drift, depletion. The Clerk, the Auditor and the Action Hero have collapsed toward truth and live in its: the still face, the number, the fix. The Radiator and the Ostrich have left the field altogether — one for the mirror, the other for the sand.

Lay them on the torus and each is a broken form: jet, sink, closed loop, broadcast, or a point that will not re-emit.

Lay them on Papworth's four steps and each is missing one. The Ostrich lacks awareness, or refuses it. The Clerk and the Auditor lack feeling. The Rescuer, the Martyr and the Action Hero lack appraisal. The Radiator and the Thermostat lack response — they have a great deal of display and no act.

And every one of them is, by their own lights, being kind or being fair. None is a villain. Each has taken one true thing about love — that it is warm, that it helps, that it is fair, that it is close, that it is peaceable, that it matters, that it gives, that it does not intrude, that it acts — and let it stand for the whole. That is deparadoxification, nine times over. The caricatures are what the proposition's state looks like when it has been reduced to one of its parts, which is the first thing this work said could not be done.

The Danish authors' instruction, having shown the gallery, is not to pick a better character. It is to notice one's reflex, with a laugh if possible, and so acquire a half-second in which something else might be done. The file can add nothing to that.

Apparatus IX · Twelve Questions for a Board

Boards do not discuss love and should not be asked to. They can, however, ask questions whose answers reveal whether the thing this work describes is present, protected, or being destroyed. These twelve are drawn from the argument. Each can be put in ordinary governance language, and each has an answer that can be evidenced.

1. To what does this organisation relax? When something goes wrong — a loss, a complaint, a failed audit — what do people here do first? Protect themselves, find someone to blame, hit the number, or turn toward whoever was harmed? (Chapter 20.)

2. How long does bad news take to reach us, and what has happened to the people who brought it? Name the last three. Where are they now? (Chapters 23, 28, 37.)

3. When did someone last disagree with the chief executive in front of others, and what followed? If no one can remember, that is the answer. (Chapters 21, 36.)

4. Who are the people everyone goes to when things are bad — and who looks after them? If the executive cannot name them, it does not know how the organisation is surviving. (Chapter 32.)

5. Do the people who do the work ever meet the people it is for? Where is the return path, and where has it been cut by structure? (Chapters 9, 35, 38.)

6. How did we treat the last person we dismissed, the last supplier we dropped, the last customer who could not pay? In detail. Would we be content to hear it told? (Chapters 31, 40.)

7. What in our procedures was put there to prevent panic or abuse — and what else is it now preventing? (Chapter 21.)

8. Which of our measures of care have become targets? And what is being performed in order to meet them? (Chapters 33, 35.)

9. What are the stories told here to new joiners, and who tells them? Are they of people at their best, or of what one can get away with? (Chapter 33.)

10. If the three people most responsible for the atmosphere of this place left tomorrow, what would it relax to? Is what we value held by an institution or by a few individuals? (Chapters 20, 28.)

11. What have we done in the last year, at cost, for someone who could do nothing for us — and did we publicise it? (Chapter 40.)

12. What is not for sale? Is there anything this institution would refuse to trade for its own survival or growth — and is that thing for others, or for us? (Chapter 41.)

A board that can answer all twelve with evidence is governing something worth governing. A board that finds the questions odd has learned something about its own order parameter.

Apparatus X · What the File Could Not Settle

An experimental file should end with its open questions stated as questions. These are the ones on which the argument turned and which it did not resolve. Several are researchable; they are offered to anyone with the means.

Is there a single phenomenon? Chapter twenty-six claimed that companionate love, high-quality connection, compassion, relational energy, emotional energy, positivity resonance and psychological safety are aspects of one field-state. This could be tested: measure all seven in the same teams over time and see whether one latent variable accounts for them, and whether it behaves as a slow variable should.

Does physiological synchrony in working groups run along bonds? The fire-walk says it does in ritual. Whether it does in meetings, whether it rises with what participants report as contact, and whether it predicts anything, is unknown. The equipment is cheap.

Is there a threshold? The Kuramoto model predicts discontinuous onset. Do teams actually change in that way — long plateaux and sudden transitions — or gradually? Fine-grained longitudinal data would show it. Practitioners' experience says threshold; practitioners' experience is subject to every bias in Apparatus VII.

Is fear's coupling really obligatory and love's voluntary? Chapter thirty-seven's asymmetry is plausible and untested. If it is true it is among the most important facts about organisations. If it is false, the file's pessimism about the default is unwarranted.

Can the photonic language be faked at scale? Duchenne's marker is harder to counterfeit than a smile, not impossible; and synthetic faces and voices now exist which are built to produce it. If the grammar of the face can be forged by a machine, the corridor's infallibility — on which this work has leaned heavily — is at an end. The file has no answer to that and thinks it the most urgent question on the list.

Does anything persist in places? Contra II. Whether atmospheres attach to rooms independently of the people now in them, or whether that is a romance, could be studied by anyone with access to an organisation moving buildings.

Does appraisal cool the heart? Papworth's third step is needed. Might it also, practised as a habit, damp the immediacy on which the first two depend? The contemplative traditions say that discernment deepens love and does not thin it. Whether that holds for a manager running four appraisals in the space of a breath, the file does not know.

How is agape extended without thinning? Sorokin's trade-off; Mozi against Mencius; Contra III. It is the oldest question on the list. Those who appear to have managed it describe it as received and not achieved, which is not an answer that can be operationalised.

What is owed to those outside the room? Contra V. The file's account of love is, almost throughout, an account of presence. McQuade's field is those who are never present — at the far end of the chain, in the next generation. Whether the proposition's state has any form in which it can reach them, or whether at that distance love must become something else — justice, law, structure — and be content to, is the question on which this work stops.

And is the seventh claim true? Not researchable. Filed.

Apparatus XI · A Working Week

Last, the four words of chapter twenty-nine — see, weigh, choose, hold — laid across five days, as a rule of life might be laid across the hours. It is the shortest form in which the argument can be carried in a pocket.

Monday · See. Before the first meeting, find the chest. In the first meeting, look at each person once as though for the first time: who is here, and how? Give one person two minutes of whole attention. Notice the white space — what is not being said. Put nothing right today. Awareness is the primary movement. A face that moves is already a response.

Tuesday · Weigh. One impulse to help, to correct, to step in, will come. Take a breath before it. Intention: for them or for me? Pattern: have I been here before? Resources: have I got this to give? Role: is it mine? Then act, or leave it. The fountain needs a nozzle.

Wednesday · Choose. Somewhere this week the room is carrying its past into its future through you. Find the place. Consult the other axis: what do I actually hold, and who do I mean to be? If they clash, say so, in the active voice. If it is grey, keep the doubt, consider everyone it touches, and choose what gives most life. Take it as your own decision. The meaning will be in the response. Stay for it.

Thursday · Hold. Something will not resolve — a tension between two goods, a person in a long difficulty, a decision that must wait. Do not close it to relieve yourself. Name both poles; lean toward the one you neglect; tell those concerned what is known and not known. And find out who is holding you. Most bad decisions are made to relieve the deciders.

Friday · Return. What came back this week, and from where? Who should hear what became of their work? What is unfinished between you and someone — and could it be finished before you go home? Tell one story of someone at their best to someone who was not there. Then stop. Go home. The return path is half the form.

And on any day, whatever else: decency to whoever is in front of you, most of all those who can do nothing for you.

That is the whole of it. A proposition about light crossing a room, a Signature about what circulates, three books on what the heart must learn; and, at the end, something that can be tried on Tuesday.

Experiential

First-person report is admitted as evidence of a particular kind. It cannot be overruled by an instrument — an instrument can only bear on what the experience was an experience of. Its strengths are immediacy and, where several independent witnesses agree, structure. Its weaknesses are suggestion, shared scripts, memory, and the writing-up of events long after. The file uses E for the witnesses of heart-burst, for composed scenes, and for the corridor's testimony. When you meet an E, ask who is reporting, how soon after, what they expected to find, and whether anyone outside their tradition says the same.

Adjacent possible

Person

Adrienne von Speyr

Von Speyr qualified in medicine against family opposition, practised in Basel, and was twice married to professors there. After her reception into the Catholic Church she reported continuous mystical experience, including yearly participation in the Passion and the descent into hell, which shaped Balthasar's theology of Holy Saturday. He published her commentaries through the Johannes Verlag. Critics of Balthasar question how far a theologian should rest on unverifiable private revelation; he insisted the two bodies of work were halves of one. The file records both views. Her importance to its argument is that the community she co-founded was the one thing he would not trade.

Concept

Affective-cognitive

One act in which being moved and knowing are not yet two things. Lewin's valence, Balthasar's beholding-and-rapture, and the Chinese heart-mind all describe it.

Concept

Affective-cognitive

Modern thought usually splits love into a feeling that knows nothing or a judgement that feels nothing extra. The hyphen refuses both. Lewin's valences show perception already tilted; Balthasar's aesthetics makes seeing the form and being seized one event; Scheler holds that love opens the eye to value; Murdoch that it corrects the eye. The file later gives the hyphen a dynamical meaning: love is neither affect nor cognition but an order parameter to which both conform — which is why it survives days without warm feeling and days of poor judgement.

First met in the text · The Proposition, As Filed

Love is an affective-cognitive cardial-toroidal state where the noetic-communicative energetic field it creates and emanates extends beyond the human body in a super-luminous way, as a wavefront, to the point where light becomes a photonic language and has real substance and you can feel it crossing the room.

Agape

Rare in earlier Greek, chosen by the Septuagint and the New Testament writers. Anders Nygren opposed it sharply to eros; later writers have softened the contrast. Former director of Anti-Slavery International. Ethical Leadership (2022) asks why some people do not go along, and answers with the Cruciform of Agency: choice made where one's own values cross the pressure of the situation.

Person

Aidan McQuade

An engineer by training, McQuade worked in humanitarian operations in Ethiopia, Eritrea, Afghanistan and Angola before leading Anti-Slavery International from 2006 to 2017. His book grows from doctoral research on moral choice and combines social psychology, sociology of agency and case narratives. He holds that most people conform, that dissent draws on values laid down over a life, and that doing good is no protection against doing harm. The file uses his Cruciform as the geometry of the moment love is tested, his "assonance" for honest doubt, and his objection about political economy as one it cannot meet.

While this file was being drafted, three further books were laid on it with the instruction to analyse, synthesise, distil and apply: Kirstie Papworth on compassionate leadership, Aidan McQuade on ethical decision under pressure, and Rikke Kristine Nielsen and colleagues on navigating paradox.

Antonio Damasio

Born 1944. Neurologist whose Descartes' Error argued that feeling is the brain's reading of the body and that reasoning cut off from it fails. He called the body the theatre of the emotions.

Person

Antonio Damasio

A Portuguese-born neurologist working in Iowa and then Southern California, Damasio studied patients whose frontal injuries left intellect intact but decision-making ruined, and proposed the somatic marker hypothesis: bodily feelings tag options and guide choice. Later books developed a layered account of self grounded in the body's regulation. The somatic marker hypothesis has critics, but the broad claim that emotion and bodily state are part of reasoning is widely accepted. The file uses him to support the hyphen in "affective-cognitive" from the laboratory side, and to argue that an organisation ignoring what people feel in their chests is discarding information.

Concept

Bifurcation

Near equilibrium, fluctuations are damped and the system is lawful and dull. At a bifurcation a chance fluctuation is amplified and decides the new order. The file reads the Overture this way: in the first ten minutes the look would have been absorbed; in the third hour, with the old pattern unstable, it selected the branch. It concludes that crisis is not the enemy of love in organisations — comfortable equilibrium is.

Bénard cells

The honeycomb of convection cells that forms in a liquid heated from below once a critical temperature difference is passed. Each cell is a small torus. Turn off the heat and they are gone.

Concept

Bénard cells

Named for Henri Bénard, who observed them in 1900. Below the critical temperature difference heat conducts and the liquid is still; above it, hexagonal cells appear in which fluid rises at the centre and sinks at the edges. Trillions of molecules move in concert over distances far beyond any intermolecular force. Nobody arranges them. They are the standard laboratory example of order that exists only in a flow.

Concept

Cardial

The word holds together what Harvey's successors separated. Hebrew lev, Greek kardia and Chinese xīn all name one centre of thought, feeling and decision. Modern physiology gives the organ more than plumbing: it has its own neurons, sends most of its traffic upward to the brain, and its beat times perception. Schmitz's phenomenology adds that the chest is where the felt body chiefly narrows and widens. The file affirms "cardial" in all three senses and denies a fourth — that the heart's magnetic field carries love between people.

1447–1510. Mystic who ran her city's largest hospital through the plague. Her saying that her Me is God is the boldest Western statement of what the proposition's seventh claim means.

Person

Catherine of Genoa

Caterina Fieschi, of a noble Genoese family, was married unhappily at sixteen. After a sudden conversion in 1473 she gave herself to nursing at the Pammatone hospital and became its director; her husband joined her in the work. Her teaching on purgatory as the fire of love was written down by followers. Baron von Hügel made her the subject of his study of mysticism. The file uses her as a hard-headed administrator who made the boldest statement of union in the Western tradition, and as evidence that such claims are compatible with running a hospital in a plague.

First met in the text · Chapter 39

Peter's second letter speaks of becoming partakers of the divine nature. Catherine of Genoa, a fifteenth-century hospital administrator — she ran the largest hospital in the city through an outbreak of plague, and is as hard-headed a witness as the tradition affords — put it in a sentence that shocked her confessors: my Me is God, nor do I recognise any other Me except my God himself.

Christiaan Huygens

1629–1695. Dutch physicist. Gave the principle that every point on a wavefront is a new source, and — ill in bed in 1665 — noticed two pendulum clocks on one beam falling into step. Both findings carry much of this file.

Person

Christiaan Huygens

Huygens discovered Saturn's rings and its moon Titan, invented the pendulum clock, and wrote the first treatise on probability. His wave theory of light was eclipsed by Newton's corpuscles for a century until Young and Fresnel revived it. His letter of 1665 on the "sympathy" of two clocks is the first record of spontaneous synchronisation. The file uses both discoveries as models: wavefronts advance by re-emission, so receiving love is passing it on; and coupled rhythms lock without a conductor. That the same man found both, the second while watching from a sickbed, is a small gift to the argument.

Christian von Ehrenfels

Ehrenfels's 1890 essay "On Gestalt Qualities" started from a puzzle of Ernst Mach's: a melody played in another key shares no notes with the original and is recognised at once. So the melody is not its notes. He named what persists a Gestaltqualität. Wertheimer was his student in Prague. The file uses transposability as a working test of love: the same form can appear in a hand on a shoulder, a blunt truth, or a silence, across people and cultures with no behaviours in common, and be recognised immediately. A checklist of behaviours can therefore be met in full while the form is absent.

Person

Confucius

Kong Qiu taught in the state of Lu and sought office without lasting success. The Analects, compiled by followers, present humaneness, ritual and the cultivated person as the basis of order. First met in the text · Chapter 30

Chinese political thought drew a near line between 德, dé — the moral force of a person, which draws others without coercion, as the pole star keeps its place and the other stars turn toward it — and 勢, shì, positional advantage, the power that belongs to the seat whoever sits in it. Confucius held that governing by dé was the only kind that lasted.

Person

Tronick, at the University of Massachusetts Boston, developed the still-face paradigm in the 1970s; it has been replicated many times and across cultures. His "mutual regulation model" holds that infant and carer jointly manage the infant's state, and that messiness — mismatch followed by repair — builds resilience and trust. He estimates matched states at roughly thirty per cent of interaction time in ordinary pairs. The file transfers both ideas to institutions as analogy, not finding: unresponsive organisations produce protest then withdrawal, and the measure of a loving one is how reliably it comes back.

In Köhler's strict sense: a single extended whole in which the state at each point depends on the state at every other. Applied to a room: the web of mutual perception and readiness. Under Stacey's correction, a pattern of interaction and not a stuff.

Concept

Field

Three senses are distinguished. Weakly, a sphere of influence. Strongly, Köhler's: an extended whole that settles into a form, where changing one region changes all. Phenomenologically, an atmosphere met on entering a room. The file proposes that the medium is the web of mutual perception — each perceiving each perceiving — and the quantity distributed over it is readiness to open or guard. It then accepts Stacey's correction that no such thing stands over the people as an agent. "The field" is shorthand for what these people are doing with and to one another now, and each of them is answerable for it.

File note registers

Each chapter ends by saying how its claims were made: E, experiential report; M, measured by a study or instrument; A, argued on the page; C, conjecture. The device exists to stop the work borrowing authority it has not earned.

Concept

File note registers

The four letters are a discipline imposed by the request to file the work as experimental and experiential. They let a reader see at a glance what kind of ground a chapter stands on, and they prevent the commonest fault of writing in this area: quoting a measurement to lend authority to a speculation. The Contra and Apparatus VII both test whether the file kept to them. Turn any file note over for a fuller account of what its registers mean for that chapter and how its claims could be checked.

Concept

Intrinsic cardiac nervous system

The network of neurons within the heart itself, able to sense and regulate locally. Popular claims run well beyond the evidence; the finding is that the heart is a sensing organ.

Concept

Intrinsic cardiac nervous system

Ganglia in the fat pads of the atria and ventricles contain afferent, interconnecting and efferent neurons. They process local mechanical and chemical information and modulate rate and force beat by beat; a transplanted heart, cut off from the brain, still regulates itself. Claims that this system stores memories or emotions have no support. The file's use is modest: the organ at the centre of the proposition is a sensing, integrating one.

The Gestalt image is of food swallowed unchewed: taken in, never broken down, never assimilated, lying heavy. Each oscillator's phase advances at its own rate plus a term pulling it toward the others, scaled by the coupling. An order parameter between nought and one measures synchrony. Koffka brought Gestalt psychology to English readers with a 1922 paper and then Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935), written at Smith College. He also applied the approach to child development. The correction for which the file cites him matters more than it seems. "Greater than the sum" suggests the parts plus a bonus, which invites managers to add behaviours until love appears. The treatise's opening claim — that love cannot be assembled from countable acts of care — is Koffka's sentence applied.

Person

Kurt Lewin

1890–1947. Founder of field theory in social psychology and of action research. Behaviour is a function of person and environment as one field, the life space, whose regions pull and repel. From him: love does not add courage; it changes the geometry of the room.

Person

Kurt Lewin

Wounded in the First World War, Lewin wrote "War Landscape" on how terrain looks to a soldier, then built in Berlin a psychology of fields and tensions. In America he founded group dynamics and action research and coined the three-step picture of change that management textbooks flattened. He contrasted "Aristotelian" explanation by a thing's nature with "Galilean" explanation by its field. The file follows the Galilean line strictly: support does not put courage into a person; it removes a barrier from the space they move in. That shifts responsibility for candour from those who stay silent to those who shape the room.

First met in the text · Overture

GESTALT asks what kind of whole love is, and finds in Wertheimer's lamps, Köhler's physical fields, Lewin's rooms and Perls's contact boundary a grammar for it — before arriving at Balthasar, for whom Gestalt was the form through which glory shines.

Lasing threshold

The sharp point at which one light wave begins to recruit faster than it leaks and captures all the emitters. Below it a lamp; above it a beam; almost no more power.

Concept

Lasing threshold

Below it, raising the pump gives a slightly brighter lamp. At it, the character of the output changes discontinuously. Two conditions are needed besides pumping: a mode able to win, and mirrors to return the light through the medium. The file applies all three to persons and organisations — commitment, something that can be willed as one thing, and structures that return one's own emission for a second pass.

Concept

Law of closure

The field completes what is incomplete: a circle with a gap is seen as a circle with a gap. The file's image for how love judges — it sees the defect as a defect in a whole.

Concept

Law of closure

The eye completes a broken outline. The file's use is exact: a circle with a gap is seen as a circle and as having a gap. To perceive someone lovingly is to see their defect against the whole they belong to — which is the only way a defect can be seen as something to be mended. This is why love and accurate judgement are not opposed. The indifferent eye sees fragments, correctly; the loving eye sees what the fragments are fragments of, also correctly. People tend to rise toward the form in which they are steadily beheld.

Concept

Life space

Lewin's term for the whole psychological field in which a person moves at a given moment: regions, barriers, paths and pulls. It is the space people actually act in, and it can change while the room stays the same.

Concept

Life space

Lewin's formula makes behaviour a function of person and environment together, as they exist for that person now. The life space has regions separated by boundaries, some hard to cross. It is contemporaneous: the past acts only as present tension. The file's use: before the look, the man's field had a front and a barrier between him and candour; afterwards the barrier was gone and he walked straight across. Nothing was added to him. The practical consequence is that those who shape the space — usually the senior — are responsible for what can be said in it.

Four senses are separated in the file: the body's real infrared and faint visible glow; the face as shaper of light; coherence, as in a laser; and the claim of the Tabor tradition, reported and untested.

Concept

Light-emitting

The file refuses to choose one sense and blur the rest. Physically, a body radiates about a hundred watts net in the far infrared and a faint visible glimmer, strongest from the face; neither is perceptible as radiance. Optically, a face shapes ambient light into signal. Dynamically, a person whose acts are in phase carries, focuses and recruits like a laser — this is the sense the file stands behind. Theologically, the hesychast tradition holds that saints shine with uncreated light seen by bodily eyes; the file reports this and cannot test it.

Born in Prague, trained in Berlin and Würzburg, Wertheimer ran the apparent-motion experiments at Frankfurt with Köhler and Koffka as subjects, and published them in 1912. His laws of perceptual organisation — proximity, similarity, closure, common fate, good form — remain in every textbook. The file uses him for three things: wholes are given directly and not assembled; a crossing can be fully real though nothing travels; and the crossing lives only within a narrow window of timing. That last point is carried from milliseconds up to meetings.

"Species" here means an emitted likeness, not a class. Fire warms at a distance by multiplying its species; a colour is seen the same way. Roger Bacon made a science of it. Its corollary is strict — no technique of communication lets one radiate a form one lacks.

Concept

Phi phenomenon

Wertheimer's name for movement seen between two lights flashed in quick succession — at one timing, movement with no moving object at all. It is given directly, not inferred, and it lives in a narrow window of timing.

Concept

Phi phenomenon

Wertheimer flashed two lights in succession and varied the interval. Long intervals gave succession, very short ones simultaneity; around sixty milliseconds observers saw one light move. At a slightly different timing they saw motion with nothing moving. The older psychology had to call this an inference from two sensations. His observers saw it directly. The file draws three lessons: the crossing belongs to the relation, not to either pole; nothing need travel for it to be real; and it exists only within a window of timing, which organisations routinely miss.

The face has some twenty pairs of muscles attached to skin, visible changes of colour, and eyes whose direction can be read across a room. Put charge on a conductor and its distribution at each point depends on the shape of the whole; alter one end and it changes everywhere. An excited atom may drop spontaneously, in a random direction and phase, or be triggered by a passing photon of the right energy, in which case the new photon matches the first exactly. The file reads it as the mechanism by which a coherent person affects others: they do not put their content into people; they induce others' own disordered states to drop into step.

Not faster than light. Dionysius's hyperphōtos: more than light, in light's direction, so that "light" fails as a description. In people: the one by whose presence you see everything else, and whom you hardly see.

Concept

Super-luminous

In physics "superluminal" means faster than light, and no signal can be. The proposition's hyphenated word has another ancestry. Dionysius coined hyperphōtos for a reality that is light, is not the light we know, and exceeds light in light's own direction — experienced as a dazzling dark. Read so, the word says the nearest name for what crosses the room is "light" and that the name is not enough. The file adds a practical sense: the luminous person draws attention to themselves; the super-luminous one is hardly noticed, and by them everything else is seen. The danger of unfalsifiability is addressed with three stated tests.

Concept

Torus

The ring-shaped form of a flow that leaves a centre, curves round, and returns through that centre. The simplest shape of giving that is fed by what it gives. The heart's magnetic field has it; so does a smoke ring.

Concept

Torus

Geometrically, sweep a circle round an axis in its own plane. What matters is the flow it permits: up through the hole, out over the top, down the outside, back underneath. Nothing is lost at an edge because there is none. The file uses it as a gestalt — a form transposable to any medium — and not as a claim about magnetism. It yields diagnostics for a person, a team and an institution: where does what is given come back from, and does it return through the same centre it left? Davies's gyre, the Gestalt cycle of experience, perichoresis and a Bénard cell all have this shape.

Concept

Wavefront

The surface a wave has reached. By Huygens's principle every point on it becomes a new source, so the wave advances by re-emission. Applied to love: no one who receives it is a terminus.

Concept

Wavefront

Four properties separate a wave from a parcel. It moves through a medium without carrying the medium, so the source is not depleted. Every point reached re-emits, so there are no end-recipients. Waves add according to timing, so the same contributions can cancel or reinforce. And a front's shape depends on its sources: one point radiates a sphere that fades quickly, many in step make a plane wave that travels. The file draws organisational consequences from each — the layer of managers who absorb and do not re-emit, the cold room of warm people out of phase, and the difference between a good manager and a culture.

Person

Wolfgang Köhler

Köhler studied physics under Max Planck before turning to psychology. Stranded on Tenerife from 1913, he wrote The Mentality of Apes and then Die physischen Gestalten (1920), arguing that physical systems such as charged conductors and fields settle as wholes. He directed the Berlin institute, publicly protested the dismissal of Jewish colleagues in 1933, and emigrated to Swarthmore. His theory that perception rests on electrical fields in the cortex was refuted experimentally. The file keeps his grammar and drops his mechanism: a room is a field in his strict sense, and — his conductor again — its charge crowds at the points, where the most exposed person stands.

Translators write "heart-mind" because neither English word suffices. In Mencius it houses the four sprouts of virtue and performs reflection. In Neo-Confucianism it is where principle is found. The proposition needs three hyphenated English adjectives to say what this one character says. The Chinese Register in Apparatus II gathers the related terms and marks where the Chinese view differs: the heart's humaneness is original and recovered, not received in a burst.

First met in the text · Chapter 7

In classical Chinese the word is 心, xīn, and the difficulty of translating it is so notorious that sinologists have given up and write "heart-mind." The character is a drawing of the organ.

Person

Yoshiki Kuramoto

Born 1940. Japanese physicist whose 1975 model of coupled oscillators shows synchrony appearing suddenly at a critical coupling, not gradually. The source of the file's threshold.

Person

Yoshiki Kuramoto

Kuramoto, at Kyoto, simplified Arthur Winfree's model of biological oscillators into one that can be solved exactly. Each oscillator has its own frequency and is pulled toward the average phase; a single parameter sets the pull. The model has since described fireflies, heart cells, power grids and neurons. The file applies its qualitative results to groups as suggestion, not proof: a threshold below which nothing shows; a first cluster forming among those nearest the middle; diversity raising the threshold without preventing the transition; and agreement in timing without sameness of nature.

First met in the text · Chapter 21

In 1975 the Japanese physicist Yoshiki Kuramoto wrote down the simplest model he could of this class of phenomena.

Concept

Zeigarnik effect

Unfinished tasks stay active in memory because the intention behind them remains charged. The file applies it to institutions: unfinished apologies and unmourned losses go on bending the corridor.

Concept

Zeigarnik effect

Zeigarnik's subjects recalled interrupted tasks about twice as often as completed ones. Lewin explained it by tension systems that remain charged until discharged. Later replications are mixed. The file's extension to organisations is its own and is marked as such. It lists what stays charged: the apology not made after a restructuring, the founder never thanked, the colleague dismissed and never mentioned. New joiners learn the detours without learning the reasons. Completing one such act is experiment 14 in the rule.

Every organisation carries a vast Zeigarnik load of interrupted relational acts.

Term

和光同塵

Hé guāng tóng chén: soften the glare, be one with the dust. Dao De Jing 4 and 56. The file's test for telling real light from the kind that needs to be seen.

Term

和光同塵

The four characters appear in chapters 4 and 56 of the Dao De Jing, among a list of ways the sage blunts sharpness and untangles knots. The same text says of the best rulers that the people say "we did it ourselves". The file sets this beside Philip Neri's clowning and Seraphim's years of obscurity: the truly luminous tend to hide it, because they are not trying to be seen.

First met in the text · Chapter 15

The Chinese tradition has a phrase for it — 和光同塵, hé guāng tóng chén: to soften one's glare and merge with the dust — and the Dao De Jing says of the best rulers that when their work is done the people say, we did it ourselves.

Term

惻隱之心

Cèyǐn zhī xīn: the heart of alarm and compassion (Mencius 2A6), felt by anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well.

Term

惻隱之心

Mencius argues that anyone would feel it, and not to win favour with the parents, gain praise, or avoid the sound of crying. It is the sprout of rén. Papworth would add that a sprout must be tended into right action: feeling is the second step, not the last.

First met in the text · Chapter 7

Mencius, in the fourth century before Christ, says that the function of the xīn is to think — 思, sī — and in the same breath locates in it the four "sprouts" of virtue, the first of which is the feeling that seizes anyone who sees a child about to fall into a well: 惻隱之心, the heart of alarm and compassion.

Term

明明德

Míng míng dé: to make bright the bright virtue. The opening of the Great Learning. The radiance is original; the work is to un-dim it.

Term

明明德

The first of the Great Learning's three aims, followed by renewing the people and resting in the highest good. The file sets it against "you become light-emitting" to mark a real difference between the Chinese and the proposition's register: one is not made radiant; one's radiance is uncovered.

First met in the text · Chapter 39

The classic on which he was commenting begins with the phrase 明明德 — to make bright one's bright virtue.

Term

萬物一體

"The myriad things as one body": Wang Yangming's statement of what the great person perceives.

Term

萬物一體

From the Inquiry on the Great Learning. Wang says one feels alarm for a child, pity for a bird, regret for a broken plant, even for a shattered tile, and that this shows one's humaneness forms one body with them. The file offers it as a parallel to Paul's body and not as an identity.

First met in the text · Chapter 39

Wang Yangming, the Ming-dynasty general and philosopher, taught in his Inquiry on the Great Learning that the great person regards Heaven, Earth and the myriad things as one body — 以天地萬物為一體.
